Pending carries an arrow because it leaves the section: pending assets are reviewed in Approvals, and a second queue here would be a second inbox.

Reference: Inventory & Lenses.

docs.title: All assets
docs.text:
The default lens, and the one that answers "what is out there". It has three controls above the table and a facet rail beside it.

The filter rail (left) builds the query for you. Facets: Class, Status, Environment, Site, Prefix, Owner, Business unit, Tag, Risk, Provenance, and a findings toggle. Each value carries its own count.

  • Class is a tree. Picking Hardware selects everything beneath it; drill down to Server to narrow. Only one class at a time — the taxonomy is a hierarchy, and a multi-select over it reads as nonsense.
  • Status is Monitoring / Pending approval / Denied / Archived.
  • Risk bands are Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational and Not assessed — a separate band, because "we have not scored this" is not the same claim as "this is fine".
  • Provenance is how the class was decided: Discovered (something measured it), Declared, Imported, Proposed.

Values within one facet are OR-ed; different facets are AND-ed.

The query box (top) holds the same thing the rail writes, in one readable line. You can type in it directly: it autocompletes fields, operators and values, and a query it cannot parse tells you where it is wrong and what to write instead, rather than just "invalid". The rail and the box are never two different filters — the query is the state, and the rail is a way of writing it.

Query applied. Under the box, the predicate the server actually ran. It is often not identical to what you typed, because the read path adds its own default scope — status:monitoring, which steps aside as soon as your query names a status itself. When the two differ you get a not what you typed marker explaining why. This is how you find out that the asset you expected is missing because it is still pending approval.

Saved views (the Views button) name a query so you can come back to it, or share it. Build a filter, open the menu, and choose Save current query… — give it a name and decide whether to share it with your organization. Shared views carry a marker; only the owner can delete one. Only a query that parses can be saved: a saved view is a predicate other people will run.

The language is documented in full at Query.

Other controls. New asset (top right) creates one by hand. The header strip shows the running count, and a warning band appears above the table whenever items are awaiting review, with a Review button into Approvals.

The empty state differs on purpose: a filtered no-match offers to clear the query, while a genuinely empty inventory offers the three ways to get some — run a discovery, import a spreadsheet, or add one by hand.

docs.title: The asset page
docs.text:
Click any row to open the asset. Overview lives at the bare URL and each other tab deep-links, so the link you copy off the first tab is the short one. The tabs:

  1. Overview — Identity (what this thing is called), Identifiers (every way it is known, each with its kind, value, source, confidence and when it was last seen; an address marked static is pinned, and still identifies this asset on a network flagged DHCP), the class attributes for its class, Risk, Context (environment, business unit, owner, support group, location, prefix — with via its gateway when the prefix's router has been interrogated), Status, and Tags. A router or firewall also shows Networks routed: each network it is the gateway of, its address there, the VLAN, DHCP, how many assets are on it (click for the list) and whether a sensor covers it.
  2. Services & Endpoints — every network face it has: address, port, transport, service, exposure, status and last seen. An asset with no network face simply has none, rather than a fabricated port.
  3. Interfaces — its physical and virtual interfaces, addresses and VLAN modes (Interfaces).
  4. Ports — the faceplate, with Connect, Trace and the cryptography overlay (Cabling).
  5. Hardware — device type, modules, inventory items and virtual chassis.
  6. Relationships — what it is attached to, where each edge came from, and what is affected if it changes.
  7. Cryptography — its cryptographic configurations, each drilling through to the protocol, cipher suite and certificate behind it.
  8. Findings — what is open against it, and what was not assessed.
  9. Software — what is installed, from a host agent or an uploaded SBOM.
  10. History — reclassification, context edits, merges and approvals, recorded as they happen.
  11. Changes — who changed each field, from where, with a diff, plus the journal (Changes and journal).
  12. Config Context — the merged JSON that applies to the asset (Config contexts).

An asset placed in a rack also shows its Placement, and an asset with a device type, contacts or custom fields shows those on the page too.

docs.title: The drawer
docs.text:
Clicking a row in a cryptography lens opens a drawer — the peek, rather than the whole record — and the drawers stack: configuration → asset → certificate, so you can drill in and close back out one layer at a time.

The asset drawer shows a risk gauge, the asset's identity and primary address, its cryptographic configurations, and its details. Open full page is the way out of the peek and into the asset page.

docs.title: Acting on an asset
docs.text:
From the asset drawer:

  • Active Scan — probe this asset now and catalogue its TLS cryptography. Results arrive once the probe completes.
  • Edit — open the asset form.
  • Delete — soft-delete. It leaves active inventory and can be restored.
  • Restore — brings a deleted or archived asset back.

These need the matching permission; without it the button is simply not there.

docs.title: Adding an asset by hand
docs.text:
New asset opens a form whose shape is decided by the class you pick, so pick that first.

  1. Class — an indented list of the whole taxonomy. What you choose decides which attributes the asset has.
  2. Display name — what a person calls it. Usually optional, because the platform derives one from the identifiers. For a service class it is required: a service identifies by its name, having no address or serial to be known by.
  3. Identifiers — the ways this thing can be recognised later, so a future sighting updates it rather than creating a second copy. You can enter hostnames, FQDNs, IP addresses, MAC addresses, serial numbers, CMDB sys ids, SSH host key fingerprints and names. Two kinds are collector-minted — agent id and cloud resource id — and cannot be typed: they are identities the platform assigns, and being able to type one would let two real assets be merged into one by hand with nothing to review. An IP address you type is pinned: it keeps identifying this asset even on a network flagged DHCP. An address a sensor recorded shows a Pin box; tick it to pin that address too (for example a router's own LAN address inside the range it hands out).
  4. Class attributes — the fields that class declares.
  5. Context — Environment, Support group, Business unit, Owner email.
  6. Description, Tags, and optional Metadata (JSON) for anything the class schema does not cover.

Click Create asset. If you ask to remove an identifier the platform must keep, it is kept and you are told which and why, rather than the removal quietly failing.

Editing an existing asset uses the same form, and the class is changeable — reclassifying something that was wrongly classed is an ordinary correction, and the History tab records it.

docs.title: Uploading a certificate
docs.text:
Add certificate (in the header of the Certificates lens) adds an X.509 certificate by PEM — useful when no sensor covers the thing that presents it. Its Declare tab adds one you know exists from just its common name and expiry date, so you are alerted before it expires (see Certificate monitoring). On the Upload PEM tab, switch between Upload file and Paste PEM, drop or paste the certificate (a chain, leaf first, is accepted; 1 MiB maximum), set its ownership, and upload. The certificate is authoritative: its cryptographic details are extracted from it server-side rather than typed.

An uploaded certificate shows as Unassigned in the Certificates lens until it is linked to an asset. See Certificate Chain Management.

docs.title: The cryptography lenses
docs.text:
Each has its own shape, a search box, and an Export button for the current view.

  • Certificates — every certificate, including ones uploaded by hand, with an Ownership filter (3rd-party / Internal / Unknown).
  • Keys — the key inventory: key, algorithm, state, expiry, and Used by, which counts the assets using it ("Unlinked" when none). The drawer drills through to the using asset. See Cryptographic Keys.
  • Configuration — negotiated cryptographic configurations, grouped by the numeric risk bands Critical, High, Medium, Low and Informational, with Not assessed as its own group when no numeric evidence establishes a score. Filters for Environment and Risk band. The catalogue's qualitative strength is separate evidence and is not derived from the numeric score.
  • TLS and SSH — the same configuration lens, narrowed to one protocol.
  • Data Protection — at-rest posture across the resources that store data, with Resource type, Assessment and Risk filters. Each row names the key-custody rung it sits on.
  • 3rd Party — outbound connections your assets make to SaaS, partners and APIs. A connection you decide to track like an internal asset can be promoted: click the promote control, confirm Elevate to managed?, and it joins managed inventory. See Third-Party & External Connections.

docs.title: Map and Software
docs.text:
Map has two views, switched at the top of the page:

  • Neighbourhood — an interactive graph around one focus asset, up to three hops, with the impact overlay and a GraphML/Cytoscape export. It also opens full screen, which returns you to the lens carrying your depth and selection rather than resetting.
  • Topology — the tenant-wide "where is everything", as a site → prefix → class tree with counts.

Software is anchored on the product, not the asset: it answers "who runs this version of this thing?" Columns for product, vendor, version, end of life, vulnerabilities, identifier, licence, last checked, and the number of assets. Sort by any of them, search across name, vendor, Package URL and CPE, and click through to the assets. An Upload SBOM link sits in its header.

See The Map and SBOM Upload.

docs.title: Stale
docs.text:
Infrastructure → Stale lists assets not observed for more than 30 days. That number is the product's one definition of stale: the lens, the hygiene finding and the compliance control all mean the same thing by the word.

Tick the rows to act on — or the header, then Select all matching — and use the bar above the list: Scan, Archive, Restore, Delete, Edit or Export. Archiving asks first and says what it does: archived assets drop out of active inventory and reporting, discovery can resurface them, and you can restore them.

Thresholds and auto-archive behaviour are set by a Tenant Admin under Settings → Policies → Asset Lifecycle. See Asset Lifecycle Management.

docs.title: Exporting what you are looking at
docs.text:
Every lens has an Export button that writes the rows currently on screen to CSV, built in your browser from what is already loaded — no round trip, no template.

A page export is convenience, not evidence. For audit-grade output with provenance, a content hash and a fixed scope, generate a bill of materials instead (see below). Detail: Page-Local Exports.

docs.title: Posture
docs.text: Risk & Compliance → Posture carries three views, switched from the rail: Overview, Frameworks and Algorithm Reference. The last two exist so a verdict is never a black box — you can always read why the platform rates something the way it does.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A gauge for the share of assets at high risk, Posture trend · 30 days, per-framework standing for each framework you have activated, a Control posture grid, and Highest-priority exposures ranked for you.

docs.title: Reading a control result
docs.text:
On the control grid — and on each group under Findings → By Control — every control shows one of three results:

  • PASS — the control was checked and nothing in scope violated it.
  • FAIL — the control was checked and something violated it. One violation is enough, whatever its severity.
  • Not assessed — the control was not checked, so no claim is made either way. Hover it to see why: no measurement rule configured, nothing in scope to check, or the check itself failed.

Severity (Critical / High / Medium / Low) rates how much a failure matters — it labels each finding and weights the score — but it never decides pass or fail. Scores cover assessed controls only and are shown with a coverage line such as "8 of 11 controls assessed". A framework with nothing assessed shows —, never 100%. Controls that could not be evaluated are left out of the score entirely: they neither reward nor punish you.

docs.title: Frameworks
docs.text:
Browse compliance frameworks and, crucially, what each one actually measures. The view opens on My frameworks — the ones you have activated, which drive your compliance score — and an All published toggle reveals the full catalogue, each with a preview score showing what you would score against it today. Open a framework to see its controls; expand a control to read its measurement in plain language (for example, "Passes when RSA key size is at least 2,048 bits"). Nothing is marked failing without a rule you can read here.

Activating and deactivating frameworks is a Tenant Admin job, under Settings → Policies → Compliance Frameworks.

docs.title: Algorithm Reference
docs.text:
A read-only catalogue of every cryptographic algorithm the platform knows about, with our assessment of each. Search or filter by strength (recommended / strong / acceptable / weak), status (current / deprecated / obsolete), or quantum (post-quantum vs classical). Click an algorithm for its strength, deprecation and post-quantum status, risk score, migration guidance, and the specific alternatives to move to. This is the same rating used to flag risk across your inventory — so when something is marked "weak", this is where you see why.

See Algorithm Reference and Framework Transparency.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text: Risk & Compliance → Findings is every open problem, from every producer.

docs.title: Lenses
docs.text:
The rail groups the lenses by what they read:

Platform findings — the one findings table, every producer:

  • By Producer (the default) — the only lens that shows every producer's findings without a framework in the way, and therefore the home of end-of-life and vulnerability findings. The producers are Compliance, Cryptography, End of life, Vulnerability, Configuration, Inventory hygiene and Drift.
  • By Framework — grouped by the frameworks you have activated.
  • By Control — grouped by control, with each control's pass/fail/not-assessed result.

Crypto findings — the cryptographic-risk stream, a different data set:

  • By Severity, By Asset, By Category (protocol / algorithm / key size / certificate), By Date Observed.

The two scopes are counted separately and labelled, because switching between them changes the number on screen. That is not a counting bug: they are different sets.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Above the list: a filter box, and filter chips for Open, Critical + High, Mine and Unassigned. A producer facet gives one chip per registered producer with its count under the current filters — a producer with no findings shows a zero rather than disappearing, because zero is an answer. Export writes the current view to CSV.

Arriving from a link that narrows to one subject or severity shows a banner saying so, with a way to clear it — a page that is filtered always says it is filtered.

docs.title: The inspector
docs.text:
Click a finding to open the inspector. It carries the finding's evidence and, for some kinds, the same issue found elsewhere on your network, with a way to raise tickets for the set at once. Advisories and, for drift findings, a Baseline / Observed comparison appear where they apply.

The Workflow block is where you act:

  • Status — New, Notified, Resolved or Suppressed. Choosing Suppressed asks for a suppression reason before it is applied.
  • Assignee — assign the finding to a member of your organization, or leave it unassigned.
  • Create ticket — opens a remediation ticket pre-filled from the finding. It lands in Remediation → Queue.
  • Add to plan — attach it to an existing remediation plan, or create a plan and add it in one step.
  • Override control (justified exception) — for compliance findings only. Disregards that control in future evaluations. A rationale is required and is audited.

The Remediation block above it always shows the standard guidance for that kind of finding — in every edition, with no model involved.

Full reference: Findings.

docs.title: Bills of Materials
docs.text: Risk & Compliance → Bills of Materials produces the documents you hand an auditor: immutable, dated, content-hashed snapshots of what matched a scope at the moment of generation.

docs.title: The four kinds
docs.text:
Kind What it contains Cryptographic (CBOM) Certificates, algorithms, protocols, keys and crypto libraries Software (SBOM) Every distinct software product installed, and the assets it was found on Hardware (HBOM) Every hardware asset, with vendor, model, serial and firmware Full inventory Every asset with its endpoints, relationships, facts and open vulnerabilities

All four share one pipeline: the same scope, the same content hash, the same comparison.

docs.title: Generating one
docs.text:
Click Generate and choose:

  • Kind — one of the four above.
  • Scope — the boundary the artifact attests to. Scopes are named, versioned asset definitions managed under Risk & Compliance → Scopes; see Scopes.
  • Name — optional. For an audit submission, name it after the engagement.

The artifact captures the scope's exact version, so it stays reproducible even after the scope is later edited.

docs.title: The list
docs.text: Each row shows name, scope, kind, when it was generated, entry count and size. Filters for kind and scope sit above. Click a row for the artifact drawer.

docs.title: Downloading
docs.text:
Download offers the formats that kind supports:

  • CycloneDX 1.7 — the canonical bytes, and what the content hash covers. Available for every kind.
  • OCSF 1.9 events — JSON Lines for a SIEM: one Device Inventory Info per asset, one Vulnerability Finding per CVE. Offered for the full inventory kind only, because it is the only one with devices and CVEs to project.

docs.title: Verifying
docs.text: Verify in the artifact drawer recomputes the content hash (and the signature, where there is one) and reports the verdict. This is how you prove an artifact you were handed is the one that was generated.

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text:
Delete soft-deletes an artifact. The row stays, so a comparison that referenced it shows "deleted" rather than a dead end.

Reference: Bills of Materials and CBOM Artifacts.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
Remediation → Alerts is the inbox. Summary cards count Acknowledged, Snoozed and the rest; a severity filter and status filters narrow the list.

Each row names the alert, its type, its severity, and its subject — the thing the alert is about. Where the subject has a page of its own, it is a link: an asset goes to the asset page; a software install or a crypto configuration goes to Findings narrowed to exactly that subject; a control goes to the control lens; a certificate goes to the Certificates lens. Where there is no honest destination the subject is plain text, because a link that lands on an empty page reads as "nothing is wrong here" — the one thing it must never say.

Working an alert. Per row:

  • Acknowledge — you have seen it.
  • Snooze — put it aside until a time you choose, with a reason.
  • Unsnooze — bring it back now.
  • Resolve — close it, with a resolution note.
  • Create ticket — turn it into remediation work in the Queue. A row whose ticket already exists links straight to it.

Click a row for the detail panel: the full message, the subject, and who acknowledged, snoozed or resolved it and when.

What raises an alert. These are the types that can open against your organization:

Alert Raised when Certificate expiring A certificate is approaching, or past, expiry. One alert per certificate, escalating as expiry nears. Activated compliance policies can add earlier rungs. Control noncompliant A control in an activated framework went noncompliant. One alert per control, with the affected-asset count — not one per asset. Compliance score drop A framework's score fell more than 10 points in 24 hours. Hygiene score drop Your Inventory Hygiene score fell more than 10 points in 24 hours. Split out from the above because data quality is worth routing — and silencing — separately from security posture. Known vulnerability An installed software product matched the vulnerability catalogue. End of life Something on an asset passed, or is approaching, the date its vendor stops shipping fixes — its operating system, its hardware, or an installed package. Drift detected Something about a subject changed relative to its recent baseline: a new device class on its prefix, a protocol it has not spoken before, a different set of listening ports, a certificate from an unfamiliar issuer. Drift is not automatically bad — most are planned changes, and resolving the finding is how you tell the baseline so. Sensor offline A sensor stopped reporting, or registered and never reported at all (after a 15-minute dwell — measured from the last heartbeat, or from registration if there has never been one, so a sensor whose install silently failed is not invisible). Sensors marked air-gapped, pending or inactive are not expected to check in and do not raise this. Discovery agent offline A discovery agent stopped reporting, or registered and never reported at all (same dwell, measured the same way). Agents switched to inactive do not raise this. Discovery job failed A discovery job failed. Failed login burst Multiple failed sign-in attempts in a short window. Asset limit approaching Asset usage is nearing your plan limit.

Most resolve themselves when the condition clears — a renewed certificate is observed, a heartbeat arrives, the next run succeeds, the finding stops being detected.

Which alert types are enabled, and where they are delivered, is configured by a Tenant Admin under Settings → Notifications & Alerts.

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
Remediation → Queue is the single ticket queue: every remediation ticket in your organization, whatever raised it.

Five cards across the top double as filters: Open work, Overdue, Due soon, Resolved, and Keeping pace — the share of open work still on track. Click a card to filter to it, click again to clear.

The table lists ticket, category, external reference, SLA state and due date. Click a ticket for its drawer: description, due date, assignee, what it is linked to, and a threaded Comments section (⌘/Ctrl + Enter posts). Status changes are made from the drawer.

Categories are compliance, certificate, remediation, vulnerability, operational and general — each able to link back to the asset, certificate, configuration or finding it came from.

docs.title: Plans
docs.text:
Remediation → Plans groups related work into one initiative — a post-quantum migration, a protocol deprecation, a certificate replacement programme — and tracks it as a whole. Click New plan, give it a title, and add findings to it from the findings inspector (Add to plan). A plan's detail view shows its steps and its progress.

See Remediation.

docs.title: Global Search and Ask
docs.text:
Press ⌘K (Mac) or Ctrl+K (Windows/Linux) anywhere, or click the search icon in the header, to open the command palette.

Search is the default. Type two or more characters to search assets, certificates, devices and sensors at once; results are grouped by type. With the box empty it lists the pages you can jump to. Navigate with ↑↓, open with Enter, close with Esc, and ⌘K toggles it.

Full reference: Global search.

docs.title: The bell
docs.text: The bell in the header carries a count of unread notifications. Open it for the recent list, mark one read by clicking it, or Mark all read. Two links at the bottom go to View alerts and View delivery history.

docs.title: Your own preferences
docs.text:
My Profile → Notifications controls what reaches you, within what your organization has configured.

What you're notified about — per-category switches: Security findings & alerts, Sensors & discovery, Billing & subscription, System & maintenance, CBOM & compliance evidence, Members & access changes.

How it reaches you — In-app and Email switches, plus a Frequency: Immediate, Hourly digest, or Daily digest.

Click Save changes to apply.

You choose what and how often. The channels themselves — Slack, email, PagerDuty, a webhook — are configured for the whole organization, as are the routing rules that decide which events reach which channel and the alert rules that decide what raises an alert in the first place. Those live under Settings → Integrations and Settings → Notifications & Alerts, and are covered in the Tenant Admin Guide.

docs.title: Organization Settings at a Glance
docs.text:
Reached from the profile chip → Organization Settings. What you see depends on your permissions and your edition; the detail for each is in the Tenant Admin Guide.

Group Pages In one line Organization Overview, Branding Organization metadata, and white-labelling the console Plan & Usage Usage & Limits, Billing Consumption against plan limits, and (on the commercial editions) the subscription itself People & Access Members, Roles & Permissions, Security & SSO Who is in the organization, what each role grants, and how people sign in Integrations Integrations, AI assistant Connected systems — CMDB/ITSM, messaging, storage, SIEM — and which AI capabilities are on Notifications Routing Rules, Alert Rules Which events reach which channel and what raises an alert Discovery & Reconciliation Active Scanning, Identification rules How the platform discovers and reconciles records Policies & Trust Compliance Frameworks, Custom Policies, Asset Lifecycle, Trusted CAs The policy and trust decisions the platform applies to your data Data & Schema Custom Fields, Export Templates Tenant-wide fields and export formats

Some of these belong to the commercial editions and are simply absent from the rail on a Core deployment: Billing, Security & SSO, Custom Policies, and SIEM export among the integrations. Core has local users, invitations, roles and the free frameworks, with no subscription to manage.

Three pages are worth knowing about as a user even though you may not administer them:

  • Risk & Compliance → Scopes defines the asset boundaries a bill of materials attests to (Scopes).
  • Infrastructure → Asset Classes browses the asset class taxonomy and the attributes each class carries — which is what the New asset form is built from.
  • Policies → Identification rules shows how a new sighting is matched to an existing asset, and whether a high enough match may be accepted without you. That page's settings are what fill the Merged automatically section in Approvals.

Billing, retention, locations and prefixes are administrator work; the Tenant Admin Guide covers each.

docs.title: My Profile
docs.text: Reached from the profile chip → My Profile. Six pages.

docs.title: Personal
docs.text:
Your identity. Edit First name, Last name and Timezone, and Save changes. Upload photo takes a JPEG, PNG, GIF or WebP up to 5 MB and applies it immediately.

Email and Role are shown but not directly editable: changing your email requires confirming a link sent to the new address, and your role is assigned by your organization's admins under Settings → Members.

Your data → Export downloads everything the platform holds about you, as a file you can keep.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Password — enter your current password, a new one (8 characters minimum) and the confirmation, then Change password. You may be signed out afterwards and have to sign in again.

Multi-factor authentication — an authenticator app with backup codes is on the roadmap and will be enrolled from here. It is not available yet, and the page says so rather than offering a control that does nothing.

Account status — whether your account is active, when you joined, and your last sign-in.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: Covered under Notifications above.

docs.title: Sessions & Devices
docs.text: Every active session: device, IP address, last active, and when it was signed in. Your current session is marked. Revoke ends one session; Revoke other sessions ends every session except the one you are using — the right move after signing in somewhere you do not control. A revoked session stops working at once; your other devices quietly refresh their sign-in and carry on. Changing or resetting your password ends all your other sessions the same way, and you sign in again with the new password.

docs.title: Connected Accounts
docs.text: On a Core deployment there are no providers to link, so this page has nothing to show.

docs.title: API Tokens
docs.text:
Personal access tokens for connecting AI assistants to the read-only MCP server. They work only with the MCP server — not with Vista Platform's other REST endpoints. New token creates one: name it, choose its scopes, and copy the value — the full value is shown only once, so put it in a secret manager immediately.

The table lists name, prefix, scopes, created, expires, last used and status. Revoke kills a token. Tokens carry a subset of read-only scopes, are owned by you, and you may hold up to 25 active at a time. See API Tokens & MCP Server.

Preferences and Accessibility appear in the design but are not in this build, so they are not listed in the profile rail. Theme is switched from the profile chip menu in the meantime.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"I ran a discovery and the inventory did not change." New discoveries wait in Discovery → Approvals and are invisible to every lens until accepted. Check the pending count on the Inventory header, or Pending approval on the Dashboard's Assets Monitored hero.

"An asset I know exists is not in the list." Look at the Query applied line under the query box. The default scope is status:monitoring, so anything pending, denied or archived is excluded until your query names a status itself. Add status:pending_approval (or archived, or denied) to see it.

"Two records exist for the same thing." That is what merge proposals are for — check Approvals. If no proposal was raised, the two records may share no identifier the matcher can compare; add one to each from the asset form, and the next sighting should link them. See Asset Approval.

"An asset was merged and I did not approve it." Check Approvals → Merged automatically. A row marked Auto-accepted by the matcher means your organization's auto-accept threshold is above zero; a row marked Merged by rule means the same-device rule was sure the two records were one device, and shows the evidence. The Change these settings link goes to the settings. There is no way to reverse a completed automatic merge from that page.

"A sensor shows offline but the process is running." Offline is decided by the heartbeat, not by the stored status. Check the sensor drawer's Health tab for the last heartbeat and the reporting interval, and confirm the host can reach the platform.

"Host observations show a large Shed count." The network is busier than the sensor is sized for, so observations are being dropped rather than emitted. That is a capacity signal.

"A compliance control says Not assessed." Nothing was claimed either way. Hover the result for the reason: no measurement rule configured, nothing in scope to check, or the check failed. Not-assessed controls are excluded from the score entirely.

"My compliance score has not moved after fixing something." Evaluation is continuous but not instantaneous, and catalogue rule changes take a few minutes to propagate. Check Findings for whether the finding cleared before assuming the score is wrong.

"A risk score reads 0." Zero means not assessed — nothing resolved against the algorithm catalogue and no size or lifecycle rule fired. It is not a claim that the thing is safe. The Not assessed tile on the Dashboard lists these.

"The Dashboard says some assets have no crypto observed." They are assets with nothing cryptographic on record: no crypto configuration, no encrypted store, no TLS, SSH or IPsec endpoint, and not a key or secret store. A phone or smart plug that a sensor saw only on the local network is the usual case. There was nothing to assess, so the Cryptographic Posture ring shows them as their own grey slice, apart from Not assessed. If you expected crypto on one, it usually means no sensor could see its traffic and no scan reached an open port on it.

"My saved views will not load." The menu says so and offers a retry; your views have not been deleted. If the query box shows an error, a view can only be saved when the query parses — fix the query and save again.

"I cannot see a page or a button that the documentation describes." Two possibilities. It may be gated by permission — your role does not grant it, and your administrator assigns roles under Settings → Members. Or it may be gated by edition — the capability belongs to Enterprise, in which case a deep link shows an upgrade card rather than a broken page.

docs.title: Support
docs.text:
• In-product — About (profile chip) reports the exact version and build you are running. Quote it in any report.
  • Concepts — Concepts defines every term this guide uses.
  • Feature guides — the documentation index lists a page per feature; each goes deeper than this guide does.
  • Administrator tasks — Tenant Admin Guide, and your organization's administrators for access, roles, connected systems, notification channels and anything else under Organization Settings.

When reporting a problem, include what you clicked, what you expected, what you saw, and the version from the About page.

docs.title: Business Units
docs.text: A Business Unit is the party an asset belongs to or is billed to: a department, a customer, a cost centre. Units nest (Corporate, then Finance beneath it, and so on) up to four levels deep. A NetBox tenant maps onto a Business Unit.

docs.title: Manage them
docs.text:
Settings -> Organization -> Business Units shows the tree with the number of assets in each unit. Tenant admins can:

  • Create a unit: a name, an optional slug (derived from the name when left empty), an optional parent and a description.
  • Edit a unit, including moving it under another parent. A unit cannot go under itself or one of its own descendants, or deeper than four levels.
  • Delete a unit. While assets or prefixes are assigned to it you choose another unit to move them to; units beneath the deleted one move up a level.

Anyone who can see the inventory can see the list; changing it needs the business_units.manage permission, which only tenant admins hold.

docs.title: Assign assets
docs.text:
• One asset: the Business unit control on the asset form lists your units, None, and Create new... (type a name and the unit is created when you save).
  • Many assets: Inventory -> select assets -> Edit -> Business unit.
  • Imports: a Business unit column holding a name is matched to an existing unit (ignoring case) or creates one. A NetBox import assigns each device the unit its NetBox tenant maps to.

docs.title: Filter by unit
docs.text:
The Business unit facet in the Inventory filter rail shows unit names and counts. In the query box:

Query Finds business_unit = "Finance" assets in the unit named (or with the slug) Finance business_unit.id = "<id>" assets in the unit with that id business_unit.parent = Corporate assets in Corporate and every unit beneath it not exists(business_unit) assets with no unit

docs.title: Cabling
docs.text:
A cable joins two ends: a port on one asset and a port on another (or on the same one). Each end is an interface, a console port, a console server port, a front port, a rear port, a circuit termination, a power port, a power outlet or a power feed (see Power). Vista Platform follows NetBox here: a patch panel's front and rear ports carry a connection through the panel, and a circuit's two ends carry it across a provider's network, so a cable path can run from a switch port through several panels and a circuit to a device in another building.

You can record cables by hand, paste a whole switch's cabling from a spreadsheet, or let discovery propose them from what devices report about their neighbours. Cabling is first-class inventory, and the platform draws the cryptography it has seen behind each port on top of it.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text:
You want Go to Every cable in the estate Inventory → Cabling One device's ports, drawn as its front panel Inventory → open the asset → Ports tab (the Faceplate). The Interfaces tab has a Faceplate button that jumps to it. Where a map line physically runs Inventory → Map, then Show physical path (see below) Neighbour-reported cables waiting for a decision Discovery → Approvals → Proposed cables

You need the DCIM read permission (dcim.read) to see any of this and DCIM manage (dcim.manage) to connect, change, disconnect, approve or reject cables. Both are part of the Tenant Administrator and Security Administrator roles; Viewers can read.

docs.title: The Cabling lens
docs.text:
Inventory → Cabling lists every cable. Each row shows:

  • Label
  • A end and B end, each as asset:port. Click one to open that asset's Ports tab. A circuit end links to the circuit in Inventory → Circuits.
  • Type (CAT6, OM4, single-mode and the rest of NetBox's cable types)
  • Status: Connected, Planned, Decommissioning or Proposed. A proposed cable has a dashed marker on its row.
  • Length and Colour (a swatch)
  • Site / rack of the ends

Filter by site, rack, asset, cable type, status (Proposed (awaiting approval) is one of the choices) and port kind (interface, front port, rear port, console port, console server port, circuit termination). The search box matches a cable's label or description. Export downloads the rows on screen as a CSV file.

The lens is a place to look and to correct. A new cable is made from a port (see Connect below), not from the lens.

docs.title: The cable drawer
docs.text:
Click a row to open the cable. The drawer shows:

  • Ends: both ends with their site and rack, each with a Trace button.
  • Cable: edit the Type, Status, Label, Colour (six hex digits) and Length with its unit, then Save. Only the fields you changed are sent. Everything is read-only without dcim.manage.
  • Trace: the path from either end (see Trace a cable).
  • Changes: who changed the cable, and when.
  • Disconnect (top right) deletes the cable after you confirm. Both ports become free and the Changes log keeps the cable's history.

A proposed cable's drawer says it is waiting for approval in Discovery → Approvals.

docs.title: The cable page
docs.text: A cable row opens the cable's own page (/inventory/cables/<id>), which you can bookmark and share. It shows both ends, the cable's type, status, length and colour (editable with dcim.manage), whether an LLDP / CDP neighbour has confirmed it, and the trace from either end, then custom fields, tags, contacts, images, changes and journal. The drawer's title (open from a map or a link) goes to the same page. Back returns to the Cabling lens with its filters.

docs.title: The Ports tab and the faceplate
docs.text:
Inventory → open an asset → Ports opens with the Faceplate, a picture of the device's ports followed by tables of its port components.

The faceplate draws:

  • the asset's physical Interfaces (virtual and wireless interfaces are not drawn; the legend says how many were left out),
  • then its Console ports, Console server ports, Front ports and Rear ports, each kind in its own row group.

Ports appear in the order of the asset's device type templates (see Device types), or in natural name order when there is no template. Each row holds 24 ports, so a 48-port switch is two rows.

Each port tile shows:

  • Link state on its border: coloured for Up, Down and Disabled. Console, front and rear ports have no link state and are drawn neutral.
  • A dot when the port has a cable. A dashed border and hollow dot mean the cable is proposed or planned.
  • A tint from the crypto overlay (below).

Hover a tile for its name and state. Click it (or focus it and press Enter) to open the port panel; the arrow keys, Home and End move between tiles. The panel shows the port's name, type and state, its Cable cell (the far end as asset:port, with Connect or Disconnect and a Trace button), and the crypto behind it.

An empty faceplate ("No ports to draw") means nothing has reported or declared a physical port, not that the device has none. Apply templates on the Ports tab creates the ports and interfaces from the asset's device type; nothing already set is overwritten.

docs.title: The crypto overlay
docs.text:
The Crypto overlay checkbox above the faceplate (on by default) tints each interface by the cryptography Vista has observed behind its addresses. This is the platform's differentiator: you can see a weak TLS configuration sitting on a particular switch port.

  • Colour is the highest certified risk score among the crypto configurations on endpoints bound to the interface's addresses, banded Critical, High, Medium, Low or Informational like every other risk badge (see Assets and crypto configurations). The legend under the faceplate shows the colours.
  • Grey means Not assessed: configurations were seen but no certified score exists. It is never drawn as clean.
  • No tint means nothing cryptographic has been observed behind the port. That is not the same as safe.
  • A lock marks a weak protocol version in use.
  • Hover a tile (or open its panel) to see how many configurations sit behind it and which one is worst, with its protocol, version, cipher suite and port.

Only the asset's own endpoints count, so a neighbour's configuration never tints this device's port. The legend also names the worst open finding on this asset. If the overlay cannot load, the legend says so rather than drawing every port as clean.

The overlay tints interfaces only; console, front and rear ports are not tinted.

docs.title: Connect a port
docs.text:
1. Click a port on the faceplate (or use the Cable column on the Interfaces tab or the tables on the Ports tab) and choose Connect.
  2. Far end is: the kind of port at the other end: Interface, Front port, Rear port, Console port, Console server port, Circuit termination, Power port, Power outlet or Power feed. Kinds that cannot be cabled to this port are labelled (not compatible), and Connect stays disabled with the reason shown.
  3. For a port on an asset, optionally narrow by Site and Rack (picking a rack lists the assets placed in it), then search for the Asset by name, hostname or identifier and choose the Port. For a circuit termination, search by circuit ID and choose the side. For a power feed, pick the Site (and optionally the Rack) and choose the feed.
  4. Optionally set Cable type, Status, Label, Colour (six hex digits) and Length with a unit. A length needs its unit.
  5. Click Connect.

The rules:

  • One cable per port. A port that already has a cable (or is marked connected) cannot take another; disconnect first.
  • Compatibility. Interfaces, front ports, rear ports and circuit terminations can be cabled to each other; a console port cables to a console server port, a front port or a rear port; a power outlet cables to a power port, and a power port to a power outlet or a power feed. An interface cannot be cabled to a console port, for example. The Connect dialog shows the matrix as you choose.
  • A cable can join two ports of the same asset.
  • Virtual and wireless interfaces cannot be cabled.

Disconnect (the unplug button in the Cable cell) asks first, then deletes the cable.

You need dcim.manage, and the asset must not be archived or deleted.

docs.title: Edit cables as a table
docs.text:
For a whole switch, Ports tab → Edit cables as table opens a grid with one row per cable: Local port, Far asset, Far port, Cable type, Label.

  1. Paste a block from a spreadsheet into any cell. Tab-separated text is expected (comma-separated is accepted), and a header row is dropped. Or type the rows; Add row adds more.
  2. Click Check rows. Far assets are found by exact name and their ports are loaded. Each row says Ready or lists what is wrong: an unknown or already-cabled port, a missing or ambiguous far asset, an incompatible pair, an unknown cable type, or the same local or far port used twice.
  3. Click Apply N cables. Valid rows are connected one after another and each row reports Connected or why it was refused. A refused row does not stop the others.

docs.title: Trace a cable
docs.text:
A Trace answers "where does this port really go?". It is available from the port panel and the Cable cell on an asset, from either end in the cable drawer, and from the map.

The trace window shows a left-to-right diagram of port, cable, port, with the in-device hops between them: a patch panel's front to rear or rear to front, and a circuit's A to Z. The far end is highlighted, a planned or not-connected cable is drawn dashed, and every asset or circuit is a link. Below the diagram is the same path as a hop list, and Copy as text copies it.

Each path is labelled complete or incomplete. An incomplete path ends before it reaches a far port. A note appears when not every cable is connected or when the path splits: a rear port carrying several front-port positions, or a circuit with several terminations, cannot be followed as one line. A front or rear port can lie on several paths, and the trace then lists each. A port with no cable says Not cabled.

Paths are worked out when cables change and follow at most 64 cables. A proposed cable carries no path until someone approves it.

docs.title: Port components
docs.text:
Besides interfaces, an asset can hold console ports, console server ports, front ports, rear ports, device bays, and power ports and power outlets (described in Power). They live below the faceplate on the Ports tab, one tab per kind with its count; you need dcim.read to see them and dcim.manage to change them.

  • Add console port and the other add buttons open a drawer. A console port has a Name, Type and Speed (baud); a rear port has Positions (how many front-port positions it carries; a 12-fibre trunk has 12); a front port names the Rear port it belongs to and its Position on it. Declare rear ports first. Every kind also takes a Label and Description.
  • The rear ports table shows how many of its positions are Mapped to front ports. A rear port cannot be made smaller than a position that is already mapped.
  • A device bay holds one child asset, such as a blade in a chassis. The drawer takes the Installed asset's id; the table shows Empty or a link to the installed asset. A device bay takes no cable.
  • Apply templates instantiates every component kind from the asset's device type, interfaces included.

A patch panel is simply an asset whose device type has rear ports and front ports: cable a switch to a front port, cable the panel's rear port onward, and the trace follows the mapping through it.

docs.title: Cables from circuits
docs.text: A circuit termination is a cable end like any other. In Connect, choose Circuit termination as the far end, search for the circuit and pick its A or Z side. A trace through it crosses the circuit from one side to the other. See Circuits.

docs.title: Neighbours become proposed cables
docs.text:
Switches, routers and firewalls report which device sits on the other end of each port with LLDP or CDP. Vista Platform reads those neighbour tables when it interrogates Cisco devices (CDP and LLDP), Palo Alto firewalls (LLDP), any SNMP device that answers the LLDP or CDP tables, and UniFi controllers (the LLDP table and each device's wired uplink), and turns each into a cable instead of a loose fact. The device has to be interrogated for this; sensor captures do not currently produce cables.

For each neighbour the platform finds the far device by its chassis ID, else its system name, else its management address, and the far port by MAC address, else by name. If more than one candidate matches it does not guess.

  • Both ends known and free: a proposed cable is created between the two interfaces. It is marked as measured, appears with a dashed Proposed marker in the Cabling lens and on both ports, and waits for a person.
  • Far end not in the inventory yet: no cable can be made yet. The platform parks the observation as an unresolved termination, remembering what the neighbour announced (chassis ID, port, system name, management address). When that device or port later arrives, through discovery, an import or by hand, the cable is created as proposed. Unresolved terminations are matched after every batch of discovered interfaces and again hourly, and one that nothing matches is dropped after 30 days without a new sighting. They are not listed in the interface, so a missing far end shows up only as the absence of a cable.
  • Already agrees with a cable: nothing is proposed; the cable is stamped as confirmed by the neighbour.

docs.title: Approve or reject
docs.text:
Proposed cables are listed in Discovery → Approvals under Proposed cables, with both ends as links, the protocol that saw them and the number of observations. They count in the queue and under the Discovered source filter.

  • Approve makes the cable one of record and computes its paths (needs dcim.manage).
  • Reject keeps the cable marked as rejected, so the same pairing is not proposed again. Its ports show Rejected; disconnect it to free them.

A proposal is only made between ports that are both free, so a cable you drew yourself is not replaced.

docs.title: When a cable is contradicted: topology/cable_drift
docs.text:
When a neighbour on a port contradicts an active cable, either because the cable's far end (followed through any patch panels) is a different device or port, or because the far port the neighbour names is cabled to something else, the platform raises a topology/cable_drift finding on the local asset. It is medium severity and, being an inventory-accuracy finding rather than an exposure, does not feed risk scores.

Open it in Risk & Compliance → Findings: the Cabling versus neighbours panel lists each contradicted port with the cable of record beside what LLDP or CDP reports. The fix is on the asset's Interfaces tab. If the device really was re-patched, update the cable; if the record is right, find out what is plugged in. The finding resolves by itself when a later interrogation shows the neighbours agreeing with the cables, or as soon as one of those cables is changed. A neighbour whose far device is not in the inventory never counts as a contradiction.

docs.title: Cables on the map
docs.text:
In Inventory → Map, the Neighbourhood view has a Physical cabling toggle. It draws the cable runs between the assets on screen as thick lines, dashed while proposed and faded when not connected. The toggle is disabled, with the reason as its hover text, when no cables run between the assets shown. The legend names the relationship, cable and proposed-cable line styles.

  • Hover a cable to see its ports, its label and how many cables and patch panels it passes through.
  • Click a relationship line and choose Show physical path to trace the cable from that line's port. The item is disabled, with the reason, when no port can be named for the relationship, for example a line drawn from a cloud region rather than observed on a port.
  • Click a cable to open the trace, with Open cable to reach it in the Cabling lens.

The Topology view adds a Physical cabling toggle between prefixes, summing the cable runs between each pair of prefixes. In the Network view, a device's detail has a Faceplate link to the asset's Ports tab. See Map.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
/api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/cables lists, creates, reads, changes and deletes cables, with the filters asset_id, site_id, rack_id, location_id, type, operational_status, status, termination_kind, termination_id, label and q. POST /dcim/cables/{id}/approve and /reject decide a proposed cable. GET /dcim/{interfaces,front-ports,rear-ports,console-ports,console-server-ports,circuit-terminations}/{id}/trace answers a path's steps. GET /dcim/assets/{id}/interface-posture feeds the crypto overlay. Components are under /dcim/{console-ports,console-server-ports,front-ports,rear-ports,device-bays} and /dcim/assets/{id}/{kind}. Reads need dcim.read; writes need dcim.manage.

The inventory query language reaches cables with cable.type, cable.status and cabled_to. See Query.

docs.title: Changes, journal and tags
docs.text: Every create, change and delete of an inventory object is recorded: who made it, where it came from, when, and which fields moved. That record is the change log. Alongside it, people leave journal entries (dated notes on an object) and attach tags (labels). Together they answer "what happened to this estate, and why?". A NetBox object change, journal entry and tag map onto these one to one.

docs.title: The change log, across everything
docs.text:
Inventory → Changes (in the Lifecycle group of lenses) lists every recorded change, newest first, 50 to a page. Reading it needs the dcim.read permission.

Each row shows When, Who, Source, Kind, Object, Action (Created, Updated or Deleted) and the Fields changed. Narrow the list with the filters above it:

Filter Narrows to Object kind one kind of object (asset, interface, rack, prefix, circuit…) Object name objects whose name contains the text User changes by a person whose name or email contains the text Source Web UI, API, System, Discovery or Sync Action created, updated or deleted From / To a range of days, both days included

Clear removes the filters. The filters live in the page address, so a filtered view can be shared as a link. Export page downloads the rows on screen as change-log.csv (when, who, source, kind, object, object id, action, fields changed); it exports the page you are looking at, not the whole log.

Click a row to open its drawer: when, who, source, the object (a link, when it is an asset that still exists), the object it belongs to (an interface's asset, for example), the request id, and What changed — a table of Field, Before and After. Fields that did not exist before or do not exist after read as an em dash. A secret (a password or key field) is redacted when the change is recorded, so the table shows that it moved, never what it was.

docs.title: The change log of one object
docs.text:
An object's own page carries the same record, limited to that object:

  • Inventory → open an asset → Changes tab. It lists the asset's own changes and those of its interfaces, IP addresses, tags and journal, each line naming what changed, and the journal below it.
  • Racks (Settings → Organization → Racks, and Inventory → Racks), sites, VLANs, prefixes, circuits, clusters, tunnels, cables, ports, interfaces and business units show a Changes panel in their dialog, drawer or page.

On each line, Show changes expands the same Field / Before / After diff; Hide changes collapses it. A long history shows the latest changes and says how many there are in all.

(The asset's separate History tab is the older record of reclassifications, context edits, merges and approvals; the Changes tab is the DCIM record.)

docs.title: A person's edit and a collector's measured value
docs.text:
The Who and Source of a change tell you whether a person or the platform made it:

Source Meaning Who reads as Web UI a person edited it in the web UI the person's email API a person or token wrote it through the API the person Discovery (…) a collector reported it, named after the collector the source Sync (…) a connector brought it in, named after the connector the source System a platform job System

Filter Source to Discovery to see only what collectors measured, or to Web UI to see only what people declared. The two are kept apart on purpose: a value a collector measured is never overwritten by an import or a sync, and a person's edit is never overwritten by a collector. See Interfaces for how this looks on a field.

CSV imports are recorded with the source intake:import and so appear under Discovery.

docs.title: Journal entries
docs.text:
A journal entry is a dated, attributed note on one object — a repair, a move, a decision. Everyone in your organization who can read DCIM objects (dcim.read) sees them.

Journals are on the Changes tab of an asset and in the Journal panel of racks, sites, VLANs, prefixes, circuits, clusters and business units. People with dcim.manage get an add form: write the note (up to 10,000 characters), choose its kind — Info, Success, Warning or Danger — and press Add entry. Each entry shows its kind, author, time and text. Adding an entry also appears in the change log, as a change to the journal.

Entries are added, not edited or deleted, from the web UI.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
A tag is a label — pci-scope, decommission-q3 — that you attach to an object. The tags on an asset appear as chips under its name at the top of the asset page.

With dcim.manage, Edit tags opens a checklist of your organization's tags. Tick the ones that apply, or type a name under New tag and Create to add one to the list, then Save tags. The change is recorded on the asset as one change. A tag that is restricted to certain kinds of object is offered only on those kinds.

Config contexts can be assigned by tag; see Config contexts.

docs.title: How long the log is kept
docs.text: The change log is stored in monthly slices, and a slice is dropped whole once it is older than the retention period. The period is set once by the platform administrator for all tenants; without a setting it follows the longest general audit retention. There is no per-tenant setting: export the Changes page to keep a copy beyond it.

docs.title: API
docs.text: GET /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/changes lists the log with the filters object_kind, object_id, action, source (a value such as ui, or a family such as intake:), q (object name), user_name, since and until; include_related=true adds an object's interfaces, addresses and journal. GET /dcim/changes/{id} returns one change with its field diff. Journal: GET and POST /dcim/objects/{kind}/{id}/journal. Tags: GET and PUT /dcim/objects/{kind}/{id}/tags, and /dcim/tags to list, create, rename and delete the tags themselves. Reads need dcim.read, writes dcim.manage.

docs.title: Circuits
docs.text:
A circuit is a link you buy from someone else: an internet connection, an MPLS service, a stretch of dark fibre, a wavelength, a leased line. It has a circuit ID (the provider's reference), a circuit provider, a circuit type, a status and a commit rate, and up to two ends, A and Z. A NetBox provider, provider account, provider network, circuit type, circuit, circuit termination and circuit group map onto these one to one. A virtual circuit is the other kind: a circuit a provider delivers over its own network (see Virtual circuits).

Circuits answer "what do my sites run on, from whom, and at what rate?". A circuit end is also a cable end, so a cable trace can carry on through a circuit to the other side (see Cabling).

docs.title: Where to find them
docs.text:
You want Go to The list of circuits and each one's ends Inventory → Circuits Virtual circuits and the interfaces that terminate them Inventory → Circuits → Virtual circuits Providers, accounts, provider networks, circuit types, virtual circuit types and circuit groups Settings → Infrastructure → Circuit Providers

You need the Circuits read permission (circuits.read) to see both and Circuits manage (circuits.manage) to add, change or delete anything. Both are part of the Tenant Administrator and Security Administrator roles; Viewers can read. Cabling a circuit termination to a port is a cable, so it needs dcim.manage.

docs.title: Keep the catalogues: Settings → Circuit Providers
docs.text:
The page has six sections, each a table with an Add button and edit and delete buttons on each row you own. Build these before your first circuit.

  • Circuit Providers: the companies your circuits come from. A provider has a Name, a Slug (made from the name when left blank), AS numbers (comma-separated, shown as AS3356) and a Description.
  • Provider Accounts: your accounts with a provider, so a circuit can say which contract it is billed under. Each has the Circuit Provider, an Account number, a Name and a Description.
  • Provider Networks: a provider's own network that a circuit can end on instead of a site, such as an MPLS cloud or an internet exchange fabric. Each has the Circuit Provider, a Name, a Service ID and a Description.
  • Circuit Types: what kind of service a circuit is. Seven ship with the platform and are marked Built in, which makes them read-only: Internet, MPLS, Dark Fibre, Wavelength, Point-to-Point, Broadband and Cellular. Add your own with a Name, a Slug, a Colour (six hex digits) and a Description.
  • Virtual Circuit Types: what kind of overlay a virtual circuit is, such as SD-WAN, MPLS L3VPN or Metro Ethernet. None ship with the platform. Each has a Name, a Slug, a Colour and a Description.
  • Circuit Groups: a name for a set of circuits that belong together, such as the primary and backup links to one office. Each has a Name, a Slug and a Description.

An account or provider network belongs to one provider, and deleting a provider takes its accounts and networks with it. A provider, circuit type, provider network or virtual circuit type that circuits or virtual circuits still use cannot be deleted.

docs.title: The Circuits lens
docs.text:
Inventory → Circuits lists every circuit with its Circuit ID, Circuit Provider, Type, Status, A end, Z end and Commit rate. Search by circuit ID, filter by Status, and use the Circuit Providers button to jump to the catalogues.

Click Add circuit and fill in:

  • Circuit ID: the provider's reference. Unique per provider.
  • Circuit Provider and Circuit Type (both required), and optionally a Provider Account.
  • Status: Planned, Provisioning, Active (the default for a new circuit), Offline, Deprovisioning or Decommissioned.
  • Commit rate (kbps), Installed and Contract ends (dates as YYYY-MM-DD), and a Description.

docs.title: The circuit drawer
docs.text:
Click a row to open the circuit. The drawer has:

  • Details: status, commit rate, installed and contract dates, description. The pencil and bin buttons at the top edit and delete the circuit.
  • Terminations: the A and Z ends. Click Set (or Edit) beside an end. Lands on names the provider network the end sits on, or leave it as Not connected. Port speed (kbps), Cross-connect ID and Patch panel / port record the handoff.
  • Circuit Groups: the groups the circuit belongs to, each with an optional priority (Primary, Secondary, Tertiary or Inactive). Add to group adds one; the cross removes it.
  • Custom fields: any custom fields your organisation defined for circuits (Settings → Infrastructure → Custom Fields).
  • Changes and Journal: who changed the circuit and when, and notes people have written about it.

Deleting a circuit asks first. Its terminations and group memberships go with it.

docs.title: The circuit page
docs.text: A circuit row opens the circuit's own page (/inventory/circuits/<id>), which you can bookmark and share. It shows the same details, A and Z terminations (editable with circuits.manage) and groups as the drawer, adds a trace from each cabled end, and ends with custom fields, tags, contacts, images, changes and journal. Back returns to the Circuits lens with its filters.

docs.title: Virtual circuits
docs.text:
A virtual circuit is a circuit a provider delivers over one of its provider networks rather than as a physical link of its own: an SD-WAN overlay, an MPLS L3VPN, a Metro Ethernet virtual connection. Its ends are interfaces (the interface on each of your devices where the overlay lands), each with a role: Peer, Hub or Spoke. The model is NetBox 4.2's virtual circuit, virtual circuit type and virtual circuit termination.

Inventory → Circuits, then Virtual circuits at the top of the lens, lists every virtual circuit with its Circuit ID, Circuit Provider, Provider Network, Type, Status and its Terminations (each as role, asset and interface). Search by circuit ID and filter by Status.

Click Add virtual circuit and fill in:

  • Circuit ID: the provider's reference. Unique per provider network.
  • Provider Network and Virtual Circuit Type (both required), and optionally a Provider Account, which must be an account of the network's provider.
  • Status: the same six as a circuit's, Active by default.
  • A Description.

Click a row to open the virtual circuit: its status and description, its terminations (each links to the interface's page; the cross removes one) and its Changes. The pencil and bin buttons edit and delete it; deleting a virtual circuit removes its terminations.

An interface joins a virtual circuit from its own page (/inventory/interfaces/<id>): under Virtual circuit, Add to a virtual circuit asks for the virtual circuit and the role. An interface terminates at most one virtual circuit; the page shows which, with a link to it, and the cross takes the interface out. Deleting the interface removes its termination.

The inventory query language finds assets by the virtual circuits their interfaces terminate: virtual_circuit (the circuit ID, or the virtual circuit type's name or slug), virtual_circuit.cid, virtual_circuit.provider (by name or slug) and virtual_circuit.role (peer, hub or spoke). virtual_circuit.role != hub also matches an asset that terminates no virtual circuit. See Query.

docs.title: Circuit terminations as cable ends
docs.text:
Each side of a circuit is a circuit termination, and a termination can be cabled like a port: from a switch's or router's port (or a patch panel's front or rear port), choose Connect, set Far end is to Circuit termination, search for the circuit by circuit ID and pick the side. A termination takes one cable and can be cabled to an interface, a front port, a rear port or another circuit termination.

Once a cable reaches a termination, Trace on the port follows the path across the circuit from its A side to its Z side and onward. A circuit with several terminations on one side splits the path, and the trace says so. The Cabling lens links a circuit end straight to the circuit in this lens. See Cabling.

docs.title: API
docs.text: /api/v2/inventory-service/circuits/{providers,provider-accounts,provider-networks,circuit-types,circuits,circuit-terminations,circuit-groups,circuit-group-assignments,virtual-circuit-types,virtual-circuits,virtual-circuit-terminations} list, create, read, change and delete each object. The circuits and virtual circuits lists take operational_status and q; terminations and group assignments filter by circuit_id; virtual circuits by provider_network_id and provider_id; virtual circuit terminations by virtual_circuit_id and interface_id. Reads need circuits.read; writes need circuits.manage. GET /dcim/circuit-terminations/{id}/trace answers the cable path through a termination and needs dcim.read.

docs.title: Config contexts
docs.text: A config context is a named piece of JSON — NTP servers, a syslog target, a login banner — that applies to every asset matching a set of criteria. Each asset's page shows the rendered result: all the contexts that apply to it, merged by weight into one document. Use it to keep the settings your devices should share in one place instead of repeating them per asset. A NetBox config context maps onto this one to one.

docs.title: Where to find them
docs.text: Settings → Infrastructure → Config Contexts lists every context with its weight, whether it is Active, and what it Applies to. Everyone who can read DCIM objects (dcim.read) can open the page; adding, editing and deleting needs dcim.manage.

docs.title: Add a config context
docs.text:
Add config context opens a dialog:

  • Name (required) — unique in your organization.
  • Weight — a whole number from 0 to 32767 (default 1000). Lower weights merge first; a heavier context wins a conflicting key.
  • Active — only active contexts are used when an asset's config is rendered. Switch it off to keep a context without applying it.
  • Data (JSON object) — the document itself. It must be a JSON object, like {"ntp": ["10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2"]}; the dialog refuses anything else and says what is wrong.
  • Applies to — see below.

The pencil icon edits a context and the cross deletes it. A deleted context stops applying to assets; the deletion is recorded in the change log (see Changes, journal and tags).

docs.title: Who a context applies to
docs.text:
Applies to has one collapsible list per criterion:

Criterion Matches an asset when… Locations the asset is in the location, or in a location inside it Device types its device type is one of those picked Device roles its device role is one of those picked Platforms its platform is one of those picked Business units it belongs to one of those business units Tags it carries one of those tags

The rules:

  • Pick any number of values in a list; an asset matches the list if it matches any one of them.
  • An asset must match every list you fill in.
  • A context with every list empty applies to all assets (the table shows All assets).

Sites, regions, site groups and clusters are not yet available as criteria.

docs.title: How the merge works
docs.text:
For an asset, the platform takes every active context that applies and merges them lightest weight first (ties are ordered by name):

  • JSON objects are merged key by key, going as deep as the objects go.
  • Where two contexts set the same key, the heavier context wins.
  • Lists, numbers, text and null are replaced, not combined. A list in a heavier context swaps out the whole list from a lighter one.

For example, a context of weight 100 with {"ntp": ["10.0.0.1"], "banner": "Authorized use only"} and one of weight 500 with {"ntp": ["10.9.0.1"], "syslog": {"host": "10.0.0.9"}} render as {"ntp": ["10.9.0.1"], "banner": "Authorized use only", "syslog": {"host": "10.0.0.9"}}.

docs.title: See the result on an asset
docs.text:
Inventory → open any asset → Config Context tab. It shows the Rendered config as JSON and, under Contributed by, the contexts that produced it in merge order with each one's weight. Manage config contexts links to the settings page. If no active context matches the asset, the tab says so; that means nothing applies, not that the asset has no configuration.

The tab needs dcim.read. It is read-only: to change what an asset receives, change the contexts or the asset's location, device type, role, platform, business unit or tags.

docs.title: API
docs.text: /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/config-contexts (list, create, read, edit, delete) and GET /dcim/assets/{id}/config-context, which returns the merged document and the contributing contexts. Reads need dcim.read, writes dcim.manage.

docs.title: Contacts and images
docs.text:
A contact is a person or a team you call about something: a NOC, an on-call rota, a facilities manager, a vendor account rep. A contact role says what the contact is for on one object: Owner, Technical, Billing, On-call and NOC come built in, and you can add your own. An assignment puts a contact in a role on an object, with an optional priority (primary, secondary, tertiary or inactive).

An asset's Owner line on the Overview is still just an email address kept for convenience; it is not a contact, and the two are not linked.

docs.title: Manage contacts
docs.text:
Settings -> Infrastructure -> Contacts has two tabs.

  • Contacts: add, edit and delete contacts. A contact has a name, an optional title, email, phone, address and link, and an optional group - another contact it belongs to, so a team can hold its members. Names are unique within a group.
  • Roles: add, edit and delete your own roles. The built-in roles are marked Built in and cannot be changed. A role that is still assigned somewhere cannot be deleted.

Anyone with the DCIM read permission can see both tabs; changing anything needs dcim.manage.

docs.title: Assign a contact
docs.text:
On an asset's Overview tab, the Contacts section lists who is assigned, primary first, with each contact's role, priority, email and phone. With dcim.manage:

  1. Choose Assign contact.
  2. Pick an existing contact, or New contact... and type a name (and optionally an email)
  3. the contact is created and assigned in one step.
  4. Pick the role, and optionally a priority, then Assign.

The same contact can hold several roles on one object (an owner who is also the billing contact), but not the same role twice. The remove button on a row removes that assignment only; the contact stays. Deleting a contact removes all of its assignments.

Every assignment, edit and removal is recorded in the object's change log.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
The Images section of the same tab holds pictures of the object: a photo of a rack before the cabling work, a floor plan, a label. Upload image accepts PNG, JPEG, WebP and SVG files of up to 5 MB; the type is decided from the file's contents, not its name, so a program renamed to .png is refused. An SVG that contains a script, an event handler or an embedded object is refused as well. Click a thumbnail to open the full image; the trash button deletes the image and its stored file.

Images are kept in the object storage an administrator has configured for the platform (artifact type dcim_images, enabled the same way as CBOM artifact storage). Until that is enabled they are kept on the disk of the inventory service (DCIM_IMAGE_DIR), which is lost if the pod is replaced without a volume mounted there.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Under /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim: contacts, contact-roles, contact-assignments (list, create, read, edit, delete), objects/{kind}/{id}/contacts (list and assign), objects/{kind}/{id}/images (list and multipart upload), images/{id} (metadata, delete) and images/{id}/download (the bytes). Reads need dcim.read, writes dcim.manage.

docs.title: Custom fields
docs.text: A custom field is a field you add to inventory objects of your own choosing: an owner team on every asset, a cost centre on every prefix, a service tier on every circuit. You define it once, say which kinds of object carry it, and from then on the object's page shows it, edits it, checks it on every save, and the inventory query language can search on it. A NetBox custom field and custom field choice set map onto these one to one.

docs.title: Define a field
docs.text:
Settings → Infrastructure → Custom Fields has two tabs, Fields and Choice sets. Everyone who can read DCIM objects (dcim.read) can see the definitions. Creating, editing and deleting them needs the custom_fields.manage permission, which tenant admins hold.

On the Fields tab, Add field opens a dialog:

Field What it does Name * Lowercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter. It is how a query names the field: cf.<name>. Label The words shown on pages. Without one the name is shown. Type * See the table below. Object kinds * The kinds of object that carry the field. A filterable checklist of every object kind. Choice set * For Selection and Multiple selection only: the set the choices come from. Related object kind * For Object and Multiple objects only: the kind the value points at. Required A person saving an object must fill it in. Default A new object starts with this value. For Multiple selection, separate values with a vertical bar (\|). Minimum / Maximum For Integer and Decimal. Validation regex For Text, Text (long) and URL: a value must match it. Shown Always, If set (hidden while empty) or Hidden. Editable Yes, Read-only, or Not in the form. Group and Weight Fields with the same group are listed under a heading; lower weights come first (default 100). Cloneable Copied when an object is cloned. Description Shown as a tooltip on the field's label.

The available types are Text, Text (long), Integer, Decimal, Boolean (true/false), Date, Date & time, URL, JSON, Selection, Multiple selection, Object and Multiple objects.

The table lists each field with its cf.<name>, its type, the kinds it applies to and its group. The pencil icon edits a field and the cross deletes it. Deleting a field does not erase the values objects already hold, but they are no longer shown, checked or searchable. The deletion is recorded in the change log (see Changes, journal and tags).

docs.title: Choice sets
docs.text: A selection field draws its choices from a choice set. On the Choice sets tab, Add choice set takes a Name, the Choices (one per line, either value or value|Label), an Order alphabetically switch and a description. A set that a field uses cannot be deleted.

docs.title: Which objects carry them
docs.text:
The Object kinds checklist offers every object kind in the vocabulary, but a value can be seen and edited in the web UI where the object's page has a Custom fields panel. Today that is:

  • an asset — Inventory → open the asset → Overview tab, under Custom fields;
  • an interface — in the interface's drawer on the asset's Interfaces tab;
  • a prefix — in the prefix's panel on Inventory → Networks;
  • a VLAN — in its detail on Inventory → VLANs;
  • a circuit — in its drawer on Inventory → Circuits;
  • a business unit — in its dialog under Settings → Organization → Business Units.

If no field applies to the kind, the panel says so and points to Settings → Custom Fields.

docs.title: Fill in a field
docs.text: On any of those pages, Edit custom fields turns the panel into a form, with a control that fits each type (a date picker, a drop-down for Selection, checkboxes for Multiple selection, a text area for JSON, and so on; Object and Multiple objects take object ids). Save stores only the fields you changed. Editing needs the permission to edit the object itself: assets.update for an asset, ipam.manage for a prefix or VLAN, circuits.manage for a circuit, business_units.manage for a business unit, dcim.manage for an interface. Fields marked Required carry an asterisk.

docs.title: How values are checked
docs.text:
Values are checked on every write, whichever way it arrives: the page, the API or a CSV import. A write is refused, with the reason in words, when:

  • the value does not fit the type (text in an integer field, a malformed date or URL, invalid JSON);
  • it is not one of the choice set's choices;
  • a number is outside the Minimum / Maximum, or text does not match the Validation regex;
  • an Object value points at an object that does not exist;
  • a Required field is empty.

Two rules keep the checks from getting in discovery's way.
