Required is enforced for writes by people (the page, the API, CSV import) but not for discovery, sync or system writes, so a new required field can never stop a scan. And an update that does not mention custom fields at all is not re-checked.

docs.title: Import and export columns
docs.text:
A custom field is a CSV column named cf.<name>, for example cf.owner_team. On import, a blank cell leaves the stored value alone and - clears it, as with every other column (see Import and export); a column naming a field that does not apply to the kind is reported as an error on the row. Export writes one cf.<name> column for each field that applies to the kind, so an exported file imports as no change.

Custom field columns are available for the kinds the importer handles directly (the IPAM kinds and the device catalogue kinds that carry custom fields, such as prefixes, VLANs and IP addresses). They are not yet available for business units, sites, locations, assets or interfaces.

docs.title: Find objects by a custom field
docs.text:
In the inventory query bar, a custom field is cf.<name>, on assets and on interfaces:

cf.owner_team:payments
cf.tier in (gold, silver)
exists(cf.owner_team)

The query bar completes the names of your own fields. A value is compared as text: : ignores case, = does not. Ordering comparisons (<, >, ranges) on a custom field are refused. A name no field uses matches nothing rather than failing. See Query for the language.

docs.title: API
docs.text: /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/custom-fields and /dcim/custom-field-choice-sets (list, create, read, edit, delete). Reads need dcim.read, writes custom_fields.manage. An object's values travel in its custom_fields property on that object's own route; a PATCH names only the fields it changes.

docs.title: Device types
docs.text:
A device type is a hardware model: a Cisco Catalyst 9300-48P, a Dell PowerEdge R650, an APC AP7900B rack PDU. It records the manufacturer, the part number, the height in rack units, whether it is full depth, its airflow, and the interfaces and ports every unit of that model has (its templates). Assigning a device type to an asset tells the inventory what the box is and lets it create the box's interfaces in one step.

The catalogue follows the NetBox device-type model, so a type imported from NetBox's community library means the same thing here.

docs.title: What ships with the product
docs.text:
Every installation carries a catalogue of common models, taken from the NetBox community device-type library (public domain, CC0-1.0): Cisco Catalyst 9200/9300/9500 and Nexus 9300 switches, Arista 7050 and 7280, Juniper EX4300, EX4400, QFX5120 and SRX, FortiGate 60F to 600F, Palo Alto PA-220 to PA-3400, F5 BIG-IP i-series, Ubiquiti UniFi switches, gateways and access points, Dell PowerEdge, HPE ProLiant DL360/DL380, Supermicro 1U/2U servers and APC rack PDUs — 154 models in all. The manufacturers list also includes the vendors the platform recognises from MAC addresses.

Built-in types, manufacturers and device roles are marked Built in. Everyone can use them; nobody can change or delete them. To change one, import or create your own copy.

docs.title: Where to find them
docs.text:
Settings → Infrastructure → Device Types. Filter by manufacturer, show built-in types or your own, and search by model or part number. Click a type to see its templates by kind: interfaces, console ports, console server ports, front and rear ports, module bays, device bays, power ports and power outlets.

Next to it: Manufacturers, Device Roles (what a device does — one role ships for each hardware and virtual asset class: Switch, Router, Firewall, Server, Access point, …) and Platforms (OS) (the operating system or firmware family: IOS-XE, Junos, FortiOS, Ubuntu). These are simple lists; add your own entries there.

You need the DCIM read permission to see these pages and DCIM manage to add, edit, delete or import.

docs.title: Importing a type from the library
docs.text:
When a model you own is not in the catalogue, find its file in the device-type library (under device-types/<Manufacturer>/), then click Import from library and paste the file's contents or upload the file. Several files can go in one paste, separated by a line containing only ---.

Each file becomes your organization's own device type with all its templates; a manufacturer you do not have yet is created. A model already in the catalogue (built in or yours) is reported as Already in the catalogue and left as it is. A value the platform cannot store — an interface type it does not know yet, a port with an over-long name — is dropped or set to Other, and the result lists what was adjusted. An import is all or nothing: if one file is not a valid device-type file, nothing is imported.

Elevation images are not imported yet; the type records where the library keeps them.

docs.title: Assigning a type to an asset
docs.text:
Open the asset, click Edit, and use the Hardware fields: Device type (type to search; each choice shows its height), Device role, Platform (OS), Serial and Asset tag. A device type can only be given to a hardware asset (a switch, server, firewall, PDU, …), not to a virtual machine or a cloud resource. An asset tag must be unique among your assets.

The asset page's Hardware card shows the manufacturer, model, part number, height, serial, asset tag, role and platform.

docs.title: Apply templates
docs.text:
On the Hardware card, Apply templates creates the device type's interfaces on the asset. It merges with what discovery already found rather than adding a second copy:

  • An interface the type declares and the asset does not have yet is created.
  • An interface the asset already has under the same name — GigabitEthernet1/0/1 reported by SNMP as Gi1/0/1 counts as the same name — is kept. Its measured MAC address, speed, duplex, MTU and up/down state are never overwritten, nor its enabled flag or description. If it had no specific type (Other), it takes the template's type; a missing label or PoE setting is filled in.
  • Applying the same type again changes nothing.
  • Changing the asset to a different device type and applying again adds the new type's interfaces. An interface the old type created is removed only if the new type does not have it, no collector has ever reported it, and nothing is attached to it (no MAC address, IP address or cable). Everything discovered stays.

For example: SNMP has reported 12 ports of a switch. Assigning the Catalyst 9300-48P and applying templates gives the switch its 48 typed GigabitEthernet ports (plus its stack and management ports), the 12 measured ones keeping their MAC addresses and state.

Console, front and rear ports, power ports and outlets, and module and device bays are stored on the type but not created on the asset yet; the card says how many are waiting.

docs.title: End of sale, support and life
docs.text:
A device type and a platform (OS) each carry three lifecycle dates: End of sale, End of support and End of life. Set them in the type's or platform's form (Settings → Infrastructure → Device Types or Platforms (OS), Edit), or in a device-type or platform import file (end_of_sale, end_of_support, end_of_life, as YYYY-MM-DD).

The same form can link the type or platform to an entry in the end-of-life catalogue, the platform-curated list of product support dates (a device type links to a hardware entry, a platform to an operating system entry). A date you leave blank falls back to the linked entry: end of support takes the entry's end-of-support date, end of life its extended-support date. The catalogue has no end-of-sale date. A date you set always wins over the catalogue.

You do not have to link every entry yourself. When you create or import a device type or platform, and once a day for those already there, the inventory looks for the one catalogue entry that fits and links it. A device type matches a hardware entry whose vendor is its manufacturer and whose product is its model or part number (ignoring case and extra spaces), or, failing that, a product that opens the model at a whole word or dash (product C9300 for model C9300-48P). A platform matches an operating-system entry by its name, or by its "name release" (Ubuntu 22.04). If two or more entries fit, which happens whenever a product has several releases and the name does not say which, nothing is linked. A link you chose is never replaced, and a type or platform you unlinked stays unlinked. The edit form says whether the link was made automatically or by you; choose another entry, or None, to override an automatic one. Built-in device types and platforms are not matched.

Built-in device types and platforms cannot be edited, so their dates cannot be set; use your own copy of the type if you need them.

docs.title: Commercial lifecycle
docs.text:
The asset page's Hardware tab has a Lifecycle card with what the asset cost and who sold it, its warranty and support contract, and when it was installed and decommissioned:

Field Notes Purchase date, Purchase cost, Currency, Purchase order The cost is an amount with at most two decimals; the currency is an ISO 4217 code such as USD or EUR. Vendor (seller) Who sold it — a reseller or distributor. The maker is the device type's manufacturer. Warranty start, Warranty end The end cannot be before the start. Support contract, Support contract ends Installed, Decommissioned Decommissioned cannot be before installed.

People with the DCIM manage permission click Edit on the card; each save is recorded in the asset's Changes tab. The asset import file has the same eleven columns (purchase_date, warranty_start, warranty_end, purchase_cost, purchase_currency, purchase_order, vendor, support_contract, support_contract_end, installed_at, decommissioned_at), and the import's preview shows each one that would change.

The card also shows two states:

  • Warranty — Under warranty, Warranty ends within 90 days, or Warranty expired, from the warranty end date.
  • End of support — Supported, End of support within 12 months, or Past end of support. The date used is the earlier of the device type's and the platform's end of support (each the date set on it, or else its end-of-life catalogue entry's), and the card says which one it is and where it came from. An asset whose hardware is supported until 2030 on an operating system that lost support last year is past end of support.

When nothing is recorded, the card says Warranty not recorded and End of support not recorded. That is not the same as covered or supported: it means nobody has told the platform.

The asset list has optional Warranty end, End of support, Purchased and Vendor (seller) columns, and the list's CSV export includes them, blank when not recorded.

docs.title: Spare parts
docs.text: Parts that are not in an asset — a spare power supply, a box of optics, a unit out for return — are inventory items with a stock location instead of an asset. Installing a spare into a module bay creates a module of the module type its part number names. See Spares and RMA.

docs.title: Searching
docs.text:
The inventory search understands device_type (model, slug or part number: device_type = "C9300-48P"), device_type.manufacturer (device_type.manufacturer:cisco), device_role, platform, serial and asset_tag.

For the commercial lifecycle: warranty_end, purchase_date, support_contract_end, installed_at and decommissioned_at compare as dates (warranty_end < now+90d finds warranties ending in the next 90 days; not decommissioned_at:* finds assets still in service), vendor matches the seller (vendor = "Acme Resale"), and end_of_support is the effective end-of-support date described above (end_of_support < now finds assets past end of support). An asset with no date recorded never matches a date comparison.

docs.title: Import and export (CSV)
docs.text: Bring objects in from a spreadsheet, or take them out, one kind at a time. The same file format does both: an export re-imports to no change, so you can export, edit in a spreadsheet, and import the result.

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
Infrastructure -> Catalog & Data -> Import.

  1. Pick the kind (Business units, Sites, Locations, Manufacturers, Device roles, Platforms, Device types, Assets, Interfaces, RIRs, Aggregates, VRFs, VLAN groups, VLANs, Prefixes, IP ranges, IP addresses). The page lists the kind's columns; required ones are starred.
  2. Download template gives the header row and one example row.
  3. Drop your CSV on the page. Nothing is written yet: every row is checked and the page shows what it would do - Create, Update (with the columns it changes), Unchanged, or Error with the reason in words.
  4. Fix the file and drop it again, or press Apply. Rows with errors are skipped and reported; every other row is applied. Applying needs the permission to edit that kind (ipam.manage for IPAM kinds, business_units.manage for business units, dcim.manage for sites, locations, the device catalogue and interfaces, assets.update for assets); without it you can still check a file.

docs.title: How rows are matched
docs.text:
A row is matched to an existing object by its name, not an id, so a file is portable between organisations. A device type is a manufacturer plus a model; a prefix, IP range or address is matched inside its VRF (a blank vrf is the global table); a VLAN by its group and VID; an asset by asset_tag, else its class with hostname or display_name; an interface by its asset and name; a site by its name; a location by its site and its path inside that site. Business units and locations name their parent by path (Corporate/Finance, Floor 2 or Floor 2 / Cage A inside the row's site).

Reference columns (vrf, rir, group, manufacturer, business_unit, ...) take the referenced object's name. A row may refer to an object created later in the same file.

docs.title: Placing assets
docs.text:
The asset kind's site, location, rack, position and face columns place each asset, the same way its Placement card does:

  • location is the path inside the row's site (Floor 2 / Room 201), and rack is the rack's name inside that site - or inside the location, when the row names one. A rack name is only unique within its site and location, so a row naming a location or a rack names its site too.
  • A rack needs a position (the lowest unit the asset occupies, a whole or half unit) and a face (front or rear). The asset takes the rack's site and location.
  • On an asset already in a rack, position and face alone move it within the rack, and - in rack takes it out (it keeps its site and location). A racked asset's site is its rack's, so moving it to another site needs - in rack on the same row.
  • Units already taken, or a device too tall for the rack, are reported on that row when you apply.

Racks themselves are not an import kind yet: create them first (Infrastructure -> Facilities -> Racks -> Manage racks).

docs.title: Blank cells
docs.text: A blank cell leaves an existing value alone. A cell holding - clears it. Export writes a blank for "no value", which is why an exported file imports as no change.

docs.title: What an import records
docs.text:
Objects created by an import are marked as imported, and every change appears in the object's Changes panel with the source intake:import. The IPAM and device-catalogue kinds are checked by running the real import and rolling it back, so the dry run shows exactly the errors the apply would. Business units, sites, locations, assets and interfaces are written by their own services: the dry run checks references and values, and a rule only the service knows (for example a duplicate slug) is reported on that row when you apply.

A file may have up to 10,000 rows and 8 MiB.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
Export buttons on Inventory -> Networks (prefixes in the VRF you are looking at), Inventory -> VLANs (the selected group) and Settings -> Business Units download the rows as CSV. The columns are the kind's import columns. Through the API, GET /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/export?kind=<kind>&format=csv|json streams any kind and accepts the list filters of that kind.

Exporting needs the permission to read the kind (ipam.read, assets.read, otherwise dcim.read).

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
An interface is a network attachment point of an asset: a switch's GigabitEthernet1/0/24, a server's eth0, a firewall's port1, a link aggregation group (Port-channel1), a VLAN interface, a loopback, a virtual machine's network adapter. Physical and virtual interfaces live in one list, on whatever asset owns them.

Interfaces are where an asset meets the network. Each IP address is an address on one of an asset's interfaces (see Networks, VLANs and IP addresses); cables connect them to other ports (see Cabling). You can record interfaces, see them, and search the inventory by them.

docs.title: Where to find them
docs.text:
Inventory → open any asset → Interfaces tab.

The table shows each interface's name, type, whether it is enabled, its MAC address, speed, MTU, 802.1Q mode and VLANs, the state the device last reported (up, down, testing) and its description. A LAG member says which LAG it belongs to.

You need the DCIM read permission to see the tab and DCIM manage to add, edit or delete interfaces. Both are part of the Tenant Administrator and Security Administrator roles; Viewers can read.

docs.title: An empty tab
docs.text:
"No interfaces reported yet" means exactly that: nothing has told the platform about this asset's interfaces, and nobody has declared any. It does not mean the asset has none. Discovery fills this tab with the MAC and IP addresses it identifies the asset by: each address is an IP address on one of the asset's interfaces. When the source did not say which interface carried a value — a sensor watching traffic never knows — it is listed under an interface named observed-1, observed-2, … of type Other, and that interface is renamed when the device later reports the real name for the same MAC. The device agent's host inventory fills in the rest for the host it runs on (or collects from): one interface per real network interface the operating system reports, with its MAC, addresses (with their prefix length), MTU, link speed (Windows) and state; a VLAN sub-interface such as bond0.100 under its parent with its VLAN, and a bond's members under the bond. Virtual interfaces — loopback, container bridges and veths, tunnels — are not listed. The address the agent reports for itself becomes the asset's primary IP. A sensor does the same for the host it runs on — its interfaces by name, with MAC and addresses — and names the interface it captures on in the asset's discovery details. A device a sensor only watched shows its MAC and address on one observed-1 interface; each address records whether it was last seen over DHCP, ARP or another announcement. Generic SNMP devices (any vendor's switch, router or appliance) fill the tab the same way: every port and virtual interface with its type, MAC, MTU, speed and state, the addresses on it with their prefix length, a LAG's members, a sub-interface's parent and, where the device answers the bridge VLAN tables, each port's native and trunked VLANs. A UniFi controller's interrogation fills in the ports, LAGs and VLANs of every switch it manages, the radios of every access point and the gateway's interfaces with its addresses (see the Device Interrogation guide). A cloud discovery lists each instance's network interfaces — AWS ENIs (named eni-…), Azure network interfaces, GCE nic0, … — as Virtual interfaces with their MAC (where the provider states one) and private addresses at their range's prefix length. Interfaces you state also land here: a NetBox import's device interfaces with their addresses, a spreadsheet row's interface, and the MAC and interface given when a device is added by hand; these show as declared or imported. Cisco, Palo Alto, Fortinet and F5 interrogation fills the tab the same way: the device's ports, their addresses, the VLANs defined on it and the ARP table it can see.

An asset is recognised by a MAC on any of its interfaces, including one you add by hand, and its primary IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are chosen from its interface addresses (a management interface's first, never a link-local one) unless you have set them.

docs.title: The interface page
docs.text: Click an interface's name in its drawer (Asset → Interfaces) to open the interface's own page (/inventory/interfaces/<id>), which you can bookmark and share. It shows the asset it belongs to, its type, speed, duplex, MTU, MAC and mode, its untagged and tagged VLANs and its IP addresses (each linking onward; VLAN names and addresses need the IPAM read permission), the cable on it with the far end, and the trace, followed by custom fields, tags, contacts, images, changes and journal. Edit on the asset takes you back to the Interfaces tab, where interfaces are edited. An interface that nothing has reported on shows "State not reported" rather than a status.

docs.title: Adding and editing an interface
docs.text:
Click Add interface (or the edit button on a row). The drawer asks for:

  • Name — use the device's own long form, e.g. GigabitEthernet1/0/24 rather than Gi1/0/24. Names are unique on an asset and case-sensitive.
  • Type — the interface type list (1000BASE-T, 10GBASE-X SFP+, LAG, Virtual, Bridge, 802.11ax and the rest), the same list NetBox uses.
  • Enabled, Management only, MAC address, MTU, Speed, Duplex, Label, Description.
  • LAG — the link aggregation group this interface is a member of. Only interfaces of type LAG on the same asset are offered; a LAG cannot itself be a member of another LAG, and a virtual interface cannot be a member at all.
  • Parent and Bridge — another interface of the same asset. Choices that would make a loop are not offered.
  • 802.1Q mode — Access (an untagged VLAN), Tagged (an untagged VLAN plus at least one tagged VLAN), Tagged (All) (every VLAN; no list) or Q-in-Q. The VLAN fields switch on and off with the mode. VLANs are picked from the ones defined under IPAM (this needs the IPAM read permission; without it, a VLAN is entered by its id).

Each interface's own change record — who changed what, and when — is at the bottom of its drawer.

Deleting an interface asks first. Its LAG members and child interfaces are detached, not deleted.

docs.title: What the device says versus what you say
docs.text:
Some fields are measured — what a device reports about itself — and some are declared by a person. They are kept apart on purpose:

  • Enabled is declared. The device's own administrative state is recorded separately, and a later observation never switches Enabled back on behind your back.
  • State (up / down / testing) is measured, from the device. It is shown as reported and never edited.
  • Description is declared. A description a device reports seeds a new interface once and is never written over yours.

When discovery reports an interface under a short name (Gi1/0/24, Et1, Po10), the platform folds it onto the long name (GigabitEthernet1/0/24, Ethernet1, Port-channel10) so the same interface is never listed twice. An interface that stops being reported is marked Stale after the asset's stale window, not removed. An interface found on an asset still waiting in Approvals is Pending and follows the asset once it is approved.

docs.title: Virtual device contexts
docs.text:
Many devices partition themselves into logical devices that each own some of the interfaces: a Fortinet VDOM, a Palo Alto vsys, a Cisco Nexus VDC, an F5 route domain. Vista Platform records them as virtual device contexts (NetBox's VirtualDeviceContext).

  • Where they live. On the asset page, Hardware tab, the Virtual device contexts card lists the device's contexts: name, identifier (the device's number for the context, if it has one), status (Active, Planned or Offline), business unit, primary IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and how many of the asset's interfaces belong to each. With the DCIM manage permission you can add, edit and delete them there. An empty card means none has been recorded, not that the device has none.
  • Which interfaces belong to which. On the Interfaces tab, the Context column names each interface's contexts. Open an interface and tick its contexts under Virtual device contexts; only the asset's own contexts are offered, and the server refuses a context of another asset.
  • Primary addresses. A context's primary IPv4 must be an IPv4 address (and its primary IPv6 an IPv6 address) assigned to one of the asset's interfaces. Deleting the address clears it from the context.
  • Rules. A name is 1–64 characters and unique on the asset; an identifier is a whole number from 0 to 32767 and unique on the asset when set. Deleting a context takes its interfaces out of it; the interfaces and their addresses stay.

Every change is in the context's change record.

docs.title: Discovered contexts
docs.text:
Interrogating a device records its contexts and which interfaces each owns:

Device Context Identifier Fortinet FortiGate each VDOM an interface is in, root included none (a VDOM has no number) Palo Alto the virtual system that owns the interface (vsys1, vsys2, …) the vsys number F5 BIG-IP the route domain of each VLAN, named as BIG-IP names it (the default route domain is 0) the route-domain id Cisco Nexus (NX-OS) the VDC each port is allocated to (show vdc membership) the VDC id

Only the context's name and number are collected, plus, on a Palo Alto firewall, the display name its administrator gave the virtual system: it becomes the context's description (for example Tenant B Edge on vsys2). The description of a discovered context follows the device, so a rename on the firewall is picked up; a firewall that states no display name, or that refuses the read, leaves the description as it was. Other devices, and SNMP, do not report contexts.

  • New contexts are Pending while the asset waits in Discovery → Approvals, and become Active at the first interrogation after the asset is approved.
  • What you declared wins. A context you created, or one NetBox synced, with the same name is matched, never overwritten: its identifier, status, business unit, primary addresses and description stay as you set them. An interface you put in a context yourself stays in it.
  • Moves. When the device reports an interface in a different context, the interface leaves the discovered context it was in and joins the new one.
  • Contexts that disappear are marked Stale after the asset's stale window (the tenant's asset lifecycle policy, 30 days by default), and only by a device that still reports contexts. A discovered context is never deleted by discovery; delete it on the Hardware tab if it is gone for good.

docs.title: Finding assets by interface
docs.text:
The inventory query language reaches interfaces with interface:( … ):

interface:(mac_address:"00:11:22:33:44:55")
interface:(name = "GigabitEthernet1/0/24" and mode:tagged)
interface:(speed_kbps >= 10000000)
exists(interface) and not interface:(enabled = true)
interface:(virtual_device_context:"vsys2")

Fields: name, type, mac_address, enabled, mgmt_only, mtu, speed_kbps, mode, status, operational_status, description, virtual_device_context (the name of a context the interface belongs to). See Query.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
/api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/interfaces lists, creates, reads, changes (JSON merge-patch) and deletes interfaces, and POST /dcim/interfaces/bulk creates several at once (all or none, so a LAG and its members can arrive together). GET /dcim/assets/{id}/interfaces lists one asset's. Filters: asset_id, name, type, enabled, mgmt_only, mac_address (any of an interface's MAC addresses), lag_id, vlan, status, q.

An interface carries its contexts as virtual_device_contexts (id and name), virtual_device_context_ids and vdcs (the names). A create or PATCH sets them with virtual_device_context_ids — or, by name, vdcs — and replaces the interface's memberships. Contexts are at /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/virtual-device-contexts (list, create, read, change, delete; filters asset_id, name, identifier, status, operational_status, business_unit_id, q) and /dcim/assets/{id}/virtual-device-contexts (one asset's; create on it). Reads need DCIM read, writes DCIM manage.

docs.title: Networks, VLANs and IP addresses (IPAM)
docs.text: Vista Platform keeps an IP address management (IPAM) record of your networks alongside the asset inventory: the prefixes you run, the IP addresses in them, the VLANs that carry them and the VRFs that separate one routing table from another. The model follows NetBox, so a NetBox user will recognise every object.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text:
Page What it is for Inventory → Networks Your prefixes as a tree, one VRF at a time, with how full each one is; the panel for one prefix; the Find box Inventory → VLANs VLAN groups and the VLANs in them, with the prefixes each carries; and, under Translation policies, the VLAN translation policies interfaces apply Settings → Infrastructure → IPAM The catalogues the tree builds on: VRFs, aggregates, RIRs, prefix roles, AS numbers and ASN ranges

Reading needs the IPAM read permission; adding, editing and deleting need IPAM manage. Tenant Administrators and Security Administrators hold both; Viewers can read.

docs.title: The prefix tree
docs.text:
Pick a VRF at the top of Networks — or Global (no VRF) for addresses that are not in any VRF. Each row is a prefix, nested under the prefix that contains it: 10.10.0.0/24 sits under 10.10.0.0/16, and if you later add 10.10.0.0/22 it appears between them by itself. Nothing is stored about who is whose parent; the nesting is worked out from the addresses every time, so it cannot go stale.

Each row shows:

  • Status — Container (a block that holds other prefixes), Active, Reserved or Deprecated.
  • Role and VLAN, when set.
  • Utilisation — how full the prefix is (see below).
  • Counts — how many prefixes and addresses are inside it.

A prefix discovery found but nobody has approved yet carries a Pending approval chip.

docs.title: What utilisation means
docs.text:
• For a container, utilisation is the share of its space covered by the prefixes inside it: a /22 holding one /24 is 25 % used.
  • For any other prefix, it is the share of its usable addresses that have an IP address record, plus any IP range marked as fully used. In an IPv4 prefix the network and broadcast addresses are not usable — except in a /31 or /32, or a prefix marked as a pool, where every address is.
  • A prefix marked Treat as fully used shows 100 %.

An empty prefix shows 0 % of a known size, never a blank: the size is arithmetic, not something anyone has to measure.

docs.title: One prefix
docs.text:
Click a prefix to open its panel:

  • Utilisation with the exact counts (1 of 254), the parent prefix and what the prefix contains.
  • Child prefixes — the ones directly inside it.
  • Free space — the largest free blocks, or every free block of a size you pick (say, every free /26), each with a + to add it as a child; and how many addresses are still free, with the first few. In IPv6 the all-zeros address of a prefix is the subnet-router anycast address: it is free, but every router on the link answers it, so the panel says so.
  • IP ranges inside the prefix.
  • Discovery — what discovery reads from the prefix: whether it is declared by you or learned from a device, its network type, environment, DHCP posture (DHCP, Static or Unknown), auto-approval, the gateway an interrogated router reported, the sensor that reaches it, and any FHRP group (VRRP, HSRP, …) whose virtual address is in it. A learned prefix offers Claim as ours. See Operational context.
  • IP addresses — each with its status, DNS name and, where Vista knows it, the asset that holds it (as its primary or out-of-band address). Add address suggests the first free one.
  • Changes — every edit to the prefix: what changed, who changed it and when.
  • Journal — dated notes anyone with access can add.

docs.title: The prefix and VLAN pages
docs.text: Click a prefix's name in the panel to open the prefix's page (/inventory/prefixes/<id>), or a VLAN's row in Inventory → VLANs to open the VLAN's page (/inventory/vlans/<id>). Both can be bookmarked and shared. The prefix page shows its VLAN, role and business unit, then everything in the panel above. The VLAN page shows its group, site and status, the prefixes it carries and every interface that uses it, untagged or tagged. Each page ends with the same panels as every other inventory object: custom fields, tags, contacts, images, changes and journal. Back returns to the lens with the filters you had.

docs.title: VLAN translation policies
docs.text:
A VLAN translation policy is a named set of rules that rewrite VLAN IDs as traffic crosses an interface: a provider edge port that carries a customer's VLAN 100 as VLAN 2100 on its own side. Each rule maps one local VLAN ID to one remote VLAN ID. The model is NetBox 4.2's.

Inventory → VLANs → Translation policies lists every policy with its rules and how many interfaces apply it. Add translation policy asks for a Name and a Description. Click a policy to open its rules; Add rule asks for the two VLAN IDs (1–4094). Within one policy each local VLAN ID appears once, and so does each remote VLAN ID; a second rule for either is refused.

An interface picks its policy in its edit drawer (Inventory → open an asset → Interfaces → open an interface → VLAN translation policy), and the interface's page shows it. Deleting a policy removes it from the interfaces that applied it; it deletes no interface.

docs.title: ASN ranges
docs.text: An ASN range is a block of autonomous system numbers a registry delegated to you, from a first to a last number, such as the private 16-bit range 64512–65534. Settings → Infrastructure → IPAM → ASN ranges lists each range with its RIR and how many of its numbers your ASNs already use and how many are free; Show free lists the first free numbers, in order. Add ASN range asks for a Name, a Slug (made from the name when left blank), the RIR, the First ASN and Last ASN (the first may not be after the last) and a Description. A range only describes the block: the ASNs themselves are kept in the ASNs section above it, and a range counts every ASN whose number falls inside it.

docs.title: An asset's IP addresses
docs.text:
Inventory → open any asset → IP Addresses tab lists every address the asset holds in one table: the ones assigned to its interfaces, plus any it names as its primary IPv4, primary IPv6 or out-of-band address. Each row shows the address with its prefix length, its VRF, the interface it sits on (a link to the Interfaces tab), role, status, DNS name, where it came from (measured, declared or imported, and what last saw it) and when it was first and last seen. A Primary badge marks the asset's primary address and OOB its out-of-band management address.

Click a row to open the address: its details, its change record and Edit. Set as primary and Set as OOB (needs the IPAM manage permission) record the choice on the asset; an IPv4 address becomes the primary IPv4 and an IPv6 address the primary IPv6, and only an address the asset holds can be chosen. Choosing the same button again unsets it.

"No interfaces recorded" means the asset has not been interrogated and none of its interfaces has been declared, so it says nothing about whether the asset has addresses; "No IP addresses" means its interfaces are known and none carries one.

docs.title: Find
docs.text:
Type an address into Find — 10.10.0.5 — and Vista tells you, for every VRF that has it:

  • the most specific prefix containing it,
  • the IP address record, if there is one, with its DNS name, and
  • the asset holding it.

Addresses in different VRFs are different addresses: 10.10.0.5 in VRF blue and 10.10.0.5 in the global table are answered separately, and a prefix in one never answers for an address in another.

docs.title: Rules Vista enforces
docs.text:
• A prefix is stored as its network. Typing 10.10.0.7/24 stores 10.10.0.0/24.
  • One prefix once per VRF. The same prefix in two VRFs is two networks; twice in one VRF is refused.
  • Addresses are unique within a VRF that enforces it (the default, and always for the global table). Addresses with an anycast, VIP, VRRP, HSRP, GLBP or CARP role may be shared with other such addresses, because that is what those roles are for. A VRF can be set not to enforce uniqueness.
  • A VLAN ID is unique within its VLAN group, and must sit inside the group's VLAN ID ranges (1–4094 by default).
  • IP ranges must start and end in the same address family, start before they end, and not overlap another range in the same VRF.
  • A VLAN translation rule's local and remote VLAN IDs are each unique within its policy, and both are 1–4094.
  • An ASN range starts at or before it ends, and both ends are AS numbers (1–4294967295).
  • Something still in use cannot be deleted. A VRF that prefixes or addresses are in, or a VLAN group with VLANs, is refused with the reason.
  • Built-in catalogue rows — the regional internet registries and private address authorities, and the standard prefix roles — are listed as Built in and cannot be edited or deleted. Add your own beside them.

docs.title: Discovered networks and addresses
docs.text: Discovery and cloud enumeration record the prefixes and addresses they see. A cloud account's networks are prefixes here — an AWS VPC's or Azure virtual network's address ranges and the ranges inside them, a GCP network's regional ranges — each naming the cloud network it belongs to, and the network a cloud instance is in is the prefix its address falls in. A new one arrives pending approval; approving it is setting its status to approved. When discovery sees an existing address again it refreshes what it measured — the MAC address, how it was seen, when — and fills in a DNS name only if none is recorded. It never overwrites a description, role, status or DNS name a person set.

docs.title: Querying the inventory by network
docs.text:
The inventory query box understands an asset's addresses and networks:

Write To find assets ip.address:10.10.0.0/24 with an address in 10.10.0.0/24 ip.dns_name="pbx.corp" with that DNS name on an address prefix.prefix:10.10.0.0/16 whose address's most specific prefix is in 10.10.0.0/16 prefix.status:deprecated with an address in a deprecated prefix vlan.vid=10 with an address in a prefix carried on VLAN 10 vrf.name:blue with an address in VRF blue

"The asset's addresses" are, today, its primary IPv4, primary IPv6 and out-of-band management addresses. The prefix is always the most specific one in the address's own VRF.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
Vista Platform records how power reaches your equipment, in NetBox's shape:

  • A power panel is an electrical panel at a site, optionally in one of the site's locations.
  • A power feed is one circuit from a panel, optionally serving a rack. It has a status (Active, Planned, Offline, Failed), a type (primary or redundant), a supply (AC or DC), a phase (single-phase or three-phase), a voltage, an amperage and a maximum utilisation (the percentage of its capacity that may be drawn).
  • A power port is a socket that draws power: a server's power supply, a PDU's inlet. It can declare a maximum draw and an allocated draw in watts.
  • A power outlet is a socket that supplies power: an outlet on a PDU. It names the power port it draws from (the PDU's own inlet) and, on a three-phase PDU, its feed leg (A, B or C).

A power cable runs from a power port to a power outlet, or from a power port to a power feed. With those cables in place, a server's power supply traces through its PDU to the feed and the panel that power it.

Each feed's available power is worked out as NetBox does: |voltage| × amperage × maximum utilisation, multiplied by 1.732 for a three-phase feed. A 120 V, 20 A, single-phase feed at 80 % has 1,920 VA available; a 208 V, 30 A, three-phase feed at 80 % has 8,646 VA.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text:
You want Go to A site's power panels and their feeds Inventory → Sites → open the site → Power panels The feeds serving a rack Inventory → Racks → open the rack → Power feeds A rack's power budget Inventory → Racks → open the rack → Power, the Power overlay on its elevation, and the Power column of the Racks list Racks drawing more than their feeds supply Dashboard → Facilities → Racks over power budget, and the Over power column of its site table What a PDU measured on each socket Inventory → open the asset → Ports tab → Power ports or Power outlets → Measured A device's power supplies or a PDU's outlets Inventory → open the asset → Ports tab → Power ports or Power outlets Power port and outlet templates of a device type Settings → Device Types → open the type → Power ports or Power outlets

You need the DCIM read permission (dcim.read) to see any of this and DCIM manage (dcim.manage) to add, change or delete panels, feeds, ports, outlets and power cables.

docs.title: Power panels and feeds
docs.text:
On the site page, the Power panels card lists each panel with its location and its feeds. Each feed shows its status, type, rack, rating and available power, and which device it powers: the power port at the far end of its cable (usually a PDU's inlet), or not cabled.

  • Add panel asks for a Name, an optional Location inside the site and a Description. Two panels at one site cannot share a name.
  • The + button on a panel opens Add a feed: Name, Rack (optional; it must be at the same site as the panel), Status, Type, Supply, Phase, Voltage, Amperage and Maximum utilisation. The form previews the available power. A DC supply cannot be three-phase; the voltage cannot be zero (a negative voltage records a DC plant such as -48 V); the amperage is at least 1 and the utilisation between 1 and 100 %. Two feeds on one panel cannot share a name.
  • Deleting a panel deletes its feeds; deleting a feed detaches its cable. The change log keeps what they were.

A panel cannot move to another site while one of its feeds serves a rack at the current site; clear those feeds' racks first.

On the rack page, the Power feeds card lists the feeds declared as serving the rack, grouped by panel, with the total available power of the active ones. The Power card above it is the rack's power budget (see Rack power budget).

docs.title: Power ports and outlets on an asset
docs.text:
On the Ports tab, the Power ports and Power outlets sections list the asset's power sockets, and the faceplate draws them in their own rows.

  • A power port shows its Type, Maximum draw and Allocated draw. A draw nobody declared reads not recorded, never 0 W, and is sent as empty when you save. The allocated draw cannot exceed the maximum.
  • A power outlet shows its Type, the Power port of the same asset it draws from, and its Feed leg.
  • The Power summary above both sections totals the declared draws (and says on how many ports they were declared), lists the feeds the asset reaches with their available power, and for each power port says where its cable path ends. On a PDU, each inlet also shows how many of its outlets feed something and what those devices declare they draw.

Apply templates creates the power ports and outlets of the asset's device type along with every other component, including each outlet's power port and feed leg.

docs.title: Connect power
docs.text:
Use Connect on a power port or outlet, as for any port (see Connect a port):

  • A power outlet cables to a power port.
  • A power port cables to a power outlet or a power feed.
  • Nothing else can be cabled to a power socket, and a power socket cannot be cabled to anything else. The Connect dialog labels the other kinds (not compatible).

For a feed, choose Power feed as the far end, pick the Site (and optionally the Rack) and then the Power feed, shown as panel:feed. A feed already cabled is marked (in use). The cable type defaults to Power. A PDU's outlets and a server's power supplies can also be cabled from Edit cables as table; a feed cannot, because it is not on an asset.

docs.title: Trace power
docs.text: Trace on a power port, outlet or feed shows where the power comes from or goes to. A server's power supply traces to the PDU outlet it plugs into and, when the PDU's inlet is cabled, on through the PDU (outlet → inlet) to the feed, shown as panel:feed. When the PDU's inlet is not cabled, or the outlet names no power port, the path ends at the outlet. A feed traces to the power port it powers. A loop (a PDU's inlet cabled back to one of its own outlets) stops after 64 cables, incomplete.

docs.title: Rack power budget
docs.text:
A rack's power budget compares what its devices are allocated to draw with what the feeds serving it can supply, the way NetBox does:

  • The feeds counted are every feed declared as serving the rack, whatever its status.
  • Each feed's draw is that of the power port at the far end of its cable, usually a PDU's inlet. When that port declares an allocated draw, that figure is used. When it declares no draw, the figure is the sum of the allocated draws of the devices plugged into its outlets.
  • The rack's utilisation is the allocated draw on all its feeds, divided by their available power, to one decimal.

On the rack page, the Power card shows a bar for each feed (allocated W / available VA · %) and one for the rack. On a three-phase feed it also shows each leg, using the outlets' feed legs, against a third of the feed's available power. A bar turns amber over 80 % and red over 95 %, the same thresholds the Facilities dashboard uses for rack space. A feed whose devices declare no draw reads No draw declared, and a feed with nothing cabled to it reads Nothing cabled to it. Neither is shown as 0 W. A rack that no feed serves has no budget at all. That does not mean it draws nothing.

Turn on Power overlay above the elevation to tint each device by its own declared draw as a share of the rack's available power. The tint gets stronger as the share grows, in the same amber and red. A device whose power ports declare no draw is drawn dashed and labelled Draw not recorded. The crypto overlay is turned off while the power overlay is on.

The Racks list's Power column shows each rack's utilisation, or no feed. The Facilities dashboard counts the racks over power budget: racks whose allocated draw is more than their feeds' available power. Its site table shows the count per site, or a dash for a site where no rack has a feed declared.

Measured draws (see below) are shown beside the budget. They are never part of it: the budget is about what devices are allocated, and a reading is what they drew when the PDU was last read.

docs.title: PDU collection
docs.text:
When a rack PDU is interrogated over SNMP (see Device interrogation), Vista Platform reads what the PDU measures:

PDU MIB What is read APC rack PDUs PowerNet-MIB (rPDU2) the PDU's total load, each phase's current and load, each outlet's name, on / off state, current and power Raritan PDUs PDU2-MIB each inlet's current and power, per pole (feed leg), each outlet's name, on / off state, current and power Eaton ePDUs EATON-EPDU-MIB each input's total power and per-phase current and power, each outlet's name, on / off state, current and power Any other device ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB a power supply's watts and amperes sensors (a server's or switch's power supply, as a power port)

Each reading is matched to the PDU's power ports and outlets. A socket is first matched by name. If no name matches, it is matched by number: the PDU's outlet 3 is the one power outlet whose name ends in 3, such as Power Outlet 3 from the device type. When two sockets could match, neither is used. A matched socket keeps everything a person or a sync recorded; only its measured draw, current, on / off state and reading time are written, and an outlet's power port and feed leg are filled only when nothing was recorded. A socket the PDU lists that the asset does not have is added as discovered. It is pending until its asset is approved, and then it becomes active.

The Ports tab shows the reading in a Measured column (for example On · 40 W · 0.2 A), with the time it was taken on hover. A socket nothing has measured reads not measured.

What is not collected: anything else a PDU reports, such as its user accounts, contact or location, and the SNMP community used to read it. Only the first unit of a daisy-chained set is read. A reading is not written to an object's change log, but adding a socket is.

docs.title: Search by power
docs.text:
The inventory search reads the feeds an asset's power ports reach:

Field Example power_feed.status power_feed.status = failed — assets drawing from a failed feed power_feed.type, power_feed.supply, power_feed.phase power_feed.phase = three-phase power_feed.voltage, power_feed.amperage, power_feed.available_power power_feed.available_power < 2000 power_feed.panel, power_feed.rack, power_feed.site power_feed.panel = "Panel 1"

An asset that reaches no feed (an uncabled supply, a PDU whose inlet is not cabled) matches none of them, and satisfies !=.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Under /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim:

  • GET/POST /power-panels, GET/PATCH/DELETE /power-panels/{id} — filters site_id, location_id, name.
  • GET/POST /power-feeds, GET/PATCH/DELETE /power-feeds/{id} — filters power_panel_id, rack_id, site_id, location_id, operational_status, type, supply, phase, business_unit_id. available_power is read-only.
  • GET /power-ports/{id}/trace, GET /power-outlets/{id}/trace, GET /power-feeds/{id}/trace — the cable path.
  • GET /assets/{id}/power — the asset's power summary.
  • GET /racks/{id}/power — the rack's power budget: each feed with its allocated draw, available power, utilisation, legs and measured load, and each device's own declared draw and share. The rack list (GET /racks) carries power_utilization, or null for a rack no feed serves.
  • Power ports and outlets carry the read-only measured_draw, measured_current, measured_at (and measured_legs on a port, measured_state on an outlet).

Power ports and outlets keep their routes (/power-ports, /power-outlets, /assets/{id}/power-ports, /assets/{id}/power-outlets).

docs.title: Racks and placement
docs.text: A rack is a frame of numbered units (U) in a site, optionally in a location inside it (a row, hall or cage). An asset is placed in a rack at a position — the lowest unit it occupies — on the rack's front or rear face. A NetBox rack, rack role, rack type and rack reservation map onto these one to one.

docs.title: Maintain racks
docs.text:
Settings → Organization → Racks lists every rack with its site and location, role, status, utilisation and the number of devices in it. Tenant admins (the dcim.manage permission) can:

  • Create a rack: a name (unique within its site and location), the site, an optional location of that site, a role, a status (active, planned, reserved, available, deprecated), its height (1–100 U, default 42), its starting unit (default 1), whether its units are numbered top-down, its width, and its facility ID, serial and asset tag.
  • Pick a rack type — a model of rack — and the rack copies the type's height, numbering, width and dimensions when you save.
  • Edit a rack. Its dialog has a Changes tab (who changed what, when) and its journal. A rack cannot be made shorter than the devices in it reach. Moving a rack to another site or location moves its devices with it.
  • Reserve units on the rack's Reservations tab: the units (1-2, 7) and who or what they are held for. Reserved units cannot overlap another reservation or a device.
  • Delete a rack: its reservations go with it, and its devices leave the rack and stay in the site.

Five rack roles are provided — compute, network, storage, patching and power — and you can add your own. A rack type that a rack uses cannot be deleted; deleting a role you added clears it from its racks.

docs.title: Place an asset
docs.text:
The asset page's Placement card shows Site › Location › Rack › U · Face. Place in a rack (or Edit placement) opens a dialog: choose the site, optionally the location (it narrows the racks), the rack, the position (in half units) and the face. The asset moves to the rack's site and location. Remove from rack takes it out; it stays in the site.

The placement rules:

  • A device occupies its device type's height from its position upward — a 2U device at U10 takes U10 and U11. Positions step in half units. An asset with no device type is treated as 1U and full depth.
  • A device must fit the rack: from the starting unit up to the top unit.
  • A device is mounted on one face. A full-depth device (the device type says so) takes both faces; two half-depth devices can share a unit, one on each face.
  • A placement over units another device holds is refused, and the message names the device in the way with a link to it. So is a placement over reserved units.
  • A device in a parent device's device bay takes no rack units of its own, and a 0U device (a PDU strip mounted on the side) takes no position.
  • A racked asset's site and location are its rack's: change them by moving the asset to another rack, or remove it from the rack first.
  • Changing a racked asset's device type is refused when the new height no longer fits or overlaps a neighbour.

Two people placing devices into the same units at the same moment cannot both succeed: one placement is saved and the other is refused.

docs.title: Utilisation
docs.text: A rack's utilisation is the units its devices occupy (either face, half units counting as half) out of its height, minus the units held only by devices whose device type is excluded from utilisation (blanking panels, cable managers). An empty rack is 0 %.

docs.title: Find racked assets
docs.text:
Query Finds rack = R12 assets in rack R12 (by name or facility ID) rack.site:ams-1 assets in a rack of site AMS-1 (name or slug) rack.role = network assets in racks with the Network role position >= 40 assets whose lowest unit is U40 or higher face = rear assets mounted on a rear face exists(rack) every racked asset

The asset list's CSV export carries Site, Location, Rack, U and Face columns.

docs.title: API
docs.text: /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/rack-roles, /dcim/rack-types, /dcim/racks and /dcim/rack-reservations (list, create, read, edit, delete); GET /dcim/racks/{id}/elevation returns the rack's per-unit occupancy of both faces, its reservations and its utilisation; GET, PUT and DELETE /dcim/assets/{id}/placement read, set and clear an asset's placement. A refused placement answers 409 with placement_conflict and the blocking asset or reservation. Reads need dcim.read, writes dcim.manage.

docs.title: Saved filters and export templates
docs.text: Two tools for reusing work. A saved filter keeps a query so you, or everyone in your organization, can apply it again in one click. An export template turns the rows of a list into a text format of your choosing — a hosts file, a configuration snippet, an XML feed — instead of CSV.

docs.title: Saved filters
docs.text: A saved filter is exactly its query text, written in the inventory query language. Applying one puts its query into the query bar, so you can read what it says and change it. A NetBox saved filter maps onto this.

docs.title: Save a filter
docs.text:
1. On Inventory → All assets, build a query in the query bar.
  2. Open the Filters menu beside it and choose Save current filter…. The button is disabled until the query is valid.
  3. Give the filter a Name. The dialog shows the query in its canonical form, the same predicate however you spelled it.
  4. Tick Share with my organization if everyone should see it, then Save filter.

docs.title: Use a filter
docs.text: The Filters menu on the All assets lens lists the filters Shared with your organization first, then Mine, plus the built-in Never scanned. Choosing one fills the query bar. A shared filter shows a people icon; the trash icon deletes a filter you may delete.

docs.title: Shared and personal
docs.text:
• A personal filter is yours. No one else can see or change it.
  • A shared filter is available to everyone in your organization. Creating, editing or deleting a shared filter, or sharing a personal one, needs permission to change organization settings (settings.update). Without it the Share with my organization switch is disabled and the filter stays yours alone.

docs.title: Manage them in Settings
docs.text: Settings → Organization → Saved Filters lists every filter you can use: its name, the object kinds it Applies to, its query, and whether it is Shared or Personal. The pencil icon opens Save changes (name, query, kinds, sharing); the trash icon deletes. A shared filter you cannot change shows a lock instead. The query is checked against every kind you pick before it is saved. Listing needs the assets.read permission.

docs.title: Which kinds can have a filter
docs.text: A filter can apply to Assets, Endpoints and Interfaces, the objects the query language can search. Only the All assets lens has the Filters menu today, so filters for endpoints and interfaces are set through Settings → Organization → Saved Filters (the Applies to checkboxes) or the API. Networks, VLANs, Circuits, Tunnels and Sites have no query bar and no Filters menu.

docs.title: Export templates
docs.text: An export template is a short text template, run over the rows of a list export. The rows are the same ones the CSV export would give, with the same columns.

docs.title: Define a template
docs.text:
Settings → Infrastructure → Export Templates lists each template with the kinds it is Offered on and its file extension and MIME type. Everyone who can read DCIM objects (dcim.read) can see them; Add export template, the pencil and the cross need dcim.manage. The dialog asks for:

  • Name (required).
  • Offered on (required) — the kinds whose lists should offer the template.
  • MIME type (default text/plain) and File extension (default txt) of the downloaded file.
  • Template (required) — the text. A new template starts with {{range .Rows}}{{.name}} followed by a line break and {{end}}: one line per row.

Preview on 5 rows renders the template over the first five rows of the first kind you ticked and shows the output or the error, before you save.

docs.title: Write the template
docs.text:
Templates use Go's text/template syntax. The data you can read:

Name What it is .Kind the kind being exported .Columns the list of column names .Rows the rows; each is a map from column name to text .Count the number of rows

Inside {{range .Rows}}, .name reads that row's name column. A custom field is a column named cf.<name>, which a dot cannot spell, so read it with index: {{index . "cf.owner_team"}}. The column names are the kind's import columns, listed on Settings → Infrastructure → Import. For example, a plain list of names under a heading:

# {{.Count}} {{.Kind}}
{{range .Rows}}{{upper .name}}
{{end}}

Alongside the usual if, range and with, you can use these helpers: upper, lower, trim, replace, join, split, contains, hasPrefix, hasSuffix, default, quote, json, csv, int, float, add, sub, mul, div, mod and date, plus the standard and, or, not, eq, ne, lt, le, gt, ge, len, index, slice, print, println, html, js and urlquery.

docs.title: What the sandbox forbids
docs.text:
A template is text written by your users, so it runs in a closed box. It is checked when you save it, and again each time it runs. These are refused, with the reason shown:

  • any function not listed above — there is no file, command, environment or network access, and no call or printf;
  • template, define and block — templates cannot include or call each other;
  • reading any top-level field other than Kind, Columns, Rows and Count;
  • names such as readfile, exec, env or system, wherever they appear.

A render also stops after 10 seconds, or when its output passes 10 MB.

docs.title: Download with a template
docs.text:
On a list with an Export button, the arrow beside the button opens Export with template…: a menu of the templates offered for that kind, each with its file extension. Choosing one downloads the list's rows (honouring the filters you have on screen) through that template. If no template is offered for the kind, the menu says so and links to Settings → Export Templates. Exporting needs the permission to read that kind.

The Export button today is on Inventory → Networks (prefixes), Inventory → VLANs and Settings → Organization → Business Units. Offering a template on a kind whose list has no Export button does nothing yet.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
• Saved filters: /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/saved-filters (list with ?kind=, create, edit, delete), behind assets.read; sharing needs settings.update.
  • Export templates: /dcim/export-templates (list, create, read, edit, delete; writes need dcim.manage), GET /dcim/export?kind=<kind>&format=template&template_id=<id> to render one, and POST /dcim/export/preview for a five-row preview.

docs.title: Sites and locations
docs.text:
Every asset can say where it is: the site it is in and, optionally, the location inside that site.

Object What it is Examples Region Geography. Regions nest. Europe › Netherlands › Amsterdam Site group A functional grouping, independent of geography. Groups nest. Branches, Colo, Labs Site One place. In at most one region and one site group. AMS-1, the Boston office, an AWS account Location A place inside one site. Locations nest. Hall 2 › Cage 7 › Row C

A NetBox region, site group, site and location map onto these one to one.

docs.title: Build the tree
docs.text:
Settings → Organization → Sites shows the tree — regions, then the sites in each (under their site group), then the locations inside each site — with the number of assets in each site and location. Tenant admins (the dcim.manage permission) can:

  • Create a region or site group (a name, an optional slug, an optional parent), a site (name, status, region, site group, facility, time zone, physical and shipping address, latitude and longitude), or a location inside a site (the + on a site or location row adds one beneath it).
  • Edit any of them. The edit dialog shows the object's Changes (who changed what, when) and its Journal. A location cannot move to another site, and nothing can be moved beneath itself. Trees are at most eight levels deep.
  • Delete them:
  • a region or site group: what was in it moves up to its parent;
  • a location: the locations inside it go with it; their assets stay in the site;
  • a site: its locations go with it. While assets are in the site you choose another site to move them to (they lose their location, which no longer exists), and the site's VLANs and the prefixes scoped to it move with them.

Names and slugs are unique: a site name across the tenant, a location name among its siblings in a site.

docs.title: Place assets
docs.text:
• One asset: the asset form's Site and Location controls. The location list is the chosen site's; choosing another site clears the location. Choosing only a location places the asset in that location's site.
  • Imports: a Site column holding a name is matched to the site of that name (ignoring case) or creates it. A NetBox import places each device in its NetBox site.
  • Networks: a prefix scoped to a location places the assets whose addresses fall in it in that location and its site, unless the asset is already in another site.
  • Cloud: connecting a cloud account creates a site for the account (its facility is the provider). Each region the account's resources are in becomes a location of that site, and the account's network prefixes are scoped to their region's location. Resources are placed in their region's location.

The asset page shows Site › Location under the asset's name; click it to open the site.

docs.title: The site page
docs.text: Inventory → Sites lists every site with its region, group, facility and asset count. A site opens its page, which shows where it is (address, time zone, coordinates), what it holds (assets, locations, racks, prefixes, VLANs), its locations, its findings by environment, and its change log and journal. The asset count opens the asset list filtered to the site.

docs.title: Floor plans
docs.text:
A location — a hall, a room, a cage — can carry a floor plan: a rectangle of a width and a depth in metres or feet, drawn as a grid, with the location's racks placed on it. Open the site, then the Floor plan tab, and pick the location.

  • Set up a plan. For a location without one, a person with dcim.manage enters the width, depth and unit and presses Create plan. Edit plan size changes it later. A plan cannot be removed, change its unit or shrink past a rack placed on it; move or take off those racks first.
  • Place racks. The racks of the location that are not on the plan wait in the Unplaced racks tray. Drag one onto the plan, or press Place to put it in the middle. Drag a placed rack to move it; a position that runs past the edge of the plan is drawn in red and not saved. With a rack focused, the arrow keys nudge it (a tenth of the unit; Shift for a whole one), R turns it a quarter turn and Enter opens it. The On this plan list turns a rack or takes it off the plan.
  • Read it. Each rack is drawn at its outer width and depth, turned the way its front faces (the thick edge). A rack with no recorded outer size is drawn at 600 × 1000 mm and marked *. Utilisation colours racks by the units in use, Power by the share of the power their feeds can supply that is allocated: the accent colour up to 80 %, amber over 80 %, red over 95 % — the Facilities dashboard's thresholds. A rack whose figure is not recorded is drawn dashed, never as 0 %. Click a rack to open its page.

A rack is placed only on its own location's plan; moving a rack to another location takes it off the old plan, and deleting a location takes its racks off. A rack's place is part of its change log. Floor plans are not exchanged with NetBox, which has no floor plan of its own.

docs.title: Filter by place
docs.text:
The Site facet in the Inventory filter rail lists sites by name. In the query box:

Query Finds site = "AMS-1" assets in the site named (or with the slug) AMS-1 site.id = "<id>" assets in the site with that id site.region = Europe assets in a site in Europe or any region beneath it site.group = Branches assets in a site in the Branches group or any group beneath it location = "Hall 2" assets in Hall 2 or any location inside it location = "AMS-1 / Hall 2 / Cage 7" the same by path not exists(site) assets with no site

region and zone on their own are the text a cloud provider or an import states (for example us-east-1); they are not the Region tree.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
/api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/regions, /site-groups, /sites and /locations (list, get, create, update, delete). Reads need dcim.read, writes dcim.manage. DELETE /dcim/sites/{id}?reassign_to=<site id> moves a site's assets before deleting it; without it a site holding assets answers 409.

Floor plans: a location's floor_plan_width, floor_plan_depth and floor_plan_unit are set with PUT /dcim/locations/{id}; a rack's floor_x, floor_y (the centre of its footprint, in the plan's unit) and floor_rotation (0, 90, 180, 270) with PATCH /dcim/racks/{id}. GET /dcim/locations/{id}/floor-plan returns the plan and every rack in the location with its footprint, utilisation and power budget.

docs.title: Spares and RMA
docs.text:
A spare part is an inventory item that is not in an asset. Vista Platform keeps spares where it keeps the parts inside your equipment, so a power supply, a line card or a box of optics is one kind of record whether it is installed, on a shelf or out for repair.

Each inventory item has a stock state:

State Meaning Where it is Installed In an asset. Every part a collector reports is installed. On its asset In stock On a shelf, ready to use. At a stock location Reserved On a shelf, set aside for a job. At a stock location Out for RMA Being returned to its vendor under a return case. Still in its asset, on the shelf, or with the vendor once it has shipped Retired Gone from your estate. Nowhere

A stock location is any location of a site (a hall, a cage, a store room) — see Sites and locations. A spare also has a quantity: a box of twelve identical, unserialised optics is one row of twelve. A serialised part is a row of its own, so two spare line cards of one model sit side by side with their own serial numbers.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text:
You want Go to Every spare, and the return cases in progress Infrastructure → Catalog & Data → Spares & RMA The spares stocked at one site Infrastructure → Sites & locations → open the site → Spares Take a part out of an asset, or open a return for it Inventory → open the asset → Hardware tab → Inventory items → To stock or RMA

You need the DCIM read permission (dcim.read) to see spares and return cases, and DCIM manage (dcim.manage) to add, install, remove, reserve, retire or return them.

docs.title: Adding spares
docs.text:
On Spares & RMA, Add spare asks for a name, the part number, a serial (leave it empty for a box of identical parts), the quantity and the stock location; tick Reserved to set the parts aside. A serialised spare always counts one.

From the Stock table you can Reserve or Release a spare, or Retire it. Filter the table by state to see only what is reserved, out for RMA or retired.

docs.title: Installing a spare
docs.text:
Install on a spare that is in stock or reserved asks for the asset (search by name or hostname), the name the part takes on the asset, and — for a row of several — how many units to install. The units you install become an item on the asset; the rest stay on the shelf with the count reduced. The asset's Hardware tab lists the part straight away.

Through the API an install can also name a module bay of the asset: the part is then the module in that bay, or, when the bay is empty, a module of the module type whose part number the spare carries is installed there first (with the spare's serial), and its interfaces are created as for any module.

docs.title: Removing a part to stock
docs.text: On an asset's Hardware tab, To stock on an inventory item asks for the stock location. The part leaves the asset. An unserialised part joins a spare of the same name and part number already at that location, adding to its count; otherwise it becomes a spare of its own. A part with child items (a line card with optics in it) has to have the children removed first.

docs.title: Return cases (RMA)
docs.text:
RMA opens a return case for a part, with the vendor, the vendor's case number and notes:

  • On a part in an asset, the part is marked out for RMA and stays in the asset until it ships — the usual order when the vendor sends the replacement first. Choose a stock location in the dialog to take it out of the asset now instead.
  • On a spare, the spare is marked out for RMA. On a row of several, one unit splits off and goes out; the rest stay in stock.

A part has one open case at a time. The RMA cases table on Spares & RMA lists the open cases (tick Show closed cases for all of them) with the vendor, case number, the dates it was opened, shipped and received, where the replacement goes, and its state. Move a case on with its buttons:

Step What happens Shipped The shipped date is recorded (today) and the failed unit leaves its asset or shelf: it is with the vendor. Received The received date is recorded and the replacement lands in stock, at the location where the failed unit was when the case opened (its shelf, or its asset's location). It joins a spare of the same name and part there, or becomes a new spare. Close The case is final. A unit that shipped is retired; a unit that never shipped (still in its asset or on the shelf) goes back into service.

Shipped and received can come in either order. A case with nowhere to put the replacement (the failed unit had no shelf and its asset has no location) is refused with the reason; give the case a replacement location through the API, or add the replacement as a spare yourself.

Every add, install, removal, reservation, return step and retirement is recorded in the item's Changes, with who did it and when.

docs.title: Searching
docs.text: The inventory search understands inventory_item.stock_state: inventory_item.stock_state = rma finds the assets with a part out for RMA still in them, and inventory_item.stock_state != rma the assets with none.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Spares are inventory items: /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/inventory-items lists, creates, reads, changes and deletes them, with the filters stock_state, location_id, site_id and asset_id=null (the items in no asset) beside the existing ones. A create names an asset_id or a location_id, never both; a change may move a spare between stock locations and between in stock, reserved and retired, and never between an asset and a shelf. The transitions are their own calls: POST /dcim/inventory-items/{id}/install (asset_id, and optionally module_bay_id, parent_id, name, quantity), POST /dcim/inventory-items/{id}/remove (location_id, and optionally name, stock_state) and POST /dcim/inventory-items/{id}/rma (optionally vendor, case_number, opened_at, notes, location_id). Return cases are GET /dcim/rma-cases (filters state, inventory_item_id, open, q), GET /dcim/rma-cases/{id} and PATCH /dcim/rma-cases/{id} (state, the dates, vendor, case_number, replacement_item_id, replacement_location_id, notes). Reads need dcim.read; writes need dcim.manage.

docs.title: Virtualization
docs.text: A cluster is a group of hypervisor hosts that run virtual machines together: a vSphere cluster, a Proxmox cluster, a Hyper-V cluster, a Kubernetes cluster, or one region of a cloud account. A virtual machine is not a separate kind of record; it is an asset of the Virtual machine class, and a hypervisor is an asset of the Hypervisor class. The cluster is the object that ties them together, and it is never an asset itself. A NetBox cluster type, cluster group, cluster and virtual disk map onto the objects described here one to one.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text:
You want to Go to See every cluster, with its hosts, VMs and status Inventory → Clusters (the Assets group of lenses) Open one cluster Click its name in the Clusters lens Maintain cluster types and groups Settings → Infrastructure → Cluster Types & Groups See a VM's cluster, resources and virtual disks, or a hypervisor's hosted VMs The Virtual machine or Hypervisor card on the asset page

Reading needs the virtualization.read permission and every change needs virtualization.manage. Tenant Administrators and Security Administrators have both; Viewers can read. Without virtualization.manage the Add, Edit, Delete and Approve buttons below are not shown.

docs.title: The Clusters lens
docs.text:
The lens lists each cluster with its Name, Type, Group, Scope, Hosts and VMs counts and its Status. Filter by type with the All types menu or search by name with Search clusters. A cluster that is not yet approved carries a second chip beside its status (Pending approval, Stale and so on).

Add cluster asks for a name, a cluster type (required), an optional cluster group, a status and a description. The status is NetBox's list: Planned, Staging, Active, Decommissioning or Offline. A cluster's name is unique within its type.

If the lens is empty it says so: nothing has told the platform about a cluster and nobody has declared one.

docs.title: The cluster page
docs.text:
Clicking a cluster opens its page. The header shows the type, group and status chips, and (with virtualization.manage) Approve for a pending cluster, Edit and Delete. Below it:

  • Resources — tiles for the number of virtual machines and the total vCPUs, memory and disk of the VMs in the cluster. A VM that reports no value for a resource is left out of the total, and the tile says how many VMs report it (for example "4 of 6 VMs report it"); an unknown value is shown as a dash, never as zero.
  • Virtual machines — each VM with its status, vCPUs, memory, disk and number of virtual disks. A VM links to its asset page.
  • Hosts — each hypervisor in the cluster with its class, status and where the membership came from. Add host (a dialog titled Add host) lists hypervisor assets; the x on a row removes a host from the cluster. A host is in at most one cluster, so adding a hypervisor that is in another cluster moves it here.
  • Changes and Journal tabs — who changed the cluster and when, and notes people have written on it.

Delete asks first. A VM that was in the deleted cluster stays in the inventory without a cluster. A cluster type that clusters still use cannot be deleted.

docs.title: Cluster types and groups
docs.text:
Settings → Infrastructure → Cluster Types & Groups has two tables.

  • Cluster types — the technology a cluster runs. Nine types are built in and shown with a Built in tag, read-only: VMware vSphere, Proxmox, Hyper-V, KVM, Nutanix, AWS, Azure, GCP and Kubernetes. Add cluster type creates your own (a name, an optional slug, an optional description); a type you added can be edited or deleted.
  • Cluster groups — your own grouping of clusters, for example by data centre, environment or team. Add cluster group works the same way.

If you leave the slug blank it is made from the name.

docs.title: Virtual machines on the asset page
docs.text:
Open any asset from Inventory. An asset that is a virtual machine shows a Virtual machine card; one that is a hypervisor shows a Hypervisor card. Other assets show neither. The cards need virtualization.read.

  • Virtual machine card — the VM's Cluster (a link to the cluster page, with its type), its vCPUs, Memory and Disk, and the list of its Virtual disks by name and size ("None recorded" when there are none). Edit opens Edit virtual machine, where you choose the cluster (or No cluster) and enter vCPUs, memory in MB and disk in MB.
  • Hypervisor card — the Cluster the host is in and the Hosted VMs recorded as running on it, each with its vCPUs and memory. "No VM is recorded as running on this host" means nothing has said so, not that the host is idle.

A VM's network adapters are ordinary interfaces of type Virtual on the VM asset, so they appear on its Interfaces tab and carry its IP addresses.

docs.title: How discovery fills these in
docs.text:
• Cloud discovery. Each connected cloud account and region is mirrored as one cluster of the provider's type (AWS, Azure or GCP), named <account>/<region>, and every compute instance found there is a virtual machine in it. The mirror exists so a cloud estate looks the same as an on-premises one, and for NetBox sync; the cluster page says so. The account itself remains the inventory object.
  • Clusters a collector reports arrive pending approval. Open the cluster page and click Approve to make it active.
  • Hypervisors and their hosted VMs are recorded by hand today: create the cluster, then use Add host on its page and the Edit button on each VM's card. The platform has no collector yet that reads a vCenter, Proxmox or Hyper-V manager and fills these in by itself.

A host's source on the cluster page tells a measured membership from one a person declared.

docs.title: Finding VMs and hosts by cluster
docs.text: The inventory query language reaches the cluster with cluster, cluster.type and cluster.group; see Query.

docs.title: API
