docs.text: /api/v2/inventory-service/virtualization/cluster-types, /cluster-groups, /clusters and /virtual-disks list, create, read, change (JSON merge-patch) and delete. GET, POST and DELETE on /clusters/{id}/hosts (and /{asset_id}) manage a cluster's hosts, GET /clusters/{id}/vms lists its VMs, and GET and PATCH /assets/{id}/virtualization read and change a VM's cluster, vCPUs, memory and disk. Reads need virtualization.read, writes virtualization.manage. Virtual disks are created through the API; the asset page shows them but has no button to add one.

docs.title: VPN tunnels
docs.text: A tunnel is an encrypted link between two gateways: an IPsec site-to-site tunnel between two firewalls, a GRE tunnel, a WireGuard or OpenVPN link. Each tunnel is built from IKE (phase 1) and IPsec (phase 2) settings, and every algorithm in those settings is looked up in the platform's algorithm catalogue, so you can see which tunnels still offer a weak Diffie-Hellman group or 3DES and which will need post-quantum migration.

docs.title: The objects
docs.text: Object What it is Tunnel group A named collection of tunnels (for example one per customer or per region). Tunnel One link, with its encapsulation, status and IPsec profile. Tunnel termination One end of a tunnel: a role (peer, hub or spoke) on an interface of an asset, optionally with the outside IP address. An interface terminates at most one tunnel. IKE proposal One phase-1 transform: authentication method, encryption, integrity, Diffie-Hellman group and lifetime. IKE policy An IKE version (1 or 2) and mode, with the list of IKE proposals it offers. IPsec proposal One phase-2 transform: encryption, integrity and lifetimes. IPsec policy The IPsec proposals offered, and the perfect-forward-secrecy (PFS) group. IPsec profile An IKE policy plus an IPsec policy (mode ESP or AH). A tunnel names a profile.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text:
You want to Go to See every tunnel with its posture Inventory → Tunnels (in the Cryptography group of lenses) Maintain proposals, policies and profiles Settings → Infrastructure → VPN Policies See how many tunnels need migration The Tunnels needing migration tile on the PQC dashboard, which opens the Tunnels lens

Reading needs the vpn.read permission and every change needs vpn.manage. Tenant Administrators and Security Administrators have both; Viewers can read. Without vpn.manage the Add, edit and delete buttons are not shown.

docs.title: The Tunnels lens
docs.text:
Each row shows the tunnel's Name, Encapsulation (IPsec transport or tunnel, IP-in-IP, GRE, WireGuard, L2TP, PPTP or OpenVPN), Status, Ends, IKE version, Weakest component and PQC class. Filter by encapsulation with the All encapsulations menu.

  • Ends lists the devices and interfaces the tunnel terminates on, and any remote gateway address a collector measured whose far end is not (yet) an interface in your inventory.
  • Weakest component is the single worst catalogue risk across both phases, shown as a risk band (Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational) with the algorithm's code, for example 3DES. Hover for the phase and role it came from. A tunnel where no algorithm could be matched to the catalogue says Not assessed; that is not the same as safe.
  • PQC is the tunnel's post-quantum readiness class: Needs PQC migration (the tunnel's Diffie-Hellman groups are classical key agreement, which a quantum computer can break), PQC ready, Symmetric only or Not classified.

Click a row to open the tunnel's side panel. Its Proposals tab lists the IKE (phase 1) proposals, with the IKE version, mode and PFS group, and the IPsec (phase 2) proposals. Next to each algorithm a chip gives the catalogue's strength rating; hover for the algorithm code, its deprecation status and its risk score. An algorithm the catalogue does not know is marked unassessed. The Changes tab shows who changed the tunnel and when.

Add tunnel asks for a name, an encapsulation, a status (Active, Planned or Disabled), an IPsec profile and a description. The pencil and bin buttons on a row edit and delete a tunnel.

docs.title: Policies, proposals and profiles
docs.text:
Settings → Infrastructure → VPN Policies has five tables: IPsec profiles, IKE policies, IKE proposals, IPsec policies and IPsec proposals. Each has an Add button and an edit and delete button per row. Discovered rows arrive from interrogated devices; you can also add your own.

  • IKE proposal — authentication (pre-shared keys, certificates, RSA signatures or DSA signatures), encryption (aes-128-cbc … aes-256-gcm, 3des-cbc, des-cbc), integrity (hmac-sha1 … hmac-sha512, hmac-md5, or None (AEAD)), the Diffie-Hellman group number and the SA lifetime. The table shows each algorithm with its catalogue strength.
  • IKE policy — version (IKEv2 or IKEv1), mode (main or aggressive, for IKEv1) and the proposals it offers.
  • IPsec proposal — encryption, integrity and lifetimes (seconds and KB).
  • IPsec policy — the PFS group (empty for none) and the proposals offered.
  • IPsec profile — mode (ESP or AH), an IKE policy and an IPsec policy.

docs.title: How the catalogue scores a tunnel
docs.text:
Scoring is not done in the VPN pages. A tunnel's IKE and IPsec settings are recorded as crypto configurations, and every algorithm in them (encryption, integrity, Diffie-Hellman group, PFS group) is matched to a row of the algorithm catalogue. The tunnel's risk is the highest risk_score among those rows, banded with the platform's one severity ladder. The catalogue is maintained by the platform and tenants view it, they do not edit it; see Algorithm Reference. When a rating changes, tunnels move with it; nothing on the tunnel itself has to be edited.

The same rule means a Diffie-Hellman group or a cipher that is not in the catalogue is shown as unassessed rather than given an invented score.

docs.title: Pre-shared keys are never collected
docs.text: The platform records that an IKE policy uses a pre-shared key, and shows Configured in the Pre-shared key column, but it never reads, stores, shows or syncs the key itself. Collectors project a firewall's VPN configuration onto the fields above and drop everything else; no field in these pages accepts a key. The same goes for the vpn.manage permission: it cannot reveal a key because none is held.

docs.title: How discovery fills these in
docs.text: Interrogating a Fortinet, Palo Alto or Cisco device, or a UniFi gateway, records its tunnels, their terminations on the device's own interfaces, and their IKE and IPsec proposals, each scored against the catalogue. See Device interrogation. Cloud VPN gateways are not read yet. An empty lens means nothing has reported a tunnel and nobody declared one, not that there are none.

docs.title: Finding tunnels
docs.text: The inventory query language reaches tunnels with tunnel, tunnel.encapsulation, tunnel.ike_version and tunnel.pfs_group; see Query.

docs.title: API
docs.text: /api/v2/inventory-service/vpn/ has tunnel-groups, tunnels, tunnel-terminations, ike-proposals, ike-policies, ipsec-proposals, ipsec-policies, ipsec-profiles, l2vpns and l2vpn-terminations, each with list, create, read, change (JSON merge-patch) and delete. Reads need vpn.read, writes vpn.manage. Tunnel groups, tunnel terminations and L2VPNs are created through the API or by discovery; the pages above have no button to add them.

docs.title: Wireless LANs and links
docs.text:
A wireless LAN (WLAN) is an SSID that access points broadcast, together with how it authenticates. A wireless LAN group collects related WLANs (a campus, a controller site, a brand) so the same SSID on two sites can be told apart. A wireless link is a point-to-point wireless connection between two interfaces, such as a mesh uplink or a bridge pair. This is inventory only: there is no RF planning and no controller management.

The point of recording them is posture. Each WLAN's authentication type and cipher are looked up in the platform's algorithm catalogue, so an open network, WEP or TKIP stands out from WPA2 with AES.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text:
You want to Go to See, add and edit WLANs, groups and links Settings → Infrastructure → Wireless See the SSIDs one access point serves, or the SSID a Wi-Fi client joined Inventory → the asset → Interfaces tab, under the interface table: Wireless LANs

Reading needs the wireless.read permission and every change needs wireless.manage. Tenant Administrators and Security Administrators have both; Viewers can read. Without wireless.manage the Add, edit and delete buttons are not shown.

docs.title: Settings → Infrastructure → Wireless
docs.text: The page has three tables.

docs.title: Wireless LANs
docs.text:
Each row shows the SSID, Group, Authentication (for example WPA Personal (shared key) · AES (CCMP)), Key and Cipher risk. A row waiting for approval carries a Pending tag and, for a user with wireless.manage, an Approve button (see Approval). Add wireless LAN asks for:

  • SSID (required) — case-sensitive, up to 32 bytes.
  • Group — optional.
  • Authentication — Open (no encryption), WEP, WPA Personal (shared key) or WPA Enterprise (802.1X), or Not reported.
  • Cipher — Negotiated (AES or TKIP), TKIP or AES (CCMP), or Not reported. It is not used by an open or WEP network.
  • A pre-shared key is configured — a checkbox that records only that a key exists.
  • Status — Active, Reserved, Disabled or Deprecated.
  • Description.

docs.title: Wireless LAN groups
docs.text: Add group asks for a name, an optional slug (made from the name if left blank), an optional parent group and a description.

docs.title: Wireless links
docs.text: The table shows each link's From and To interfaces, SSID, Authentication and Cipher risk. There is no Add button: links are created by discovery or the API, because they join two interfaces by id. You can edit a link's status (Connected, Planned or Decommissioning), distance and unit (km, m, mi, ft) and description, and delete it. A discovered link waits for approval and has the same Approve button as a WLAN.

docs.title: Approval
docs.text:
A WLAN you add is active straight away. A WLAN discovery reports takes its status from the access point that broadcasts it, the same way that access point's interfaces do:

  • From an approved access point it is active.
  • From an access point still waiting for approval it is pending. It becomes active the next time the access point is interrogated after you approve the access point.
  • Approve on the row makes it active now, whichever access point reported it.

The VLAN a discovered WLAN puts its clients on follows the same rule. A WLAN you archived or rejected stays as you left it, and so does one you added yourself. A pending WLAN is still checked for weak authentication.

docs.title: How the catalogue scores a WLAN
docs.text:
The cipher risk is read from the algorithm catalogue, not from a list in the product. The catalogue has a row each for AES-CCMP, TKIP, WEP and open Wi-Fi, and a WLAN's authentication and cipher point at one of them. The Cipher risk chip shows the band of that row's risk score (Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational); hover for the score and the catalogue's strength rating. A WLAN with no catalogue row, such as a negotiated cipher or no authentication recorded, shows a grey Not assessed chip, not a clean one. The catalogue is maintained by the platform and tenants view it; see Algorithm Reference.

A weak WLAN raises a finding against the access point that broadcasts it (the weak_wireless_auth finding), with its severity taken from the catalogue. Clients that joined the WLAN are not named in the finding. See Findings.

docs.title: Pre-shared keys are never collected
docs.text: The platform records that a shared key is set (Key set in the table, No key for an open network) and nothing more. The key is never entered, read from a controller, stored or shown.

docs.title: The Wireless LANs panel on an asset
docs.text:
On an asset that has at least one wireless interface, the Interfaces tab ends with a Wireless LANs panel: SSID, Authentication, Key, Cipher risk and Status. On an access point it lists the SSIDs its radios serve; on a Wi-Fi client, the SSID it joined. It needs wireless.read; without it the panel says so. A switch with no wireless interface shows no panel.

"No wireless LANs reported" means no controller has reported an SSID on this asset and none is declared. It says nothing about what the access point actually broadcasts. A WLAN waiting for approval shows Pending approval.

The panel is on the asset page only. There is no wireless panel on the site page yet.

docs.title: How discovery fills these in
docs.text:
Interrogating a UniFi controller records each access point's radios as wireless interfaces, and its WLAN configuration as WLANs with their authentication type, cipher and whether a key is set. The passphrase itself is dropped. See Device interrogation and Interfaces. Controllers other than UniFi are not read yet, and UniFi does not report wireless links, so links come from the API.

The controller's client list also says which SSID each Wi-Fi client joined. The client's interface (the one holding its MAC address) becomes a wireless station on that WLAN, typed by the 802.11 generation it connected with, for example IEEE 802.11ax. A client is joined only to a WLAN an access point has reported, and is never used to create one. If two WLANs in different groups share the SSID, the client is not joined to either. A client using a randomised (private) MAC address is not joined, because that address is not a stable way to find its interface. A client that moves to another SSID keeps the earlier one too. The client's Relationships tab separately shows which access point it is connected to.

docs.title: Finding assets by WLAN
docs.text: The inventory query language reaches WLANs with wireless_lan.ssid and wireless_lan.auth_type. They match both the access points that serve a WLAN and the clients that joined it, so wireless_lan.ssid:Guest lists everything on the Guest network; see Query.

docs.title: API
docs.text: /api/v2/inventory-service/wireless/wireless-lan-groups, /wireless-lans and /wireless-links list, create, read, change (JSON merge-patch) and delete. GET /wireless-lans accepts an asset_id filter, which is what the access point's panel uses. Reads need wireless.read, writes wireless.manage.

docs.title: Platform catalogues and their feeds
docs.text:
Vista Platform evaluates every tenant's inventory against platform catalogues — curated reference data that carries no tenant_id and is the same for everyone on the deployment. There are five:

Catalogue Table Where it comes from Console Algorithms algorithms Shipped in the seed, hand-curated Catalog ▸ Algorithms Compliance frameworks platform_frameworks Shipped in the seed (+ the Enterprise content bundle) Catalog ▸ Frameworks End-of-life eol_catalogue Mirrored from endoflife.date Catalog ▸ End-of-life Vulnerability vulnerability_catalogue, vulnerability_matches Mirrored from NVD and OSV Catalog ▸ Vulnerability feed Classification rules classification_rules Shipped in the seed, curated in the console Catalog ▸ Classification rules

This page covers the last three: how the mirrors work, how to run them, what their sources ask of you, how to fill them on a deployment with no internet, and how to curate the classification rules that decide what a newly discovered asset is proposed as.

All five are Core — free, present in every edition, with no entitlement to check.

docs.title: Rating an algorithm
docs.text:
Catalog ▸ Algorithms is the source of truth for cryptographic algorithm assessments. Creating a row requires a Risk score from 0 through 100. Enter the score the catalogue curator actually assessed; the form has no preselected score and the API rejects a blank value. Zero remains a valid, deliberate assessment and is distinct from leaving the score unknown.

Older or operator-created rows can still have no score. They remain unscored until a curator supplies one: schema upgrades do not replace missing evidence with 0, 50, or another inferred value. Opening one of those rows for editing also leaves the field blank. Curators can update its metadata without assigning a score; the console omits the unchanged blank score from that update. Once a row has a numeric score, the console does not allow it to be cleared.

Deprecate makes an algorithm grade Critical. The Deprecate action (or setting the status to obsolete in the edit form) raises the risk score to at least the bottom of the Critical band (90), so every configuration that uses the algorithm grades Critical. The score it replaced is remembered. Setting the status back to current or deprecated restores that score, unless you enter a new one in the same edit. While an algorithm stays obsolete, a score below the Critical band is refused. Algorithms that were already obsolete before this behaviour existed keep their scores, and re-activating them leaves the score as it is. Both the raise and the restore are recorded in the audit log.

Every tenant's inventory is matched against these catalogues nightly (and after an SBOM upload): an asset's OS and hardware resolve against the end-of-life catalogue, and its installed software resolves against the vulnerability catalogue, raising end-of-life and known-vulnerability findings when there's a match. See Findings for what those look like and how to triage them.

docs.title: Who can see and change them
docs.text:
The three feed and classification pages are gated on the platform permission catalogs.manage, granted to super_admin and platform_admin by the seed. It is separate from algorithms.manage on purpose: curating crypto ratings and re-pointing the platform at a vulnerability source are different trust decisions, even though the same two roles hold both today.

Catalog ▸ Algorithms uses algorithms.manage for its write controls.

The routes live under the admin plane (/api/v1/admin-service/admin/catalogs/**), so they are served on the admin host only — never on the tenant host.

docs.title: Shipped content and upgrades
docs.text:
The frameworks (with their controls and measurement rules) and the classification rules that ship with Vista Platform are re-applied on every helm upgrade. Your changes to them win over that:

  • An edit stays. Archive a shipped framework, reword a control, retune a measurement or classification rule, and the next upgrade leaves it as you set it.
  • A deletion stays. A shipped control, measurement rule or classification rule you delete is not put back by an upgrade. The deletion is remembered, and so is the old identity of a control or rule you re-keyed.
  • Rows you have not touched keep up. If a release changes shipped content you never edited, the upgrade applies it.
  • Changes to rows you edited are offered, not applied. When a release ships new content for a row you changed, the upgrade keeps your version and the row shows Update available. Hover it to see exactly what accepting would write, field by field; clicking it shows the same list and asks you to confirm before anything is written. The row stays yours after that, so the next release's change to it is offered again. If you never accept, your version stays.

The catalogue pages mark each row Vista (shipped) or Custom (added here), and a shipped row you have changed as Modified. Accepting an update needs catalogs.manage and is recorded in the audit trail with the values before and after.

Rows you added are never touched by an upgrade, even when a shipped correction would otherwise match them. That includes a measurement rule of a type the control already has — a second tls_version pattern, a key_size floor and ceiling: an upgrade only ever removes exact leftover copies of a shipped rule that earlier releases created by mistake.

On the first upgrade to a release with this behaviour, the platform compares every shipped framework, control and classification rule with everything the release ships for it — not only the fields the upgrade used to rewrite. A row that matches is marked as shipped content you have not changed. A row that differs is kept as it is, marked Modified, and offered the shipped values: the platform cannot tell an edit you made from content that changed between releases, so it keeps your version and loses nothing. Measurement rules are placed by when they were created: one created with its shipped control is Vista (and Modified if it has been updated since); one added later is left as Custom, which an upgrade never overwrites.

Deletions are remembered only from this release on. A shipped framework, control, measurement rule or classification rule you deleted before upgrading to it left no record, so that first upgrade puts it back once. Delete it again afterwards and it stays deleted.

docs.title: The feeds
docs.text:
Three mirror jobs run inside admin-service, on a schedule and on demand:

Feed Source Fills Incremental by eol https://endoflife.date/api eol_catalogue Nothing — a full pass each run nvd https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0 vulnerability_catalogue + CPE match rules Last-modified window osv https://osv-vulnerabilities.storage.googleapis.com/<ecosystem>/all.zip vulnerability_catalogue + PURL match rules Per-ecosystem watermark, plus If-Modified-Since

Each run records its outcome in catalog_feed_state — last run, status, rows written, the error if it failed, and a bookmark — which is what the console shows. A feed error is recorded, never fatal. A mirror that cannot reach NVD does not take the admin console down with it, and the failure is visible on the page rather than inferred from a catalogue that stopped growing.

The bookmark only advances on success. A run that fails retries the same window next time rather than skipping it. OSV is the exception: its bookmark is kept per ecosystem, and an ecosystem that completed keeps its bookmark even when another ecosystem in the same run fails. Only the failed ecosystem starts over. The card lists each OSV ecosystem under the feed with its own result: rows written, how far it has imported, or the error and when it last worked. A run where some ecosystems failed shows as Partial. The Rows column counts what the most recent run wrote, including rows a failed run wrote before it stopped. Those rows are kept.

OSV downloads are large. Each ecosystem is one bulk archive, downloaded to disk and read one advisory at a time. The feed accepts archives up to 2 GiB. Ubuntu's was about 705 MiB in September 2026, Debian's about 68 MiB and Alpine's about 4 MiB. On Kubernetes the chart gives admin-service a dedicated scratch volume for this (catalogFeeds.spool.sizeLimit, default 3Gi) and requests matching ephemeral storage. Keep the size above 2 GiB. Outside Kubernetes, point CATALOG_FEEDS_SPOOL_DIR at a directory with about 2.5 GiB free.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Variable Default What it does CATALOG_FEEDS_ENABLED true Kill switch. false stops the scheduled passes and refuses Sync now (409). Bundle import still works. CATALOG_FEEDS_INTERVAL 24h Time between scheduled passes. CATALOG_FEEDS_STARTUP_DELAY 2m Delay before the first pass after a pod starts, so a rolling restart is not N simultaneous passes. NVD_API_KEY empty Raises the NVD rate limit from 5 to 50 requests per 30 seconds. OSV_ECOSYSTEMS Debian,Ubuntu,Alpine Comma-separated osv.dev bucket names to mirror. CATALOG_FEEDS_SPOOL_DIR empty (the OS temp dir) Where OSV archives are downloaded before they are read. The chart sets it to its own scratch volume.

On Kubernetes, set them through the chart's per-backend extraEnv:

backends:
  admin-service:
    extraEnv:
      - name: CATALOG_FEEDS_ENABLED
        value: "false"

Only one replica runs a given feed at a time: each run takes a Postgres advisory lock keyed on the feed name, so scaling admin-service up does not multiply the requests going to NVD.

docs.title: Rate limits, and why the first NVD run is not the whole database
docs.text:
NVD allows 5 requests per rolling 30 seconds without an API key and 50 with one, and answers 403 — not 429 — when you exceed it. NIST's published guidance is to sleep 6 seconds between unkeyed requests, which the mirror does.

Because 403 means "slow down" here rather than "you may not", a rate-limited page is waited out and retried — up to three attempts, backing off from the length of NVD's own rolling window (or from a Retry-After header when one is sent), with the retries counting against the run's request budget. Only once those are exhausted does the run fail, and the error it records says rate limit, not just "403", so nobody goes hunting for an authentication problem that isn't there. A status that is a genuine refusal (404, 401) is not retried.

Because of that, the first NVD run does not pull the entire history. It reaches back 90 days by default and advances from there, a window at a time, with a per-run request budget so a cold start cannot loop for a day. To get the full back catalogue, either let it run for several days or — much faster — import an offline bundle built on an install that already has it.

Get a key (free) at https://nvd.nist.gov/developers/request-an-api-key and set NVD_API_KEY.

docs.title: What the vulnerability catalogue does not contain
docs.text:
vulnerability_catalogue is keyed on CVE id. OSV advisories are keyed on OSV ids (GHSA-…, DSA-…, PYSEC-…) and only some carry a CVE alias; the mirror imports the ones that do and skips the rest, counting the skips in the service log. A GitHub advisory with no CVE assigned is therefore not in this catalogue. That is a real coverage gap, stated here rather than papered over by minting synthetic ids.

Similarly, a CVE mirrored only from OSV has a CVSS vector and no base score: OSV publishes no number, and this platform does not compute one from the vector. The console shows "vector only" rather than a 0.0 that would read as "not serious". When NVD later mirrors the same CVE, the score fills in.

docs.title: Running a feed now
docs.text:
Catalog ▸ End-of-life (or ▸ Vulnerability feed) → the feed card at the top of the page → Sync now.

The button answers immediately — the run is started, not finished. A pass takes minutes (NVD's rate limit alone guarantees it), so the page polls the feed status and the result appears there when the run completes. A second click while a run is in flight is refused.

If Sync now is greyed out, either a run is already going or this deployment has CATALOG_FEEDS_ENABLED=false; the card says which.

docs.title: Air-gapped installs: the offline bundle
docs.text:
A disconnected deployment cannot reach endoflife.date, NVD or osv.dev. Fill its catalogues from a bundle built on a connected install.

1. Build it with the catalog-bundle export tool, on the connected install or any machine that can reach its database. Each Core release attaches the tool to its release on the Distribution repository as a static binary for Linux, macOS and Windows (catalog-bundle-<os>-<arch>: linux-amd64, linux-arm64, darwin-amd64, darwin-arm64, windows-amd64.exe), listed in the release's signed SHA256SUMS. Download and verify it as the release's VERIFY.md describes under "The operator tools", then run it:

./catalog-bundle-linux-amd64 -database-url postgres://user:pass@host:5432/crypto_inventory

This writes catalog-bundle-<YYYY-MM-DD>.tar.gz and prints a SHA-256 and row count per file. Optionally pass -out /path/to/bundle.tar.gz. The same binaries are inside the release's tools image, so with Docker at hand (the database must be reachable from inside the container; on the database host itself add --network host):

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/vistasecurity/tools:<version> \
  catalog-bundle -database-url postgres://user:pass@host:5432/crypto_inventory -out /work/catalog-bundle.tar.gz

2. Carry it across the gap by whatever means your policy allows.

3. Import it in the disconnected install: Catalog ▸ End-of-life → Import bundle → choose the file. (Either catalogue page imports the whole bundle; it is one file covering both.)

docs.title: What is in a bundle, and what is checked
docs.text:
A gzipped tar of:

  • manifest.json — format, version, generation time, and per file a SHA-256, a row count and a byte length;
  • ATTRIBUTION.md — the upstream sources' attribution, carried with the data rather than only in the product's NOTICE, because a bundle is a file you may hand on (see "Attribution and terms" below);
  • eol_catalogue.jsonl — one end-of-life row per line;
  • vulnerability_catalogue.jsonl — one CVE per line, with its match rules inline.

On import, every file's hash and row count is verified before a single row is written. A corrupt transfer is refused with a message naming the file and the mismatch, and nothing is applied — the alternative, verifying as you go, leaves a half-imported catalogue behind a corruption error, which is precisely the failure an air-gap transfer is most likely to produce.

A bundle carries each file once, and one that repeats a name is refused. That is not tidiness: the verification records one digest per name, so a second member under a name already seen would be checked while the first was silently applied alongside it — which would defeat the manifest entirely.

The one failure that is not "nothing was applied" is a fault that happens after verification passed — a dropped database connection partway through. The console labels that case differently and names the rows already written, because telling an operator their catalogue is untouched when it is half-written is worse than telling them nothing. Re-import the same bundle; import is idempotent.

Import is idempotent: re-importing the same bundle leaves the catalogue exactly where it was.

docs.title: Reading the numbers an import reports
docs.text:
The three counts answer slightly different questions, and the second import of a bundle is where the difference shows:

Count Statement On a re-import of the same bundle End-of-life rows ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE the same number again — every row was applied Vulnerabilities ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE the same number again Match rules ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING 0 — the rules were already there

All three are what the database reported affected, not what the file contained. A second import showing "0 match rules" is the correct answer, not a failure.

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text: Both actions on these pages are written to the platform audit trail (Security ▸ audit logs): running a feed records which feed and who started it, and importing a bundle records the operator, the manifest's SHA-256 per file and the rows actually written. The hash is the part worth having — after a bad bundle the question is not whether an import happened but which bytes were applied, and only the hash settles it. A bundle refused by verification wrote nothing and is not recorded; one that failed partway through is, with what it managed to write.

docs.title: Hash, not signature — and why
docs.text:
The Enterprise content bundle (regulated compliance frameworks) is signed with an ECDSA key, because it carries licensed content and the signature is what makes it revocable by non-renewal.

These catalogues are Core. There is nothing to revoke and no entitlement to prove, so the bundle carries integrity rather than provenance: a hash per file, checked before use. That is what answers the question an air-gap transfer actually raises — "did this file arrive whole?".

If your policy also requires provenance, sign the tarball with your own key before it leaves the connected side and verify it before import. The format does not prevent that; it just does not require a key this platform would then have to manage for you.

docs.title: Classification rules
docs.text:
Catalog ▸ Classification rules is the fifth platform catalogue, and the one you can write to. It holds the evidence behind every class proposal: what kind of thing a newly discovered asset is.

When a collector sees something new, it has facts but no identity — a MAC address, an SNMP sysObjectID, a cloud resource type, an HTTP Server: header, a set of open ports, a model string. A classification rule maps one of those onto a vendor and, where the mapping is unambiguous, an asset class.

Every rule produces a proposal that goes through Approvals. Nothing on this page classifies anything on its own.

Rules you add or edit here go live within about five minutes. The classification service rebuilds its in-memory rule set on an interval (CLASSIFICATION_RULES_REFRESH, default 5m) rather than only at the next release, so a rule you save here starts affecting new class proposals shortly after — no redeploy needed. A rule that fails validation is skipped (and logged by name); the rest of the table keeps working.

docs.title: What a rule looks like
docs.text:
Field Meaning Kind How the pattern is matched — see the table below. Pattern The thing matched, in that kind's own syntax. Class The asset class to propose. Optional, and often deliberately empty. Vendor The manufacturer the pattern identifies. Optional. Model The specific model, where the pattern pins one. Rarely set. Confidence 0.50–0.95. What the rule asserts. Source Where the mapping comes from. Required for a rule that ships. Kind Pattern is Example MAC OUI The 24-bit IEEE assignment, 6 uppercase hex digits 00000C SNMP sysObjectID An OID under 1.3.6.1.4.1; longest prefix wins 1.3.6.1.4.1.9 EtherNet/IP vendor An ODVA vendor id in decimal 1 Cloud resource type The provider's own type aws_s3_bucket Service banner A regular expression over a captured banner (?i)^server:\s*nginx Port profile Ports that must all be open 631,9100 Model prefix A prefix of the stated model; longest wins C9300 Collector platform The management API the device answered fortios

The MAC OUI rules are derived, not written by hand: the platform keeps one manufacturer table (the same one the sensor uses to name a vendor from a captured frame), and each shipped OUI rule pairs a prefix from it with the class that manufacturer's products are — where there is one. That is why most of them say vendor only: two thirds of the manufacturers in the table sell more than one kind of thing.

docs.title: "Vendor only" is the normal answer
docs.text:
Most of the shipped OUI rules name a vendor and no class, and the table says "vendor only" rather than showing a gap. That is deliberate.

Dell, HP, Netgear, Ubiquiti and MikroTik each sell servers, switches, access points and printers under the same IEEE assignment. There is no majority worth guessing at, so the rule stops at the vendor and something with better evidence — an SNMP walk, a model string, an agent on the host — narrows it later.

A wrong class is worse than no class. An absent class shows as unclassified, which reads as "we have not worked this out yet" and invites someone to look. A wrong class shows as a fact, and a plausible-looking wrong proposal is the one that gets approved without a second thought.

Follow the same instinct when you add a rule: leave the class empty whenever the pattern covers more than one kind of thing, and prefer a broad class that is certainly right (network_device) over a narrow one that is probably right (switch).

docs.title: When two rules disagree
docs.text:
If two rules propose different, unrelated classes at similar confidence, the classifier proposes no class and records both. That is the intended behaviour, not a failure — it means the catalogue contradicts itself, and the fix is to correct one of the two rules rather than to let a coin-flip decide.

A rule proposing switch and another proposing network_device is not a disagreement: one is a refinement of the other, and the more specific class wins.

docs.title: Adding, editing and deleting
docs.text:
Add rule opens the form. The pattern box shows what that kind expects, and the server validates against exactly the rules the classifier applies — so a rule that saves is a well-formed rule, not one the engine will later refuse. It starts proposing classes within about five minutes (see the note above). If it is rejected, the message names what to change.

Two things are worth knowing before you edit or delete:

  • Editing a shipped rule lasts. Upgrades keep your version; if a later release changes that rule, it shows Update available instead (see Shipped content and upgrades). Adding a more specific rule — a longer sysObjectID prefix, a longer model prefix — is still the way to override a shipped answer without touching it. Rules you add are never touched by an upgrade.
  • Deleting does not rewrite history. Class proposals already made from a rule keep their own copy of it, so past decisions stay reviewable. Deleting a shipped rule is remembered, and upgrades do not put it back.

Adding, editing and deleting a rule are all recorded in the audit trail with who did it and what the rule was.

docs.title: Attribution and terms
docs.text:
These are third-party datasets. Mirroring them into your deployment is a redistribution, and the sources ask for different things:

  • endoflife.date — a community-maintained dataset. The mirror identifies itself with a User-Agent, paces itself to roughly 4 requests per second, and runs once a day. Rows are stored with the upstream product page as their source_url, and the console links to it. See https://endoflife.date/docs/api for their current terms.
  • NVD (NIST) — a U.S. government work. This product uses data from the NVD API but is not endorsed or certified by the NVD. NIST asks that you do not imply endorsement and that you identify your client; the mirror sets a User-Agent and honours the published rate limits. See https://nvd.nist.gov/developers/terms-of-use.
  • OSV (osv.dev) — the aggregated database is published under CC-BY-4.0, attributed to OSV (https://osv.dev) and to the upstream database named on each record. See also https://github.com/google/osv.dev.

The offline bundle carries this wording with it. Every bundle the catalog-bundle tool builds includes an ATTRIBUTION.md member stating exactly the three points above, so the obligations do not stay behind in the product's NOTICE when the file is carried across an air gap or handed on. The same text is in NOTICE, under "Third-party data".

Operator responsibility. If you redistribute a bundle built from this platform beyond your own organization, the attribution obligations of the upstream sources travel with it — which is what ATTRIBUTION.md is for. Redistribution itself is permitted by both sources; the review of their terms for this bundle is complete, and what it found was owed is the attribution wording above. Nothing here should be read as legal advice.

docs.title: Filling gaps in the end-of-life catalogue
docs.text:
The mirrors only know what their upstream sources publish. endoflife.date is excellent on mainstream operating systems and language runtimes and thin on appliances, network hardware and vendor-specific firmware trains — so the catalogue will not answer for everything your inventory contains.

Catalog ▸ End-of-life has three views of the same catalogue, listed under End-of-life in the left nav:

View What it is Catalogue The rows you have, with a badge saying how each one got there (mirrored, AI-proposed, declared). Proposals A review queue. Nothing in it is in the catalogue yet. Gaps The products the platform has been asked about and could not answer for, ordered by how often.

docs.title: Check a product
docs.text:
On the Gaps view, "Check a product" asks the platform what it knows about a vendor, product and version. There are four answers, and they are deliberately different from each other:

  • A date, with its provenance. Each fact carries the catalogue row it came from and the page that cites it.
  • "The catalogue has this product but publishes no end-of-life date." The release train is known and the vendor has not announced a date — including the case where the upstream source says support has ended without saying when. This is not a gap, and nothing is added to the gap list: there is nothing for anyone, model or person, to fill in.
  • "Nothing for this product — added to the gap list." The catalogue has never heard of it. This is the answer that puts it on the list a proposal run works from, which is how you deliberately queue a product up.
  • "…and the gap list could not be updated." The lookup worked and the bookkeeping write did not. Said plainly rather than reported as the previous answer, because "it is on the list now" would be false.

The matching is deliberately exact. A version whose release train is not in the catalogue resolves to nothing, not to the nearest cycle: the support date of the release beside yours is not your support date, and answering with it would be wrong in the direction that reassures. When both the question and a catalogue row name a vendor they must agree.

docs.title: Where the gaps come from
docs.text:
Most rows on this list are not put there by hand. Every tenant's end-of-life pass resolves each asset's operating system, its hardware and every installed package against this catalogue, and each lookup it cannot answer is counted here. So the top of the list is, literally, the products costing your tenants the most answers.

Two things follow from that, and both are deliberate:

  • A gap is a silence, not a clean bill of health. A product the catalogue has never heard of produces no end-of-life finding for anybody running it. Filling the gap is what makes those findings appear.
  • One pass records at most 500 new gaps. A tenant with tens of thousands of distinct unrecognised packages would otherwise fill this list in one night and bury the row worth working on. The next pass records the next slice, and anything common reappears immediately.

docs.title: Working the gap list by hand
docs.text:
Without a provider, the Gaps view is still useful on its own: it is the list to work through by hand, ordered by how much each gap costs you, and any row you add by hand is a row the mirrors will not overwrite unless the upstream source starts publishing it.

Adding a row has an effect you can see: the next end-of-life pass resolves the products that were missing it, and their findings appear on the assets running them — citing the row you just added. See Findings for what those look like to a tenant.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"Never run" and Sync now does nothing. Check CATALOG_FEEDS_ENABLED. The card shows a banner when the deployment has feeds switched off.

NVD keeps failing with 403. That is the rate limit, not authentication — and the mirror already retried it three times before recording the failure, so this means the limit is being hit persistently. Set NVD_API_KEY, or check whether something else on the same egress IP is also calling NVD.

The catalogue is not growing after a successful NVD run. Look at the bookmark on the feed card. A run that reaches its per-run request budget stops early and records the window it did finish; the next run resumes from there. Repeated runs walk forward through the history.

An import was refused. The message names the file and the check that failed. A SHA-256 mismatch means the file changed in transit — rebuild or re-copy it. A row-count mismatch usually means the manifest was edited. Nothing was applied in either case; the card says "Bundle refused".

An import says "Bundle partly applied". That is the other outcome: the manifest verified and the write then failed (most often a database connection dropping under a large import). Some rows are in. Import the same bundle again — it is idempotent, so the repair is a retry, not a cleanup.

One OSV ecosystem keeps failing. The card names it and shows its error. An error that mentions the archive cap means that ecosystem's export has grown past 2 GiB. "no space left on device" means the spool volume is smaller than the archive, so raise catalogFeeds.spool.sizeLimit. The other ecosystems are not affected either way.

An OSV ecosystem is missing. Check the name against the bucket listing at https://osv-vulnerabilities.storage.googleapis.com — OSV_ECOSYSTEMS uses the exact upstream spelling, spaces included (Rocky Linux).

docs.title: Certificate compliance refresh
docs.text:
Certificate compliance findings refresh after inventory changes and every 12 hours for certificates near or past a published policy threshold. The first scheduled pass starts three minutes after compliance-engine starts. The scan derives its window from published certificate-expiration controls, including zero-day and fractional-day thresholds, and includes a one-day boundary margin.

This updates findings and framework scores; it does not add notification thresholds. Certificate expiry notifications retain their own policy. Operators can set COMPLIANCE_CERT_BAND_SCAN_ENABLED=false on compliance-engine to stop the scheduled pass; event-driven evaluation continues, but findings can then become stale as certificates age.

docs.title: Container runtime images (source of truth)
docs.text:
Purpose: Single reference for which container images run when the platform is up, for security reviews, supply-chain questions, and registry planning.

Last updated: 2026-09-16

docs.title: How to read this
docs.text:
• Runtime image = what actually executes in a long-running container (the effective image: after build, or the final stage of a multi-stage Dockerfile).
  • First-party images = built from this repository (16 Go backend services plus the two frontends). Locally they're built by Docker from Dockerfile.dev / Dockerfile.prod; in production the Helm chart pulls pre-built, cosign-signed images.
  • Third-party images = pulled from a public or vendor registry as-is.

Default registry: References without a host (for example postgres:17-alpine) resolve to Docker Hub (docker.io).

Maintenance: When you add a service, change a FROM/ARG, or change a compose image:, update this file. Compose files are partly generated from standards/service-registry.yaml (make generate); infrastructure exceptions stay in root docker-compose*.yml.

docs.title: First-party runtime images (application workloads)
docs.text:
These images contain Vista code. 16 backend services, all Go, all built the same way:

Service Port Dockerfile (prod) auth-service 8081 services/auth-service/Dockerfile.prod inventory-service 8082 services/inventory-service/Dockerfile.prod compliance-engine 8083 services/compliance-engine/Dockerfile.prod cbom-service 8084 services/cbom-service/Dockerfile.prod sensor-manager 8085 services/sensor-manager/Dockerfile.prod cluster-sensor-service 8088 services/cluster-sensor-service/Dockerfile.prod admin-service 8089 services/admin-service/Dockerfile.prod monitoring-service 8091 services/monitoring-service/Dockerfile.prod tenant-health-service 8093 services/tenant-health-service/Dockerfile.prod device-interrogation-service 8095 services/device-interrogation-service/Dockerfile.prod audit-service 8096 services/audit-service/Dockerfile.prod notification-service 8097 services/notification-service/Dockerfile.prod pcap-processor 8098 services/pcap-processor/Dockerfile.prod discovery-processor-service 8090 services/discovery-processor-service/Dockerfile.prod mcp-service 8100 services/mcp-service/Dockerfile.prod

Build/runtime bases (all 16, pcap-processor noted separately):

  • Compile stage: golang:1.26.10-alpine (ARG GO_BUILDER_IMAGE)
  • Runtime: alpine:3.24.2 + a static Go binary (ARG RUNTIME_IMAGE)
  • pcap-processor is the one exception. It needs CGO and libpcap (packet capture is not pure Go), so its build stage adds gcc musl-dev libpcap-dev and its runtime stage adds the libpcap runtime package on top of the same alpine:3.24.2 base. This is also why pcap-processor has no Dockerfile.licensed/.dist variant in the commercial pipeline — a CGO-linked binary can't be obfuscated the way the pure-Go services are.

Frontends — Vite/React apps, built with Caddy as the runtime web server:

Service Port Dockerfile (prod) web-ui 3000 frontend-v2/Dockerfile.prod admin-ui 3006 admin-ui-v2/Dockerfile.prod
  • Build stage: dhi.io/node:24-alpine3.24-dev (Docker Hardened Images — free and open source; needs a Docker Hub account, not a paid plan)
  • Runtime: caddy:2-alpine, pinned by digest
  • admin-ui-v2 has no Dockerfile.dev. Local development for the admin console runs the Vite dev server directly (npm run dev) rather than through Docker; admin-ui-v2/Dockerfile.prod is the only Dockerfile the package ships. frontend-v2/Dockerfile.dev exists and runs on node:24-alpine (Vite dev server, not Caddy) — that's what docker compose up builds locally for web-ui. docker-compose.yml's admin-ui service in fact builds admin-ui-v2/Dockerfile.prod directly, since there's no dev variant to build instead.

docs.title: Where the running images actually come from
docs.text:
The platform's development stack (docker compose up -d in its source tree): Docker builds all 18 images from source, from the Dockerfile.dev/Dockerfile.prod variants above. That source tree is not published; this applies to Vista Security's own development only.

A Core install (the release's compose.yaml, or the Helm chart): nothing is built — both pull pre-built, signed images. The Core chart published at oci://ghcr.io/vistasecurity/vistaplatform points at ghcr.io/vistasecurity/* and digest-pins every image to the exact bytes that release was tested with: built without the Enterprise code, with the Go services obfuscated, and promoted to GHCR by digest. Every image and the chart itself are cosign-signed; see VERIFY.md in the Distribution repository.

docs.title: docker-compose.yml (local full stack)
docs.text:
Service Image reference postgres postgres:17-alpine redis (Valkey) valkey/valkey:8.1.10-alpine nats nats:2.14-alpine api-gateway traefik:v3.7.15 otel-collector otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.151.0 jaeger jaegertracing/jaeger:2.17.0 prometheus prom/prometheus:v3.11.3 grafana grafana/grafana:13.1.0-25351545110 adminer adminer:latest (local dev only — a Postgres admin UI)

api-gateway (Traefik) exists only in the Docker Compose topology. There is no in-cluster gateway pod in the Helm chart — the chart's Traefik IngressRoute/ Middleware resources route the cluster's own Traefik directly to backend Services.

docs.title: Helm chart (charts/vistaplatform/values.yaml) — in-cluster datastores
docs.text:
The chart pins its own datastore image versions, which are not always the same as docker-compose.yml's — always state which one you mean when answering a supply-chain question, the sets are not identical:

Datastore Image reference vs. docker-compose.yml postgres postgres:17-alpine same redis (Valkey) valkey/valkey:8.1.10-alpine same nats nats:2.14-alpine same

The cache is Valkey (BSD-3-Clause), a Redis-protocol drop-in maintained under the Linux Foundation. The compose service, the redis Service/hostname, the datastores.redis values key, and the REDIS_URL / REDIS_PASSWORD variables keep the Redis name because they name the protocol, not the server. Releases up to 5.0.0 shipped Redis (7.4 in the chart, 8 in compose); see Upgrading for what the switch does to an existing install.

helm test additionally runs a short-lived pod from curlimages/curl:8.22.0 (exact tag) that calls the auth-service and admin-service /health endpoints; it is not part of a running install.

Any of the four in-cluster datastores can be swapped for a managed/external instance instead (datastores.<name>.enabled: false plus the corresponding *-url secret key) — see the comments above the datastores: block in values.yaml.

docs.title: Environment summary
docs.text:
Concern docker-compose.yml (local dev) Helm chart (production) Builds images from source Yes, all 18 (the platform's own development stack) No — pulls pre-built, signed images (as does a Core install's compose.yaml) API gateway (Traefik pod) Yes (api-gateway service) No — cluster's own Traefik routes directly Observability stack (otel-collector, jaeger, prometheus, grafana) Bundled for local exploration Not installed by the chart — bring your own adminer Bundled Not applicable

For compliance answers, state which environment defines the deployment you're describing — a laptop docker compose up -d and a production Helm install run different image sets, at different versions, from different registries.

docs.title: Maintenance in the Admin Console: Back Up, See What's New, Update
docs.text:
The admin console has a Maintenance section (left rail, Platform group) with two pages:

  • About & Updates shows which version of each service is running, whether a newer Vista Platform release exists, and updates the platform.
  • Backups takes a backup of the platform database, optionally with the encryption keys a restore needs, and keeps the newest few for you to download.

Everything on this page is part of Vista Platform Core. Enterprise and MSP installs use the same pages.

These pages work on installs made with the Helm chart on Kubernetes. A Docker Compose install (evaluation only) shows "Not available in this deployment"; back that database up with pg_dump. If the Maintenance section is missing altogether, it has been turned off; see Turning it off.

Who can use it. Anyone who can see System Health can read these pages. Taking, downloading and deleting a backup, checking for updates and running an update need the separate permission platform.maintenance, which the built-in Platform Administrator role has. See Permissions.

docs.title: Create a backup
docs.text:
1. Sign in to the admin console and open Maintenance → Backups.
  2. Choose Create backup.
  3. Decide whether to tick Include encryption keys and install secrets (see the next section). If you do, enter a passphrase of at least 12 characters twice.
  4. Choose Create. A row appears as "Running". The platform keeps working while the backup runs. When it finishes the row says "Ready" with its size.

Only one backup (or other maintenance run) can run at a time. Run history, below the list, records who started each backup and update, when, and how it ended. A failed run keeps the end of its log so you can see why.

docs.title: What is inside a backup
docs.text:
Every backup holds the platform database (crypto_inventory), taken with pg_dump in custom format, plus a small manifest.json that says which version took it. What you download depends on the tick box:

Option File you download Contains Keys not included vista-platform-backup-<date>-<version>.tar manifest.json, database.dump Keys included vista-platform-backup-<date>-<version>.enc the same two files plus secrets.yaml, encrypted with your passphrase
  • database.dump is everything in the platform database: tenants, inventory, findings, configuration. It is not a copy of any keys.
  • manifest.json records the Vista Platform and chart versions, the database schema version, the edition, the install ID and the Helm release name and namespace.
  • secrets.yaml holds the install's Kubernetes Secrets: the encryption master key, the JWT signing key, the install identity, the generated database, Redis and NATS passwords, and the key that signs CBOM artifacts.

docs.title: Do you need the keys?
docs.text:
Tick the box if you ever want to restore onto a fresh install and have it behave like the old one. Without the keys:

  • Credentials the platform stored encrypted (integration and device credentials, collector agent secrets) cannot be decrypted. You re-enter them and re-enroll the collectors.
  • Everyone is signed out, because the JWT signing key is new.
  • CBOM artifacts signed before the backup no longer verify.
  • The install identity is new, so an install-bound licence must be re-issued.

Warning: the passphrase is not stored anywhere. Not in the platform, not in the database, not in the backup. It is the only way to open an encrypted backup. If you lose it, that backup cannot be restored and Vista Security cannot recover it. Keep it in your password manager, separately from the file. The encrypted file contains your install's master keys: treat it, and the passphrase, as you would the cluster's Secrets.

The encryption is AES-256-GCM with a key derived from your passphrase using Argon2id. The keys are never served unencrypted; that is why a passphrase is required.

docs.title: Download, retention and delete
docs.text:
• Download streams the file to your browser. A backup that lives only on the platform's own volume is not off-site, so download it and keep it somewhere else. Every download is recorded in the activity trail.
  • Retention. The newest maintenance.backups.retention ready backups are kept (default 5). After each new backup the oldest beyond that are removed.
  • Delete removes one backup now.

docs.title: Where backups are stored
docs.text:
Backups are written to a volume the chart creates for the maintenance service. The chart values (maintenance.backups.*):

Value Default Meaning enabled true false creates no volume; the page says "Backup storage is not configured" size 20Gi Size of the volume. Make it at least a few times your database size times the retention retention 5 How many ready backups to keep storageClassName empty Empty uses datastores.storageClassName accessMode ReadWriteOnce ReadWriteOnce or ReadWriteMany

With the default ReadWriteOnce, only one node can mount the volume at a time, so the backup runs on the same node as the maintenance service and the service restarts without a surge pod (the old one lets go of the volume before the new one starts). That works with no action from you; it matters only if that node is full or drained, when a backup may wait for room. A ReadWriteMany storage class removes both limits. ReadWriteOncePod does not work and the chart refuses it.

helm uninstall keeps the volume, so removing the platform does not delete your backups.

docs.title: External databases
docs.text: If you run PostgreSQL yourself (datastores.postgres.enabled=false), backups work the same way: the backup job dumps the database named by the platform's database-url Secret. The database user must be allowed to read everything in crypto_inventory. The job runs pg_dump from the chart's schemaMigration.image (PostgreSQL 17), and the database must be reachable from the cluster namespace.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
Restoring is a documented procedure, not a button, in this release. It puts a backup onto a fresh install of the same version, then you upgrade normally.

You need: the backup file; its passphrase if it is an .enc file; kubectl and helm pointed at the target cluster; and your own values file. If you have never used kubectl, ask whoever installed the platform to run the commands below with you; every step says what it does.

  1. Open the file. For an .enc backup, decrypt it with the bundle-decrypt tool. Each Core release attaches it to its release on the Distribution repository as a static binary for Linux (linux-amd64, linux-arm64), macOS (darwin-amd64, darwin-arm64) and Windows (windows-amd64.exe), named bundle-decrypt-<os>-<arch> and listed in the release's signed SHA256SUMS. Download the one for the machine you restore from, with SHA256SUMS and its Sigstore bundle, from the release of the platform version you are restoring, and verify it before you run it:
VERSION=v5.3.0   # the platform version of the backup
TOOL=bundle-decrypt-linux-amd64
for f in "$TOOL" SHA256SUMS SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json; do
  curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Distribution/releases/download/${VERSION}/${f}"
done
cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform/.github/workflows/release-core.yml@refs/tags/core-${VERSION}" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS
chmod +x "$TOOL"

This downloads the tool, checks that the release's file list was signed by the Core release workflow (cosign v3; add --new-bundle-format with v2.4 or later), and checks the tool against that list (shasum -a 256 on macOS). The Windows and macOS binaries carry no native code signature (no Authenticode, no notarization): the signed SHA256SUMS is what verifies them. Releases up to 5.2.1 attached no tool; the tool of a later release opens their backups, since the encrypted format has not changed. The same binaries are inside the release's tools image (ghcr.io/vistasecurity/tools:<version>, named in IMAGES.txt), so where Docker is at hand you can run the tool from it instead of downloading it:

VISTA_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE='your passphrase' docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -e VISTA_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE -v "$PWD:/work" "ghcr.io/vistasecurity/tools:${VERSION}" \
  bundle-decrypt -in /work/<backup>.enc -out /work/bundle.tar

Then decrypt (the passphrase is read from the environment so it does not appear in your shell history or process list):

VISTA_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE='your passphrase' "./$TOOL" \
  -in vista-platform-backup-20261014-031200-4.6.0.enc -out bundle.tar

This writes the tar inside the backup. A wrong passphrase, or a file that was cut short or changed, fails with an error and writes nothing. A .tar backup needs no decryption.

tar -xf bundle.tar
cat manifest.json

This unpacks manifest.json, database.dump and, for an encrypted backup, secrets.yaml. In manifest.json note chart_version, release.name and release.namespace. Use those same values below.

Delete the unpacked secrets.yaml and bundle.tar when the restore is finished.

  1. Put the Secrets back first (encrypted backups only). Do this before installing, so the new install keeps your original keys instead of generating new ones:
kubectl create namespace <namespace>
kubectl apply -n <namespace> -f secrets.yaml

The first command creates the namespace; the second recreates the Secrets with their original values. Their Helm labels let the install adopt them. Use the same release name and namespace as manifest.json; a different namespace makes Helm refuse the Secrets ("invalid ownership metadata"). For a .tar backup, skip this step and expect the consequences listed under Do you need the keys?.

  1. Install the same version.
helm install <release> oci://ghcr.io/vistasecurity/vistaplatform \
  --version <chart_version> -n <namespace> -f <your values file> --wait --timeout 30m

This installs a clean platform with an empty database, as for any new install. Use the chart source and values you normally install with.

  1. Stop everything that writes to the database.
kubectl -n <namespace> scale deployment --all --replicas=0

This stops all the services. PostgreSQL keeps running, because it is a different kind of workload.

  1. Replace the database. Drop the new, empty database and create it again, then load the dump into it:
kubectl -n <namespace> exec postgres-0 -- psql -U <database user> -d postgres \
  -c 'DROP DATABASE crypto_inventory WITH (FORCE)' \
  -c 'CREATE DATABASE crypto_inventory OWNER <database user>'

This deletes and recreates the database. <database user> is datastores.postgres.user from your values.

kubectl -n <namespace> exec -i postgres-0 -- pg_restore \
  -U <database user> -d crypto_inventory --exit-on-error < database.dump

This streams the dump into the empty database. It must finish with no errors.

Drop and recreate the database. Do not use pg_restore --clean over the fresh install's database: it cannot drop the partitioned tables' constraints and reports dozens of errors.

With an external database, run the same two commands against it from any machine with PostgreSQL 17 client tools, replacing -U … -d … with the connection string (-d "$DATABASE_URL"); dropping the database needs its owner or your provider's administrator login.

  1. Start the platform again.
helm upgrade <release> oci://ghcr.io/vistasecurity/vistaplatform \
  --version <chart_version> -n <namespace> --reuse-values --wait --timeout 30m

This brings the services back with their normal replica counts. The chart version is unchanged, so --reuse-values is safe here. If you want a newer version, restore first and update afterwards, as in Updates.

  1. Check it.
  2. In the admin console open Maintenance → About & Updates: every service should show the backup's version and "All services aligned".
  3. Sign in as a tenant user. An integration with a stored credential should still connect, which proves the master key came back.
  4. The backup run that was in progress when the dump was taken is marked "failed" on the first start. That is expected and needs no action.

Restoring into the same release name and namespace is the supported path. Restoring across versions is not: restore into the version in manifest.json, then update.

docs.title: Knowing a new release exists
docs.text:
When a newer Vista Platform release is available, every admin console page shows a banner under the top bar: "Vista Platform 4.6.0 is available · What's new". You can dismiss it; it comes back for the next version. It appears only for users who may see System Health, never for tenants.

Maintenance → About & Updates is the full picture:

  • Running versions lists each service and the version it runs, with a badge: All services aligned, Version skew detected (two services report different versions, usually an interrupted upgrade), Degraded (aligned but a service cannot be reached) or Version unknown.
  • How this install is managed says whether the console can update this install (see Installs managed outside Helm).
  • Updates says "Up to date · checked 2 hours ago", or "Vista Platform 4.6.0 available" with a What's new link to the release notes, or why the check could not run. Check now runs a check immediately.

docs.title: Where "latest" comes from
docs.text:
The platform lists the version tags of the chart's repository in the OCI registry it was installed from, picks the newest release, and compares it with what is running. The registry is derived from your image settings (image.registry and image.repoPrefix), so an install that pulls from your own mirror checks your mirror. It is anonymous unless your first image.pullSecrets entry has a credential for it. Nothing about your install is sent anywhere else.

Override the repository with maintenance.chartSource if the chart lives somewhere other than the images, for example oci://registry.example.internal/vistaplatform.

Value Default Meaning maintenance.updateCheck.enabled true false stops the periodic check and refuses a manual one: no outbound call is made maintenance.updateCheck.interval 24h How often to check (a duration such as 12h; minimum 1m) maintenance.updateCheck.includePrereleases false true also offers release candidates (for example 4.6.0-rc.1) maintenance.updateCheck.notesBaseUrl the Vista Security release-notes page Root of the release-notes page for sources other than ghcr.io; the version is appended maintenance.chartSource derived from image.* OCI repository to check and to update from

Release notes for each version are its page under Release notes on this documentation site; the Distribution repository's release of the version carries its install files.

Air-gapped sites. Set maintenance.updateCheck.enabled=false so the platform makes no outbound call; the Updates card then says "Update check is off". Mirror the chart and images into your own registry as described in OFFLINE.md, point image.registry (and maintenance.chartSource if needed) at the mirror, and either leave the check on against the mirror, which works the same way, or turn it off and update on your own schedule.

docs.title: Updating from the console
docs.text:
When an update is available, Update to 4.6.0 on the Updates card opens the update dialog. You need platform.maintenance.

  1. Pre-flight checks. The dialog first checks the install and lists every result, so you can fix everything in one pass. A Blocks the update result must be fixed before Update is enabled; a Warning does not stop you.
Check Outcome What it means Managed by Helm Blocks if not Helm manages the install and no GitOps controller owns it. Otherwise see Installs managed outside Helm Version available Blocks if not The version is published at the chart source and newer than the running one Chart signature Blocks if it fails; Warning when verification is turned off The chart's cosign signature matches the Vista Security release identity Image pins in your values Warning A image.tag, backends.<service>.image.tag or image.digest you set (often for a hotfix) is carried into the update, so that service would stay on the pinned image. The warning names them; remove them first unless the pin is intended Cluster size Warning on a single node A rolling update starts each new pod before the old one stops, which can need more CPU than one node has and stall the update. The warning lists the services that roll rather than recreate Database schema Warning The schema marker could not be read, or was last written by a different chart than the running one (a previous update may not have finished) No other maintenance running Blocks if one is A backup, update or rollback is already in progress Recent backup Warning if none Whether a ready backup from the last 24 hours exists. The update takes its own fresh one regardless, unless you tick the box below. With backup storage turned off it warns that you must back up yourself

  1. Confirm. The dialog lists what will happen and asks you to type the version number to enable Update.

  2. Backup first. Every update starts with an automatic backup of the database. It is database only: it does not include the encryption keys. If you want a backup with the keys, take one from Backups first. Tick I have my own backup — skip the backup step to skip it; the run records that step as skipped by the operator. On an install with backup storage turned off (maintenance.backups.enabled=false) the console refuses to start an update unless that box is ticked.

  3. The run. The progress page walks through four steps with a live log: Back up the database, Verify the chart's signature, Upgrade: apply the schema and restart every service, and Check every service runs the new version. The upgrade step runs as a Kubernetes Job, not inside the console, as helm upgrade <release> <chart source> --version <version> --reset-then-reuse-values --wait --timeout 30m, the same command as the manual procedure. Only one maintenance run can be active; starting a second is refused.

  4. Expected downtime. Services on the default rolling strategy keep serving while new pods start, but each waits for the database schema migration to finish, so an update that changes the schema takes as long as the migration plus the rollout. Services set to strategy: Recreate (such as pcap-processor and sensor-manager) are unavailable for that whole window. The admin console restarts too: the progress page shows "Services are restarting — this page will reconnect" and keeps trying for up to 15 minutes. The update carries on without it, so you can close the page and come back; the run is also in Run history.

  5. Done or failed. On success the page says "Running Vista Platform 4.6.0" and the banner goes away. On failure it shows the step that failed with the end of its log.

  6. If it failed at the backup or signature step, the page says nothing was changed and your current version is still running.
  7. If it failed at the upgrade or version check step, the cluster may have changed and the page offers Roll back to 4.5.0.

Change a chart value such as maintenance.updates.timeout (default 30m, a whole number of s, m or h) if a large install needs longer than 30 minutes to roll.

docs.title: Rolling back
docs.text: Roll back runs helm rollback to the previous release revision in a Job, then checks every service runs that version. It returns the Kubernetes side (images and configuration) to the previous release. It does not undo the database: the schema changes are additive, and the previous version runs on the newer schema. If you need the database as it was before the update, restore the backup the update took, following Restore.

docs.title: Signature verification, mirrors and credentials
docs.text:
• Verified by default. Before every update the chart is verified with cosign against the Vista Security release signing identity. A chart that does not verify blocks the update.
  • Air-gapped mirrors that cannot re-sign. If your mirror copies the chart without its signature, set maintenance.updates.skipSignatureVerify=true. Pre-flight then shows Chart signature as a warning, not a pass, the update's verify step is recorded as skipped by configuration, and the chart is installed unverified. Turn this on only when you trust the mirror's contents; prefer mirroring with signatures intact.
  • Mirrors without TLS. maintenance.updates.plainHttp=true pulls the chart over HTTP.
  • Mirrors signed by your own CA. If the registry that holds the chart presents a certificate from a private CA (an internal Harbor, an air-gapped mirror), the update check reports x509: certificate signed by unknown authority and the update's verify and upgrade steps fail the same way. Give maintenance-service the CA the way monitoring-service takes one for its synthetic checks: mount the PEM from a Secret and point EXTRA_TRUSTED_CA_PATH at it. The service adds it to the public trust store (never replacing it, so a public registry keeps working), cosign gets it as SSL_CERT_FILE, and the update Job carries the same env and mount, so helm upgrade trusts it too.
backends:
  maintenance-service:
    extraEnv:
      - name: EXTRA_TRUSTED_CA_PATH
        value: /app/certs/mirror-ca/ca.crt
    extraVolumes:
      - name: mirror-ca
        secret:
          secretName: mirror-ca        # kubectl create secret generic mirror-ca --from-file=ca.crt=…
    extraVolumeMounts:
      - name: mirror-ca
        mountPath: /app/certs/mirror-ca
        readOnly: true

A missing or unreadable file is logged at start-up and the service runs with the public trust store, as it does without the variable. - Private registries. The registry credential is the first image.pullSecrets entry. It is never written to the run log.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The updater runs under its own namespace-scoped service account and cannot grant itself new permissions. Kubernetes refuses to let an account apply a Role that gives out permissions the account does not hold. So if a release's notes say the maintenance updater's role changed, that one update cannot be applied from the console: it fails at the upgrade step and offers a rollback. Apply it once from the command line as an administrator, using the manual procedure below. The console update works again from then on.

docs.title: Installs managed outside Helm
docs.text: If a GitOps controller (Argo CD or Flux) manages the platform, or it was applied some other way than helm install, About & Updates says so ("Managed by GitOps" or "Not installed with Helm") and the Update button is off. The console cannot update it: the controller would undo the change on its next sync. Update it from your values repository, changing the chart version there, using the notes in the production checklist. The update check and the banner still work, and so do backups.

docs.title: Updating by hand
docs.text: The manual Helm procedure is unchanged and always works; the console automates it. It is the way to update a GitOps install and the fallback if the console is unavailable. See the Helm guide's "Upgrade" and Upgrading in the production checklist. Back up first, either way.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
What Permission See running versions, the update status, the backup list and run history platform.health Check for updates now, create / download / delete a backup, run an update, roll back platform.maintenance

platform.maintenance is separate on purpose, so an operator who may watch the dashboards cannot also download a copy of the database or rewrite the cluster. The built-in Platform Administrator role has it. To give it to another platform role, see Staff & Access in the Platform Administrator Guide. Every write action, including each download, is recorded in the activity trail.

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text:
Set maintenance.enabled=false in your chart values and run a normal helm upgrade. That removes the maintenance service, its service accounts and permissions, and the backups volume, and the console hides the Maintenance section. Nothing else changes. Download the backups you want to keep first: with the maintenance component off, the chart no longer manages the backups volume.

To keep the page but stop the outbound registry call, set only maintenance.updateCheck.enabled=false.

The service holds the only credential in the platform that can talk to the Kubernetes API, and it is limited to the platform's own namespace: no cluster-wide role is created. You can see the exact permissions in charts/vistaplatform/templates/maintenance/.
