docs.title: Support
docs.text: For issues or questions: 1. Check service logs: docker-compose logs admin-service 2. Review audit logs: Query platform_integration_audit_log table 3. Check encryption service logs for initialization errors 4. Verify RBAC permissions for your user account

docs.title: Deployment Documentation
docs.text: Deployment guides and checklists for Vista Platform.

docs.title: Deployment Guides
docs.text:
• Production Checklist - Comprehensive production deployment checklist
  • Database Migrations - Database migration procedures
  • Service-mesh mTLS - Staging internal mTLS across upgrades, managed-Postgres/NATS notes

docs.title: Installing
docs.text: Vista Platform Core is distributed as signed container images on ghcr.io/vistasecurity and a signed Helm chart; no source checkout and no local build are involved. Each release's install files (a Docker Compose file, a Helm values example, the image digests and the verify instructions) are attached to that release in the Distribution repository, whose INSTALL.md is the full walkthrough.

docs.title: Evaluate it (Docker Compose, one host)
docs.text: Download compose.yaml and env.example from one release, verify them, generate the secrets into .env and run docker compose up -d; see INSTALL.md, Docker Compose. It is an evaluation install: one host, bound to 127.0.0.1, no service mesh, and agents on that host only.

docs.title: Production Deployment
docs.text:
Production installs use the Helm chart:

  1. Production Checklist
  2. helm install vista oci://ghcr.io/vistasecurity/vistaplatform --version <chart version> against your cluster, following the Distribution repository's Helm guide. It needs cert-manager, Stakater Reloader, Traefik with a TLS-passthrough entrypoint for the agents, and the two agentMtls passthrough hostnames: agent and sensor mTLS and the service mesh are mandatory, with no opt-out, and the install stops with an error naming what is missing. If you are staging internal service-mesh mTLS on an existing cluster, see Service-mesh mTLS.

docs.title: Deployment Environments
docs.text:
• Evaluation: the Docker Compose file of a release, on one host.
  • Production: the Helm chart oci://ghcr.io/vistasecurity/vistaplatform, at an exact version, on any Kubernetes cluster.

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text: • Operations Monitoring - Monitoring setup

docs.title: Database Migration Guide
docs.text: 1.0.0 is a fresh install only. The general asset inventory release dropped the port-as-asset tables (network_assets, devices) and the asset_type enum rather than migrating them, and moved credential encryption to v2 — old credentials cannot be decrypted under it. There is no migration path from a core-v0.x database to 1.0.0; start a new database and pg_dump the old one first if you want to keep it for reference (the 1.0.0 release notes say more).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You never apply schema changes by hand. Each release carries its database schema in its schema image (ghcr.io/vistasecurity/schema:v<version>), which holds schema.sql, seed.sql and their SHA-256 sums, and the install applies it for you, on a fresh database and on every upgrade:

  • Helm chart: the schema-migration Job applies schema.sql with ON_ERROR_STOP=1 and records the schema's hash in public.schema_migration_status; the seed-data Job applies seed.sql after it. Each Postgres-backed service waits (its wait-for-schema init container) until that hash is recorded, so no new pod runs against an old schema.
  • Docker Compose: the release's compose.yaml does the same with its schema and db-migrate services, described below.

Both refuse a schema.sql whose hash is not the one the chart or compose file was stamped with, so the SQL that runs is always the release's own. The schema is written to be applied again and again: every statement is idempotent, and an upgrade is the newer release's schema applied over the existing database.

docs.title: Docker Compose install
docs.text: The compose file each release attaches applies the schema the way the Helm chart's Jobs do, on every docker compose up: the schema container fills a named volume with schema.sql and seed.sql from that release's schema image, and the one-shot db-migrate container checks that schema.sql hashes to the value the compose file was stamped with, applies it with ON_ERROR_STOP=1, records the completion marker in public.schema_migration_status, gives the row-level-security roles their login, and applies seed.sql. The services that use the database start only after db-migrate exits 0. The schema is idempotent, so the same steps upgrade an existing database to a newer release: back up first (pg_dump, as in the Distribution repository's INSTALL.md).

docs.title: Kubernetes (Helm chart)
docs.text: helm install and every helm upgrade run the Jobs above against the bundled PostgreSQL. The schema-migration Job is an ordinary release resource, not a hook, so it runs alongside the new pods, which wait for it. Size helm upgrade --wait's timeout to cover the migration. Back up before every upgrade (the admin console's Maintenance → Backups, or pg_dump).

docs.title: An external PostgreSQL (Amazon RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure Database)
docs.text: Set datastores.postgres.enabled: false and put the connection string in the platform Secret's database-url key (PostgreSQL 17, the database already created). The same Jobs then apply the schema and seed to that database through DATABASE_URL; there is no manual psql step and nothing to copy into the cluster. The user in database-url must be able to create tables, types, functions, policies and roles in that database, because the schema creates the two row-level-security roles the services connect as (crypto_app, and crypto_bypass with BYPASSRLS) and the rls-roles Job gives them their logins. Whether a given managed service lets its database owner do that has not been tested by us for every provider; if yours does not, the schema-migration Job fails with a permission error naming the statement (see Troubleshooting).

docs.title: Reading the SQL a release applies
docs.text:
To review the schema before an upgrade, or to keep it with your change records, copy it out of the release's image:

docker create --name vista-schema ghcr.io/vistasecurity/schema:v<version>
docker cp vista-schema:/sql/. ./schema-v<version>/
docker rm vista-schema
(cd ./schema-v<version> && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS)

Verify the image's signature first, as the release's VERIFY.md describes.

docs.title: The algorithm catalogue risk scores (ADR-0016)
docs.text: The ADR-0016 catalogue migration removes the old algorithms.risk_score database default of 50. Applying it does not re-grade any existing row: explicit scores, old rows that previously received 50, and NULL scores are preserved. New algorithm rows must include a deliberate integer score from 0 through 100 through the catalogue API. An insert-only database guard also rejects direct inserts without one. NULL remains allowed for historical or operator-created rows because the migration has no authoritative evidence with which to grade them; those rows can still receive unrelated corrections until a curator supplies the missing score.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: After an install or upgrade, check that the schema was recorded and tenant isolation is in place.

docs.title: Check the recorded schema
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM public.schema_migration_status;

The row names the schema hash, the platform and chart versions that applied it, and when.

docs.title: Check RLS is enabled
docs.text:
SELECT tablename, rowsecurity
FROM pg_tables
WHERE schemaname = 'public'
AND tablename IN ('sensors', 'pending_sensors', 'sensor_discoveries', 'assets', 'asset_endpoints', 'crypto_implementations');

-- Should show rowsecurity = true

docs.title: Check RLS policies exist
docs.text:
SELECT schemaname, tablename, policyname, permissive, roles, cmd, qual
FROM pg_policies
WHERE schemaname = 'public'
AND tablename IN ('sensors', 'pending_sensors', 'sensor_discoveries', 'assets', 'asset_endpoints', 'crypto_implementations');

-- Should show policies for each table

docs.title: Check the tenant-context functions exist
docs.text:
SELECT proname, proargtypes
FROM pg_proc
WHERE proname IN ('set_tenant_context', 'clear_tenant_context');

-- Should return 2 rows

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
A schema change is not rolled back by applying an older schema: the schema only adds and alters, so an older release's file leaves the newer objects in place. To return to an earlier release, restore the backup you took before the upgrade, then install that release (the admin console's update offers a one-click rollback that does this; see Maintenance).

Do not disable row-level security to work around a problem: it is the database-level tenant isolation every service relies on.

docs.title: Pods stay in Init after an upgrade
docs.text:
Each Postgres-backed service waits in its wait-for-schema init container until the schema-migration Job has recorded this release's schema hash. A stuck migration shows as Init:Error after about ten minutes while the old pods keep serving.

kubectl -n <namespace> logs job/<release>-schema-migration-<hash>
kubectl -n <namespace> logs <pod> -c wait-for-schema   # names the wanted and latest hashes

docs.title: The migration fails with a permission error
docs.text: On an external database, the user in database-url lacks a privilege the schema needs (creating roles, types, functions or policies). Grant it, or use the database owner, and run helm upgrade again: the Job re-applies the whole idempotent schema.

docs.title: The schema image is refused
docs.text: "the schema image carries schema X, stamped for Y" means the schema image is not the one of this release: the chart (or compose file) and the image are from different versions. Use the files of one release together.

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• Production Checklist - Production deployment checklist
  • Maintenance - Backups, updates and rollback from the admin console

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The device agent is a downloadable binary that customers deploy in their on-premises or air-gapped environments to perform device interrogations. The agent communicates outbound-only with the platform service, receiving jobs and submitting results.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The device agent operates in a hybrid deployment model:

  • Platform Internal Agent: Runs as a background worker in the device-interrogation-service, handling cloud provider APIs and internet-accessible devices
  • Downloadable Binary: Customer-deployed agent for on-premises/air-gapped environments

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Network access to the platform API gateway (outbound HTTPS)
  • Registration key from the platform
  • Appropriate credentials for target devices (configured in platform)

docs.title: Minimum supported Windows version
docs.text:
Windows Server 2019 or later (or Windows 10 1809 and later) — for the host the agent runs on, and for any Windows host it collects from in remote mode. Remote host-inventory collection on Windows uses PowerShell over SSH, which needs the OpenSSH Server feature; that feature is available from these versions. WinRM is not supported (see "Exactly what runs, per OS" below).

Which operating systems and architectures you can install on is decided per platform build: the registration dialog lists every system the agents are built for and says which ones have a qualified agent (see Getting the binary).

docs.title: Getting the binary
docs.text:
The registration dialog (Discovery → Sensors & Agents → Register → Device interrogation agent, or Enroll on a pending registration) prints the download, verification and install steps for every operating system and architecture. They come from the platform's qualified mapping: the one release of the Vista Platform Agents repository whose signed compatibility record says it was tested with this platform version and edition. The dialog names that record (Qualified by record and its id), and each file carries the SHA-256 the platform pinned and its Sigstore signature bundle. There is no "latest" download and no other source: a system the mapping has nothing for shows No qualified agent for this platform build on <os>/<arch> and no link. A nightly build is offered only by a candidate platform build qualified with one, after you tick Use a nightly build.

There is no in-product download endpoint: the platform does not serve agent binaries over HTTP, so a curl/Invoke-WebRequest against the platform itself will not work. The files are release assets of the Agents repository, named vista-device-agent_<version>_<os>_<arch> (.exe on Windows), with install-device-agent.sh and a <file>.sigstore.json bundle for each.

What the signatures do and do not cover. The agents are open source under the Apache License 2.0 in the same repository; a binary you build yourself is not the one the platform qualified. Every file carries a Sigstore signature, which the steps verify. Windows binaries are not Authenticode-signed and macOS binaries are not notarized, so Windows SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper warn when you run one: that warning is expected, and the Sigstore verification is how you know the file is ours. Each agents release run-tests its Linux builds (amd64 and arm64); its Windows and macOS builds are compiled and signed but not run-tested.

Consoles of Vista Platform 5.2.1 and earlier point their download links at release assets of the former Core repository that no longer exist; upgrade the platform to get working downloads.

The full verification procedure, with every signing identity, is Verifying a release in the Agents repository. The sections below assume the verified binary has been copied to device-agent (device-agent.exe on Windows), as the steps do.

docs.title: Linux (recommended): the installer
docs.text:
The registration dialog shows these steps with the exact release, digests, your platform URL and key filled in (here for a stable release <tag>):

# 1) Download the agent and its installer with their signature bundles
curl -fsSLo vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_amd64 https://github.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Agents/releases/download/<tag>/vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_amd64
curl -fsSLo vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_amd64.sigstore.json https://github.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Agents/releases/download/<tag>/vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_amd64.sigstore.json
curl -fsSLo install-device-agent.sh https://github.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Agents/releases/download/<tag>/install-device-agent.sh
curl -fsSLo install-device-agent.sh.sigstore.json https://github.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Agents/releases/download/<tag>/install-device-agent.sh.sigstore.json

# 2) Check the SHA-256 digests the platform pinned (one line per file and bundle)
echo "<sha256>  vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_amd64" | sha256sum -c -
echo "<sha256>  install-device-agent.sh" | sha256sum -c -

# 3) Verify the signatures
cosign verify-blob --bundle vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_amd64.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity 'https://github.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Agents/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/<tag>' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_amd64
cosign verify-blob --bundle install-device-agent.sh.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity 'https://github.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Agents/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/<tag>' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com install-device-agent.sh

# 4) Install and enroll (runs it as a service)
install -m 0755 vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_amd64 device-agent
sudo bash install-device-agent.sh --url https://platform.example.com --key YOUR_REGISTRATION_KEY

A nightly is signed by https://github.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Agents/.github/workflows/nightly.yml@refs/heads/main instead; the steps use the identity of the release they name.

The installer is the device agent's counterpart of the sensor installer. It installs the agent to /opt/crypto-device-agent as the crypto-device-agent systemd service, running as its own user. It keeps the agent's certificate and the platform's CA under the install directory, starts the service, and waits until the agent has enrolled, then prints its agent ID and version. If the platform rejects the key (expired, invalid or already used), it stops the service and says so. Re-running the same command on that host keeps the agent's enrollment and replaces only the binary, which is how to upgrade it. For a platform whose certificate this host does not already trust, add --ca-fingerprint <sha256> (see Platforms with a privately-signed certificate).

A --key on the command line is visible to other users in the process list. To keep the key out of it, set VISTA_REGISTRATION_KEY in the environment (sudo VISTA_REGISTRATION_KEY=... bash install-device-agent.sh --url ..., which passes the variable through sudo directly) or pipe it in with --key-stdin. The installer never prints the key in full, and writes every value it puts in the config file as a quoted YAML string.

Exit status 78. A start that only a person can fix, namely a registration key the platform rejected, a config file that cannot be parsed, or a data directory the agent cannot write, makes the agent exit with status 78 (EX_CONFIG). The installed systemd unit sets RestartPreventExitStatus=78, so the service stops and stays stopped instead of retrying every 10 seconds; check journalctl -u crypto-device-agent, fix the cause (usually: generate a new key and re-run the installer), then systemctl start crypto-device-agent. Any other failure, such as the platform being unreachable, still restarts and retries. Windows services and macOS launchd have no equivalent exit-status exclusion, so a rejected key under those supervisors still exits 78 but may be restarted by the supervisor.

bash install-device-agent.sh --check-dependencies checks the binary runs on this host without installing anything. On ARM hosts use the linux/arm64 steps.

docs.title: Linux (AMD64): running the binary yourself
docs.text:
# after downloading and verifying vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_amd64 (steps 1-3 above)
install -m 0755 vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_amd64 device-agent

# Run it — with no arguments the agent walks you through setup and then starts
./device-agent

Data path. The agent's default data path on Linux is /var/lib/crypto-device-agent, which only root can create. Run it as root, or choose a data path your user can write. The agent checks it can save its enrollment before it sends the registration key, and refuses to start with "cannot store its enrollment" if it can't. The key is then still unused.

Running the binary with no arguments opens the interactive installer: it asks for the platform URL (and tests reachability), the registration key, the data path and the poll interval, enrolls the agent, writes <data_path>/agent-config.yaml, and then starts polling for jobs immediately. Verbose logging is on by default. On every later start the agent finds that config file and runs straight away — no flags, no second command.

To configure a host without answering prompts, write the config file yourself and the installer stays out of the way:

cat > device-agent.yaml <<EOF
platform_url: https://platform.example.com
registration_key: YOUR_REGISTRATION_KEY
poll_interval: 30s
verbose: true
EOF

./device-agent --config device-agent.yaml

A config file that exists but cannot be read or parsed (a typo such as a line missing its :) is fatal: the agent logs the file's path and the parse error and exits non-zero, rather than starting against built-in defaults with no identity. The environment-variable fallback applies only when no config file exists.

docs.title: Linux (ARM64)
docs.text:
# after downloading and verifying vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_arm64
install -m 0755 vista-device-agent_<version>_linux_arm64 device-agent

# Follow same configuration steps as AMD64

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
# after downloading and verifying vista-device-agent_<version>_windows_amd64.exe
# (the dialog's Windows steps check it with Get-FileHash and cosign verify-blob)
Copy-Item vista-device-agent_<version>_windows_amd64.exe device-agent.exe

# Run it — with no arguments the agent walks you through setup and then starts
.\device-agent.exe

As on Linux, a config file suppresses the installer:

@"
platform_url: https://platform.example.com
registration_key: YOUR_REGISTRATION_KEY
poll_interval: 30s
verbose: true
"@ | Out-File -FilePath device-agent.yaml -Encoding utf8

.\device-agent.exe --config device-agent.yaml

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
# after downloading and verifying vista-device-agent_<version>_darwin_amd64 (Intel)
# or vista-device-agent_<version>_darwin_arm64 (Apple Silicon); the dialog's
# macOS steps check it with `shasum -a 256 -c` and cosign verify-blob
install -m 0755 vista-device-agent_<version>_darwin_arm64 device-agent
xattr -d com.apple.quarantine device-agent 2>/dev/null

# Follow same configuration steps as Linux

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
The agent can be configured via environment variables or a YAML file:

  • PLATFORM_URL: Platform API gateway URL (default: http://localhost:8080)
  • PLATFORM_URL_OVERRIDE: set to 1 to force PLATFORM_URL on an already-enrolled agent (see below)
  • REGISTRATION_KEY: Agent registration key (required)
  • AGENT_ID: Agent ID (set after first registration)
  • POLL_INTERVAL: Job polling interval (default: 30s)
  • VERBOSE: Enable verbose logging. Verbose is on by default; set VERBOSE=false (or verbose: false in the config file, or -verbose=false on the command line) to quiet a long-running install.
  • HOST_INVENTORY_ENABLED: set to true to have the agent inventory its own host on a schedule (default: false). See Host inventory.
  • HOST_INVENTORY_INTERVAL: how often it does so (default: 24h, minimum 1h — a shorter value is raised to the minimum and logged).
  • HOST_INVENTORY_CONNECTIONS_ENABLED: explicit opt-in for collecting a bounded remote-peer list (default: false). Destinations can reveal application and browsing activity, so host inventory alone does not enable it.

These are a starting position, not the source of truth. Once the agent is enrolled, POLL_INTERVAL, HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL, VERBOSE and the inventory schedule/interval settings are managed from the console. The connection opt-in remains local to the agent, alongside the credentials and endpoint. The managed settings are shown under Discovery → Sensors & Agents → the agent → Settings, and a later local edit to them is overwritten at the next check-in. See Agent and sensor settings.

docs.title: Configuration File
docs.text:
Create a device-agent.yaml file:

platform_url: https://platform.example.com
registration_key: your-registration-key-here
poll_interval: 30s
verbose: true

# Optional: inventory this host as well as interrogating network devices.
host_inventory_enabled: true
host_inventory_interval: 24h

docs.title: Registration key type (required)
docs.text: Create a pending registration from the tenant web UI (Operations / Sensors, or the enhanced registration flow) and select Device interrogation agent so the profile is device_interrogation. Keys issued for network sensors are rejected by POST /api/v1/device-interrogation-service/agents/register.

docs.title: Gateway-first
docs.text:
Enrolled agents pin their own endpoint. Every call after enrollment uses agent mTLS (managed protocol 1 has no other mode), and registration saves the advertised TLS-passthrough URL into the agent's config, and that saved value wins over PLATFORM_URL on subsequent starts. This is deliberate: the agent's client certificate is bound to that endpoint, and letting a stale bootstrap PLATFORM_URL win would send post-registration traffic back through the edge proxy, where TLS terminates, the client cert is lost, and the agent gets 401s.

The agent logs a line when it ignores PLATFORM_URL for this reason. To repoint an enrolled agent deliberately, set PLATFORM_URL_OVERRIDE=1 alongside the new PLATFORM_URL — expect to re-enroll, since the existing certificate will not be valid for the new endpoint. The sensor has the equivalent pair (CONTROL_PLANE_URL / CONTROL_PLANE_URL_OVERRIDE).

Set platform_url (or PLATFORM_URL) to the API gateway base URL (for example https://platform.example.com or http://localhost:8080). Do not point the agent at individual backend service ports.

docs.title: First-time enrollment
docs.text:
1. Option A — just run the binary (default): device-agent with no arguments prompts for the registration key, enrolls, saves the config, and starts the agent in one step. Nothing to prepare beforehand.
  2. Or, to prepare the config yourself, add registration_key to your YAML file or environment and pick one of the following.
  3. Option B — explicit register flag: device-agent -register -config device-agent.yaml Then run the agent normally: device-agent -config device-agent.yaml.
  4. Option C — auto-enroll on start (sensor-style): If registration_key is set and agent_id is empty, the agent registers once on startup, saves certificates under <data_path>/certs, and updates the config file with agent_id. If you did not pass -config, it writes <data_path>/agent-config.yaml by default.
  5. After a successful enrollment, the server marks the key as used. Keep agent_id and the saved certificate paths for subsequent runs.

docs.title: What the agent keeps after enrollment
docs.text:
The registration key is single-use and is not kept once enrollment has succeeded. At enrollment the platform also issues the agent a random agent secret, once, alongside its client certificate. That secret is what protects the device credentials the platform sends with each job (F5, Cisco, Fortinet, Palo Alto and UniFi administrator passwords), so it replaces the registration key as the thing worth stealing.

What Where Notes Client private key, certificate, platform CA <data_path>/certs/client.key (0600), client.crt, ca.crt Written as one unit. Agent secret <data_path>/certs/agent-secret.json (0600) Written atomically with the certificate, so a rotation replaces both or neither. The platform stores only its encrypted form and cannot show it again. Registration key Nowhere. The config file holds registration_key_sha256 (a fingerprint) in its place. The fingerprint lets install-device-agent.sh recognise "this host already enrolled with this key" on a re-run. The key itself is removed from the config only after the agent secret is safely on disk; if the save failed, the key stays where it was. The platform always issues the secret (managed protocol 1), and the agent refuses an enrollment answer without one.

Setting REGISTRATION_KEY in the service environment after enrollment has no effect on credential decryption; an enrolled agent never derives its key from it.

docs.title: Certificate rotation also rotates the agent secret
docs.text: Every certificate rotation (an agent rotates when its certificate is within 30 days of expiry) issues the agent a new agent secret, saved with the new certificate. The secret it replaces stays valid on the agent for 24 hours, so a job the platform sealed just before the rotation still decrypts; after that the old secret is discarded from memory and from agent-secret.json. The platform seals every job with the current secret only.

docs.title: Agents enrolled by an earlier release
docs.text:
An agent enrolled before agent secrets existed keeps working with no re-enrollment. It keeps decrypting with its registration key until its next certificate rotation, when it receives its first agent secret, switches to it, and removes the registration key from its config. The registration key keeps decrypting jobs sealed in the 24 hours around that switch, then is discarded too. An agent binary older than this feature never asks for an agent secret, so the platform never switches it away from its registration key.

Job polling, results, and heartbeat use agent mTLS (client certificate) when certificates are present; they do not use tenant user JWT cookies.

docs.title: Platforms with a privately-signed certificate
docs.text:
If the platform's edge certificate comes from an internal CA this host does not trust, enrollment fails certificate verification before it can start — registration is itself an HTTPS call. The agent resolves this with an explicit one-time trust decision rather than by skipping verification.

  • Interactive: the default install path — plain device-agent, or device-agent --interactive to force the dialogue on a host that already has a config file — shows the CA the platform presents, with its SHA-256 fingerprint, and asks whether to trust it. Accepting pins it to the agent's config; every later connection is verified against it.
  • Unattended: pass --ca-fingerprint <sha256>. The agent pins the CA only if it hashes to that value and aborts on a mismatch. With neither a fingerprint nor an operator to ask, it refuses rather than pinning an unapproved CA.
  • Alternative: install the CA into the host's system trust store, after which no flag is needed.

The expected fingerprint is shown in the web UI when you mint the registration code (Discovery → Sensors & Agents → Register, on the confirmation screen), so you can compare it against what the agent displays. Read it there rather than trusting the connection you are trying to validate. If the platform cannot inspect its own certificate, get it from the host directly:

openssl s_client -showcerts -connect <platform-host>:443 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -outform PEM | openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256

Before offering you a CA to approve, the agent checks that the certificate the platform presents is valid for the hostname you gave it. If it is not, the agent refuses and names what the server is actually serving — commonly an ingress controller's placeholder such as a1b2c3d4.traefik.default, which means the platform's TLS certificate was never installed. Trusting a CA cannot fix this: verification checks the hostname before it checks the signature, so the connection would fail either way, and approving one would look like a completed security step while changing nothing. Fix the platform's certificate and run setup again. The same refusal applies on the --ca-fingerprint path.

Full explanation, including the trust-on-first-use caveat: Sensor Registration → Trust Bootstrap.

docs.title: Job Polling
docs.text:
The agent polls the platform every 30 seconds (configurable) for pending jobs. When a job is available:

  1. Agent receives job with encrypted credentials
  2. Credentials are decrypted in-memory
  3. Device interrogation is executed
  4. Results are submitted back to platform
  5. Credentials are cleared from memory

Timeouts, retries and shutdown. The agent runs one job at a time, and each job is bounded: 5 minutes unless the job carries its own timeout_seconds (capped at 1 hour). A device that does not answer in time fails the job with a "timed out" reason and the agent moves on to the next one. A crash inside one device's interrogation is reported as a failed job too, not a dead agent. If the platform cannot be reached when a job finishes, the agent retries the result five times over about two minutes before giving up; a result still undelivered after that is lost, and the job shows as failed or stuck on the platform. On SIGTERM or SIGINT (and on a service stop) the agent takes no new jobs, lets a job already running finish and submit its result, and exits, waiting at most 30 seconds. Set your service manager's stop timeout above 30 seconds.

Adding devices through the agent. When a device is reachable only from this agent, Add device can route its identification here (Reach it from in the form). That is a device_discovery job, assigned to this agent alone: the agent logs in, reads the device's identity with the same calls the platform uses, and reports only that identity — or the reason it could not. On each poll the agent tells the platform which job types it supports; an agent older than the platform does not, and is never handed a discovery it cannot run. Add device refuses to queue on an agent that has not polled in the last 10 minutes.

docs.title: Supported Device Types
docs.text: Currently supported: - Fortinet FortiGate - SSL VPN, IPSec tunnels, certificates - F5 BigIP - Virtual servers, SSL profiles with cipher lists, cert chains (iControl REST API) - Palo Alto Networks - SSL/TLS policies, certificates (PanOS XML API) - Cisco - Crypto maps, IPSec/IKEv2 SAs, SSL/TLS configs, SSH metadata (SSH/CLI) - Ubiquiti UniFi - Controller TLS configs, device enumeration, site settings (REST API) - Generic HTTP - REST API certificate extraction with TLS deep scan - Generic SNMP - SNMPv2c system information collection

docs.title: Host inventory: local and remote modes
docs.text:
The tenant-facing view of this — what it collects, what the result becomes, and where it shows up in the console — is Host Inventory.

Beyond interrogating network devices, the agent can build a general inventory of a host — its operating system and kernel, hardware identity, installed packages, listening sockets, and installed certificate stores. One collector, reached two ways:

Local Remote What it describes The machine the agent is installed on Another machine, over SSH Credentials None — it is already there The target's stored SSH credentials Started by The agent, on a schedule A job you queue against a device Identity Strongest: the agent's own id, plus the host's serial and MACs Whatever the host reports Sees loopback sockets and the package database Yes Yes, subject to the login account's privileges

Local mode is off by default. Turn it on from the console — Discovery → Sensors & Agents → the agent → Settings — or, for an agent that has not enrolled yet, with HOST_INVENTORY_ENABLED=true (or host_inventory_enabled: true in the config file). The agent then collects on start and every HOST_INVENTORY_INTERVAL (default 24 hours, minimum 1 hour) and posts the result to the platform. An agent you installed to interrogate firewalls will not start enumerating its own host's software just because it was upgraded.

Turning it on from the console takes effect at the agent's next check-in, without a restart and without touching the host. Turning it off stops the collection, rather than collecting and discarding the result.

Remote mode is queued like any other job, against a device that already has SSH credentials configured:

POST /api/v1/device-interrogation-service/devices/{id}/interrogate
{
  "job_type": "host_inventory",
  "mode": "remote",
  "transport": "ssh",
  "agent_id": "<the agent that can reach the target>"
}

mode must be remote: local collection is agent-originated, so a local-mode job would sit in the queue with nothing to claim it. agent_id is required — the collection runs from an agent that can reach the target host.

docs.title: Preview what would be sent
docs.text:
./device-agent --host-inventory-once

Collects this host once, prints the ordinary report as JSON, and exits. It contacts nothing and needs no enrollment. The preview excludes outbound connection peers; those remain behind the separate scheduled or requested collection opt-in. It exits 2 if some sections did not complete (the report is still printed).

docs.title: Exactly what runs, per OS
docs.text:
Everything below is read-only. Nothing is written to the host, no configuration is changed, and no command takes an argument from outside the agent.

Linux

What Command or file OS name and version /etc/os-release Kernel uname -r Host and domain names uname -n, hostname -f Hardware vendor, model, serial, UUID, BIOS /sys/class/dmi/id/{sys_vendor,product_name,product_serial,product_uuid,bios_version} Interfaces and addresses ip -d -j addr (-d adds each link's kind and VLAN id) Installed packages dpkg-query -W -f=…, or rpm -qa --queryformat=…, or apk info -v Listening sockets and UDP bindings ss -ltnup, falling back to /proc/net/{tcp,tcp6,udp,udp6} Outbound peers (opt-in) ss -tnup, falling back to /proc/net/{tcp,tcp6,udp,udp6} Trust stores find /etc/ssl/certs /etc/pki/tls/certs -maxdepth 1 -type f …, then reads the certificate files it lists

product_serial and product_uuid are root-readable only on most distributions. An agent running unprivileged simply does not report them — the fields are absent, never blank, because a blank serial shared across the estate would merge every host into one asset.

macOS

What Command or file OS name, version, build sw_vers Kernel uname -r Host and domain names uname -n, hostname -f Hardware model, serial, platform UUID, boot ROM system_profiler SPHardwareDataType -json Interfaces and addresses ifconfig -a Installed packages pkgutil --pkgs, plus each /Applications/*/Contents/Info.plist for names and versions Listening sockets and UDP bindings lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN, lsof -nP -iUDP Outbound peers (opt-in) lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:ESTABLISHED and connected UDP rows Trust stores /etc/ssl/cert.pem, /private/etc/ssl/certs

The System and login Keychains are not read. Reading a keychain means asking for access to a store that also holds private keys and passwords, which a host inventory has no business holding.

Windows (PowerShell, run as powershell -NoProfile -NonInteractive -EncodedCommand …)

What Command OS name, version, build, machine and domain names Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem, Win32_ComputerSystem Hardware vendor, model, UUID, serial, BIOS Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystemProduct, Win32_BIOS Installed programs Get-ItemProperty over the Uninstall keys under HKLM:\SOFTWARE\… and HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\… Interfaces and addresses Get-NetAdapter, Get-NetIPAddress Listening sockets and UDP bindings Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen; Get-NetUDPEndpoint is retained separately with unknown role Outbound peers (opt-in) Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established; this API exposes no UDP peer Certificate stores Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\{Root,CA,My} — subject, issuer, thumbprint and expiry only

Remote collection on Windows uses PowerShell over SSH, which needs the OpenSSH Server feature enabled. The minimum supported Windows version is Windows Server 2019 or later (or Windows 10 1809 and later) — that is where the OpenSSH Server feature is available. WinRM is not supported: its Go client would add sixteen modules, including a Kerberos stack, to a cross-compiled agent in order to run one PowerShell command over a channel SSH already provides. Asking for "transport": "winrm" returns an error that says so.

docs.title: What is never collected
docs.text:
• No private keys, ever. Certificate stores are read for certificates only: a PEM block that is not a CERTIFICATE is skipped without being decoded, and the shape a certificate is stored in has four fields — subject, issuer, SHA-256 fingerprint, expiry — with nowhere for key bytes to go. A private key found loose in a trust directory is reported only as a count of non-certificate blocks.
  • No passwords, tokens or keys of any kind. Nothing here reads a configuration file, an environment block, or a credential store.
  • No command transcripts. A step that fails records the step name and a short message, never the output it could not parse.
  • No process arguments. A listening socket records the process name that holds it, which is the service identity; a command line can contain a password.
  • No file contents beyond /etc/os-release, the DMI fields listed above, application manifests, and certificate files.

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text: A collection reports each section as ok, failed or unsupported. This matters: a host with no packages listed and packages: ok genuinely has none, while packages: failed means the agent could not look. The two are never collapsed, so an unanswered question is not displayed as a clean answer.

docs.title: If a report is too large
docs.text:
A very large host can produce a report the platform will not accept. The agent logs this distinctly:

Host inventory NOT submitted — report too large: 41231922 bytes exceeds the
platform's cap. This will not fix itself: the next collection (in ~24h) will be
the same size.

That is not a transient failure and the agent does not retry it — the same host produces the same size every run. Either reduce what is collected on that host or raise the platform's cap. The cap is 32 MiB, which is roughly three times the largest report the collector's own limits can produce (20,000 packages and 1,500 trust-store certificates), so reaching it means something unusual: check the package count in --host-inventory-once output first.

docs.title: What appears in the inventory after a collection
docs.text:
One asset per host, and everything the collection learned about it:

You will see Where The host, awaiting approval Discovery → Approvals, class Unknown host Its OS, kernel, hardware vendor/model/serial and interfaces The asset's Facts One entry per listening socket, with the process holding it and whether it is reachable from the network The asset's Endpoints Its installed packages The asset's Software tab, and the Inventory Software lens "Last host inventory: 2h ago — 412 packages, 18 listeners" Discovery → Sensors & Agents, on the agent's row The same counts per run Discovery → Discovery Jobs, under the run's status

The asset arrives pending approval, like everything else the platform discovers: it appears in Approvals for someone to admit deliberately, and does not count against your inventory until they do.

The class is left as Unknown host, on purpose. The agent measures an operating system and a hardware model; deciding that those make the machine a server rather than a laptop is a rule, not a measurement, and a plausible-looking guess is the kind that gets approved without being read. Set the class yourself when you approve the asset.

A second collection updates the same asset. It is matched on the agent's own installation id, which is the strongest identifier the platform has — so re-collections do not create duplicates, and packages that have been uninstalled are marked removed rather than deleted, which is what keeps "this library was here in March and is gone now" answerable.

If a section failed, nothing is invented for it. A host whose package database could not be read reports no package count and no software changes at all — it is not recorded as a host with no software, and its existing software list is left exactly as the last successful collection left it. The same applies to its listening sockets: a collection that could not read the socket table leaves the endpoint list alone rather than reporting every service as stopped.

A service that stops listening is marked closed, not deleted. The agent reads the machine's own socket table, so it is the only thing that can tell you a port is genuinely no longer served — a network scan can only report what answered, and silence there might be a firewall. On the next collection a socket that has gone shows as closed on the asset's Endpoints tab, keeping its history; if it comes back it goes active again. Endpoints that something else found — an active scan, a cloud connector — are never touched by this, because the agent is only authoritative about its own host. Sockets are closed only by a collection the platform recognised as this host: a report that could only be held for review in Discovery → Observations closes nothing.

Addresses. Every address the host reports is used to recognise it, plus the address the platform reached it at (a remote collection) or the address the agent reported for itself, so a collection without a network-interfaces section still lands on the right asset. Addresses on virtual interfaces — container bridges, veths, tunnels — are recorded on the asset as evidence but never used to match it, because the same bridge address exists on every host running the same software.

The Endpoints tab's Exposure column has three states, and blank is one of them. "Bound to localhost" and "reachable" are both measurements the host itself made. A blank means nobody established it, which is every endpoint found by a network scan — a scan sees what answers, not what a socket is bound to. It is deliberately not shown as "reachable": that would be an exposure claim nobody measured.

If the same agent id turns up on different hardware — a restored image, a cloned VM, a replacement chassis with the agent's state copied over — the platform does not silently merge the two. It opens a merge proposal in Approvals naming both, because two different hardware serials are two different machines whatever else they have in common, and asks you to settle it.

Collections taken before this shipped are not back-filled. They are still on the job, complete, and nothing was lost — but they were collected under an older projection and replaying them would produce assets identified by rules that no longer apply. The next scheduled collection from each agent lands normally, so on the default 24-hour interval every agent's host appears within a day of upgrading. There is no reprocess action and none is planned.

docs.title: Heartbeat
docs.text: The agent sends a heartbeat to the platform every 60 seconds to indicate it's alive and ready for jobs. The heartbeat also reports the agent's binary version and the addresses bound on its host, which is how the fleet list shows a multi-homed agent's full address inventory — the platform cannot observe those itself, because NAT and ingress rewrite the connection source.

docs.title: Viewing the fleet
docs.text:
Enrolled agents appear under Discovery → Sensors & Agents, in their own Discovery agents table below the network sensors. Sensors and agents are different things and are listed separately: the table shows, per agent, the host and its addresses, what the agent is permitted to interrogate, when it last ran a job and how many it has run in total, its version, and whether it is currently checking in.

An agent that has reported a host inventory also shows "Last host inventory: 2h ago — 412 packages, 18 listeners" on its row. That is a separate line from the job counts because it answers a different question: a host inventory is not work anybody queued, so an agent busy interrogating firewalls that has never described its own host looks perfectly healthy on "47 jobs · 2h ago". The line is absent when the agent has never reported one, which usually means HOST_INVENTORY_ENABLED is not set.

An agent whose last heartbeat is stale shows as offline even if its status column still reads active — nothing rewrites that column after enrollment, so the heartbeat is the authority.

docs.title: Removing an agent
docs.text:
Discovery → Sensors & Agents → Discovery agents → ✕ on the row, then confirm. Requires the discovery.manage permission.

Removing an agent:

  • takes it out of the fleet list and stops it being assigned any further work;
  • revokes its client certificate;
  • returns its queued jobs to the pool, so another agent — or the platform's own in-cluster worker — picks them up. A queued job that names no device cannot be reassigned and is marked failed, because nothing else can resolve its target;
  • marks any job it was currently running as failed. That job is not retried automatically, since the agent may have already carried out the work before it was removed; re-run it from the device if you need the result.

This does not uninstall the agent. The binary keeps running on its host and will keep polling. Stop and remove it separately on its host (stop the service, then delete its install directory and config). Until you do, its polls are rejected with a 404 — harmless, but noisy in its logs, and covered under Troubleshooting below.

docs.title: Credential Handling
docs.text:
• Credentials are encrypted at rest in the platform database
  • Credentials are wrapped in an AES-256-GCM envelope per job (key derived from the job ID and the agent's secret, which the platform issues at enrollment)
  • Agent decrypts credentials in-memory only during job execution
  • Backward compatible: accepts pre-decrypted credentials if encrypted_data field absent
  • Credentials are never written to disk or logged
  • Credentials are cleared from memory after job completion

docs.title: Network Security
docs.text:
• Agent uses outbound-only HTTPS communication
  • No inbound ports required
  • All communication is initiated by the agent
  • TLS 1.2+ required for all connections

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text:
• Registration key required for initial bootstrap only, and not kept on the agent afterwards
  • Client certificate (issued at registration) and agent ID are used for job polling and results
  • Job credentials are protected by a per-agent secret issued at enrollment and rotated with the certificate (see What the agent keeps after enrollment)
  • Jobs are scoped to specific agents
  • Agent can only access jobs assigned to it

docs.title: HTTP 401 on job polling or heartbeat
docs.text: Usually means the agent request hit a route that still required a tenant JWT (browser session) instead of agent mTLS. Ensure the platform runs a build where outbound routes (/agents/:id/jobs, /results, /heartbeat) are protected by agent auth, not only JWT. Also confirm agent_id in the config file matches the enrolled agent (after registration, the agent should persist agent_id automatically).

docs.title: "This agent cannot store its enrollment"
docs.text:
The agent could not create or write its data path (<data_path>/certs) or its config file, so it stopped before contacting the platform. The registration key is still unused. Install with install-device-agent.sh, run the agent as a user that can write the data path, or set data_path in its config to a directory that user can write.

Agents older than this check sent the key first and then failed to save. They logged Failed to save certificates to disk, and every later call failed with certificate signed by unknown authority. That enrollment cannot be recovered: delete the agent in the console, generate a new key, and install again.

docs.title: Behind an egress proxy
docs.text: The agent honours the standard HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY environment variables both before and after enrolment, including after its mTLS client certificate is issued or rotated. Set them in the agent's service environment (for the systemd unit, an Environment= line) and restart it. The proxy must allow a tunnelled connection (CONNECT) to the platform's mTLS endpoint, because the agent presents its client certificate end to end.

docs.title: The agent reports "rotated" but you see lock-outs after a restart
docs.text: Certificate rotation revokes the old certificate on the platform. If the agent cannot save the new one (a full disk, a read-only data directory) it keeps running on the new certificate in memory, logs Certificate rotated on the platform but the new certificate could NOT be saved at error level, and repeats the message on every heartbeat while retrying the save. Fix the permissions or free space on the data path; the next heartbeat saves the certificate and logs that it did. Restarting before that point leaves the agent unable to authenticate, and it must be re-enrolled.

docs.title: Invalid or rejected registration key
docs.text:
• Wrong key type: use a device interrogation pending key, not a network sensor key.
  • Key expired, already used, or database was reset: create a new pending key and enroll again.

docs.title: The platform is presenting a certificate for another hostname
docs.text: Setup stops before offering you a trust decision, and names the certificate's real identity. A name like <hash>.traefik.default means the platform's TLS secret is missing and its ingress controller is serving a self-issued placeholder. This is a platform-side fix; no CA you pin on the agent changes the outcome, because hostname verification runs before signature verification. See Platforms with a privately-signed certificate.

docs.title: HTTP 404 "Agent not registered" on every poll
docs.text:
The agent was deleted from the platform (Discovery → Sensors & Agents), but the binary is still installed and running. This is the expected, deliberate response: a removed agent is rejected at the door and receives no jobs and no credentials, even though its certificate file is still on disk.

It is not a network fault and there is nothing to fix on the platform side. Either stop and uninstall the agent on this host, or — if it was deleted by mistake — mint a fresh registration key and enroll it again. The old key cannot be reused.

docs.title: Agent Not Receiving Jobs
docs.text:
1. Verify registration key is correct
  2. Check agent status in platform UI — if the agent is missing from the Discovery agents table entirely, it has been deleted (see the 404 entry above)
  3. Verify network connectivity to platform
  4. Check agent logs for errors

docs.title: Job Execution Failures
docs.text:
1. Verify device credentials are correct in platform
  2. Check device connectivity from agent location
  3. Review job error messages in platform UI
  4. Enable verbose logging: VERBOSE=true

docs.title: Connection Issues
docs.text:
1. Verify PLATFORM_URL is correct
  2. Check firewall rules allow outbound HTTPS
  3. Verify TLS certificate is valid
  4. Check DNS resolution for platform URL

docs.title: systemd (Linux)
docs.text:
Create /etc/systemd/system/device-agent.service:

[Unit]
Description=Device Interrogation Agent
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=device-agent
WorkingDirectory=/opt/device-agent
ExecStart=/opt/device-agent/device-agent --config /etc/device-agent/config.yaml
Restart=always
RestartSec=10

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Enable and start:

sudo systemctl enable device-agent
sudo systemctl start device-agent

docs.title: Windows Service
docs.text: Use NSSM (Non-Sucking Service Manager) or similar to run as a Windows service.

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text: The agent sends periodic heartbeats to the platform. Monitor agent status in the platform UI.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Logs are written to stdout/stderr. For production, redirect to log files:

./device-agent --config device-agent.yaml >> /var/log/device-agent.log 2>&1

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
To update the agent:

  1. Download new binary version
  2. Stop current agent
  3. Replace binary
  4. Restart agent

The agent will automatically re-register with the platform if needed.

docs.title: Support
docs.text: For issues or questions: - Check platform documentation - Review agent logs - Contact platform support

docs.title: Production Deployment Checklist
docs.text: Vista Platform ships as a Helm chart — production installs run on Kubernetes, against the chart at oci://ghcr.io/vistasecurity/vistaplatform. This checklist covers the pre-flight, the install itself, and post-install verification for a real deployment. The Docker Compose file each release attaches is for evaluating the product on one host, not for running it: see INSTALL.md in the Distribution repository, which also carries the full Helm guide and a values file to start from.

docs.title: Cluster prerequisites the chart does not install
docs.text:
• cert-manager — required by default. It issues the per-service certificates for encrypted internal transport (serviceMtls, on by default) and, with tls.mode: certManager, the browser-facing certificate too. The install stops with a clear error if its CRDs are absent. It is not optional: agent and sensor mTLS (agentMtls) is mandatory under managed protocol 1 and reuses the serviceMtls certificates, so the chart refuses serviceMtls.enabled or agentMtls.enabled set to false.
  • Stakater Reloader — required whenever serviceMtls is on (the default). It restarts pods when a certificate rotates. Nothing fails at install time without it; internal mTLS quietly breaks at the first renewal, ~60 days in.
  • Traefik, with its CRDs. The chart creates IngressRoute and Middleware resources; it does not install the controller or the CRDs that define them. Traefik v3.4 or newer is required when serviceMtls is on: the chart's ServersTransport uses the rootCAs field, which older releases do not know.
  • A StorageClass for the PostgreSQL, Redis, NATS and upload volumes. The chart defaults to datastores.storageClassName: "", which omits storageClassName so your cluster's default StorageClass is used; check that kubectl get storageclass shows one marked (default). If there is no default (or you want a specific class), set datastores.storageClassName (or a per-datastore datastores.<store>.storageClassName, which wins) to a class that exists; otherwise the PersistentVolumeClaims stay Pending.

Upgrading an existing release: pin its class first. Earlier chart versions defaulted this value to longhorn, and StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates are immutable, so helm upgrade with the new empty default fails with a Forbidden error. Before upgrading, read the class off your existing volumes (kubectl -n <ns> get pvc) and pass --set datastores.storageClassName=<class> (or put it in your values file).

Full detail on the internal-mTLS options — what each toggle covers, how to stage them across upgrades, and how to run against a managed PostgreSQL — is in Service-mesh mTLS. If your edge certificate comes from an internal or corporate CA rather than a public issuer, see Running with an internal CA for the supported way to make in-cluster callers trust it.

docs.title: values.yaml
docs.text:
• [ ] Set tls.dnsName and tls.adminDnsName — where users reach the web UI/API and the admin console.
  • [ ] Set tls.issuerRef to a cert-manager ClusterIssuer you already have (for tls.mode: certManager), or configure your own certificate path.
  • [ ] If you use tls.mode: certManager with an HTTP-01 issuer, the chart already allows the cert-manager solver pod (label acme.cert-manager.io/http01-solver, port 8089) through its default-deny ingress NetworkPolicy, from networkPolicy.ingressControllerNamespace (default kube-system; set it to the namespace your ingress controller runs in). Your issuer must still be able to reach your ingress from the Internet on port 80. A DNS-01 issuer creates no solver pod and needs nothing extra from the NetworkPolicy.
  • [ ] If you turn on networkPolicy.egressEnabled and use an external PostgreSQL or Redis (datastores.postgres.enabled: false / datastores.redis.enabled: false), list the database's address range in networkPolicy.externalDatastoreCIDRs (for example ["10.20.30.0/24"]). The chart then allows egress to those CIDRs on TCP 5432 (PostgreSQL) and 6379 (Redis); without it the default egress deny blocks every backend and Job from reaching the database, so the chart refuses to render with an empty list.
  • [ ] Create platform.existingSecretName yourself, out of band, and name it in values — otherwise the chart generates platform secrets on first install and keeps them. Either way, treat ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY the way you'd treat a database encryption key: if it changes, every stored integration credential encrypted under the old key becomes permanently undecryptable. The chart reads the existing Secret back on upgrade rather than regenerating it, but only if you haven't overridden that behavior.
  • [ ] External PostgreSQL or Redis (datastores.postgres.enabled=false / datastores.redis.enabled=false) requires platform.existingSecretName. The chart-generated Secret cannot carry your connection strings, so the render stops with an error unless you supply a Secret that also holds database-url (external Postgres) and/or redis-url (external Redis), alongside jwt-secret, internal-auth-secret and encryption-master-key.
  • [ ] External NATS is not supported. datastores.nats.enabled=false is refused at render time; keep the bundled NATS.
  • [ ] If you apply the schema yourself (schemaMigration.enabled=false) and keep serviceRls.enabled on (the default), your schema must create the crypto_app (NOLOGIN NOBYPASSRLS) and crypto_bypass (NOLOGIN BYPASSRLS) roles with the grants from schema.sql. The rls-roles Job still runs and waits for them, then grants LOGIN; backends stay in Init until it does.
  • [ ] The chart creates the namespace only with createNamespace=true; that namespace is kept on helm uninstall (with its PVCs and Secrets). Delete it yourself when you mean to destroy the data.
  • [ ] Size the node(s) for roughly double your steady-state CPU request during upgrades if you're running a single-node cluster — see "Single-node clusters" below.

docs.title: Optional prerequisites
docs.text:
• [ ] A model provider, if you want AI-assisted seams (finding explanations, remediation drafting, EOL gap-filling proposals) to use a real model instead of the rule-based default every one of them falls back to. See Connecting a model provider — nothing here blocks an install; every AI capability works without it.
  • [ ] The offline End-of-life/Vulnerability bundle, for an air-gapped install with no route to endoflife.date/NVD/OSV. See Air-gapped installs: the offline bundle.

docs.title: Legal documents
docs.text: • [ ] Replace the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy templates. The chart ships templates — real structure with [BRACKETED] blanks and a banner saying they are not legally binding — and every user is asked to accept them at sign-up. See Legal documents for operators.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
helm install vista oci://ghcr.io/vistasecurity/vistaplatform \
  --namespace vista --create-namespace \
  --values values.yaml

A minimal production values.yaml:

tls:
  mode: certManager           # a real certificate, renewed automatically
  dnsName: vista.example.com  # where users reach the web UI and API
  adminDnsName: admin.vista.example.com
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-prod    # a cert-manager ClusterIssuer you already have
    kind: ClusterIssuer

platform:
  # Recommended: create this Secret yourself, out of band, and name it here.
  # Otherwise the chart generates these on first install and keeps them.
  existingSecretName: vista-platform-secrets

agentMtls:
  # Required by default: sensors and discovery agents authenticate with client
  # certificates over a TLS-passthrough listener, one hostname per service.
  # Each must differ from the other and from tls.dnsName, and resolve to a
  # Traefik passthrough entrypoint (agentMtls.entryPoint, port 8444) you provide.
  backends:
    sensor-manager:
      dnsName: sensors.vista.example.com
    device-interrogation-service:
      dnsName: agents.vista.example.com

The install fails without the two agentMtls hostnames; there is no opt-out — see Agent and sensor mTLS.

There is no separate "start infrastructure, then services, then gateway" sequence to run by hand — helm install reconciles everything (Postgres, Redis, NATS, every backend, both frontends, and the schema-migration and seed-data Jobs) in dependency order, and --wait returns once every pod is ready. Give the first install a few minutes: it's applying the schema, seeding reference data, and pulling ~18 images.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• [ ] All pods are ready: 
    kubectl -n vista get pods
  • [ ] The web UI and admin UI load at tls.dnsName / tls.adminDnsName
  • [ ] Sign in with a seeded platform administrator and complete the mandatory password rotation (see the Platform Admin Guide)
  • [ ] A backend answers on its plaintext health port (used for probes; mTLS is not required against it even when serviceMtls.enabled is on): 
    kubectl -n vista exec deploy/auth-service -- wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/health
  • [ ] The MCP service is healthy and requires INTERNAL_AUTH_SECRET/a tenant API token — an unauthenticated request to /api/v1/mcp-service/mcp must return 401.
  • [ ] Test your configured notification channels (Settings → Notification Delivery) and confirm delivery history records the attempt.
  • [ ] Take a backup and prove it. Admin console → Maintenance → Backups → Create backup, download it, and keep a copy outside the cluster. If you tick "Include encryption keys and install secrets", store the passphrase in your password manager: it is not recoverable. Walk through the Restore procedure in Maintenance on a scratch cluster before you need it.
  • [ ] Decide on update checks. maintenance.updateCheck.enabled is true by default and makes one outbound registry call a day. On an air-gapped site set it to false (and point image.registry / maintenance.chartSource at your mirror); see Maintenance.

docs.title: Verify what you're running
docs.text: Every Core image and the chart are cosign-signed with the signing identity being the release workflow. The Distribution repository's VERIFY.md gives the identity and the cosign verify commands, and each release attaches a copy for that version with IMAGES.txt, every image by digest. helm install prints the verify command for the chart version you installed at the end of its run.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
• [ ] Configure monitoring alert thresholds and notification channels — see Monitoring Setup
  • [ ] Set up log aggregation for your cluster's logging stack
  • [ ] Set up uptime monitoring against the public hostname

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• [ ] Verify HTTPS is enforced end to end (browser → ingress)
  • [ ] Test authentication and authorization
  • [ ] Review the Security & Trust → Dashboard posture view

docs.title: GitOps (Argo CD / Flux)
docs.text:
By default the chart generates its passwords and keys with lookup, which reads the Secret back on helm install / helm upgrade. A template-only render (Argo CD, Flux's dry runs, helm template | kubectl apply) cannot lookup, so every sync would write new random values: a new database password against the old volume, and a new encryption-master-key that makes every stored integration credential undecryptable. For these tools, set platform.generateSecrets: false and create the Secrets yourself (Sealed Secrets, SOPS, External Secrets, or kubectl create secret). The render then contains no generated Secret at all, and fails, listing the keys, if you have not named them.

platform:
  generateSecrets: false
  existingSecretName: vista-platform          # jwt-secret, internal-auth-secret, encryption-master-key
  existingDatastoreSecretName: vista-datastores   # postgres-password, redis-password, nats-token
install:
  existingSecretName: vista-install           # install-id, signing-key.pem
  # ...or pin BOTH install.id and install.signingKeyPEM instead (from an encrypted values file)
jwtSigning:
  existingSecretName: vista-jwt-signing       # signing-key.pem (skip if jwtSigning.enabled: false)
cbomSigning:
  existingSecretName: vista-cbom-signing      # signing-key.pem (or pin cbomSigning.keyPEM)
tls:
  mode: certManager                           # or existingSecret; selfSigned is refused (it generates a cert)
Secret Keys Value platform.existingSecretName jwt-secret, internal-auth-secret, encryption-master-key 64 random alphanumeric characters each. Add database-url / redis-url only for an external database or Redis. platform.existingDatastoreSecretName postgres-password, redis-password, nats-token 32 random alphanumeric characters each. install.existingSecretName install-id, signing-key.pem A UUID, and an ECDSA P-256 private key in PEM. On an existing install copy both from the current <release>-install Secret. jwtSigning.existingSecretName signing-key.pem An ECDSA P-256 private key in PEM. On an existing install copy it from <release>-jwt-signing so live sessions survive. cbomSigning.existingSecretName signing-key.pem An Ed25519 private key as a PKCS#8 PEM. On an existing install copy it from <release>-cbom-signing so artifact signatures keep their key id.

To adopt an existing release, copy the values out of the Secrets the chart created (kubectl get secret <release>-generated -o yaml, and the -platform, -install, -jwt-signing siblings) into your own Secrets before switching the flag; the chart-created Secrets carry helm.sh/resource-policy: keep, so they are not deleted when they leave the render.

Keep generateSecrets: true for plain helm install / helm upgrade.

Migration Jobs. The schema-migration and rls-roles Jobs have no ttlSecondsAfterFinished, so a controller never sees them disappear and re-apply them. Their names embed a hash of the rendered pod template: the same chart and values render the same Job, and a schema or chart change renders a new one. At most one finished Job of each kind is kept; the next change renames it and Helm (or Argo CD / Flux with pruning enabled) deletes the superseded one. The seed-data Job is a Helm hook (post-install/post-upgrade) and is cleaned up as one.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
From the admin console. The usual way to back up and update is the console's Maintenance section: Backups → Create backup first, then About & Updates → Update. See Maintenance in the admin console. Installs managed by Argo CD or Flux are updated from the values repository instead (the console says so), and the manual Helm procedure below always works and is the fallback.

ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY encrypts stored integration credentials — see Secrets Management. The chart reads the existing Secret back on upgrade rather than generating a new one.

Use --reset-then-reuse-values for a cross-version upgrade, not --reuse-values. --reuse-values carries every previous release's user-supplied value forward verbatim — including any per-service backends.<svc>.image.tag override you set for a one-off hotfix — which then silently pins that service to the OLD image even though the chart version (and every other service) moved forward. helm upgrade reports success either way. --reset-then-reuse-values resets to the new chart's defaults first, then reapplies only the values you still have set in your -f/--set flags, which is what you want when moving to a new chart version. Reserve plain --reuse-values for a same-version re-run (e.g. rolling a single service's tag by hand). The chart's NOTES.txt repeats this on every helm upgrade.

Back up before every upgrade. The chart re-applies scripts/database/schema.sql on every helm upgrade; NOTES.txt reminds you of this on every run. Use Maintenance → Backups → Create backup in the admin console, or pg_dump yourself; the console's update takes a backup automatically as its first step.

docs.title: The cache server changed from Redis to Valkey
docs.text:
Releases up to 5.0.0 shipped Redis (redis:7-alpine in the chart). Later releases ship Valkey 8 (valkey/valkey, BSD-3-Clause), a Redis-protocol drop-in. The values key (datastores.redis), the redis Service, the redis-password / redis-url secret keys and the REDIS_URL variable are unchanged, so your values file needs no edit.

Valkey cannot read the files Redis 7.4 wrote (RDB format 12; it stops with Can't handle RDB format version 12). So the chart gives Valkey its own files on the same volume (valkey-dump.rdb, valkey-appendonlydir/) and the cache starts empty on the first upgrade. The Redis files stay where they are, untouched, so a helm rollback to the previous chart finds them again.

Redis holds caches and short-lived state, not records — inventory, users, sessions' refresh tokens and jobs are all in PostgreSQL. After the upgrade:

  • pending password-reset and email-verification links stop working (request new ones), and SSO or login flows in progress must be restarted;
  • rate-limit and login-throttle counters start from zero (account lockout lives in PostgreSQL and still applies);
  • token revocations from the last access-token lifetime are forgotten. Logging out, changing or resetting a password, revoking a session, deactivating or erasing a user, and ending an impersonation all revoke access tokens in the cache. A token revoked in the hour before the upgrade (JWT_EXPIRY, default 1h) is accepted again until it expires. Refresh tokens are revoked in PostgreSQL and stay revoked, so no new access token can be minted. If this matters, upgrade at least one access-token lifetime after the last such action.

--reuse-values keeps the previous chart's defaults, so it would leave you on redis:7-alpine: use --reset-then-reuse-values (above). If you set datastores.redis.image yourself (a mirror, for example), point it at a Valkey 8 image. An external Redis-protocol server (datastores.redis.enabled: false) is not affected.

docs.title: Single-node clusters
docs.text:
A default helm upgrade rolls every backend with a rolling-update strategy, so old and new pods briefly coexist — on a one-node cluster that can surge pod CPU requests past what the node has to give, which can leave a recreated postgres-0 unable to schedule and every backend's init container hanging waiting on it. Size the node for roughly double your steady-state CPU request during upgrades, or set strategy: Recreate on the backends you can afford brief downtime on (the chart already does this for pcap-processor). A wedged upgrade recovers with helm rollback.

Switching a backend that is already deployed to Recreate needs one extra step under Helm's server-side apply (the default in Helm 4). Kubernetes filled in rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 25%} when the Deployment was created; server-side apply leaves a field it never set in place, so the upgrade that sets strategy: Recreate fails with spec.strategy.rollingUpdate: Forbidden: may not be specified when strategy type is 'Recreate' — and the whole upgrade stops there. Clear the field first, once per backend, then run the upgrade:

kubectl -n <namespace> patch deployment <backend> --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate","rollingUpdate":null}}}'

The patch does not restart anything, since the strategy is not part of the pod template. Helm 3's client-side apply clears the field without the patch. It is only needed when you move a live backend to Recreate, not on a fresh install.

docs.title: Pods not starting
docs.text:
• Check logs: kubectl -n vista logs deployment/<service>
  • Verify the chart's prerequisites (cert-manager, Reloader, a StorageClass) are actually installed and healthy
  • Check kubectl -n vista get pvc for volumes stuck Pending

docs.title: Database connection errors
docs.text:
• Verify kubectl -n vista get pods shows postgres-0 Running/Ready
  • Check datastores.postgres.tls.enabled matches whether serviceMtls.enabled is on — the datastore TLS toggles require the mesh toggle
  • Check firewall/security-group rules if using a managed PostgreSQL instead of the chart's in-cluster instance — set datastores.postgres.enabled: false and provide a database-url key in your platform secret, per the comments above the datastores: block in values.yaml

docs.title: PostgreSQL JIT (your own or a managed PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
PostgreSQL's just-in-time (JIT) compiler speeds up long analytical queries and slows down short ones. Vista Platform's tables are split into partitions, so even a simple lookup builds a large query plan, and with JIT on the compile time can dwarf the work itself (the same query went from tens of seconds to about a tenth of a second with JIT off). The platform therefore asks for jit=off on every connection it opens. Nothing needs to be configured for this, and your other databases and applications on the same server are not affected.

  • To keep your server's own JIT setting instead, set appConfig.dbJit: true in your values. It is one value for every backend service (the chart passes it to them as the DB_JIT environment variable), and the backends restart on the upgrade that changes it. A DB_JIT entry under backends.<service>.extraEnv overrides it for that one service.
  • If a connection pooler such as PgBouncer sits between the platform and PostgreSQL and rejects the connection with unsupported startup parameter: jit, either add jit to the pooler's ignore_startup_parameters setting, or set appConfig.dbJit: true and set jit = off for the platform's database or role on the PostgreSQL side (ALTER DATABASE crypto_inventory SET jit = off;). Running behind a pooler or a managed database proxy is described here but is not something the project tests.

docs.title: Frontend not loading
docs.text:
• Verify tls.dnsName / tls.adminDnsName resolve to your ingress controller
  • Check the Traefik IngressRoute/Middleware resources the chart created: kubectl -n vista get ingressroute,middleware
  • Check browser console for CORS or certificate errors

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
helm rollback vista --namespace vista

Restore your pg_dump backup if the upgrade already wrote schema changes you need to undo — helm rollback reverts the release's Kubernetes objects, not data already written to the database.

Restore a whole dump (schema and data) into an empty database. If you restore data only into a database that already has the schema, pass pg_restore --data-only --disable-triggers: without it, the triggers that tell shipped catalogue content from your own mark every restored shipped framework, control and rule as Custom, and upgrades stop keeping them current (see Shipped content and upgrades).
