docs.title: Certificate Security
docs.text:
• Key Storage: Private keys generated and stored ONLY on sensor hosts (never transmitted to platform)
  • CSR-Based Flow: Certificates issued via Certificate Signing Requests - private keys never leave sensor
  • CA Security: Tenant CA private keys encrypted with AES-256-GCM and stored in database
  • Key Rotation: Automatic rotation when certificates expire within 30 days
  • Access Control: Certificate operations require admin authentication
  • Audit Logging: All certificate operations logged

docs.title: Operational Security
docs.text:
• Certificate Expiry: Monitor and rotate before expiration
  • Revocation: Immediate revocation for compromised certificates
  • Backup: Secure backup of CA certificates
  • Recovery: Documented certificate recovery procedures

docs.title: Agent Binaries Before Enrollment
docs.text:
The certificates above start with an agent the operator installed, so the chain of trust starts with the binary. Sensors and device agents are downloaded from releases of the Vista Platform Agents repository, only through the console (Discovery → Sensors & Agents → Register), which prints steps for the exact release the platform's signed compatibility record qualifies for this platform version and edition, and for nothing else (no "latest" release, no other source).

  • Digest: each file's SHA-256 comes from the platform, not from the download site; the steps check it with sha256sum -c, shasum -a 256 -c or Get-FileHash.
  • Signature: each file has a Sigstore bundle, verified with cosign verify-blob against the exact identity of the agents release workflow (release.yml at the tag for stable releases and release candidates, nightly.yml on main for a nightly) and the issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com. Full procedure: Verifying a release.
  • Platform CA: on a platform with a privately-signed certificate, the registration dialog shows the platform CA fingerprint. The agent shows the same fingerprint during enrollment; compare them before approving, or pass it to the device agent installer as --ca-fingerprint for an unattended install.

Consoles of Vista Platform 5.2.1 and earlier point their download links at release assets of the former Core repository that no longer exist; upgrade the platform to get working downloads.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: All platform services use mTLS for secure service-to-service communication. Each service runs in dual-mode: - HTTP (port 8080): Health check endpoints (no authentication required) - HTTPS (port 8443): API endpoints with mTLS authentication

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Generate the platform service CA (one-time operation):

./scripts/generate-service-ca.sh

This creates: - Platform service CA certificate and encrypted private key (stored in database) - CA certificate available for service configuration

docs.title: Generate Service Certificates
docs.text:
Generate certificates for all platform services:

./scripts/generate-service-certificates.sh

This creates certificates for all services: - auth-service - inventory-service - compliance-engine - cbom-service - sensor-manager - cluster-sensor-service - admin-service - monitoring-service - tenant-health-service - device-interrogation-service - audit-service - notification-service - discovery-processor-service - pcap-processor - mcp-service - api-gateway (client certificate for backend connections; Docker Compose only — the Helm chart has no gateway pod)

Certificates are stored in: - Database: platform_service_certificates table - Filesystem: ./service-certs/{service-name}/ directory

docs.title: Certificate Files
docs.text:
After generation, each service has the following files:

service-certs/{service-name}/
├── server-cert.pem      # Server certificate for HTTPS API (port 8443)
├── server-key.pem       # Server private key
├── client-cert.pem      # Client certificate for inter-service calls
├── client-key.pem       # Client private key
└── platform-ca-cert.pem # Platform service CA certificate

docs.title: Development Environment
docs.text:
Generate the certificates once (needs Postgres up and ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY set in .env — see scripts/generate-service-ca.sh's prerequisites):

docker compose up -d postgres
./scripts/generate-service-ca.sh
./scripts/generate-service-certificates.sh
  1. Service CA is created if it doesn't exist
  2. Service certificates are generated for all services
  3. Certificates are mounted into containers via docker-compose.yml

docs.title: Kubernetes (Helm chart) — production
docs.text: You don't run the scripts above for a chart deployment. The chart's serviceMtls toggle (on by default) provisions and rotates every service certificate itself, from a cert-manager-issued Platform CA — see Service-mesh mTLS for the full toggle set, staging guidance across upgrades, and the Postgres/NATS TLS options that build on it. The manual generate-service-ca.sh / generate-service-certificates.sh flow above and the service-certs/{service}/ directory it produces are a Docker Compose mechanism only.

docs.title: Docker Compose "production-style" stack
docs.text:
If you're running a production-style Compose stack rather than the Helm chart (see production checklist for why that's not the recommended path for a real deployment):

  1. Generate Certificates: 

    ./scripts/generate-service-ca.sh
./scripts/generate-service-certificates.sh

  2. Store Certificates Securely:

  3. Use secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault)
  4. Store in encrypted storage

  5. Never commit to version control

  6. Set Permissions: 

    find service-certs -type d -exec chmod 755 {} \;
find service-certs -type f -name "*.pem" -exec chmod 600 {} \;

docs.title: Service Configuration
docs.text:
Each service is configured with mTLS via environment variables:

USE_MTLS=true
TLS_PORT=8443
SERVICE_CERT_PATH=/app/certs/server-cert.pem
SERVICE_KEY_PATH=/app/certs/server-key.pem
CLIENT_CERT_PATH=/app/certs/client-cert.pem
CLIENT_KEY_PATH=/app/certs/client-key.pem
PLATFORM_CA_CERT_PATH=/app/certs/platform-ca-cert.pem

docs.title: API Gateway Configuration
docs.text:
The API Gateway (Traefik) uses mTLS client certificates when connecting to backend services via a serversTransport configuration:

# Traefik dynamic config (config/traefik/dynamic-development.yaml)
http:
  serversTransports:
    mtls:
      certificates:
        - certFile: /etc/traefik/certs/api-gateway-client-cert.pem
          keyFile: /etc/traefik/certs/api-gateway-client-key.pem
      rootCAs:
        - /etc/traefik/certs/platform-ca-cert.pem
      serverName: ""
      insecureSkipVerify: false

  services:
    auth-service:
      loadBalancer:
        serversTransport: mtls
        servers:
          - url: "https://auth-service:8443"

docs.title: Testing mTLS
docs.text:
There is no bundled test script for this — verify each check by hand:

Certificate files exist and are valid: 

for f in service-certs/auth-service/*.pem; do
  echo "== $f =="
  openssl x509 -in "$f" -noout -checkend 0 -dates 2>/dev/null \
    || echo "  (not a cert, or expired)"
done

Health endpoint works on HTTP (port 8080), no certificate required: 

docker compose exec auth-service curl -sf http://localhost:8080/health

API endpoint works on HTTPS with mTLS (port 8443), using the client cert: 

docker compose exec auth-service curl -sf --cacert /app/certs/platform-ca-cert.pem \
  --cert /app/certs/client-cert.pem --key /app/certs/client-key.pem \
  https://localhost:8443/health

Services reject connections without a valid certificate: 

docker compose exec auth-service curl -sk https://localhost:8443/health
# expect a TLS handshake failure (curl exit 56), not a 200 response

docs.title: "Failed to create mTLS server"
docs.text:
Cause: Certificate files missing or invalid

Solution: 1. Verify certificate files exist in service-certs/{service-name}/ 2. Check file permissions (should be readable by service user) 3. Regenerate certificates if missing: ./scripts/generate-service-certificates.sh

docs.title: "mTLS certificate validation failed"
docs.text:
Cause: Certificate not signed by platform service CA

Solution: 1. Verify certificate is signed by platform service CA 2. Check certificate expiration date 3. Regenerate certificate if expired or invalid

docs.title: "Service-to-service communication fails"
docs.text:
Cause: Client certificate missing or invalid

Solution: 1. Verify client certificates exist for both services 2. Check client certificate is signed by platform service CA 3. Verify service is using mTLS client when making calls 4. Check service logs for mTLS connection errors

docs.title: "Health check fails"
docs.text:
Cause: Service not responding on HTTP port 8080

Solution: 1. Health checks use HTTP (not HTTPS) on port 8080 2. Verify service is listening on port 8080 3. Check service logs for startup errors

docs.title: Running with an internal CA
docs.text:
If your edge certificate (tls.dnsName / tls.adminDnsName) is issued by a private or corporate CA rather than a public one, anything inside the cluster that calls the edge hostname over HTTPS fails TLS verification. A pod carries only the base image's public CA bundle — it does not inherit the node's OS trust store, so the fact that your laptop or a cluster node already trusts that CA proves nothing about what a pod trusts.

This is separate from service-mesh mTLS, which already handles service-to-service, Postgres, and NATS traffic with its own cert-manager-provisioned Platform CA. The gap this page covers is narrower: anything that calls back out to your edge hostname from inside the cluster.

docs.title: Where this actually bites
docs.text: Today the one place is monitoring.syntheticChecks (see the Distribution repository's Helm guide and the monitoring: block in the chart's values). Each check is a real HTTPS GET that monitoring-service issues against your customer-facing URL — DNS, ingress, TLS, and every middleware in between, the same way a browser would. Against an internal-CA edge cert, that GET fails certificate verification, and the only toggle offered for it in values.yaml is insecureSkipVerify: true — which turns the check off rather than fixing what it's checking. For a product built around certificate hygiene, "turn verification off" cannot be the only documented answer, so here is the supported one.

docs.title: The supported fix: mount your CA into the pod
docs.text:
The chart supports arbitrary extra volumes, mounts, and environment variables per backend (values.yaml → backends.<service>.extraVolumes / extraVolumeMounts / extraEnv). Combine that with SSL_CERT_FILE, which Go's standard library honors on Linux, and a backend can trust your CA without any image change.

1. Build a combined bundle. Go's cert loader does not merge SSL_CERT_FILE with the image's default trust store — setting it replaces the default list outright. If you hand it only your internal CA, the pod loses the ability to verify anything signed by a public CA too (an SMTP relay, a webhook target, an update check). Concatenate both:

# The Core runtime images are Alpine-based with ca-certificates installed,
# so their default bundle is /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt. Grab a copy
# from any Alpine box (or `docker run --rm <runtime-image> cat
# /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt`) and append your CA to it:
cat ca-certificates.crt your-internal-ca.pem > ca-bundle.pem

2. Put it in a ConfigMap in the release namespace:

kubectl create configmap internal-ca-bundle \
  --namespace vista \
  --from-file=ca-bundle.pem=./ca-bundle.pem

3. Mount it and point the backend at it, in your values.yaml. Today that's monitoring-service, since that's the only backend calling the edge by hostname out of the box:

backends:
  monitoring-service:
    extraVolumes:
      - name: internal-ca-bundle
        configMap:
          name: internal-ca-bundle
    extraVolumeMounts:
      - name: internal-ca-bundle
        mountPath: /etc/ssl/internal
        readOnly: true
    extraEnv:
      - name: SSL_CERT_FILE
        value: /etc/ssl/internal/ca-bundle.pem

4. helm upgrade with that values file. No insecureSkipVerify needed — the check now verifies your edge cert against a trust store that actually includes the CA that issued it.

This has been verified against the chart with helm template: the volume, the mount, and SSL_CERT_FILE all render correctly onto the monitoring-service Deployment with the overlay above. It has not been verified against a live install — a real internal CA and a syntheticChecks target were not available to test end to end, so treat "the config is correct" as proven and "the probe goes green against your CA" as expected but unconfirmed until you try it.

docs.title: What insecureSkipVerify is actually for
docs.text:
monitoring.syntheticChecks[].insecureSkipVerify skips TLS verification for that one probe only. It predates the CA-mount option above and exists because a throwaway cluster needs something that works without a CA-provisioning step.

  • Acceptable: a lab or evaluation cluster where you already click through the browser's certificate warning yourself, and the synthetic check exists only to keep the dashboard from showing a spurious "down."
  • Not acceptable on anything you'd call real: it silently disables the one check in the product whose entire job is to catch a broken or misconfigured edge — which is exactly the failure class an internal-CA mismatch is. Use the CA mount instead.

docs.title: If you add another backend that calls your own edge hostname
docs.text: The same recipe applies to any backend, integration, or webhook target that calls back into your edge hostname from inside the cluster: mount the CA via that backend's extraVolumes / extraVolumeMounts, and point it at the bundle with SSL_CERT_FILE via extraEnv. SSL_CERT_FILE is a Go/OpenSSL convention honored by every Go service in this chart on Linux — it is not a chart-specific mechanism, so the same variable works for anything you add that also happens to be a Go binary.

docs.title: Secrets Management Guide
docs.text: This guide covers how secrets are managed in Vista Platform, including the encryption master key for platform integrations.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The platform uses various secrets for different purposes: - Database credentials: PostgreSQL, Redis - JWT secrets: Token signing keys - Service secrets: API keys, webhook secrets - Platform integration credentials: AWS, cloud providers, SaaS integrations (encrypted)

docs.title: Docker Compose install
docs.text:
The compose file each release attaches reads six secrets from .env and refuses to start until every one is set; none has a default. Generate them, one random value each:

umask 077
for v in POSTGRES_PASSWORD REDIS_PASSWORD NATS_PASSWORD JWT_SECRET INTERNAL_AUTH_SECRET ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY; do
  echo "$v=$(openssl rand -hex 32)"; done > .env

The services run with ENV=production, so each also refuses at startup a secret shorter than 32 bytes or one of the published development defaults (see Minimum strength). Keep .env with your backups: ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY encrypts the device and integration credentials you store, and a different key makes them unreadable. To rotate the others, change the value and run docker compose up -d again. The Distribution repository's INSTALL.md covers the rest of the compose install.

docs.title: Production Environment (Helm chart)
docs.text:
Production runs the Helm chart, not a .env file — see the production checklist. The chart handles ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY (and the other platform secrets — JWT signing key, internal-auth HMAC secret) one of two ways:

  • Chart-generated (default). If you don't supply platform.existingSecretName, the chart generates the platform Secret on first install and keeps it — every subsequent helm upgrade reads the existing Secret back rather than regenerating it.
  • Operator-supplied (recommended for anything you'd call real). Create the Kubernetes Secret yourself, out of band, and reference it via platform.existingSecretName in values.yaml. This is what lets you source ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY from whatever your organization already uses — a SealedSecret, the External Secrets Operator pulling from AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault, or a plain kubectl create secret generic against a value you generated with openssl rand -base64 32.

Never rotate ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY on a live deployment. Whichever way you manage the Secret, changing its value after you have live integrations makes every credential encrypted under the old key permanently undecryptable — see Cannot Decrypt Existing Credentials below.

docs.title: Session-token signing and the legacy shared secret
docs.text:
Session tokens are signed with ES256 (jwtSigning.enabled, on by default). The private key lives in the chart's <fullname>-jwt-signing Secret and is mounted only into the two services that issue tokens, auth-service and admin-service; every other service verifies with the public key it fetches from auth-service's JWKS endpoint.

Before ES256, every service verified HS256 tokens with one shared secret (platform.jwtSecret, injected as JWT_SECRET). Any service holding that secret can forge a session for any user and tenant, so the migration is only finished once it is removed from the services that merely verify. That is jwtSigning.acceptLegacyHmac, and its default, auto, does it for you on install and upgrade:

Situation Legacy HS256 accepted? Fresh install No. Every session is ES256 from the first token. The upgrade that first switches ES256 signing on Yes — every live session is still HS256. Later upgrades, signing key younger than jwtSigning.legacyHmacWindowHours (192h: the 7-day refresh-token lifetime plus a day) Yes The first upgrade after that No. JWT_SECRET is removed from every service except the two issuers. jwtSigning.enabled: false Yes — HS256 is the only scheme. acceptLegacyHmac: true or false As set.

The window closes at an upgrade, not on a timer: an install that is not upgraded after the window passes keeps the secret until its next helm upgrade. The install and upgrade notes print which way it went and why.

auth-service keeps JWT_SECRET regardless (it uses it for CSRF binding and for pre-cutover refresh tokens), so removing the variable is not what stops it accepting HS256. The chart sets JWT_ACCEPT_LEGACY_HMAC on auth-service from the same decision: when the window is closed it is false, and a token signed with the shared secret is refused there too. Outside the chart the variable defaults to true; it is ignored (with a warning) while no ES256 signing key is configured, since the service then signs HS256 itself.

GitOps and helm template. auto reads the signing Secret with Helm's lookup, which returns nothing when Helm is not talking to a cluster (helm template, a client-side --dry-run, Argo CD). Rather than guess, it then keeps legacy acceptance on. If you deploy that way, set the value yourself: true while ES256 signing is younger than the window, false after.

--reuse-values carries the previous release's chart defaults forward, so an upgrade with it from a chart that defaulted to true stays true. Use --reset-then-reuse-values across chart versions.

To confirm the result on a service that only verifies:

kubectl -n <namespace> get deploy inventory-service \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[*].name}' | tr ' ' '\n' | grep JWT_SECRET

No output means the legacy secret is gone from it. Check that the pods actually restarted rather than trusting a green helm upgrade — environment variables are read at pod start.

docs.title: Minimum strength (enforced at startup)
docs.text:
When ENV=production (the chart's default, appConfig.env), every service checks its platform secrets before it serves, and stops with a message naming the variable if one is wrong:

Variable Production rule INTERNAL_AUTH_SECRET Required, at least 32 bytes ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY Required, at least 32 bytes. An absent key is refused rather than run with credential encryption off JWT_SECRET If set, at least 32 bytes. May be absent on services that only verify tokens once ES256 verification is configured and legacy HS256 is no longer accepted (jwtSigning.acceptLegacyHmac resolves to false — see Session-token signing); auth-service and admin-service still require it

The published development defaults are refused as before. Anything generated by the chart or by openssl rand -hex 32 (64 bytes) or openssl rand -base64 32 (44 bytes) passes. Outside production the same problems are logged as warnings and the service keeps running; a service that stores credentials also reports "credential_encryption": "disabled" in its /health payload while ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY is unset.

Upgrading an install that supplied its own short secret. The new pods exit at startup with a line such as refusing to start in production: INTERNAL_AUTH_SECRET is 12 bytes; production requires at least 32, so a rolling upgrade stops with the old pods still serving. Replace the value in your platform Secret (platform.existingSecretName, or platform.* values), then re-run the upgrade:

  • INTERNAL_AUTH_SECRET: set a new random value. Services restart together; it is only used to sign calls between them.
  • JWT_SECRET: set a new random value, or remove it from verifier services once ES256 is on. Existing legacy HS256 sessions are invalidated.
  • ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY: there is no in-place re-key. The data key is derived from the exact string, so a new key cannot read credentials stored under the old one. Set the new key, then re-enter the integration, device and connector credentials you want to keep (they were encrypted under the old key and will report as undecryptable until replaced).

docs.title: How Encryption Works
docs.text:
When a platform admin creates an AWS integration:

  1. User enters credentials in the admin UI (plaintext)
  2. Frontend sends to backend API
  3. Backend encrypts sensitive fields (access_key_id, secret_access_key, etc.) using ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY
  4. Encrypted credentials are stored in platform_integrations.config (JSONB column)
  5. When retrieved, credentials are automatically decrypted

docs.title: Encryption Details
docs.text:
• Algorithm: AES-256-GCM (authenticated encryption)
  • Key Derivation: HKDF-SHA256 from ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY (format v2)
  • Nonce: Random for each encryption operation
  • Sensitive Fields: access_key_id, secret_access_key, session_token, api_token, api_key, password, client_secret

docs.title: Security Features
docs.text:
• Encrypted at rest: All credentials stored encrypted in database
  • RBAC protected: Only platform admins with platform.settings permission can access
  • Audit logging: All credential changes logged to platform_integration_audit_log
  • No plaintext storage: Credentials never stored in plaintext

docs.title: Sourcing the key from a key management service
docs.text: The platform reads ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY from its Secret; it does not call a key management service itself. To keep the key in AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault or similar, have that system deliver the value into the Secret the chart reads (platform.existingSecretName), for example with the External Secrets Operator, as described under Production Environment. The value must then never change: there is no re-keying of stored credentials (see Cannot Decrypt Existing Credentials).

docs.title: "Platform integration management will be disabled" Warning
docs.text:
Problem: ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY is not set.

Solution: 1. Docker Compose: set ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY in .env (see Docker Compose install) 2. Helm: verify platform.existingSecretName (or the chart-generated Secret) actually contains encryption-master-key 3. Restart the admin-service pod/container

docs.title: "Failed to encrypt config" Error
docs.text:
Problem: Encryption service failed to initialize.

Possible Causes: - ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY is empty - Key derivation failed - Key management service unavailable

Solution: 1. Verify ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY is set and not empty 2. Check service logs for detailed error messages 3. Verify key management service is accessible (if using one)

docs.title: Cannot Decrypt Existing Credentials
docs.text:
Problem: Error decrypting credentials after key change.

Cause: The encryption master key was changed, but existing credentials were encrypted with the old key.

Solution: - DO NOT change the encryption key if you have existing integrations - If you must change the key: set the new key, then re-enter every integration, device and connector credential you want to keep (each reports as undecryptable until replaced). There is no in-place re-key.

Prevention: keep the key with your backups, and deliver it from a secrets manager through platform.existingSecretName so it never changes by accident.

docs.title: Client address behind a proxy (auth-service)
docs.text:
auth-service keys its per-address sign-in and registration limits on the caller's address, and writes it to audit rows and impersonation tokens. It takes that address from the TCP connection, and reads X-Forwarded-For only when the connection comes from a peer listed in TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS (comma-separated IPs or CIDRs); it then uses the first address in the header that is not itself a trusted proxy. With the variable unset it trusts no one.

The chart sets it from trustedProxyCIDRs, which defaults to the private address ranges (where an in-cluster ingress controller lives). Narrow it to your ingress controller's pod CIDR if you can. Setting it to an empty list trusts nobody, so every request appears to come from the ingress controller and the per-address limits share one bucket. A Docker Compose install does not set it, with the same effect.

Failed sign-ins are counted per account and client address, and only failures count: signing in correctly never moves an account toward a lockout, and a stranger's failures from their own address cannot lock the owner out. When a lockout expires the account's failure count starts again from zero, so one typo afterwards does not lock it a second time.

Deactivating or deleting a user, resetting or changing a password, and revoking a session each write a per-user "tokens issued before this moment are invalid" entry to Redis, which every service's JWT middleware consults. It expires on its own once every older access token has (JWT_EXPIRY plus a few minutes). Because the check needs Redis, a service without REDIS_URL skips it and the token stays valid until it expires; every service that verifies tokens is deployed with Redis by the chart and by a release's compose.yaml. If Redis is unreachable the check fails open.

docs.text:
1. AWS KMS Integration - Direct integration with AWS KMS for key management
  2. Key Rotation - Automatic key rotation without downtime
  3. Multi-Key Support - Support for multiple encryption keys (for migration)
  4. Credential Rotation - Automated credential rotation for integrations

docs.title: Service-mesh mTLS
docs.text:
This covers the chart's in-cluster (service-mesh) mTLS — separate from and independent of your edge/browser-facing TLS certificate (tls.mode, tls.dnsName; see the Distribution repository's Helm guide). It encrypts and mutually authenticates traffic inside the cluster — every service-to-service call, plus the connections to Postgres and NATS — so that a compromised pod or a network tap inside the cluster cannot read or impersonate the platform's internal traffic.

If your edge certificate itself is issued by an internal/corporate CA (rather than a public one), that's a different gap — a pod calling back out to your edge hostname won't trust it either, since pods don't inherit the node's OS trust store. See Running with an internal CA for that case.

This is ON by default. A stock helm install ships encrypted internal transport. That means the two prerequisites below are required, not optional. The chart validates cert-manager's presence and fails the install fast with a clear message if its CRDs are absent, rather than failing mysteriously mid-apply.

There is no opt-out of the mesh. Agent and sensor mTLS (below) is mandatory under managed protocol 1 and its listener reuses the per-service mesh certificate, so the chart refuses serviceMtls.enabled set to false. The two datastore toggles, datastores.postgres.tls.enabled and datastores.nats.tls.enabled, stay separate choices: either may be false to keep that hop in the clear, and both require serviceMtls.enabled.

docs.title: Prerequisites (cluster infrastructure — the chart does not install these)
docs.text:
1. cert-manager — issues the per-service certs. See the prerequisites in the Distribution repository's Helm guide.
  2. Stakater Reloader — restarts pods when their auto-rotated cert Secret changes, so a renewal doesn't require a manual rollout: 
    helm repo add stakater https://stakater.github.io/stakater-charts
helm install reloader stakater/reloader \
  --namespace reloader --create-namespace

    If your cluster enforces the restricted Pod Security Standard, the Reloader chart's default container securityContext is rejected and its pod never starts (FailedCreate / 0 replicas). Add the two required fields: 

    helm install reloader stakater/reloader \
  --namespace reloader --create-namespace \
  --set reloader.deployment.containerSecurityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false \
  --set "reloader.deployment.containerSecurityContext.capabilities.drop={ALL}"
    Verify Reloader is actually 1/1 Running before enabling mTLS — if it isn't, certs rotate but pods never restart and mTLS breaks at the ~60-day renewal boundary.

docs.title: How the trust works
docs.text:
By default the chart provisions a self-signed Platform CA (a cert-manager Issuer + a 10-year CA cert) and issues every service a 90-day cert from it (rotationPolicy: Always, renewed 30 days out). This CA is private to the mesh — it is unrelated to your edge/browser certificate. The three data-plane toggles are decoupled so you can roll them out in stages:

serviceMtls:
  enabled: true            # HTTP service-to-service mTLS (gateway → backends, and S2S)

datastores:
  postgres:
    tls:
      enabled: true        # Postgres requires TLS; backends connect sslmode=verify-full
  nats:
    tls:
      enabled: true         # NATS requires a client cert (the shared token is retired)

Order of rollout — a fresh install gets all three at once. A brand-new helm install with the defaults brings up serviceMtls + Postgres TLS + NATS TLS together cleanly (there's no running datastore to migrate). The staging rule below matters for existing releases, not fresh installs.

Upgrading an existing release that ran with all three OFF (staged, not all-at-once). Do not flip all three in a single helm upgrade. Enable serviceMtls.enabled first (one upgrade — it provisions the Platform CA and the per-service certs the Postgres and NATS layers reuse), let the HTTP layer go healthy, then enable datastores.postgres.tls.enabled and datastores.nats.tls.enabled in a later upgrade. Each datastore toggle requires serviceMtls.enabled — they draw their certs and the in-pod ca.crt from it.

Toggling postgres.tls on a live release changes the schema-migration Job pod template. The schema-migration and rls-roles Job names embed a hash of the rendered pod template, so any pod-template change (TLS toggles, chart version bumps) creates a fresh Job instead of colliding with an immutable existing one — no manual Job deletion needed.

docs.title: Advanced: chain the mesh off your own root
docs.text:
If your security policy forbids any self-signed CA, even an internal one, point the Platform CA at an intermediate issued from your corporate root instead of the chart's self-signed bootstrap. Provide a Secret containing tls.crt + tls.key + ca.crt:

serviceMtls:
  enabled: true
  platformCa:
    externalCaSecretName: vistaplatform-platform-ca   # your intermediate CA

The entire mesh then chains to your root. This is a power-user option; the default self-signed Platform CA is appropriate for the large majority of deployments.

Bring-your-own Postgres/NATS (managed services). When datastores.postgres.enabled: false (e.g. a managed Postgres) the chart can't mint the Postgres server cert. Point serviceMtls.postgres.caSecretName / clientCertSecretName at your provider's CA and your client cert, and set serviceMtls.postgres.mode to match what the managed service enforces (require / verify-ca / verify-full).

docs.title: Agent and sensor mTLS (agentMtls) — required by the managed protocol
docs.text:
This is a separate toggle from serviceMtls, covering the outbound calls device agents and sensors make into the platform after they enroll: job polling, result submission, heartbeats, discovery submission, command acknowledgement and certificate rotation.

Agents and sensors speak managed protocol 1, which has no unauthenticated mode: every call after enrollment presents the client certificate issued at registration, and the backends refuse anything else. The certificate must reach the service intact, its CN must be the agent/sensor id, it must chain to that tenant's CA, and it must be that identity's current certificate. A path UUID is never a credential.

Enrollment always sends a certificate signing request: the agent's private key never leaves the machine it runs on, and the platform never generates one. The platform issues the agent's secret at enrollment and at every certificate rotation, and seals each job's credentials with that secret only.

Certificate rotation requires the current certificate. Rotation mints a new, legitimately CA-signed certificate and supersedes the old one. An agent or sensor that has lost its certificate cannot rotate — re-enroll it with a registration key.

docs.title: Prerequisites (cluster infrastructure — the chart does not install these)
docs.text:
1. serviceMtls.enabled: true (the default). The agent listener reuses the per-service mesh certificate as its server certificate.
  2. A cluster-Traefik TLS-passthrough entrypoint on agentMtls.port (default 8444). The edge must not terminate this traffic, or the client certificate never reaches the backend. The chart owns only the IngressRouteTCP, not Traefik's static entrypoint configuration.
  3. A DNS name per backend resolving to that entrypoint, set in values:
agentMtls:
  enabled: true
  backends:
    sensor-manager:
      dnsName: sensors.example.com
    device-interrogation-service:
      dnsName: agents.example.com

Both backends need their own hostname. They share one passthrough entrypoint and are told apart by HostSNI, so a single name cannot serve both. Keep them distinct from each other and distinct from tls.dnsName — that host is terminated at the edge.

The chart fails the install rather than open a listener nothing can reach. It fails if either hostname is missing, and also if a backend entry is deleted — removing a key does not opt a service out. The deployment template keys AGENT_MTLS_REQUIRED off the presence of that entry, so a missing key emits no value and the service falls back to its built-in default of true, demanding a client certificate that no route can deliver.

The Docker Compose install needs no DNS entries. The compose file each release attaches sets AGENT_MTLS_REQUIRED=true for both services and publishes their agent listeners on 127.0.0.1 (SENSOR_MANAGER_AGENT_HOST_PORT, default 8444, and DEVICE_INTERROGATION_AGENT_HOST_PORT, default 8446). With no Platform CA of its own, each service creates a listener certificate for localhost on first start (AGENT_TLS_CERT_DIR, kept in a Docker volume across restarts) and hands that CA to the agent at enrollment. An agent on the same host enrolls over plain HTTP through the gateway (http://localhost:8080) and switches to https://localhost:<agent port> on its own; an agent on another host cannot use that certificate, which is why compose is a single-host evaluation install. Compose runs no service mesh.

docs.title: Migrating an existing install (do this before upgrading)
docs.text:
Agents and sensors enrolled while agentMtls was off call the edge host and hold no usable transport for their certificate. After the upgrade they are rejected with 401 until migrated.

  1. Inventory what is enrolled. Discovery → Sensors & Agents lists every agent and sensor with its last check-in.
  2. Provision the passthrough entrypoint and DNS (prerequisites 2 and 3 above) before the upgrade, and verify the host resolves and accepts TCP on the port.
  3. Upgrade with the dnsNames set. Every backend restarts.
  4. Re-point or re-enroll each agent/sensor. Re-registering with a registration key is the reliable path: the registration response hands back the client certificate, the Platform CA as server trust anchor, and the passthrough URL, which the agent persists and uses from then on.
  5. Confirm. Each agent/sensor returns to a healthy last-check-in; a failure shows as 401 in the sensor-manager / device-interrogation-service logs naming the missing or mismatched certificate.

Staging the upgrade in two steps (mesh first, agents second) keeps the blast radius small, exactly as with the datastore toggles above.

docs.title: Turning agent mTLS off is refused
docs.text: There is no opt-out. The backends demand the agent's client certificate on every call after enrollment (managed protocol 1), so a release without the agent listener would enroll agents and sensors and then answer every later call with 401. The chart therefore refuses to render when agentMtls.enabled is set to false, and names the two hostnames to set instead. A values file that still carries the key must drop it (or set it to true).

docs.title: Single-node clusters: avoid the rolling-upgrade CPU deadlock
docs.text:
On a one-node cluster, a helm upgrade that rolls every service at once briefly runs old + new pods together, doubling CPU requests (the scheduler packs by requests, not usage). If that exceeds the node's allocatable CPU, the recreated postgres-0 can't schedule, the schema migration can't connect, and the upgrade hangs until it times out. Either size the node for ~2× steady-state CPU requests before upgrading, or set strategy: Recreate on the backends so pods replace in place without surging (brief per-service downtime; on a release that is already deployed, see the production checklist's Single-node clusters for the one-time patch that switch needs). If an upgrade does wedge, helm rollback restores the previous release.

This applies to config-only upgrades too, not just version bumps: the pod templates carry a checksum/config hash of the app ConfigMap, so changing any value that lands there (tls.dnsName, appConfig.*, …) deliberately rolls every backend — env vars are injected at pod start only, and without the roll the running pods would silently keep the old config.

docs.title: Asset Approval Workflow Issues
docs.text:
Discovery ran, and Inventory does not show what you expected. This page is organised by symptom, and the first one is by far the most common — and is not a fault at all.

The model this page assumes. An asset is one thing — a server, a switch, a bucket, a service — with a class, the identifiers it is known by, and the endpoints it listens on. A host exposing five services is one asset with five endpoints, not five assets. Queries below read assets, asset_identifiers, asset_endpoints and asset_history. If you arrived here with older notes, see What replaced what at the bottom.

Substitute your tenant's UUID for <tenant> throughout. Every query is written against a single tenant on purpose: every table here is row-level-security scoped, and a query without a tenant predicate is a query that will surprise you.

docs.title: Symptom: discovery ran, but Inventory is empty
docs.text:
Sensors are reporting, batches are processed, external connections appear — and Inventory shows nothing, with certificates and crypto_implementations at zero rows.

This is the designed approval workflow, not a broken pipeline. New assets land with asset_status = 'pending_approval', and their certificates and crypto configurations are deliberately deferred — held with the pending asset — until it is approved in Discovery → Approvals. Only approval materializes them into the inventory tables. Auto-approval is per prefix and is off by default.

Confirm it in one query:

SELECT asset_status, count(*)
FROM assets
WHERE tenant_id = '<tenant>' AND deleted_at IS NULL
GROUP BY asset_status
ORDER BY asset_status;

A large pending_approval count and a small (or zero) monitoring count is the answer: the work is waiting for a person, in Discovery → Approvals.

To see what is being held with each pending asset — the certificates and crypto configurations that will appear the moment it is approved:

SELECT a.id,
       a.display_name,
       a.class_key,
       count(d.id) AS deferred
FROM assets a
LEFT JOIN deferred_crypto_findings d
       ON d.tenant_id = a.tenant_id AND d.asset_id = a.id AND d.replayed_at IS NULL
WHERE a.tenant_id = '<tenant>'
  AND a.asset_status = 'pending_approval'
  AND a.deleted_at IS NULL
GROUP BY a.id, a.display_name, a.class_key
ORDER BY deferred DESC
LIMIT 20;

deferred_crypto_findings is a holding pen, not an attribute of the thing: a row is replayed (replayed_at set) when its asset becomes monitoring, by whatever route. A pending asset with 0 deferred findings is normal — it means nothing cryptographic was observed on it yet. Under identity admission enforce, a finding waits on its observation instead (observation_id set, asset_id empty until it is replayed).

If an asset is monitoring and rows for it still show replayed_at empty with a last_error, the replay failed and is retried every five minutes; the inventory-service log names the asset.

Two things exist to make this self-evident before anyone reaches for SQL: the discovery-processor batch log reports internal findings split by monitoring/pending and notes the deferral rather than printing 0 asset findings, and the Inventory page shows a pending-approval banner with a count and a link to the queue.

docs.title: Symptom: assets keep queuing when you expected auto-approval
docs.text:
Two independent gates decide this, and both are off until someone turns them on.

1. The right switch for the source. Sensor discoveries are auto-approved by a prefix's Auto-approve setting (Inventory → Networks, open the prefix). Cloud resources are not — they are auto-approved by their account: the "Auto-approve resources" switch on the integration under Discovery → Cloud (on by default).

-- Sensor discoveries: the prefix setting, and the rule it generates.
SELECT prefix, description, network_type, auto_approve_discoveries, auto_approve_sources
FROM prefixes
WHERE tenant_id = '<tenant>' AND vrf_id IS NULL AND status NOT IN ('rejected', 'archived')
ORDER BY prefix;

-- Cloud resources: the account switch, and the account each integration names.
SELECT integration_name, integration_type, account_id, auto_approve_resources
FROM platform_integrations
WHERE tenant_id = '<tenant>' AND deleted_at IS NULL
ORDER BY integration_name;

auto_approve_discoveries = false is the default for every prefix. For cloud, the usual answer when resources still queue is an empty account_id: an AWS integration learns its account on the first successful Test connection, and until then there is no account for a rule to be about. A resource whose own ARN names a different account than the integration's is approved only by that account's switch.

2. The tenant's auto-approval rules, which are queries now. A rule is a query-language string over the observation target, not a JSON object interpreted by a hand-written evaluator:

SELECT name, is_active, query
FROM discovery_auto_approval_rules
WHERE tenant_id = '<tenant>'
ORDER BY name;

Read the query column as the rule: class:server and environment:production approves exactly what it says. Two things worth knowing when one does not fire: an empty query matches every observation (a rule that auto-approves everything — deliberately expressible, and deliberately something a person has to type), and a query is validated when it is saved, so a rule that stored at all is a rule that parses. A rule that parses and never matches is a rule about the wrong thing, not a typo.

docs.title: Symptom: the queue is full of merge proposals, and nothing new appears
docs.text:
Discovery → Approvals holds two kinds of work. Pending assets are one; the other is a merge proposal — the identification engine's report that a new sighting matched more than one existing asset, or matched one it is not confident enough to fold into. Nothing is ever merged for you: a proposal waits for a person to say "these are the same thing" or "keep them separate".

Merge proposals are rows in asset_history, not a table of their own:

SELECT seq,
       asset_id,
       created_at,
       changes_json ->> 'fingerprint' AS fingerprint,
       changes_json
FROM asset_history
WHERE tenant_id = '<tenant>'
  AND action = 'merge_proposed'
  AND COALESCE(changes_json ->> 'status', 'pending') = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at DESC;

changes_json carries the candidate assets and the identifiers that matched them — which is what the Approvals row renders. Deciding a proposal writes status into it, so it drops out of the query above.

One proposal per question. A unique index on (tenant_id, changes_json->>'fingerprint') for pending proposals means a collector that re-observes the same conflict every fifteen minutes does not deposit 96 identical work items a day. If you see many proposals with DIFFERENT fingerprints for what looks like one machine, that is a real signal: something is producing observations that identify differently each time.

To see why the engine thinks a particular asset is ambiguous, read its identifiers — the scope is usually the answer, because a hostname or an IP identifies only within its prefix:

SELECT kind, value, scope, source_kind, source_ref, last_seen_at
FROM asset_identifiers
WHERE tenant_id = '<tenant>' AND asset_id = '<asset>'
ORDER BY kind;

And the asset's own story, in order:

SELECT seq, action, source, actor_user_id, created_at, changes_json
FROM asset_history
WHERE tenant_id = '<tenant>' AND asset_id = '<asset>'
ORDER BY seq;

Order by seq, never by created_at: several history rows are written inside one transaction and therefore carry the same timestamp, so ordering by time returns them in whatever order the planner chose.

docs.title: Symptom: cloud discoveries are not reaching Inventory
docs.text:
Cloud discoveries go through the same pipeline as sensor discoveries:

  1. device-interrogation-service discovers the cloud resources (AWS, Azure, GCP).
  2. They are written to sensor_discoveries with metadata->>'discovery_method' = 'cloud_api'.
  3. discovery-processor-service is woken as soon as they are written and processes the batches (a 60-second poll catches anything it was not woken for).
  4. A cloud discovery is classified by its cloud_provider/cloud_region — the per-region cloud prefix — not by its address. Most cloud resources have no address at all, and an asset with no endpoint is a real answer rather than a gap: a bucket or a key store has nothing listening on a port.
  5. Assets land monitoring when their account's "Auto-approve resources" switch is on (the default), and pending_approval in Discovery → Approvals when it is off. Either way they hang off the account's Cloud Account asset.

Check that the discoveries arrived at all:

SELECT batch_id, count(*) AS rows, min(created_at) AS first_seen
FROM sensor_discoveries
WHERE metadata ->> 'discovery_method' = 'cloud_api'
GROUP BY batch_id
ORDER BY first_seen DESC;

Unprocessed rows:

SELECT id, batch_id, created_at
FROM sensor_discoveries
WHERE metadata ->> 'discovery_method' = 'cloud_api'
  AND processed_at IS NULL
ORDER BY created_at;

If rows are arriving and never processed, check the processor:

docker compose logs discovery-processor-service

Cloud discovery runs through the Platform Device Interrogation Agent system sensor — verify that sensor exists and is active for the tenant.

docs.title: What replaced what
docs.text:
Older runbooks (and older habits) reach for tables and a screen that no longer exist. A query naming any of these fails at runtime with relation … does not exist, per query — which is exactly the error this codebase has historically swallowed behind a 200, so it is worth recognising.

If your notes say Read instead network_assets (any form) assets — one row per thing, with class_key / class_path an asset's ip_address / port asset_endpoints — one row per network face an asset's asset_type assets.class_key, or class_path for a whole subtree devices assets joined to asset_management (a device is an asset with management configured) discovery_approval_queue sensor_discoveries + the approval state on assets — this table is dropped, not merely deprecated "import the discovery results" Nothing to do: a job's findings reach inventory server-side. No API accepts a caller-supplied approval status.

  • Infrastructure Assets and Crypto Configurations — assets, endpoints, classes and what hangs off which.
  • Database Migrations — there is no separate migration file; schema changes live in scripts/database/schema.sql.
  • Device auto-discovery troubleshooting.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Guide
docs.text: This guide covers common issues and their solutions.

docs.title: Login Screen Not Loading / Stuck on Loading
docs.text:
Symptom: Login page shows a loading spinner indefinitely and never displays the login form.

Cause: Cached authentication state — expired or invalid cookies — can cause authentication initialization to hang. Auth uses httpOnly cookies exclusively; there is no localStorage token to clear.

Immediate Fix:

  1. Clear site data (Recommended) Clear cookies and site data for the app origin (e.g. http://localhost:3000):
  2. Chrome/Edge: Application tab → Storage → Clear site data
  3. Firefox: Application → Storage → Clear All

  4. Or clear cookies for the site in browser settings and refresh.

  5. Clear All Site Data (if step 1 doesn't resolve it):

  6. Chrome/Edge: Settings → Privacy → Clear browsing data → Cookies and other site data
  7. Firefox: Settings → Privacy & Security → Cookies and Site Data → Clear Data
  8. Safari: Develop → Empty Caches

Prevention: The application now automatically: - Validates token structure and expiration - Clears invalid/expired tokens automatically - Shows a "Clear cache" button if stuck loading - Has a 10-second timeout on authentication initialization

docs.title: Token Expired Errors
docs.text:
Symptom: "Token expired" or 401 Unauthorized errors.

Fix: The application should automatically refresh tokens. If it doesn't: 1. Log out and log back in 2. Clear cache as described above 3. Check browser console for errors

docs.title: Go Version Mismatch
docs.text:
Symptom: go: go.work requires go >= 1.26.0 (running go X.X.X)

Fix: Upgrade Go to 1.26: 

# Download and install Go 1.26
cd /tmp
wget https://go.dev/dl/go1.26.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz
sudo rm -rf /usr/local/go
sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.26.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz
sudo update-alternatives --install /usr/bin/go go /usr/local/go/bin/go 100
sudo update-alternatives --set go /usr/local/go/bin/go

docs.title: Docker Build Failures
docs.text:
Symptom: Docker builds fail with "go.work not found" or module resolution errors.

Fix: 1. Ensure build context is repository root (.) 2. Check Dockerfile uses WORKDIR /workspace and builds from workspace root 3. Verify GOTOOLCHAIN=local is set in Dockerfile

docs.title: Services Not Starting
docs.text:
Symptom: Services fail to start or crash immediately.

Fix: 1. Check logs: docker compose logs <service-name> 2. Verify environment variables: docker compose config 3. Check database connectivity: docker compose ps postgres 4. Restart services: docker compose restart <service-name>

docs.title: Port Conflicts
docs.text:
Symptom: "Port already in use" errors.

Fix: 1. Find process using port: lsof -i :8080 (or your port) 2. Stop conflicting service or change port in .env 3. Restart: docker compose down && docker compose up -d

docs.title: Slow Builds
docs.text:
Symptom: Builds are slower than expected.

Fix: 1. Validate cache: make validate-cache 2. Clean cache if needed: docker builder prune -f 3. Pre-warm cache: make install-deps

docs.title: Docker Cache Issues
docs.text:
Symptom: Docker builds not using cache.

Fix: 1. Check Docker BuildKit is enabled: export DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 2. Verify .dockerignore is correct 3. Check Dockerfile layer ordering 4. Clean and rebuild: docker builder prune -f

docs.title: API Gateway Not Responding
docs.text:
Symptom: 502 Bad Gateway or connection refused.

Fix: 1. Check gateway logs: docker compose logs api-gateway 2. Verify Traefik config: docker compose exec api-gateway traefik healthcheck 3. Check service health: docker compose ps 4. Restart gateway: docker compose restart api-gateway

docs.title: CORS Errors
docs.text:
Symptom: CORS errors in browser console.

Fix: 1. Verify API Gateway is running: curl http://localhost:8080/health 2. Check CORS configuration in Traefik dynamic config (config/traefik/) 3. Verify frontend origin matches CORS allowed origins 4. make test-cors is internal CI tooling and is not in this repository; to check manually, curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:8080/api/v1/auth-service/health -H "Origin: http://localhost:3000" -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: GET" and confirm an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header comes back

docs.title: Migration Failures
docs.text:
Symptom: Database migrations fail or services can't connect.

Fix: 1. Check Postgres logs: docker compose logs postgres 2. Verify database exists: docker compose exec postgres psql -U crypto_user -l 3. Check connection string in .env 4. Reset database if needed: make db-reset (⚠️ destroys data)

docs.title: Connection Pool Exhausted
docs.text:
Symptom: "too many connections" errors.

Fix: 1. Check connection pool settings in service configs 2. Reduce concurrent connections 3. Restart Postgres: docker compose restart postgres

docs.title: "Sensor limit exceeded: 0/0" registering the first sensor
docs.text:
Symptom: Sensor registration returns HTTP 402 with Sensor limit exceeded: 0/0, on a tenant that has no sensors. Adding an asset fails the same way.

Cause: The tenant has no subscription tier. Every capacity limit then falls back to the platform default, which is deliberately conservative — 0 sensors, 0 assets. It is a misconfiguration wearing a quota error's clothes: since v0.5.1 the message says so explicitly, but a tenant that signed up on v0.5.0 or earlier reports the bare 0/0.

Fix: Upgrade to v0.5.1 or later — the seed applied on every helm upgrade puts tier-less tenants on the community tier (unlimited capacity, no paid capability), and new signups are placed there at creation. To confirm, or to repair without upgrading:

SELECT t.name, COALESCE(st.name, '(no tier)') AS tier
FROM tenants t LEFT JOIN subscription_tiers st ON st.id = t.subscription_tier_id;

A platform admin can also assign a tier per tenant from the admin UI under Tenants.

Related setting: DEFAULT_SIGNUP_TIER on auth-service selects which tier new tenants land on. It defaults to community and should stay there for any self-hosted install; set it only if you are running a multi-tenant service that wants signups on a trial tier. In the Helm chart, set it via backends.auth-service.extraEnv.

docs.title: Cloud Discoveries Not Appearing in Discovery Approvals
docs.text:
Symptom: Cloud discovery jobs complete successfully, but discovered assets don't appear on the Discovery → Approvals page.

Troubleshooting Steps:

  1. Check sensor_discoveries table for cloud entries: 

    SELECT batch_id, COUNT(*) as count, MIN(created_at) as first_seen, 
       MAX(processed_at) as last_processed
FROM sensor_discoveries 
WHERE metadata->>'discovery_method' = 'cloud_api'
GROUP BY batch_id
ORDER BY first_seen DESC
LIMIT 10;

  2. Verify discoveries are unprocessed: 

    SELECT COUNT(*) as unprocessed_count
FROM sensor_discoveries 
WHERE metadata->>'discovery_method' = 'cloud_api'
AND processed_at IS NULL;

  3. Check discovery-processor-service logs: 

    docker compose logs discovery-processor-service | grep -i cloud

  4. Verify discovery-processor-service is running: 

    docker compose ps discovery-processor-service

  5. Check for processing errors: 

    SELECT batch_id, error_message, created_at
FROM sensor_discoveries 
WHERE metadata->>'discovery_method' = 'cloud_api'
AND error_message IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;

Common Causes: - discovery-processor-service is not running or crashed - Batch processing failed due to validation errors - Prefix classification failed - Inventory service API errors during asset import

Fix: 1. Restart discovery-processor-service: docker compose restart discovery-processor-service 2. Check service health: docker compose logs discovery-processor-service --tail 100 3. Verify Platform Device Interrogation Agent system sensor exists and is active 4. Check inventory-service is responding: curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/inventory-service/health

docs.title: Cloud Discovery Batch Stuck in Processing
docs.text:
Symptom: Cloud discoveries remain in sensor_discoveries with processed_at IS NULL for extended periods.

Troubleshooting: 1. Check if batch is locked (being processed): 

SELECT batch_id, COUNT(*) as count, MIN(created_at) as created
FROM sensor_discoveries 
WHERE metadata->>'discovery_method' = 'cloud_api'
AND processed_at IS NULL
GROUP BY batch_id;

  1. Review discovery-processor-service logs for that batch_id
  2. Check for database locks or connection issues
  3. Verify batch has valid data (IP addresses, ports, protocols)

Fix: If batch is truly stuck, you may need to manually mark it as failed or restart the discovery-processor-service to retry processing.

docs.title: Vista Platform Core 1.0.0 — full list of changes
docs.text:
Released 2026-09-21. The release summary — highlights, what breaks, what each edition includes, and how to verify the signatures — is in the CHANGELOG published with that release. This page is the complete, per-change record behind it.

1.0.0 replaced the asset model, so its entry is far longer than a release entry normally is; keeping it here rather than in the changelog is what lets the changelog stay readable.

docs.title: Trustworthy discovery RC rollout
docs.text:
The staged RC enhancements distinguish established, operator-confirmed and legacy identity from monitoring approval, type and assessment coverage. Weak observations are retained outside Inventory, with source evidence, explicit confirmation/link/ dismiss decisions and separate counts. Reviewed merges select a survivor and sources, check a current server preview and preserve associations and audit history. There is no merge undo or split workflow.

The coupled enrichment release queries configured sources before bounded DNS and TLS/SSH checks through a suitable observing collector. Existing credentials, network exclusions, protocol policy and sensitive-device restrictions still apply. The tenant's Trustworthy discovery settings control prospective activation and pause; existing records remain visible and keep their identities and associations. Once activated, pause retains incoming evidence instead of restoring permissive asset creation. See the operator guide.

Admission-enabled acceptance passed all 310 required checks across the three estates, every reference stage, restart/resume and two distinct certificates on one asset. Canary baseline reconciliation, the required 24-hour/two-cycle canary and live Windows deployment acceptance remain separate operational gates. Historical failed acceptance runs remain preserved.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Inventory shows a device heard advertised on another, configured tenant network as a provisional item — visible, unverified, excluded from the asset allowance until a collector on the device's own network corroborates it in place (same asset id, same history). (#1898, #1900, #1901)

  • Tickets can be raised directly from Remediation → Queue, for any subject, without starting from a finding or an alert. Filing a ticket no longer requires the permission to resolve one — a viewer who spots a problem can report it; editing, commenting and deleting stay privileged. (#1911)

  • Ticket categories now follow the finding producer one for one — compliance, cryptography, post-quantum, certificate, vulnerability, lifecycle, inventory, configuration and drift — so the work queue's category filter separates them. Every new ticket also carries a default due date derived from its priority, which is what the overdue and due-soon views and notifications act on. (#1911)
  • Remediation → Progress: opened against resolved over time, average resolution time, per-category backlog and post-quantum readiness. (#1911)
  • Tickets can be edited in place — assignee, category, priority, severity, due date, tags, resolution notes and an external ticket link — and deleted, with the deletion and the ticket's content recorded in the audit trail. (#1911)

  • Three further dashboards under one Dashboard section — Assets, Compliance and post-quantum readiness — alongside the existing Overview, which is unchanged. The post-quantum page surfaces the per-algorithm-family migration worklist and the catalogue's recommended replacement. (#1907)

  • Device agents can report bounded outbound connections on segments without a sensor. Deploy the updated device-agent binary first, then opt in locally with HOST_INVENTORY_CONNECTIONS_ENABLED=true, or set collect_connections: true on a remote host-inventory job. Existing agents and default settings do not begin collecting peers after a platform upgrade. Each snapshot is coalesced and capped at 256 peers; local ephemeral ports do not create new identities, and accepted TCP connections are excluded. Public destinations become external connections attributed to the reporting host. Private destinations follow existing network ownership and approval rules; registering an auto-approving network promotes the existing pending asset on a subsequent collection. Windows peer collection is TCP-only; Linux and macOS also report connected UDP peers when the OS exposes them. Peerless UDP bindings remain unknown-role facts, rather than claimed listening services. The support command --host-inventory-once excludes outbound peers. See Host inventory. (#1876)

  • An endpoint that has gone quiet is now marked stale. asset_endpoints.status has allowed active / stale / closed since the table was written and nothing ever wrote stale, so a filter on it returned nothing. The hygiene pass now moves an endpoint to stale once nothing has observed it for 30 days — the same boundary as the Stale finding — and back to active when something sees it again. closed is untouched: that is an authoritative "the host says this socket is gone", and only a host inventory writes it. The exposure rules stop judging an endpoint once it goes stale — an unobserved socket is not a measured exposure — but they no longer resolve its findings either, and port-profile drift still counts the port as present: "nothing has looked" must not reach a user as "the port closed" or as "the exposure is fixed".

  • Port-profile drift findings name the endpoints that changed. A port_profile_changed finding listed the ports that opened and closed but not which face they appeared on; it now carries each endpoint's address and id, so a host with several addresses says which one moved.

  • Vulnerable to quantum attack findings now name the KEY, not only the service and the certificate. The finding registry has always declared pqc_vulnerable as being about a crypto configuration, a certificate or a key, and nothing produced the third. The key is usually the subject a migration is planned against: a public key is recorded once in the key inventory and shared by every certificate and service presenting it, so one RSA key across forty hosts is one migration rather than forty. The crypto producer now classifies each key in use against the same NIST IR 8547 denylist of Shor-breakable primitives it applies everywhere else — symmetric keys raise nothing, post-quantum keys raise nothing, and a key whose algorithm resolves to no catalogue row is unclassified rather than assumed either way. Only keys actually linked to an asset are judged. Key findings are reachable from every asset using the key — finding:(…), the has_findings facet, the asset page's Findings tab and the risk roll-up all resolve through the one subject walk, which learned the key path in the same change.

  • A sortable "Last checked" column on Inventory → Software, and a "least recently checked" sort. When the lifecycle catalogue last had an answer for a product was already recorded but reached the UI only as a tooltip, so "which of my products has nobody looked at lately?" could not be answered without hovering every row. Products no completed pass has ever recorded an answer for sort FIRST, ahead of long-ago-checked ones: that is the weaker state, not a missing value. GET /software/products gains sort=eol_checked.

  • The command palette's ask mode now renders asset-class and relationship rows too, like its search mode — it rendered asset rows alone, so the same question offered different answers depending on whether it was typed as a search or asked in words.

  • A Class history panel on every asset, recording every class it has held. Core. An asset's class is an input to most of the platform — which findings a producer writes, which approval rules match, which compliance measurements apply — and it lived in a single mutable column. Change it and the previous answer was gone: nothing anywhere could say a printer had ever been a printer, so a finding written before the change was indistinguishable from one written after it, and "was this thing reclassified?" had no answer. A new asset_class_history table records one row per transition, with both ends named, the mechanism that moved it (set at discovery, accepted in Approvals, edited by a person, stated by an import), the person when there was one, and the rule ids or model id behind it. Written at all three places a class can move, inside the same transaction as the change. Read it on Inventory → an asset → History, above the general change log. An empty panel says "no recorded class change", not "never changed" — an asset created before this record exists has no entry, which is a different claim.

  • An interrogated neighbour's class is now argued from what it advertised, not from its MAC prefix alone. Core. A device reported over LLDP or CDP — by a Cisco switch, a Palo Alto firewall or a UniFi controller — reached the classifier as a MAC address and nothing else. An OUI names a manufacturer, and every manufacturer that matters makes switches, access points and desk phones alike, so almost every neighbour came back "Unknown host" while the interrogators were parsing, and then discarding, the device's own statement of what it is. The advertised product, software version and 802.1AB/CDP capability bits now travel with the peer and reach the classification rules. Each is a strict projection, never a copy: the product is the segment before the first comma of a system description and the version is the version token, because a system description is free text an operator can put a secret into. And a segment that names a credential at all — "snmp community …", a password, a key — is dropped whole rather than kept, so the defence does not rest on the operator having typed the product first.

  • A "Changed since baseline" alert. Core. The drift producer has been writing findings — a device class never seen on a segment before, a protocol an asset has not spoken, a changed set of listening ports, a certificate from a new issuer — with nothing on the Alerts page ever mentioning them. There is now a drift_detected alert type, on by default and switchable under Settings → Notifications & Alerts → Alert Rules, raising one alert per subject and grading it by the worst open drift finding. Its severity is the finding's own: drift has no second scale (no CVSS, no deadline) to grade on, so inventing one would be a second opinion about a judgement already made. It auto-resolves when the findings stop being detected — which includes somebody resolving one because the change was planned.

  • The subject of an alert is a link. Core. Remediation → Alerts rendered the Subject column as plain text, so the page that exists to be triaged told you which asset and then left you to go and find it. Asset, software install, crypto configuration, control and certificate subjects now drill straight through. Subject types with no id-addressable destination yet (sensor, agent, discovery job, framework, and the platform-track subjects) stay plain text deliberately: a link that lands on a page which cannot resolve the subject reads as "nothing wrong here". The install and configuration links name the findings lens explicitly, because the Findings page's crypto-risk lenses cannot honour a subject filter — landing on one would have shown an unfiltered list under a banner claiming it was filtered.

  • The End of life column on the Software tab and the Software lens now gives a supported package its credit. Core. It used to read "Not assessed" for every install without an end-of-life finding, because nothing on the install said whether the lifecycle catalogue had resolved it to a supported cycle, had it with no published date, or had never heard of it — so a supported package and an unknown one looked identical. The eol producer now records, per install and in the same transaction as its findings, what the catalogue resolved, and the column reads that record: Supported until 2028-04-01, No date published, Not in catalogue, or Not assessed — the last now meaning only that no completed check has recorded an answer (the check has not run since the install was seen, the install is no longer present, or its finding was closed). Hover a cell for the date the catalogue was last checked. Nothing re-runs the resolution in a list query; a closed finding does not turn into "Supported". GET …/software and GET /software/products carry the widened eol_state and a new eol_assessed_at.

  • The auto-accept threshold now covers every way a sighting reaches us (asset-inventory workstream 4.6a, ADR-0002 D3). Core.

Setting a matcher score at or above which the platform may merge two of your assets without asking used to govern inventory intakes only. Device interrogation, the cloud collectors, and the neighbours an interrogated device reports went through a different identification engine that did not read the setting — so those sightings were never auto-accepted, whatever you had set. That failed safe, and it was disclosed rather than hidden, but the same host reaches the platform both ways: which collector happened to see it decided whether your threshold applied.

It applies to all of them now. The threshold is read per sighting, on the transaction that resolves it, so turning it off takes effect on the very next observation. Nothing else about it changed: the same four conditions still have to hold — you set a threshold above zero, the score is at or above it, no serial / cloud id / agent id / CMDB sys_id disagrees, and every asset involved is already in service, not still waiting in Approvals — and every auto-accepted merge still writes an audit event and appears on Discovery → Approvals under "Auto-merged by the matcher (last 30 days)", whichever collector's sighting caused it.

The scope sentence on Settings → Policies → Identification rules and in the Asset approval guide has been corrected to match.

  • Interrogated neighbours can now be classified through Approvals (asset-inventory workstreams 4.6a, closing a 2.10b/4.2 limit). Core.

When a switch or firewall reports its neighbours, the platform runs your classification rules over what it learned about each one. Where a neighbour was a host the inventory already held, the answer was computed and then thrown away: a device your rules clearly identify stayed Unknown host for ever, and nothing said an answer had been discarded.

Those answers now appear as class proposals on Discovery → Approvals, exactly as they do for a host a sensor discovers — with the rule they came from cited, and the class the asset holds today shown beside the proposed one. A class is still never overwritten, and a class the learned classifier proposed is still marked as inferred rather than as a rule, so what argued for a class stays auditable.

  • A model provider can now be configured through the chart (ADR-0008, gate 4). A new ai: block in values.yaml — provider, baseUrl, model, allowPrivateEndpoints, maxTokens, timeout, and an apiKey block naming the environment variable and an operator-supplied Secret — renders the AI_* settings into the shared app ConfigMap and injects the credential on every backend. Before this there was no AI_* value anywhere in the chart, so on the shipped Helm path no generative capability could ever answer, whatever edition was installed.

It is off by default and the product is complete with it off: every AI capability has a rule-based behaviour behind it, and Settings → AI assistant states what that behaviour is per capability. When ai.provider is empty the block renders nothing at all, so an existing release's ConfigMap is byte-identical across the upgrade and the checksum/config annotation does not roll every backend.

The credential reaches every backend rather than only the four that own a seam, deliberately: GET /tenant/ai is the single availability answer both UIs read before rendering any AI control, auth-service serves it and owns no seam, and the Anthropic client refuses to construct without a key — so a narrower injection would hide every AI control in the product while the capability underneath it worked. A misspelled provider is refused at install time by values.schema.json rather than degrading to "no provider" with a warning in a pod log. New operator guide: docsv4/core/operate/configuration/ai-provider.md.

  • The drift finding producer (asset-inventory workstream 4.7, ADR-0005 D3). Four kinds, judged against the tenant's own recent history rather than against any catalogue: new_class_in_segment, unexpected_protocol, port_profile_changed and new_issuer. All four write through the shared shared/findings/producer writer and run in the nightly finding-producer job beside eol and vulnerability.

The baseline is a window, and the window is the tenant's. tenant_admin_settings.config.drift.baseline_days (default 30, bounds 7–365) is read on every pass and never cached, and is edited under Settings → Asset Lifecycle → Drift baseline. Everything first observed inside the window is a candidate; everything older is the baseline. No new table: every baseline is derived from timestamps the inventory already carries (assets.first_discovered_at, asset_endpoints.first_seen_at/last_seen_at, crypto_implementations.first_discovered_at).

Nothing is drift without something to compare against. A tenant observed for less than one full window raises nothing and sweeps nothing — "we have not been watching long enough to tell" is not "the condition went away", and a new organization is not told that every asset it owns is new. The same rule applies per subject: an asset with no protocol, port or certificate history older than the window, and a network segment newer than the window, are reported as un-evaluable rather than as changed.

A drift finding closes when the change ages INTO the baseline, as well as when the condition disappears. And an observation_key on every finding means a person's decision survives: resolving "started speaking SSH" is not undone by the next pass, while a genuinely different observation on the same host re-opens the finding rather than being swallowed by the earlier resolve. Suppression, being a standing decision about the condition, is never re-opened.

Coverage is what the pass could compare. Every completed pass records its coverage through Writer.MarkAssessed, in the same transaction as its findings and its sweep (workstream 3.2), so drift joins an asset's risk_assessed_by — but only where that asset had a history of its own to be compared against, plus any asset a finding was raised on. An asset first seen inside the window, and every asset of an organization still warming up, are deliberately NOT claimed: "we could not compare yet" must not read as "we compared and it was fine".

Evidence carries the baseline, the observation, the window bounds and the timestamps — and for new_issuer, the issuer DN and the certificate fingerprint, never the certificate body. Loopback-bound sockets (bound_local = true) are excluded from the port profile; sockets whose binding is unknown are kept, because that is every endpoint a network scan found. The Findings inspector renders the two sides of the comparison side by side.

  • The configuration and hygiene finding producers (asset-inventory workstream 3.5, ADR-0005 D3), on the shared writer the eol and vulnerability producers landed with.

Configuration judges how a device is managed and what it exposes. Two sources, both already collected: the mgmt.plaintext / mgmt.protocol facts device interrogation writes — the SNMP v2c seed is the first plaintext_management finding — and a reviewed Go rule table over asset_endpoints covering Telnet, FTP and SNMP v1/v2c management, plus unauthenticated datastores (Redis, memcached, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, etcd, CouchDB), the plaintext Docker API and kubelet read-only port, rsh/rlogin, and NFS/rpcbind/TFTP. Three restraints are the substance: a port rule is suppressed the moment something MEASURED the service and it was not that one (the host naming HAProxy on 6379 beats the port); no rule fires on an endpoint measured behind TLS or SSH; and a loopback-bound socket is not an exposure, with bound_local kept three-valued so "nobody established it" never renders as "reachable". Every finding records which signal fired and cites the rule id.

Inventory hygiene judges the record rather than the thing: no_owner, no_class, no_location, duplicate_suspected (raised on BOTH halves of a pending merge proposal, and resolved when Approvals decides it), stale on a 30/90/180-day ladder across assets, endpoints and software installs, and orphan_relationship on edges whose other end was archived or deleted. Every kind is feeds_risk: false and scores 0 — data quality is reported beside risk, never inside it.

Both producers record what they examined in the coverage record, which is what turns the controls that COUNT their findings — Inventory Hygiene IH-005 and IH-006, and the new mgmt_plaintext — from "not assessed" into a real number, including a real zero. Configuration claims only assets it had something to look at: a host with no management fact and no active endpoint is read and deliberately NOT claimed, so "nothing was collected here" cannot read as "we looked and it is fine". Hygiene never reaches the risk-assessed array — it feeds no score, and an asset whose only evaluation was a missing owner has not had its risk assessed.

default_credentials_exposed stays registered and unproduced, deliberately: nothing in the product records that a vendor default was ACCEPTED, and raising the kind from anything weaker would report an inference as a measurement.
