New measurement type mgmt_plaintext over the finding shape, with a new via: asset_or_endpoint so a control counts a Telnet listener found on an endpoint as well as one recorded on the asset.

  • Ask about your inventory in words, and get back a query you can edit (asset-inventory workstream 4.4b, ADR-0006 D2/D9, ADR-0008 D1). Enterprise.

The Query seam had a constructor and no caller. It has three now: a POST /api/v{1,2}/inventory-service/ask endpoint, the vistaplatform_ask MCP tool, and an Ask mode in the ⌘K command palette.

What comes back is a query, not a chat reply. A question becomes ONE line of the query language, validated against the production catalogue before anything runs; the response is the canonical predicate that ran — the platform's own default scope AND-ed in — then the assets it selected, then a summary in which every sentence cites one of those assets. "Open in Inventory" takes the predicate into the query editor, where it can be changed, re-run and saved as a view. A client rendering only the query and the rows has the whole answer.

A refusal is an answer. When the model cannot write a query that validates, the endpoint returns 422 carrying the validator's own {code, message, span, suggestion} diagnostics, in the same wire shape a hand-typed query's 400 uses, and the palette renders them through the query editor's own renderer with a button to open the attempt for editing. "No field hostnaem on assets — did you mean hostname?" is a better answer to a mistyped question than a confidently wrong list of servers.

Nothing matched is a fact about the query. Zero rows gets a fixed sentence the platform writes itself and no narration turn at all: an asset nobody has recorded and an asset that does not exist look identical from here.

The route is mounted in every edition and a Core build answers 402 — the availability question already has one deployment-wide answer at GET /tenant/ai, and a 404 would be indistinguishable from a broken route. 403 for the tenant kill switch, 503 for no provider. Gated on assets.read, the permission the MCP asset tools already declare for the same rows, pinned both in the middleware and in the routing table.

The MCP tool refuses honestly. On a deployment that cannot answer it returns {"available": false, "reason": …} as a result, naming which of edition / provider / a tenant switch is in the way and what to use instead — never a fabricated answer, and never a tool error for something a retry cannot fix. A permission failure stays a real error: the kill-switch 403 identifies itself with reason: assistant_disabled, and every other 403 — a role without assets.read, a scope-narrowed API token, a missing CSRF token — falls through to a real error carrying the platform's own sentence, rather than being told the organization switched something off.

Its bounds are the endpoint's own. A question past the published 4096-byte cap is a 400 naming the cap, not a 500, and one question is bounded end to end by a budget that fits inside the connection's write timeout — so a slow answer arrives as an error somebody can read instead of as a dropped connection.

The question is never written to the MCP audit rail. It is the one argument on that surface that is a prompt, and ADR-0008 D4.7's opt-in is enforced at the provider boundary; a copy elsewhere would be an opt-in honoured in one place and bypassed in another. The canonical query is recorded either way — it is the platform's own output, and it is what answers "which assets did that call select".

The palette also gains ADR-0006 D9's two missing result kinds in ordinary search: asset classes (from the generated taxonomy, no request, opening the whole subtree) and relationships of the best asset match, which is the shortest route to "this switch is being replaced on Friday — what is behind it?". Both modes now share one result model, so an asset row cannot look different depending on how it was found.

  • Per-asset risk is recomputed across every producer, and says who has looked (asset-inventory workstream 3.2, ADR-0005 D4).

The crypto producer. The cryptographic judgements the product has always made are now findings like everyone else's: crypto/weak_configuration on a configuration whose components the algorithm catalogue rates weak (worst component wins, with every component and its rating carried as evidence), crypto/weak_certificate on a certificate whose key algorithm, key size or signature is weak — the SP 800-131A floor applied per algorithm FAMILY, so a healthy 256-bit elliptic-curve key is not measured against the RSA floor — and crypto/pqc_vulnerable on either, from the same NIST IR 8547 denylist /pqc/progress counts with. Nothing here holds a second opinion: the catalogue roles, the PQC classification and the key-size and broken-hash rules all moved to one place each (internal/cryptoassess, shared/cryptoparse) and both callers read them.

One rollup, over findings. assets.risk_score is now MAX over the asset's OPEN risk-feeding findings — the asset itself plus its endpoints, configurations, certificates and software installs — filtered by the registry's feeds_risk flags rather than a list in code, so a hygiene finding can never inflate a security score. It replaces a statement that could only see crypto configurations, which meant an end-of-life OS or a critical CVE moved no asset's number. Parity with the old statement is PROVEN rather than asserted: both are computed over the same rows in one test before the old one was deleted.

Coverage is recorded, not inferred. A new producer_assessments table records which producer has completed a pass over which asset, written inside the pass's own write transaction — so a failed pass claims nothing. assets.risk_assessed_by is derived from it as its RISK-feeding subset: the record covers every producer, the array carries only the ones whose findings can move the score, so an asset only inventory hygiene has visited still reads NOT ASSESSED for risk. Score 0 with producers named is "assessed, nothing found"; score 0 with an empty array is NOT ASSESSED, and the asset page says which in those words. The asset's Overview tab also names the single finding its score came from, and clicking it opens the Findings tab with that finding highlighted. Compliance's finding measurement shape now gates on the full coverage record rather than the array, which is what makes an assessed_by: hygiene control answerable. A subject reachable from several assets covers all of them — a wildcard certificate served by four hosts raises four assets' risk, so it marks four.

Every producer pass now ends with one generic set-based recompute, so the configuration, hygiene and drift producers get it without knowing it exists. Discovery that writes a crypto configuration triggers a pass for that tenant rather than computing risk in the ingest path.

  • Three new alert types: vulnerable software, end of life, and an inventory hygiene score drop (asset-inventory workstream 3.9, ADR-0005 D7).

Vulnerable software. An installed package matching a published advisory now opens ONE alert for that installation — not one per CVE, because the fix is the same either way — graded on the CVSS qualitative severity bands (Medium from 4.0, High from 7.0, Critical from 9.0) by the worst advisory that matched, escalating in place when a worse one turns up. Advisories below CVSS 4.0 and advisories the feed has not scored stay visible as findings on the asset and open no alert: a notification threshold, never a claim of cleanliness.

End of life. An operating system, a package or a piece of hardware approaching or past the date its vendor stops shipping fixes opens ONE alert for the SUBJECT — an asset whose OS and whose hardware are both affected is one piece of work, graded by whichever is worse and naming both — on a ladder in days: 180 low, 90 medium, past high, past by more than a year critical. The alert grades the deadline; the finding behind it still grades the blast radius, and it is the finding that moves the asset's risk score.

Both are driven by the eol and vulnerability producers' OPEN findings, read through the ONE generated open-finding predicate (shared/findings.OpenSQL), and both auto-resolve when nothing on the subject crosses a rung any more. A pass raises only when the alert is new or the rung has risen.

Inventory hygiene score drop. The Inventory Hygiene framework's score falling more than 10 points in 24 hours is now its own alert type rather than a compliance_score_drop, so it can be routed — or silenced — separately from security posture. It is the SAME detector, routed by framework code; the two types gate independently.

The alert registry gained a second ladder shape to carry these: a fixed ladder, declared whole in standards/alert-registry.yaml as rungs: [{threshold, severity}], for types whose boundaries come from a published standard or from the finding ladder the alert is driven by. Nothing in a fixed ladder is tenant-tunable, so Settings → Notifications & Alerts → Alert Rules shows its rungs with no editor beside them.

  • Dashboard: an Inventory health hero beside cryptographic posture (asset-inventory workstream 3.8, ADR-0006 D5). Assets by top-level class, pending-approval and stale counts, and the free Inventory Hygiene framework's score with its passing / failing / not-assessed coverage. On the same page as the posture hero rather than on a dashboard of its own: the ops reader takes the left half and the compliance reader the right, and both are looking at one estate.

Three-valued throughout. The class bars are ROOT classes only — the class facet is hierarchical by design, so summing every bucket counts most of an estate two or three times. A facet level that failed renders "—" and "Couldn't load", never 0, because zero is the most reassuring thing several of these tiles can say. A hygiene score of null reads Not assessed — it is null both before the first evaluation and after one in which no control could be assessed — and never 100%.

  • The map's second view: Topology (workstream 3.8, ADR-0006 D4). A tenant-wide site → segment → class tree with counts and cross-segment connection summaries, behind a ?view= switch on the Map lens and linked from the dashboard hero. Not a graph of every asset: D4 rules that shape out, and the tree is an index into the inventory list instead — every count links through to exactly the rows it counted. A class chip uses class=<key>, the exact form: the tree groups by class, and plenty of classes are not leaves, so the subtree form would open a list three times the size of the chip that was clicked. The unsegmented bucket becomes not exists(segment_id) because the query language has no null literal.

Nothing is dropped. Assets with no site land under an explicit Unassigned node and assets with no segment under Unsegmented, which on a fresh inventory is most of them; the total is counted independently of the tree, and the view says so when the two disagree. Pending relationships and containment edges are excluded from the connection counts, with the page saying which.

New: GET /api/v2/inventory-service/infrastructure-assets/topology.

  • End-of-life and vulnerability columns on both software surfaces (workstream 3.8). The asset page's Software tab and the Inventory Software lens now show what the eol and vulnerability producers found, rolled up onto the list responses so the tab stays one request rather than one per row. Each cell with a finding behind it links to Findings narrowed to that install.

None known and Not assessed are deliberately different answers: the producer matches on Package URL and CPE only, so a product carrying neither was never checked, and rendering that as "0" would claim a check that never ran. An ungraded CVE reads "not scored", never 0.0. A missing end-of-life finding reads Not assessed, never "Supported" — it collapses a catalogue miss, a dateless catalogue row, a date beyond the warning window and a skipped non-active install, and nothing on the row tells them apart.

The catalogue rollup folds every install a tenant has, so it joins the findings plainly rather than once per install — the per-row form cost 702ms against 101ms on a 60,000-install tenant, on every page of the lens. One row per install is still guaranteed, by the findings_open_subject_uniq constraint rather than by a LIMIT.

  • GET /findings can be filtered to one subject. subject_type + subject_id, together or not at all — either alone is a 400, because a lone id can collide across subject vocabularies and a lone type is the producer filter under a worse name. Applied server-side so a subject past the page cap still returns its findings, and the Findings page says when it is filtered and offers a way out.

  • A learned classifier, underneath the rules and never in front of them (asset-inventory workstream 4.2, ADR-0008 D1/D2/D3/D4.3).

Most OUI rows in the classification catalogue are vendor-only, because most manufacturers sell across several classes under one assignment. So an HP MAC on a box with 9100 open and an embedded web server is obviously a printer to a person and unknown_host to the catalogue. That population — the rules were silent, or the rules contradicted each other — is what this is for, and it is all it is for.

The Classifier seam is now a chain. The curated rules run first and are unchanged: a rule that decides gets the answer, with rule provenance, and the model is not consulted, cannot outrank it and cannot soften its confidence. The model speaks only where they could not, and even then it must clear four further refusals — a 0.80 probability floor, a class the LIVE rule vocabulary contains, and, on a rules conflict, one of the classes the rules themselves named. Each refusal was mutation-checked by deleting it and watching a named test fail.

It proposes; it never sets a class. Not on an existing asset, and — the half that is easy to get wrong — not on a new one either. A rule-derived class IS written at creation, because the asset waits in Approvals and approving it approves the class; a model's answer always becomes an Approvals row instead, stamped class_source_kind: inferred with class_source_ref: model:<id> rather than rule. Both spellings satisfy every database constraint, so nothing but that distinction stands on the one column a reviewer uses to audit a class.

The row says "proposed by model (P=0.87)" and lists the three feature contributions the score is literally made of — "port 9100 is open", "the MAC prefix is registered to Hewlett Packard". A model cannot link to a source the way a rule can, so those reasons are the whole of its argument; and they name features and evidence, never a hostname or an address, because the classifier's entire input carries neither.

shared/classify/model: a multinomial logistic regression over hashed categorical features — OUI vendor, SNMP enterprise arc, product-id family, Server: banner tokens, 64 well-known ports chosen for what they separate, mDNS service types, LLDP/CDP capability bits, tokenised cloud resource type, and the rule engine's own output — a ~1,000-name space of which 260 carry a trained weight. Weights embedded in the binary, evaluated in pure Go. No ONNX runtime, no CGO, no new dependency — which closes the "in-process inference runtime" question the build plan had left open. Trainer at cmd/train-classifier over 184 committed fixtures, 131 of which the shipped rules are silent on, including the traps: a VM with a Cisco product id, a printer serving Apache, one Ubiquiti prefix that is both an access point and a switch, and ten class_rejected rejections trained as constraints rather than invented labels. Weights are reproducible from the fixtures by test, and the temperature is calibrated on held-out logits — fitted in-sample it is a sharpener, not a calibration, and would have made every probability read 0.999 and the floor meaningless. 1.0000 in-sample, 0.9310 five-fold held out, and — the number a reviewer actually experiences — 0.9640 precision above the 0.80 floor on the inputs the chain would raise a proposal for. The floor bounds the wrong proposals rather than eliminating them, which is what a calibrated threshold can do; a person accepting the row is what stops one reaching an asset. Both the per-class calibration table and the held-out log-loss are measured at the temperature that ships.

Operators can turn the model half off with CLASSIFIER_MODEL_ENABLED=false and keep the rules; Classifier: "none" still turns the whole seam off.

  • The eol and vulnerability finding producers, on a shared producer writer (asset-inventory workstreams 3.3 / 3.4 part 2, ADR-0005 D3).

One writer, not seven. shared/findings/producer is the single implementation of the finding lifecycle: Upsert creates the finding or reuses the open row — bumping occurrence_count, merging evidence, and bringing an INACTIVE row back to ACTIVE with resurfaced_at stamped — Resolve inactivates one subject, and Sweep inactivates everything the producer no longer asserts. Severity and score are validated against standards/findings-registry.yaml: a ladder kind must write one of its rungs verbatim, and a kind whose feeds_risk is false must write score = 0. producertest is the contract suite each producer runs with its own key and kinds against a real Postgres, so what it proves is that those findings obey the lifecycle.

End of life. Each asset's os.name/os.version and hw.vendor/hw.model facts, and every active software install, resolve against eol_catalogue. Findings escalate through the registry's rungs as the date recedes; a product whose support ends beyond the warning window gets the eol.* fact and no finding. Every finding cites the catalogue row id and the page that published it, and a lookup the catalogue cannot answer is counted on the gap list — bounded per run, and reported as bounded rather than as complete.

Vulnerability. Active software installs match vulnerability_matches by CPE and Package URL, comparing versions through ast.VersionSortKey so 1.10 is above 1.9 and never below it. One finding per install carries every matched CVE, worst-first, each with its NVD link; severity is the worst CVSS base score times ten, the convention models.RiskBands is anchored to. A CVE the catalogue never scored still raises a finding, marked not scored. A product with neither a CPE nor a PURL is counted as unidentifiable, never as clean.

The catalogue lookup moved to shared/catalogs so the producer and the Enricher seam's rule default resolve the same subjects against the same rows through one ResolveEOL — the eol.os.date fact on an asset and the end-of-life finding beside it cannot come from different catalogue rows.

Both producers run nightly over every tenant and are triggered after an SBOM upload, coalesced per tenant.

  • Risk & Compliance → Findings lists every producer. GET /findings carried a compliance-only scope, so the page the product points a person at for triage would have been the one surface omitting end-of-life and vulnerability findings — the asset page's Findings tab, finding:(…) and the has_findings facet all showed them.

A By Producer lens groups them by who judged what, and producer chips filter any lens. Each chip carries a count computed by the server under the same filters as the list minus the producer one, so a facet's number and the rows it leads to cannot describe different sets. The framework and control lenses still group by framework control, which only compliance findings have, and the page says so instead of rendering a blank list.

The inspector renders what each producer wrote: cycle, dates, days past and the catalogue citation for eol; every matched CVE with its CVSS and NVD link for vulnerability — all of them, since one finding per install carries the lot. An unscored CVE reads "not scored", never 0.0. "Create ticket" on a software-install finding links the host it is installed on, and the ticket's category follows the producer instead of filing every CVE under compliance.

The framework ACTIVATION gate now applies to compliance rows only: it asks whether a finding's CONTROL belongs to an activated framework, and a finding with no control has none — applied unconditionally it hid every end-of-life finding behind a framework subscription.

  • Remediation guidance on every finding, and — with Enterprise — a drafted plan built from it (asset-inventory workstream 4.8, ADR-0008 D1/D4/D5).

The Core half, and the larger one. Every finding kind in standards/findings-registry.yaml now carries guidance: customer-facing text saying what a person does about a finding of that kind. It renders in the Findings inspector in every edition, resolved from the generated registry with no model and no endpoint involved. It is deliberately separate from the description beside it, which is written for us and carries table names and workstream numbers — the generator refuses a kind whose guidance is a copy of it, and make audit catches drift in either registry.

The Enterprise half. Risk & Compliance → Findings → a finding → Remediation → "Draft a remediation plan" turns that generic guidance into a numbered plan for the thing actually in front of you — the version that was measured, the algorithm that was negotiated, the vendor whose command it is. Each step cites the evidence it rests on ([ev:<key>]) or the guidance ([guide]), and a step that cites nothing, or cites a measurement this finding does not have, is discarded before you see it; the panel says how many were. Every step that changes a system is tagged Manual step: the platform executes nothing, and the tag says so out loud. The classifier that applies it runs independently of the model's own flag and can only ever raise it.

It never replaces the guidance with an error. No provider, provider down, rate limit, rejected credential, refusal, unreadable answer, or an answer whose every step failed citation validation — all return the finding's own guidance with a reason naming which it was. The one exception is a tenant who has turned the AI assistant off in Settings, who is told that plainly (403) rather than handed a plan labelled like any other.

Accepting is the approval. Accept as plan writes one remediation_plan_items row with the steps as its notes, carrying source_kind: inferred, source_ref: remediator:<model id> and the accepting user — and Remediation → Plans badges it AI drafted and now renders those notes, which it never did — an accepted draft is an ordinary plan item there, managed like any other. POST /findings/{id}/remediation/draft persists nothing at all.

What crosses the boundary is an allowlist a reviewer can read in one function: the finding's kind, severity, subject label, summary and evidence, the registry guidance, and the subject's class, OS name/version and hardware vendor/model. No asset id, no hostname, no address, no serial. Evidence is redacted before it is bounded (a truncated PEM stops matching by shape), and the redacted form is the one thing sent, cited against and — only behind the tenant's Record the questions we send opt-in — audited.

Both endpoints are Core code mounted in every edition and answer 402 in Core, 503 on Enterprise with no reachable provider, and 403 for the tenant kill switch. GET /api/v1/auth-service/tenant/ai now reports the remediator seam as built and live-per-edition, and the Findings inspector asks it before offering the button, so Core shows the guidance and nothing else.

  • Four kinds of bill of materials on one artifact pipeline, and an OCSF export (asset-inventory workstream 3.7, ADR-0005 D6).

The CBOM was never a format — it was a subset. POST /cbom/generate gains kind: cbom (unchanged, and the default), sbom, hbom or inventory. CycloneDX 1.7 already models the union — device, operating-system, platform, application, library and data components, services for network faces, dependencies for edges, vulnerabilities for CVEs — so all four share one format, one content hash, one signature and one comparison rather than each inventing a serialisation. A request that omits kind is unchanged in meaning as well as in shape, and a CBOM's canonical bytes are byte-for-byte what they were: every new CycloneDX field is omitempty and appended, never inserted, because those bytes are what every stored artifact's hash and signature refer to.

What each kind holds. An SBOM is one component per software product — a fleet of 500 hosts running the same OpenSSL is one thing to patch, with the hosts underneath it as evidence.occurrences — and carries no dependencies graph, because an install record says a product is present, not that anything depends on it. An HBOM is one device per hardware-class asset with its hw.* facts, membership decided by the class registry so it cannot drift from the taxonomy. An inventory is every asset typed by its class, endpoints as services, approved relationships as the dependencies graph, facts and identifiers as properties, and open vulnerabilities.

Only the vulnerability producer's findings become CycloneDX vulnerabilities. Compliance failures, EOL, hygiene, configuration and drift are findings; none is a CVE, and every tool reading CycloneDX treats that array as CVEs. A missing asset owner listed there would be read as a remote code execution. A CVE the catalogue has not scored carries no rating at all — a 0.0 reads as "scored, and harmless".

OCSF 1.9.0 export, Core, at ?format=ocsf on an inventory artifact: JSON Lines, one Device Inventory Info (class 5001) per asset and one Vulnerability Finding (2002) per vulnerability. It is a projection of the stored artifact, so what a SIEM ingests is exactly what the content hash covers, stamped with the artifact's own generation time rather than the download's. Where OCSF defines a field nothing measured, the field is absent — not "", 0 or "Unknown" — and an asset class with no OCSF counterpart is type_id: 0 (Unknown), never 99 (Other): "we do not know" is a claim about us and true, "OCSF does not model this" is a claim about OCSF we are not entitled to make. This reaches parity with runZero, the only other product in the category exporting CycloneDX CBOM or OCSF.

Refusals rather than plausible-looking output. Comparison is same-kind only (400): two kinds identify contents in disjoint ways, so a cross-kind diff would report the entire base removed and the entire head added — precise, confident, meaningless. OCSF is defined only for inventory, and other kinds get a 400 naming the kind rather than an empty stream that reads as "no assets". SPDX and PDF stay CBOM-only, after the existing 402 edition gate so Core's answer is unchanged.

UI: Risk & Compliance → Bills of Materials (was "CBOM" — a user wanting an SBOM would never have looked there; the route is unchanged). The Generate dialog gains a Kind picker with one line per kind saying what it contains; the list gains a Kind column and filter; the download control offers only the formats that artifact's kind can produce; Compare restricts each side to the other's kind and says why.

Two bugs the tests caught before shipping: Contains(os_name, "ios") reported FortiOS, IOS-XE and Cisco IOS as Apple mobile devices, and a fact with two sources is stored per-source, so the OCSF lookup found nothing for exactly the assets carrying the most evidence.

  • Registry-driven compliance measurement, and two new Core frameworks — Inventory Hygiene and Lifecycle (asset-inventory workstream 3.6, ADR-0005 D5).

What a control can measure is declared, not coded. It used to live twice: as a switch of nineteen hand-written SQL blocks in the compliance-engine, and as nineteen INSERTed rows in seed.sql, with nothing holding the two together — a control could name a measurement type the extractor did not implement (it evaluated to nothing and read as "not assessed" forever), and the extractor could implement one no seed row offered. Both halves now come from standards/measurement-types.yaml. A row declares a whitelisted shape (one of five reviewed FROM/JOIN skeletons), a value that shape offers, and a query-language predicate compiled by shared/query; one executor runs all of them. No SQL comes from the registry, and the statement each row compiles to is pinned in a golden file, so a registry change is reviewable as the query it will actually run.

The refactor changed nothing, and that was proven rather than asserted. The old extractor was kept for exactly one commit as a test oracle, and both implementations were run over one deliberately awkward fixture — a soft-deleted asset, a soft-deleted configuration, a certificate with no algorithm at all, a CA certificate, a post-quantum key belonging to neither key-size family, an endpoint with no address, a configuration with no endpoint — and required to agree on all 74 measurements, tenant-wide and per-subject. They did. The oracle is gone; the golden it recorded stays, so every future change to a shape, a transform or a predicate is still measured against what the original extractor produced.

Inventory Hygiene (6 controls) scores the inventory record: is every asset owned, classified, located and recently seen, and are there suspected duplicates or relationships pointing at deleted assets? Nothing here feeds an asset's risk score — a host with no owner is not less secure, it is less manageable. Lifecycle (4 controls) tracks what has outlived its vendor: operating systems past end of life and within 90 days of it, software past end of life, hardware past end of support. Both are Core, both activatable like Certificate Hygiene, and both ship in the free seed rather than the Enterprise content bundle.

Both are three-valued, which is the point. A lifecycle control over an asset whose operating system the end-of-life catalogue never resolved a date for reads not assessed, never "supported": "we could not find out" and "it is fine" are different answers, and a report that conflates them is worse than none. The two counting hygiene controls read not assessed until the platform's hygiene checks have actually evaluated the asset, so a count of zero from a check that never ran is not shown as a clean bill of health.

  • Merge proposals are now ranked, and every score shows its working. When the identifiers disagree about whether a sighting is something you already have, Discovery → Approvals has always asked you rather than guessing. It now puts the strongest candidate first and tells you why.

  • A score and its reasons on every candidate card. A percentage bar, and under it the three signals that moved that score most, each with an arrow saying whether it counted for the merge or against it — "a one-per-asset identifier matches", "different network segments", "the names differ only in a trailing number, like web01 and web02". The reasons that count against are shown too: a proposal is a question, and hiding the evidence against would make the panel a case for merging rather than a summary of what was weighed.

  • 50% means "as likely as not". The score is a calibrated probability from a small model that ships inside the platform — it runs locally, sends nothing anywhere, and looks at nothing but comparisons between the two records: which identifier kinds agree and how many, how alike the names are, the network segment, the vendor and model, how close in time the sightings are, and whether two different kinds of source agree. It never sees key material, raw captures or configuration text.
  • 0% still means "nothing scored this", not "certainly wrong", and shows as an absence rather than an empty bar.
  • Optionally, a high enough score can settle it for you. Settings → Policies → Identification rules gains an auto-accept threshold. The default is Never, which is not a low bar — it is off, and no score bypasses it. The page states plainly that an auto-accepted merge cannot be undone from the UI.
  • Two things are never auto-accepted, whatever the score. A sighting whose serial number, cloud resource id, agent id or CMDB sys_id disagrees with the candidate's — two different serials are two different machines — and anything involving an asset still waiting for approval, because admitting an asset and merging two assets are separate decisions.

  • Everything it does is listed. Discovery → Approvals gains "Auto-merged by the matcher (last 30 days)", with the score, the reasons and a link to the asset, so an unattended decision is still one a person can check. The section is absent entirely while the threshold is Never. Each auto-accept also writes an audit event naming the model and the score.

  • NetBox connector, and a Settings → Integrations page driven by the connector registry (asset-inventory workstream 2.7, ADR-0001 D3 Q3, ADR-0004 D5).

The catalogue is the registry. Settings → Integrations grew an Available connectors panel that answers from standards/connectors.yaml (new Core endpoint GET /api/v2/inventory-service/connectors), grouped by kind, with each connector's status, edition and whether this tenant may add it. The page used to carry a hand-kept list of platform names in a modal file, which nothing could see drift.

Four connectors were claiming to be shipped and were not. hashicorp_vault, github, gitlab and bitbucket sat in the platform_integrations CHECK marked live with no collector anywhere — a tenant could save one and it would do nothing, forever, with no error. Neither guard could catch it, because the CHECK and the registry AGREED; what neither knew was whether any Go file dispatches on the key. The registry gained a third status, registered (the schema accepts it, nothing implements it), those four moved to it, and shared/connectors/implementations.go now names the package behind every live key with a test that fails when one is missing or names a package that does not exist. The UI renders a registered connector greyed out and not selectable — and deliberately not as an upgrade prompt, because offering to sell something that does not exist is the worse of the two mistakes.

The NetBox connector (Enterprise, connector_netbox) pulls sites, prefixes, VLANs, device types and devices. Prefixes become network_segments with imported provenance; devices become observations through the identification engine, so a device a sensor also found is one asset. Sites become site/region on the asset; hw.vendor/hw.model land as facts with provenance, so a later interrogation disagrees visibly instead of overwriting. Class comes from the NetBox device role through a mapping table (extensible per connection); an unrecognised role gives unknown_host, never a nearest guess, and the run reports how many it could not map. Imported devices wait in Approvals unless the segment auto-approves.

It never writes to NetBox. The token needs read access only, and drift is a read-only view: what NetBox lists and we do not, and what we hold and NetBox does not, each row linking into NetBox. Filling a source of truth with our own guesses would destroy the only thing that makes comparing the two worth doing. Run-now and a real scheduler (hourly/daily/weekly) both go through one code path, and every run records its counts — zeros included, so a run that imported nothing is distinguishable from one that never happened.

Private endpoints, deliberately. A NetBox is on-premises by construction, so this connector kind permits an RFC1918 target by default, per connection, with an audit entry on save and a platform-wide operator switch (CONNECTOR_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS). The other half of the SSRF guard is not negotiable: loopback, link-local and the cloud metadata endpoints are refused at connect time whatever the setting says. Pointing the connector inside the customer's network is the point; pointing it inside ours never is.

The connector also stays where it was pointed: it refuses a redirect that leaves the NetBox URL the tenant gave it, including a same-host downgrade to http://. A redirect is a destination the server picks, and the API token travels with it.

Custom fields and config contexts — where a real NetBox keeps SNMP communities, TACACS keys and RADIUS secrets — are never collected: devices are fetched with exclude=config_context, and every response is projected onto a typed shape that discards what it does not name.

Where your roles have local names, Settings → Integrations → the connection → Device-role mapping maps them onto asset classes. A mapping naming a class that does not exist is refused on save rather than ignored at import time.

Customer doc: docsv4/enterprise/integrations/netbox.md.

  • Vista Platform now works out what a thing IS, and shows you why. The classification rules a platform administrator curates — MAC prefix to manufacturer, SNMP object id to product family, advertised service to device type, and now CDP/LLDP capabilities and mDNS service types — finally reach the inventory.

A newly discovered device arrives already classed. A printer that advertises its print service is a Printer in Discovery → Approvals, not an "Unknown host", and approving the asset approves the class with it. The asset's History records which rule decided it, so six months later the answer traces back to a specific row rather than to "the system".

For a device already in your inventory, a rule that disagrees raises a class proposal — the fourth kind of row on the one Approvals queue, beside discovered assets, merge proposals and relationship proposals. The row shows what the asset is classed as now, what the rules say, and which rules matched, with a link to the source each mapping comes from. A rule you cannot check is one you can only rubber-stamp.

Four things it will not do:

  • It never changes a class you set yourself. A class a person chose is never proposed against, at any confidence.
  • When two rules disagree it proposes nothing, and shows you both candidates to pick between. Two rules arguing is a problem with the rules, and that is a thing to fix rather than a coin to flip.
  • A rejection sticks. Say no once and the same class is not proposed again for that asset — otherwise a printer announcing itself every few minutes would put the same question back in your queue all day.

  • It never guesses. A device nothing recognises stays "Unknown host".

  • Rules added in the admin console are live within about five minutes. Until now, Catalog ▸ Classification rules stored, validated and audited a new rule and then changed no classification until the next release — the page said so. The services read the table at runtime and rebuild on an interval (CLASSIFICATION_RULES_REFRESH, default 5m). A rule that fails validation is skipped and logged by name; the rest of the table keeps working.

  • Three new kinds of classification rule. mdns_service (what a host advertises about itself on the LAN — _ipp._tcp and friends), lldp_capability and cdp_capabilities (what a device declares it DOES, over the two neighbour-discovery protocols). These are the strongest passive signals on a wired segment and nothing could use them before.

The restraint is deliberate: 802.1AB bridge on its own proposes nothing, because access points and desk phones bridge too; telephone proposes nothing because the taxonomy has no phone class to map it to; and a device advertising that it BOTH routes and switches is proposed as a Network device rather than guessed at, because a layer-3 switch and a router with a switch module advertise exactly the same thing. A wrong class is worse than none.

  • The host agent's inventory of its own machine now becomes an asset. Since the last release the agent has been able to describe the host it runs on — OS and kernel, hardware identity, installed packages, listening sockets, trust stores — and the platform stored every collection and did nothing with it. It now materialises.

After a collection you get one asset per host, waiting in Discovery → Approvals, carrying:

  • its facts — OS, kernel, hardware vendor/model/serial, interfaces, and two new ones summarising its trust stores (how many certificates, and how many things in them are not certificates at all);
  • one endpoint per listening socket, with the process holding it and an Exposure column reading "bound to localhost" or "reachable" — the half of a host's exposure a network scan structurally cannot see. That column is blank for everything a scan found, deliberately: a scan sees what answers, not what a socket is bound to, and showing those as "reachable" would be an exposure claim nobody measured. It is filterable too (endpoint.bound_local = false);
  • its installed packages, in the asset's Software tab and the Inventory Software lens, beside anything an SBOM upload put there.

Things it deliberately does not do:

  • It does not guess what kind of machine it is. The class stays Unknown host until a classification rule decides otherwise. An OS name and a hardware model are evidence; calling that a server is a judgement, and a plausible-looking guess is the kind that gets approved without being read.
  • It does not merge two machines that share an agent id. A restored image or a cloned VM carries the agent's identity onto different hardware; the platform opens a merge proposal naming both rather than quietly giving one asset two hardware serials.
  • It does not report a failed step as an empty answer. A host whose package database could not be read records no package count and leaves its software list exactly as the last good collection left it — rather than marking everything on it as uninstalled. The same holds for its listening sockets.
  • Nothing is deleted. A package that is gone is marked removed and a socket that has stopped listening is marked closed; both keep their first-seen date, so "this was here in March" stays answerable. Endpoints that an active scan or a cloud connector found are never retired by an agent — it is only authoritative about its own host.

Where to see it: Discovery → Sensors & Agents now shows "Last host inventory: 2h ago — 412 packages, 18 listeners" on each agent's row (absent when an agent has never reported one, which usually means local collection is switched off), and Discovery → Job Logs shows the same counts per run.

Collections taken before this release are not back-filled — they were collected under an older projection and replaying them would produce assets identified by rules that no longer apply. Local agents collect on a timer, so every host appears within one interval (24 hours by default) of the upgrade.

  • Devices your sensor only ever overhears are now in the inventory. A sensor has been decoding host announcements since the last release — ARP, DHCP, mDNS, NetBIOS, and the LLDP/CDP advertisements a switch or a phone makes about itself — but those observations stopped at the inventory boundary and went no further. They now become assets, through the same identification engine every other intake path uses, and wait in Discovery → Approvals like any other discovery.

This is how the inventory finds what the crypto pipeline structurally cannot: printers, cameras, controllers, anything on the network that never opens a TLS connection past the sensor. An uploaded PCAP is decoded the same way, which is often the only practical way to inventory a segment that cannot host a sensor.

What the platform will and will not say about such a device:

  • A hardware address alone is enough. An ARP frame from a camera that answers no name and holds no address still says the camera is there. It becomes an asset keyed on its MAC, and the next sighting — with a name, or a new address — updates that asset rather than adding a second one.
  • Its name is what it called itself. No reverse lookup is performed on these devices: internal host names stay internal. That is now enforced by a test that drives the real ingest with the resolver replaced and fails if anything reaches it.
  • Its type comes from the classification rules, or stays "Unknown host". A device advertising printing is a printer, and saying so is a rule's conclusion with a citation behind it — see the classification entry above. A device no rule recognises stays "Unknown host", which reads as "we have not worked this out" rather than as an answer.
  • A randomised (locally administered) MAC is not used as identity. Phones and laptops rotate those, and keying on one would add a new asset every rotation.
  • It has no ports, services or certificates, because nothing connected to it. A blank crypto section on one of these means nobody looked, not that it came back clean.

Auto-approval rules can name these rows specifically — kind:host_observation and network.segment_id=… — so a tenant can accept the devices a sensor sees on a segment they own without also auto-approving every TLS endpoint that sensor reports. A segment is matched from the device's address, so a device seen without one (an LLDP frame carrying only a chassis ID, an ARP probe from a host that has not been given an address) still waits for a person. We would rather queue it than place it on a segment nothing measured.

  • A sensor's host-observation counters are visible. The sensor has been reporting eight of them on every heartbeat, and sensor-manager mapped a fixed set of columns onto the metrics table and dropped the rest — so they were documented, sent, and stored nowhere. Discovery → Sensors & Agents → a sensor → Health now shows how many devices the sensor has seen this way over the selected range, how many observations it had to shed, and how many subjects are accumulating right now. A non-zero shed count means the segment is busier than the sensor is sized for, and devices on it may be missing.

  • The inventory has a map. Inventory → Map goes live (it was a phase-2 placeholder): the neighbourhood around one asset, drawn as a graph rather than listed as two tables. Reached from the lens, from an asset's Relationships tab ("View on map"), from ⌘K, or full-screen at its own URL.

  • Class and status are two separate channels. A node's colour and icon say what kind of thing it is; a ring around it says whether it is monitored, waiting for approval, or archived. An asset awaiting approval is still a server and still looks like one.

  • Pending relationships draw dashed, and rejected ones never draw at all. Somebody decided a rejected relationship was wrong; redrawing it would put a settled decision back up for grabs. Pending edges are off by default and come in behind a toggle.
  • "Show impact of focus" tints the blast radius by distance and dims — rather than hides — everything outside it, because "nothing else is affected" is only readable if the something-else is still on screen. It reads the same closure as the Relationships tab, so it keeps the same rules: no connects_to, no unconfirmed proposals, and a capped answer reported as "at least N" rather than as a total.
  • A truncated graph says so, with both counts. The map draws at most 500 assets and 2,000 relationships; past that a banner reads "Showing 500 of 812 assets and 2000 of 3104 relationships", because a picture that silently caps is the thing the endpoint's cap bit exists to prevent.
  • Deterministic layout. The same neighbourhood is drawn the same way every time (dagre, hierarchical), so a screenshot pasted into a ticket matches what the person reading it sees. A force layout settles somewhere different on every run and would not.
  • GraphML and Cytoscape JSON export of the graph on screen, for Visio, yEd, Gephi and Cytoscape. Documented as convenience, not evidence: written in the browser with no provenance or content hash, and truncated when the map is. Audit-grade output is still a CBOM artifact.
  • The graph library is code-split. @xyflow/react and dagre (both MIT) load only when a map is opened. The bundle every user downloads in order to look at a table grows by 0.8 kB gzipped — most of that ten new icon glyphs, not the graph — while the 85.2 kB the map itself costs is paid only by somebody who opens one.

  • Docs: The Map.

  • Assets now record how they are connected, and the platform can tell you what breaks if one changes. The asset page's Relationships tab goes live (it was a phase-2 placeholder), and relationship proposals join Discovery → Approvals as a third row kind beside discovered assets and merge proposals.

  • What depends on this. The tab leads with the impact question — how many assets are affected if this one changes, how far away each is, and which ones. It counts the nine dependency relationship types and deliberately not connects_to: two machines exchanging packets says nothing about whether one stops working when the other does, and because nearly every asset connects to something, counting those would make almost every answer "the whole estate", which is the same as no answer. The vocabulary actually walked is reported alongside the number.

  • Each relationship is followed the way its own meaning points. Ask what breaks if a wireless controller dies and you get the access points it manages; ask it of a virtual network and you get its subnets; ask it of a server and you get the applications running on it. A business service you have declared an asset to impact is included, and the answer stops there rather than continuing into everything that service touches.
  • Only confirmed relationships count. A proposal nobody has accepted is shown on the tab but excluded from impact. Nobody should plan a maintenance window around a guess.
  • Where each relationship came from is on the row. Measured, Declared, Imported or Inferred — the four are not worth the same, and Inferred, the one nothing has confirmed, is the one that is highlighted and the one that always waits for a person.
  • One relationship, two readings. An edge is stored once in its canonical direction, so the application's page reads "runs on" and the server's page reads "runs" — from the same row, with no second copy to fall out of step.
  • Declaring one shows you the sentence first. Direction is the easiest thing to get backwards, and a relationship pointing the wrong way is not obviously wrong on the page — it quietly inverts every impact answer built on it. The modal previews payments-api runs on app-server-04 before you save.
  • Measured relationships cannot be deleted, and the platform says why. A collector saw it, so the next run would re-create it: the delete would appear to work and then silently undo itself. Those retire by going stale, the same way a stale asset does. Relationships you declared delete normally.
  • The caps report honestly. Impact reaches 10 hops and 500 assets, the neighbourhood 3 hops, 500 assets and 2000 relationships. Past either, the answer says it is a floor and gives the real totals rather than quietly returning less than it found.
  • Three read-only MCP tools — relationships, neighbourhood and impact — so an AI agent can answer these questions with the same caveats a person gets: that inferred is not confirmed, that impact covers nine types and not ten, and that an empty result means nothing is recorded, which is not the same as nothing depending on the asset.

Customer documentation: docsv4/core/features/relationships.md.

  • Settings → AI assistant: what this deployment has turned on, and the two switches that are yours. A new Core page under Settings → Integrations (Tenant Administrator), behind one endpoint, GET/PUT /api/v1/auth-service/tenant/ai.

The page carries no entitlement lock, deliberately: it explains the edition rather than being gated by it. A Core tenant opening it sees each generative capability marked "Enterprise" — or "Not yet built", where nothing implements it in any edition, which an upgrade would not change — beside the rule-based behaviour that answers instead. The product is AI-native and never AI-dependent (asset-inventory ADR-0008), and an upgrade card would hide the settings a Core tenant genuinely has.

  • A capabilities table with one row per AI seam: where you meet it, what answers when no model does, and a four-valued status that keeps "not part of this edition" separate from "nobody has configured a provider" — one is a purchase, the other is ten minutes of an administrator's time.
  • The AI assistant kill switch. Off, and no generative capability runs for that organization, whatever the deployment has configured. Everything falls back to the deterministic path it already has; nothing errors. Enforced at each call site and again inside the provider boundary, so a capability added later inherits it rather than having to remember it.
  • The question-recording opt-in (ADR-0008 D4.7). Off by default: the audit trail records that a call happened, who made it, which model answered and a fingerprint of the request, but not the text anyone typed. On, and the redacted prompt is stored beside the fingerprint, bounded and marked when truncated. Implemented once at the boundary rather than per seam.
  • No credential and no endpoint address ever crosses: the response carries the provider kind and the model id only, pinned by a test that configures a provider and greps the raw response body.

The tenant's two controls live in the existing tenant_admin_settings.config blob — no new table, and the settings-audit trigger records every change against the acting user, the first save included. tenant.authoring_disabled is reported read-only alongside them: it is the interim platform-wide pause on custom-policy authoring (#1439), not a tenant decision, and a request trying to write it is refused rather than accepted and ignored.

Reading the status needs only a signed-in tenant user — it carries no credential and no endpoint address, and any surface can use it to explain why a generative capability is absent. Changing either switch needs settings.update, which is also what the Settings rail entry is gated on.

  • Cloud discovery now inventories your compute and network estate, not just its cryptography. A run against AWS, Azure or GCP records the account's compute instances, virtual networks, subnets and security-group membership alongside the load balancers, key stores and buckets it already found — the thing an ops buyer expects from a cloud collector and the frame the rest of a run hangs on. A TLS listener on a machine that is not in your inventory is half an answer.

  • One switch, on by default. Discovery → Cloud → Edit integration gains Inventory compute, networks and subnets, with the exact extra API calls and the IAM role that covers them stated next to it, per provider. An integration created before this release carries no setting and enumerates; turning it off stops the calls.

  • It is the same identity as everything else. Each resource goes through the identification engine on its provider resource id — an ARN, an Azure resource id, a GCP partial resource name — so an instance found here and the same host seen by the sensor or named in a CMDB pull are ONE asset, new assets land in Pending approval like any other discovery, and a re-run updates rather than duplicating. A name that is not globally unique is not used as one: EC2's IP-derived private DNS name repeats wherever a private address repeats, so it is recorded as a description rather than as the instance's hostname.

  • Two machines that share a private address stay two machines. A CIDR is not unique in a cloud account — two VPCs from one Terraform module both get 10.0.0.0/16 — so a network segment now carries the VPC, VNet or network it belongs to and two subnets with the same CIDR are two segments rather than one. And where an address genuinely is reused inside ONE subnet, the replacement is recorded as its own asset with a review item in Approvals asking whether it is the machine that used to answer to that address: from outside, an address that changed hands and a machine that was rebuilt look identical, and the platform does not guess.

    Underneath, agent_id, cloud_resource_id, serial_number and cmdb_sys_id are now singleton identifier kinds — an asset holds at most one of each — and an observation that disagrees with the one an asset already carries opens a merge proposal instead of quietly adding a second. This closed a real auto-merge: two EC2 instances sharing a private address became one asset carrying two ARNs, inheriting the first one's approval state and findings, with nothing in Approvals to say so. The same rule covers the LAN twin (two chassis behind one address are two serials, so two assets). - Containment is drawn from the provider. VPC contains subnet and subnet contains instance, from the provider's own placement rather than inferred, and a subnet's CIDR becomes a network segment — which is what lets an instance's private address resolve to the same asset when an agent inside it, or the sensor on the wire, reports the same address. - Instances are not crypto findings, and are not recorded as any. An instance negotiates no protocol and states no at-rest encryption, so it writes no discovery row at all rather than the TLS-on-443 the findings pipeline would otherwise have invented for it. - Security groups are membership, never rules. The group a resource is IN is recorded; IpPermissions, securityRules and a GCP firewall's allowed/sourceRanges are not read. On GCP, where there is no security-group object, membership is computed from firewall tag targeting — and a rule targeted by service account is not claimed to apply, because the platform does not collect an instance's service account and a false membership is worse than a missing one. - User data is never requested. Not projected away, not redacted: DescribeInstanceAttribute(userData), Azure's osProfile.customData and GCP's metadata.items are the three richest sources of secrets in a cloud account, and none of them is asked for. Neither are EC2 block-device mappings, GCP disks[] (which carries a customer-supplied disk key), or service-account scopes. EC2 key pairs are recorded by name only. - No guessed operating system. None of the three providers states a guest OS product on a list call — a billing string, an OS family and an image reference are not what the machine runs — so the OS fields stay empty rather than carrying a value that would silently mismatch the end-of-life catalogue. - The Job Logs row says what it found, and distinguishes a run that enumerated an empty account from one that did not enumerate.

  • Upload a bill of materials and it becomes software inventory. Discovery → Sources → SBOM Upload takes a CycloneDX (JSON 1.4–1.7) or SPDX (JSON 2.2/2.3) document, up to 32 MB, and turns its components into a per-tenant software catalogue and a record of which asset carries what. The platform already emits CycloneDX; this makes it an input as well (ADR-0004 D3, workstream 2.6b — the parser shipped in #1642).

  • The format is read from inside the document, never from the filename or the Content-Type — both are supplied by whoever is uploading and neither is evidence. The endpoint takes a form upload or a raw body, so a build pipeline can curl --data-binary @bom.json without a multipart encoder.

  • Where it shows up. An asset's Software tab; Inventory → Software for the whole catalogue, with a click through to the assets that carry each product; software:(name:openssl and version < 3.0) in the query language; and vistaplatform_list_asset_software over MCP. The tab and the lens were phase-3 placeholders waiting on the host agent — SBOM ingestion reaches the same rows first.
  • The result says what it did, against what you gave it. "412 of 480 components ingested · 68 excluded by the document", plus every warning the parse produced. A bare "412 imported" is a number you cannot check against your own build output.
  • An empty software list is not "no software". It means nothing has enumerated any, and the page says that in those words rather than showing a clean table that reads as a clean bill of health.
  • Re-uploading replaces the imported list for that asset, and what the new document does not list is marked no longer listed rather than deleted — so its first-seen date survives, "this library was here in March" stays answerable, and a later document that lists it again brings it back. Nothing a sensor or agent measured is touched.
  • Products deduplicate on the strongest identifier the document gave: purl, else CPE, else name and version. CPE attribute values are stored lowercase, because CPE 2.3 makes them case-insensitive and NVD publishes them that way — so OpenSSL and openssl are one product line and one vulnerability match, not two. Versions order on a normalised key, and a version with no numeric part has none at all rather than a wrong one.
  • A document with no target asset can create one from its own subject, and uploading the same artefact again lands on the same asset. It arrives in Approvals labelled Declared from SBOM upload and is not in your inventory until someone accepts it: an asset you create in the UI is approved because a person decided in front of the inventory, and an upload is a file arriving at an endpoint. Only an application subject can become an asset; a library or container subject is refused by name, with the remedy in the message.
  • The dependency graph is not stored, and says so. A document's dependencies are edges between components, and the platform's relationships are between assets. They are counted on the result card ("56 dependency edges not kept") rather than dropped in silence.

Not yet: vulnerability matching and end-of-life dates. The identifiers are stored so both become possible; neither is claimed today. Guide.

  • Host inventory: one collector, local and remote, held at intake. The device agent can now inventory a host as well as interrogate a network device — its OS and kernel, hardware identity, installed packages, listening sockets, and installed certificate stores (asset-inventory ADR-0004 D3, workstream 2.11a).

One collector library, two ways in. shared/hostinventory runs the same command set through a Runner: locally via os/exec, or remotely over SSH with the device's stored credentials. The parsers take command output or file bytes and nothing else — they never touch os/exec, read a local path, or consult runtime.GOOS — so local and remote parity is a property of the shape rather than something anyone has to maintain. A test drives one fixture through both transports and requires byte-identical reports.

  • Local mode is off by default (HOST_INVENTORY_ENABLED, HOST_INVENTORY_INTERVAL, default 24h with a 1h floor). It is not a job: the agent describes its own host on its own schedule, with no credentials, and posts to a new agent-authenticated intake route. An agent installed to interrogate firewalls does not start enumerating its own host because it was upgraded.
  • Remote mode is a host_inventory job queued against a device that already has SSH credentials, and requires mode: "remote" plus an agent_id — the collection runs from an agent that can reach the target.
  • --host-inventory-once collects this host, prints the report as JSON and exits, contacting nothing. It is how an operator sees exactly what would be sent before enabling the schedule.

Windows is reached by PowerShell over SSH, not WinRM. The intended client (github.com/masterzen/winrm) is Apache-2.0 itself and its graph carries no GPL or AGPL — but two MPL-2.0 modules and an ISC one, none on this project's MIT/Apache/BSD list, and it would add sixteen modules including a Kerberos stack to a cross-compiled agent to run one PowerShell command. Windows Server 2019+ ships OpenSSH Server, so transport: "ssh" reaches Windows too. "winrm" is a recognised-and-refused value whose error names the reason and the alternative.

Posture, never key material. Certificate stores are read for certificates only: a PEM block that is not a CERTIFICATE is skipped before being decoded, and the stored shape has four fields — subject, issuer, SHA-256 fingerprint, expiry — with nowhere for key bytes to sit. The Windows script asks Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\… for three properties rather than taking the certificate objects, which can carry a private key. A private key found loose in a trust directory is reported as a count and nothing else. No command transcripts, no process command lines, and no PID inside the durable socket fact. A fixture carrying a real private key appended to a certificate proves none of it reaches the report.

Three-valued honesty throughout. Each section reports ok, failed or unsupported, and a failed section emits no fact — an absent fact means "not measured", where a fact with an empty value would mean "measured, and the answer is nothing". sw.package_count is emitted for an enumeration that genuinely found zero packages and never for one that failed. Hardware serial and UUID are absent rather than blank when DMI is unreadable, because a blank serial shared across an estate merges every host into one asset.

A report too large to accept is its own answer. Intake refuses an over-cap submission with 413 naming the cap and what the agent declared it was sending, and the agent logs the size it actually measured and says plainly that waiting will not help — an over-cap report is the same size on the next run. Previously this and a malformed body both answered 400, so a host too big to report retried forever and never appeared in the inventory. The cap is derived from the collector's own ceilings rather than picked: at 20,000 packages and 1,500 trust-store certificates the worst legal submission is ~9.3 MiB, and the cap sits at 32 MiB, with a test pinning the relationship so the two cannot drift apart.

Results are stored and HELD. Nothing yet creates an asset, an endpoint, a finding or a fact row — that is workstream 2.11b. The same reasoning as #1633's hold on sensor host observations: a host-inventory result carries one endpoint per listening socket with no crypto posture and an identity made from the host's own MACs and serial, and through the crypto ingest that is a finding per socket, a loopback endpoint routed to external_connections, and a fresh nameless server every collection. The held run is visible with an honest headline (materialized: 0, fully_materialized: false, and a line saying why) rather than absent, and the whole payload stays on the job row.

Operator guide: docsv4/core/operate/deployment/device-agent-deployment.md — including the exact command list per OS. Developer contract: docsv4/internal/developer/standards/HOST_INVENTORY.md, which also carries the osquery input-adapter query list (documented, deliberately not embedded).

  • What a device is is now argued from a curated rule table, not from constants in Go. The fingerprint rules behind every class proposal — MAC OUI, SNMP sysObjectID, EtherNet/IP vendor id, cloud resource type, service banner, port profile, model prefix, and the management platform the device answered — live in standards/classification-rules.yaml, generate into both a compiled-in Go table and seeded classification_rules rows, and are curated by platform admins at Catalog ▸ Classification rules (catalogs.manage, full CRUD, audited). This is asset-inventory ADR-0004 D6: the catalogue grows without a release.

shared/classify is the engine — pure Go, no database, no CGO, so the sensor and the device agent classify identically to a service. It is also the Classifier seam's default implementation (ADR-0008 D1's "rule-based default" column, not the null one); Classifier: "none" still selects a classifier that proposes nothing.

The posture is the feature:

  • A wrong class is worse than no class. Two thirds of the shipped OUI rules name a vendor and deliberately no class, because Dell, HP, NETGEAR, Ubiquiti, Cisco Meraki and Zebra each sell three or four different kinds of thing under one IEEE assignment. class_key is nullable so that is expressible, and a test fails if the ratio ever inverts.
  • Two rules that disagree produce nothing. Unrelated classes within 0.10 confidence of each other yield no class and report both — a contradiction in the catalogue, named, rather than a coin flip. A refinement (switch under network_device) is not a disagreement and resolves to the specific class.
  • Every rule cites a source, and a prefix IEEE never assigned does not get to cite IEEE: the locally-administered virtualisation markers (FA:16:3E, 02:42:AC, 52:54:00) cite the platform that documents the convention, and make audit fails if one does not.
  • One manufacturer, one name. OUI → vendor has a single owner (standards/oui-vendors.csv, the same table the sensor compiles in), the OUI rules are derived from it, and the generator refuses any hand-written rule that spells a manufacturer differently.

shared/deviceinterrogation/classhint.go is now a thin adapter over the engine; a parity test transcribes every pre-existing hint and fails by name if one disappears. Rules added in the console are stored, validated and audited but not yet consulted at run time — the classifier reads the shipped set, and both the page and the operator guide say so. (#1646)

  • End-of-life answers now come with the row that said them — and where the catalogue is silent, AI proposes and a person decides. Catalog → End-of-life gains two views beside the catalogue table: Proposals and Gaps.

This is ADR-0008 D1's Enricher seam, and unlike the narrator and the author its Core path genuinely answers:

  • Ask what the platform knows. "Check a product" on the Gaps view resolves a vendor/product/version against eol_catalogue and against the CPE names advisories already use, and shows each fact with its source_kind, the row id that stated it, and the page that cites it.
  • It will not answer approximately. A version whose release train is not in the catalogue resolves to nothing, never to the neighbouring cycle — that would be a support date wrong in the direction that reassures. A row that publishes no end-of-life date, or carries no source URL, produces no fact.
  • And it does not round its answer down to "nothing". "The catalogue has never heard of this" and "the catalogue has it and the vendor has not announced a date" are different answers with different fixes, and only the first is a gap — so the second says so and adds nothing to the gap list.
  • Every gap is counted. A lookup that resolves nothing lands on catalog_lookup_misses with a count, so the Gaps view is ordered by what is actually costing you answers rather than by what happened to be logged.
  • AI proposals are Enterprise, and they are proposals. With a provider configured, a run over the top gaps asks a model for an end-of-life row with a vendor page to cite. Proposals with no usable citation, an unparseable or self-contradicting date, or a URL pointing at a private address are discarded before anyone sees them; "unknown" is an expected answer and costs nothing. The pass also runs after each nightly mirror pass, in that order, so nothing is asked about a gap the feed has just filled.
  • Accepting is the only thing that writes the catalogue. A proposal is reviewed beside its cited URL; accept writes the row and marks the proposal in one transaction, with source_kind = inferred, the citation, and the reviewer's name. The citation is re-checked at that moment rather than trusted from write time, because that is when a claim becomes data every tenant is evaluated against. The table badges such a row AI-proposed permanently, so it never becomes indistinguishable from a mirrored fact. Rejecting writes nothing and keeps the proposal as a record of what was wrong.
  • No provider, no button. A new availability endpoint answers in every edition — {"available":false,"reason":"edition"} in Core, "no_provider" where nothing is configured — so the action is never offered where it would answer 503, and the page says which of the two is missing.

Subjects are redacted at the provider boundary before they are sent, and every call is audited (seam, provider, model id, prompt hash, tokens, invoker — never the prompt). Accept, reject and run-now land in the platform audit trail with the subject, the dates, the model and the cited URL. (#1644)

  • Ask the inventory a question and get back a query you can edit, plus the rows it selected. ADR-0008 D1's Query seam (shared/ai/ee/query), Enterprise, behind the provider boundary. This release ships the seam; the surfaces that call it — the MCP ask tool, the inventory endpoint and the command-palette mode — follow.

The design is that a model never returns rows. It returns one line of the query language, which is parsed and validated against the catalogue, run by the read-only MCP tools under your own row-level security, and shown to you, editable. So an answer you disagree with is a predicate you can correct, and an answer you like is a view you can save.

  • It refuses rather than guesses. A query that does not validate gets one repair turn carrying the validator's own diagnostics, and is then refused with those diagnostics attached — "no field hostnaem on assets, did you mean hostname?" — instead of returning confidently wrong rows.
  • Every sentence cites a row, by asset id, and a sentence citing a row the model was not given is discarded. If nothing survives, the rows are still returned with a plain note saying the summary was discarded and why.
  • Nothing matched is not nothing is there. A query that selects no assets gets a fixed sentence saying exactly that, and the model is not asked to describe an absence it cannot cite.
  • Bounded, in code: two translation turns, three tool calls, three narration turns. After the rows are in, the model may ask for one of three read-only tools — asset detail, the class list, facet counts — and nothing else.
  • Your question is redacted before it is sent (a pasted private key never reaches a provider) and the call is audited: seam, provider, model id, prompt hash, tokens, invoker, plus the canonical query that ran. The question itself is recorded only if the tenant opts in.

Core is unaffected: it has the whole query language, the facet rail and saved views, and the seam is null. (#1643)

  • SBOM parsing: CycloneDX and SPDX documents into a normalised software model. Two new shared packages — shared/software and shared/sbom — turn a bill of materials into the shape software_products and software_installs rows have. This is ADR-0004 D3's "SBOM ingestion first", and it makes CycloneDX an input to the platform as well as an output.

This is the parser library (workstream 2.6a). The upload endpoint, the Discovery → Sources page and the asset Software tab are 2.6b; nothing here is reachable by a user yet.

  • CycloneDX JSON 1.4–1.7 and SPDX JSON 2.2/2.3, detected from the document's own declaration rather than from a filename or Content-Type, neither of which is evidence. Nested CycloneDX components are flattened with containment recorded; SPDX primaryPackagePurpose is mapped onto the CycloneDX type vocabulary so a consumer reads one vocabulary whichever format arrived; cpe22Type external references are converted to CPE 2.3 so the two spellings of one product dedupe to one row.
  • One identity rule, matching the database. Product.Identity() is coalesce(purl, cpe, name || '@' || coalesce(version, '')) — including the inner coalesce, without which an unversioned product produces a NULL key and NULLs do not conflict, so every re-observation would insert another row. VersionSort() delegates to ast.VersionSortKey, the definition of version_sort and of the query language's version < 3.0; a second implementation would have the writer and the translator disagree silently.
  • Cryptographic components are skipped, with a counted warning. They are the CBOM path's business and an algorithm does not belong in a software catalogue. The fixture set includes the cbom-service formatter's own output, so a document this platform emits is one it accepts.
  • Nothing is silent. A malformed component, licence, edge or relationship is skipped with a warning rather than failing the document; a dropped purl or CPE names itself; a declared subject that cannot be read or resolves to no package says so rather than simply coming back absent; the two caps (32 MiB, 100,000 components) refuse the document rather than truncating it, because a half-ingested SBOM shows a software list that looks complete. An SPDX LicenseRef-… is dropped with a warning: it is an id its own document defines and nothing else, so two unrelated build systems both emitting LicenseRef-0 would merge two licences under one catalogue value.
  • No key material. redact.TextPEM runs over every string returned, warnings included — a warning quoting a malformed field is a leak path too, and it is the one nobody inspects. CERTIFICATE blocks survive: they are posture, and an over-strict scrubber is the same bug pointed the other way.
  • FuzzParse ships a committed seed corpus and asserts, on every input, no panic, a writable component with a non-empty identity, resolvable edges and no string that redaction would still change.

Contract and the mutation table for every guard: docsv4/internal/developer/standards/SBOM_INGESTION.md.

  • Draft compliance controls from a pasted standard — cited, unpublished, and evaluated by the engine, never by the model. Both compliance-authoring surfaces gain a Draft from a standard… action: Catalog → Frameworks for platform admins and Settings → Policies → Custom Policies for Enterprise tenants. Paste the text of a standard, or one section of it, and the platform proposes controls with measurement rules for you to review.

This is ADR-0008 D1's Author seam (services/compliance-engine/ee/author), and the honesty rules are the feature:

  • Every draft cites the passage it came from, by byte span, highlighted in your pasted text beside the draft. A draft whose citation does not resolve against the text we sent is discarded before anyone sees it.
  • Rules use only the measurement catalogue this deployment has, validated with the same MeasurementValidator the create-measurement endpoint runs. A rule naming an unknown measurement, an illegal operator, or a pattern that could never match the values its measurement can take is dropped and the control kept without it — with a note saying the control will score Not assessed, which is not a pass.
  • Everything discarded is reported, with the reason and the subject, so a model that cannot count bytes is distinguishable from a catalogue that is missing the measurement your standard is about.
  • Nothing is written by the drafting endpoints. Accepting a draft calls the ordinary create-control endpoint — same route, same validation, same permission — with source_kind: inferred and source_ref: author:<model>. Both control tables gained those two nullable columns and both control lists badge a drafted control. Publishing the framework is still the approval step, and the platform endpoint refuses a framework that is already published.
  • No provider, no button. A new availability endpoint on each plane answers in every edition — {"available":false,"reason":"edition"} in Core, "no_provider" where nothing is configured — so neither UI offers an action that would answer 503. The tenant endpoint is additionally gated on the custom_policies entitlement.

The pasted text is redacted at the provider boundary before it is sent, and the call is audited (seam, provider, model id, prompt hash, tokens, invoker — never the prompt). (#1639)

  • The CBOM comparison summary is now the Narrator seam, and it cites its sources. The prose above a CBOM diff has always been rule-written; it is now an implementation of seams.Narrator (ADR-0008 D1), alongside a second implementation that asks a configured model.
