Every deployment gets the deterministic one by default — nothing leaves the process, and the wording is unchanged.

Both narrators cite. DiffChange gains a row_id (r1, r2, …) and the summary carries inline [row:<row_id>] markers, which the compare page renders as links that jump to the change being counted. A new narrative_detail on the comparison response carries the marked-up text, the citation list, ADR-0008 D4.1 provenance, and source: rules | model plus model_id — so the panel can say "Summarised by rules" or "Summarised by \<model>" rather than leaving a reader to guess which they are reading. narrative itself is unchanged: the same plain sentence, markers stripped.

With AI_PROVIDER configured, the model is shown only the categorised rows — category, component name, and the one-phrase reason — never the CBOM documents, capped at 40 rows chosen worst-first, with the prompt stating explicitly how many rows were withheld. It goes through ai.Boundary, so it is redacted and audited. Every sentence whose citations do not resolve, and every sentence with no citation, is discarded before the user sees it; if nothing survives — or the provider is unreachable, unauthorised, rate-limited, slow, or returns no model id — the rule narrative answers. The narrator never returns an error to the user and never leaves an empty panel. (#1632)

  • audit.NewAISink adapts ai.AuditSink onto the platform audit rail every backend already wires, so an ADR-0008 D4.7 record (seam, provider, model id, prompt hash, tokens, invoker — never the prompt) lands in the same activity log as every other audited action. Reusable by the next service that wires a provider.

  • End-of-life and vulnerability catalogues, with their mirror feeds and an offline bundle. Platform admins get two new pages under Catalog beside Algorithms and Frameworks — End-of-life (eol_catalogue, mirrored from endoflife.date) and Vulnerability feed (vulnerability_catalogue + vulnerability_matches, mirrored from the NVD 2.0 API and osv.dev's bulk exports). Each page is a searchable, paginated table plus a feed-status card showing the last run, its outcome, the rows written and the bookmark, with a Sync now button and an Import bundle upload.

The feeds run daily inside admin-service, are incremental (NVD by modification window, OSV by per-ecosystem watermark), take a Postgres advisory lock so scaling the service does not multiply the requests going to NVD, and record every outcome in a new catalog_feed_state table. A feed error is recorded, never fatal, and the bookmark only advances on success — so a failed run retries its window instead of skipping it.

For air-gapped installs, make build-catalog-bundle DATABASE_URL=… exports both catalogues as a tarball with a SHA-256 and row count per file; importing it verifies every file before writing a single row, so a corrupt transfer cannot leave a half-imported catalogue. Integrity rather than a signature: these catalogues are Core, so there is nothing to license.

New platform permission catalogs.manage (granted to super_admin and platform_admin), kill switch CATALOG_FEEDS_ENABLED, optional NVD_API_KEY to raise NVD's rate limit from 5 to 50 requests per 30 seconds, and OSV_ECOSYSTEMS to choose which osv.dev buckets to mirror. Operator guide: docsv4/core/operate/catalogs.md, including the sources' attribution terms.

Two limits stated plainly rather than papered over. The catalogue is keyed on CVE id, so an OSV advisory with no CVE assigned is not mirrored (the skip count is logged and the page says so); and a CVE mirrored only from OSV carries a CVSS vector with no base score, which the console shows as "vector only" rather than a 0.0 that would read as "not serious".

This fills the catalogues. Nothing evaluates them against tenant inventory yet — the end-of-life and vulnerability producers are the next slice and depend on the asset-model rewrite. (#1605)

  • AI model providers behind the existing boundary (Enterprise). The two generative endpoints ADR-0008 specified now exist: Anthropic (Messages API) and an OpenAI-compatible client that covers hosted OpenAI, vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio and the gateways that imitate that shape. Both are pure net/http with no new dependencies, and both sit behind the redaction and audit decorators that shipped in 0.5 — a prompt that has not been through the redactor is refused at the provider itself, not only at the boundary.

Configuration is AI_PROVIDER / AI_BASE_URL / AI_MODEL / AI_API_KEY_ENV / AI_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS (plus AI_MAX_TOKENS and AI_TIMEOUT), all documented in env.example. The API key is never stored in configuration — only the name of the environment variable holding it, read at the moment of use — so a configuration row that leaks is a configuration row.

AI_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS (default false) is the knob worth knowing about: pointing the platform at your own Ollama or vLLM on a private address is a legitimate setup and an SSRF target wearing the same clothes, so it is an explicit operator decision rather than a guard quietly dropped. With it off, a private endpoint is refused twice — at configuration time for a literal IP, and at connect time for a hostname that resolves to one.

Unchanged for Core and for anyone who configures nothing: AI_PROVIDER still defaults to none, every seam still returns its documented null answer, and nothing is sent anywhere. A Core build does not contain the providers at all and says so — naming one yields the no-AI provider plus a logged warning, never a silent half-configured state.

Streaming is deliberately not implemented yet; the seams that need it arrive with the grounded-query work.

  • The has_findings inventory facet is back (withdrawn in Gate 1), as a tri-state control on the filter rail — has open findings / has none / any. It counted compliance_findings while the rail's click wrote a finding:(…) term over the unified findings table, so the number described a different set from the list it led to. The repair is not a second expression pointed somewhere else: the facet now produces its count by COMPILING the exact query text the rail writes, through the same translator the asset list compiles, and that text is generated into Go (findings.OpenQuery) and TypeScript (OPEN_FINDINGS_QUERY) from one line of standards/findings-registry.yaml. One integration test drives the facet and the list against a single fixture and fails if they diverge. "No open findings" still means producers looked and found nothing — for assets nobody has looked at, Risk → Not assessed is the honest third answer.

  • Release-candidate verification runs itself. scripts/rc-verify.sh installs a published chart version on a cluster the way a customer does (helm upgrade --install from the OCI registry, polling until the version exists), waits for the rollout, ensures a verification tenant exists through self-service signup (scripts/rc-verify-tenant.sh), runs rc-smoke.sh and helm test, and writes a one-page Markdown summary. It refuses to run unless every node name matches --expect-nodes, so a wrong kubeconfig fails before helm is called. Internal only for now — both scripts, and the rc-verify.yml workflow that drives them on the dev cluster, are dropped by the public-tree export, because rc-verify.sh cannot start without rc-smoke.sh and that has never shipped. The workflow runs after an -rc.N publish only while the repository variable RC_VERIFY_AUTO is true (absent = off: a shared cluster is not upgraded because a tag was pushed, and a re-run of an older publish is refused outright); it can be dispatched for any version in upgrade or fresh (no-migration, destructive, dispatch-only) mode. Guarded by scripts/test-rc-verify.mjs in make standards-check, which executes the workflow's resolve step rather than reading it.

  • The data path verifies itself too. tools/qa-platform/cmd/rc-verify-data registers a sensor exactly as a real one does (CSR-issued certificate, agent-mTLS passthrough), pushes a committed golden dataset through the sensor plane, and asserts what the tenant API reports: hosts → exactly that many monitoring assets, endpoints, crypto configurations, certificates and their expired state, legacy-TLS risk banding, risk-band sums, PQC summary/progress agreement, Core framework scores, findings. Counts are derived from the dataset; product behaviours are pinned in expected.json. Runs in rc-verify.yml after the install smoke; tested against a fake platform with one failing check per mutation.

  • The UI journeys verify themselves too. A new e2e/ workspace (Playwright, pinned to the browser build the lab runners already hold) logs into the deployed tenant UI through the real two-step login as the verification-data tenant and drives ledger journeys J3, J5, J9, J11, J13, J14 and J15 — dashboard counts and risk index against /risk/summary, PQC readiness against /pqc/progress, framework cards and "not assessed" against /frameworks/available, the Certificates and Configuration lenses against their APIs, Sensors & Agents rows, and a CBOM generated, listed with its hash, opened and verified from the page. Every number on screen is compared with the API the page itself calls. Runs in rc-verify.yml after the data path; ci.yml type-checks the package on every PR.

  • rc-verify can seed a fresh verification-data tenant. The workflow's dispatch takes a data_tenant suffix; the data path and the browser journeys then run against rc-verify-data-<suffix>@rc-verify.invalid, a tenant nothing has ever approved by hand, so "exactly N monitoring assets" proves segment auto-approval itself rather than a prior manual approval. Empty (the default) reuses the standing tenant.

  • Discovery → Discovery Jobs now lists every scan, not just device interrogations. discovery_jobs — Active Scans, Discover wizard runs, and the automatic-scan sweep — had no listing page anywhere; a scan sent to a tenant sensor was visible only as a feedback panel on the page that started it, or a stub run list under Settings → Active Scanning. The existing Discovery Jobs table (no new route, no new nav entry) now merges those jobs with device-interrogation jobs into one list, with Kind (Interrogation / Discovery / Automatic scan), Status and Executor filters. Clicking a discovery or automatic-scan row opens a detail panel with the dispatch timeline (queued → dispatched to \<sensor> at t → picked up → completed/ failed), its targets, and the findings/materialization split; Cancel is offered wherever cluster-sensor-service already supports it. (#1858)

  • Sensors report their own host, so it's a named, classed asset the platform never scans. The machine a sensor runs ON used to be visible only if some OTHER sensor happened to see it passively (ARP/mDNS), landing as an anonymous unknown_host carrying nothing but a MAC and an IP — even though the sensors row for that same host already knew its name, platform and profile. A sensor now reports its own hostname, FQDN (cached, never a blocking DNS call on the heartbeat path), OS/arch and per-interface MACs at registration and (throttled — at most once an hour unless it changed) on heartbeat. sensor-manager turns that into a host observation through the same ingest path every passive capture already uses, tagged with agent_id — the strongest identifier kind there is, so it can never mis-merge with an unrelated host sharing an address — plus a class hint from the sensor's platform/profile. An asset already seen passively (a real-deployment case: another sensor's capture created an anonymous MAC/IP-only unknown_host before this sensor ever self-reported) is retro-matched and upgraded with a name and a class, never overwritten if a rule or a human already classified it. The Sensors & Agents drawer shows a Host line linking to the resolved asset once one exists. Active-scan auto-routing (#1839) now excludes a sensor's own addresses from its targets — a sensor is never dispatched to scan the host it runs on. sensors.asset_id is nullable and absent (not blanked) for an older sensor build that sends no host block.

  • Active scans can run from the sensor that actually sees the host. A host reachable only from inside an organization's network used to get a passive partial observation forever, because every active scan ran from the platform sensor inside the cluster. Discovery → Active Scan gains a Run from control — Auto (observing sensor), Platform sensor, or a named tenant sensor — and automatic scans choose the same way behind a new Prefer the observing sensor switch (default on) on Settings → Discovery → Active Scanning. The observing sensor is the one whose passive capture last recorded the host; failing that a sensor on the same segment; failing that the platform. A scan sent to a sensor that is offline fails immediately and says so — it is never run from the platform instead — and a sensor that goes quiet after being handed a job fails it, naming the sensor and its last check-in, once the time its own reporting cadence allows has passed. Where scans are visible they now say who ran them and in what state — the Active Scan page keeps a Scans started from this page panel (executor, Queued · Awaiting · Running on · Completed · Failed: sensor offline with the sensor's last check-in, and the dispatch timeline, updating while the scan runs), and the Active Scanning settings run list shows the same for automatic scans. The permission follows the action: running from a sensor needs the same assets.update as running from the platform. A dispatched job's results take the sensor's ordinary discovery route and land on the asset as active observations. The legacy tenant-JWT POST /discovery/jobs/{id}/results intake, which a sensor could never authenticate to and which fed nothing inventory read, is removed. (#1839)

  • Automatic active scanning. The platform now builds the inventory without being asked: a new internal host is actively scanned for its cryptography as soon as it appears — from a sensor, an interrogated device, a scan or an import — and every internal host is scanned again once the organization's rescan interval (24 hours by default) has elapsed. Tenant admins control all of it, including turning it off, at Settings → Discovery → Active Scanning, which also shows what the platform has been scanning. Only internal addresses are ever scanned automatically: private ranges, or a network segment the organization registered as its own and typed private, VPN or cloud. Public addresses, segments the organization typed public, third-party-owned assets, shared carrier space and the platform's own addresses are never probed; scanning stops for an organization whose account is cancelled or suspended; and the default port set is narrower than the Discover wizard's, leaving file-sharing and industrial-control ports out of a scan that repeats unattended. (#1809) Upgrading to this release starts scanning your existing internal inventory on the first sweep — every internal host already in the inventory is due, and is scanned again every 24 hours by default. Tenant admins can turn it off at Settings → Discovery → Active Scanning; operators who would rather stage it can hold the worker off cluster-wide with DISCOVERY_AUTO_SCAN_WORKER_ENABLED=false and release it later.

  • The Active Scanning page now says what it did not scan. A Not scanned panel lists, by reason, the hosts the last pass looked at and refused — public addresses, carrier-grade NAT space, the platform's own addresses, link-local and the rest — with a count, and for the first two a link to register the range as a network segment. Carrier-grade NAT (100.64.0.0/10, RFC 6598) is now named as its own reason rather than folded into "public", because Tailscale, ZeroTier and mobile carriers hand out that range and an estate built on one of them was seeing "Automatic scanning: on" over a sweep that scanned nothing. What is refused has not changed.

  • Platform admins can set a tenant's email-verification and onboarding overrides again. admin-ui-v2 gains a Settings tab on the tenant drawer (Tenants → a tenant → Settings), where a platform admin with tenants.manage can require or waive email verification, and require or waive the onboarding walkthrough, for one customer organization. Each control is three-way — Platform default / Required / Not required — and the first option names what the platform default currently resolves to, so the choice is not made blind; leaving a setting on the platform default keeps that tenant tracking later changes to it rather than freezing today's value. auth-service has read both of these overrides all along, but the UI that set them lived in the v1 admin console and was dropped in the v1→v2 rebuild, so for the whole v2 era the per-tenant tier of both settings could not be reached. Operators without tenants.manage see the same panel read-only.

  • Automatic scans now count as scans on the Active Scan coverage list. An automatic scan that completes and records a finding for an endpoint stamps that endpoint as scanned, so a host the platform has already probed no longer sits on Discovery → Active Scan as never scanned. Only assets in monitoring are stamped — a host still waiting in Approvals has its findings held, so it stays on the list until it is approved or scanned by hand.

  • Processed sensor_discoveries rows are now purged after a retention window instead of accumulating forever. discovery-processor-service's raw ingestion queue kept every row indefinitely once it had been materialized, suppressed, deferred or routed — a one-sensor lab accumulated 13,779 rows in 24 hours with nothing bounding the total. A new bounded sweep (its own ticker, a cross-replica advisory lock so only one pod runs it at a time, deletes in 5,000-row batches) purges rows where processed_at IS NOT NULL and older than the retention window; an unprocessed row — still awaiting the poller — is never touched, however old. Default window 7 days (SENSOR_DISCOVERY_RETENTION_HOURS, default 168); kill switch SENSOR_DISCOVERY_RETENTION_ENABLED (default on). A supporting partial index (idx_sensor_discoveries_part_processed_at) keeps each sweep from sequentially scanning the table.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The dashboard's overdue-ticket card opens the work queue rather than the remediation plans grid, which lists a different object. (#1911)
  • A ticket's resolution time is stamped once, when it first reaches a terminal status, instead of being rewritten when it is later closed. Reopening a resolved ticket clears it. Average resolution time and the resolved-per-day trend were both inflated by the rewrite. (#1911)
  • A ticket created with a category the server does not accept now answers 400 naming the field and the value, instead of a generic 500. (#1911)
  • A host the tenant's own device agent is installed on is approved into inventory by its first local host inventory, instead of waiting in Discovery → Approvals. Installing and enrolling the agent is the decision the queue was asking for; the history row names the agent as the approver. Remotely collected hosts, and hosts a person has denied, are unaffected.
  • Identity enrichment's executor selection is no longer tied to the collector that heard a device advertised: any of the tenant's eligible collectors on the observed network can execute enrichment, while the observing collector is preserved as provenance. (#1898, #1901)
  • Existing retained observations that never produced an asset are automatically re-checked and materialized into provisional inventory items after upgrade, with no re-registration required. (#1898, #1901)
  • Automatic enrichment can refresh an explicitly configured source through a durable, deduplicated job, with tenant policy and executor checks and honest completion after ingestion. Admission and enrichment remain separately gated.
  • Observation details explain retained host, peer, cloud and cryptographic evidence with original source/times and safe certificate validity summaries.

  • Identity enrichment records durable source-first work, collector capability blockers and bounded scoped DNS/TLS/SSH attempts. Replays retain job identities and observation clocks; admission pause also pauses automatic asset scans.

  • Inventory distinguishes unevaluated identity records from established and operator-confirmed identities, independently of approval and assessment.

  • Discovery observations have durable source evidence and replay-safe receipt tracking, with an observation browser and identity coverage counts. Prospective activation is tenant-scoped and requires the coupled release acceptance gates.

  • Retained observations support reasoned confirmation, explicit linking, and dismissal. Confirmation preserves separate monitoring approval and checks the asset allowance. Deferred certificate evidence survives processing restarts.

  • Existing-asset reconciliation supports explicitly selected candidates, server previews, stale-evidence refresh, field decisions and durable merge audit. Archived sources redirect to the survivor; merge undo remains unavailable.

  • Trustworthy discovery settings separate admission from automatic enrichment, require a reason and current version, and retain incoming evidence while paused. Existing records stay visible as unevaluated without a bulk rewrite.

  • "Stale" means one thing now: 30 days. The Inventory → Stale lens cut at 14 days while the Stale finding's first rung, the Inventory Hygiene control IH-004 and everything else that judges freshness started at 30 — so a record could be listed as stale with no finding, no failing control and nothing anywhere agreeing that it was. The lens now reads the same ladder the finding does, so it lists fewer records than before. Both sides come from one constant and a test fails if they part company again.

  • The hierarchical class facet — the dashboard's costliest query — is about nineteen times faster (243 ms → 13 ms on a seeded 50,000-asset tenant, identical rows). It counts the distinct class paths before expanding them into ancestor prefixes rather than after. The cost was never the work: the expansion itself was 76 ms, but generate_series(1, <expr>) carries no row estimate, so the planner costed the join at fifty million rows and crossed the JIT threshold — two thirds of the time went on compiling a plan for a query that touches 1,389 pages.

  • A class argued from a rule is now recorded as such. class_source_kind on an asset gained a fifth value, rule, alongside measured, declared, imported and inferred, and class_source_ref names the rule row. Calling a rule-derived class "measured" would claim we measured the mapping (we measured the MAC); calling it "inferred" would call a deterministic, citable rule a model. Both are false provenance on the one field used to audit a class.

  • The Approvals count and the Inventory banner include class proposals. Approvals is one queue, and a count that covered three of its four row kinds pointed at a page with more work on it than the number admitted.

  • proposed_by in the query language now finds rule-derived classes. The Inventory facet listed them and filtering on one returned nothing, because the predicate behind it named only the older machine-proposed kind. Filtering on a facet bucket and getting an empty page is a bug that reads as an answer.

  • An unknown host is now recognised by its serial number. "Unknown host" is the class for something in your own space that nothing has identified further — and, now, for a serial nothing has classified yet. A serial names one chassis globally, so two sightings carrying the same one are the same machine whatever either sighting managed to work out about it; withholding that from the least-identified class did not make it more honest, it made it unable to recognise something it had already seen. This affects every way assets arrive, not only the NetBox connector.

Nothing about conflicting evidence changed: when a sighting's serial disagrees with the one an asset already carries — a restored image or a cloned machine carrying an agent's identity onto different hardware — you are still asked, in Discovery → Approvals, rather than told.

  • A host-inventory submission is about half the size it was. The package list used to be sent twice in every report — once in the collector's own record and once in the observations the platform materialises. It is now sent once, with the omission marked explicitly so an empty list cannot be misread as a host with no packages, and --host-inventory-once still prints the full local report. On a 20,000-package host the worst-case submission falls from ~9.3 MiB to ~5.1 MiB, against an unchanged 32 MiB cap.

  • An asset is a thing, not a listening port. The inventory's unit is now a configuration item with a class, identifiers and endpoints: a host exposing five services is ONE asset with five endpoints, where it used to be five assets. network_assets and devices are replaced by assets, asset_endpoints, asset_management and asset_credentials; the four-value asset_type enum is replaced by the class registry; and the address, port and identified service move from the asset to the endpoint. What that removes, and why nothing is carried forward, is under Removed below. Phase 1 of the general asset inventory initiative (ADR-0002, ADR-0007); no public release is cut until core-v1.0.0.

  • One identification engine behind every intake. Sensor ingest, active scan, cloud discovery, PCAP, spreadsheet import, CMDB pull and manual create all build an observation and resolve it through shared/identity instead of the four different dedupe keys they used before (manual create did not dedupe at all). A hostname or an IP now identifies only within its network SEGMENT, a serial or a cloud resource id identifies globally, and identifiers that resolve to more than one asset open a merge proposal in Approvals rather than merging anything.

  • Asset risk can go down. The per-asset score is recomputed as the maximum over the asset's scored crypto configurations. The previous write was GREATEST(old, new), so removing the last weak configuration left the asset reporting its old maximum forever. risk_assessed_by records which producers have looked, so a score of 0 with an empty array (not assessed) is distinguishable from 0 with {crypto} (assessed clean).

  • asset_history has a writer. Every asset creation, match, merge proposal, context change and status change records an entry with its provenance. The table has existed since the beginning with no writer at all — not Go, not a trigger.

  • BREAKING (API): a finding names its SUBJECT, and severity is one lowercase ladder. With the unified findings table (see Removed), every finding shape on the wire changed. A client reading the old names silently gets undefined rather than an error, so this list is the upgrade:

was is asset_id on a finding subject_id asset_type on a finding (network_asset/certificate/crypto_implementation) subject_type (asset/certificate) severity Low/Med/High/Critical info/low/medium/high/critical severity_counts.med severity_counts.medium finding_asset_type / finding_asset_id on a remediation plan item finding_subject_type / finding_subject_id

Findings additionally gained producer, kind, score and subject_label. GET /assets/{assetId}/findings now answers for the asset and its descendants, from every producer, and returns only OPEN findings — detection_state = ACTIVE and workflow_status NOT IN (RESOLVED, SUPPRESSED). The MCP vistaplatform_get_control_findings tool description changed with it.

  • network_segments records its provenance. New nullable source_kind / source_ref columns (ADR-0005's vocabulary). NULL means "drawn before this column existed" and is deliberately distinct from declared — a segment somebody drew two years ago has no recorded provenance, and labelling it would invent a fact. A NetBox prefix that matches an existing segment stamps the provenance and leaves the tenant's name, environment, tags and auto-approval settings alone.

  • Two unused search indexes on the findings table are gone. They were trigram indexes meant to speed up the Findings page's free-text search, and Postgres could never use them: the search matches a term against the summary, the subject label, the finding kind OR the host, and a disjunction that includes the host lookup cannot be served from an index at all. Measured on a 50,000-finding tenant, the query plan is identical with them and without them, while the two indexes cost ~18 MB and were rewritten on every producer pass. Removing them changes no result and no timing; it removes write cost and the impression that the search is indexed.

  • Risk & Compliance → Findings now opens on By Producer. The page's nav home was the By Severity lens, which reads inventory-service's crypto-risk stream — a different data set from the one the page is documented to show ("every open finding for your organization, from every producer"). End-of-life, vulnerability, configuration, hygiene and drift findings were therefore invisible until the reader changed lenses, on the one surface the product points a person at for triage. The Dashboard's "Critical findings" tile links here explicitly rather than riding the default, and counts the Criticals in the same every-producer set this lens groups.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Sensor self-reports use a separate installation identifier from device agents, preventing false conflicts when both run on one host. Existing sensor identifiers retain their asset association on upgrade.

  • Enrichment distinguishes offline collectors from online collectors without an eligible interface in the target network, including reflected advertisements.

  • New password and social signups start with identity admission and automatic enrichment enabled, with an audited initial policy. Existing tenant policies are preserved. Inventory describes unevaluated identities without the misleading “legacy” label and explains inactive or paused assessment.

  • Sensors report a restart requirement only for capture settings that differ from the running capture configuration. Changes are saved before acceptance, persistence errors are surfaced, and pending values are not reported as running.

  • The Linux sensor installer checks startup dependencies before installation and explains libpcap and loader failures; --check-dependencies supports a check without root access or registration.

  • Cloud discoveries retain encrypted provider context while identity is unresolved, then replay facts and crypto evidence with original observation timestamps. Cloud job logs distinguish retained evidence, created/matched assets and approval.

  • Approving an asset no longer refreshes its observation time or clears its stale state. Existing observation timestamps are not rewritten.

  • The platform interrogation worker uses one fleet identity. The unused device-agent auto-registration route, token, bootstrap certificate and synthetic heartbeat have been retired. The existing system sensor continues to identify the worker and attribute discovery results. Operator-installed agents retain enrollment, certificate rotation and heartbeats. Historical duplicate device-agent rows may appear offline until an operator deletes them through the normal fleet lifecycle; the platform-managed system sensor remains protected. (#1875)

  • An asset is re-classified when a host inventory arrives, and the classifier can finally read an operating system. Classification ran exactly once, when an asset was created, and nothing re-asked the question when better evidence turned up minutes later: a laptop first seen passively was created unknown_host from an address and a MAC, and a device agent's full host inventory for the same asset three minutes later — OS, vendor, model, serial, 106 software installs, 83 listening sockets — changed nothing. It also could not have: a general-purpose computer matches no rule kind the catalogue had, since its OUI is vendor-only by design and its model is a consumer product line. Two halves, both needed:

  • A new os_name classification-rule kind (RE2 over the reported os.name), seeded with rules for client Windows and macOS → computer and Windows Server → server. Linux and the BSDs get no rule on purpose — a distribution name is not a statement of function. Curated like every other kind under Catalog ▸ Classification rules.
  • The host-inventory intake now applies the rules' class to an asset it creates, and PROMOTES an existing asset that is still on the unknown_host floor, writing the move to asset_class_history. A human-declared class is never touched, an asset already holding a real class gets a proposal in Approvals instead, and a class the learned model proposed is never applied. Only first-hand evidence may promote: an interrogated peer, which is described by a third party, still proposes.
  • A matched asset is also named. The identification engine writes display_name only at creation, so an asset the platform knew the hostname of went on being displayed as a bare IP address; a display name that is an address is now replaced by the hostname, and one that is a real name is left alone.
  • A reverse-DNS guess no longer overwrites the hostname a sensor measured. Third-party connections in Inventory → 3rd Party showed a generic cloud PTR name (ec2-54-163-235-119.compute-1.amazonaws.com) in place of the vhost the client actually asked for (slack.com), because the active TLS enricher's row carries no SNI of its own and fell through to reverse DNS. Two fixes: a discovery now inherits the SNI its own passive sibling captured in the same batch (refusing to guess when one address was contacted under two names), and external_connections.dest_hostname gained a provenance (dest_hostname_source_kind, the ADR-0005 measured/inferred vocabulary) that the upsert enforces — an inference can never replace a measurement, and a measurement can always correct one. Existing rows are unlabelled and keep their names; a real SNI now repairs them on the next observation.
  • A sensor or discovery agent that never reported can now go offline. The offline detector measured the dwell from last_heartbeat alone, behind an AND last_heartbeat IS NOT NULL guard, so a subject that registered and then never checked in — the ordinary shape of a failed install, where registration succeeds and the service then fails to start or is firewalled — showed active in the console indefinitely and raised no sensor_offline or discovery_agent_offline alert, ever. It now measures from COALESCE(last_heartbeat, created_at), the form sensor-manager's reaper has always used; the two code paths had disagreed, so such sensors were flipped to offline while the alert path stayed silent about them. An alert for a subject that has never reported says so rather than rendering a zero timestamp, and clears on the subject's first heartbeat. Sensors an operator marked air-gapped are now excluded from the detector — the flag means the sensor is not expected to check in at all.
  • Certificate controls could report a clean pass on a certificate nothing had evaluated. The per-asset compliance reconcile behind every asset-change event folded certificate-subject controls against the asset's id, which matches no certificate, so those controls produced no measurement and no finding — and the score rollup, which derives a control's verdict from the absence of an active finding, read that silence as a pass. A tenant whose only certificate had 56 days of validity left scored 100/100 on "Certificate expires within 90 days"; the same pass also cleared the PQC-readiness certificate controls. An asset-change reconcile now covers the certificates bound to the asset, mirroring the fan-out a certificate change already performs in the other direction, and the stale-finding sweep is scoped to the subjects the pass actually evaluated.
  • An automatic active scan whose sensor refused the job no longer counts as a scan. The stamp that takes an asset off the rescan queue is written at dispatch — right for a probe that went unanswered, wrong for a sensor that never ran the job at all — so an asset whose sensor rejected the command sat out a full rescan interval on the strength of a scan that never happened. The sweep now hands those assets back on its next pass.

  • A discovery job that ends no longer leaves its targets queued. Only the in-cluster executor and the sensor's own completion report ever settled discovery_targets, so a job that failed before either ran left its target rows at pending indefinitely and the Jobs page showed work still queued under a job that had finished. Unfinished targets are now settled with the job, carrying its reason; targets that already reached a terminal state keep the outcome they earned.

  • Certificate expiry controls refresh as time passes, even when no asset or certificate is changed. The platform checks the expiry window three minutes after startup and every 12 hours thereafter, reconciling affected tenants through the existing evaluation path. Zero-day, negative and fractional policy thresholds are included. This covers published platform frameworks; tenant-authored custom-policy evaluation remains disabled. See Compliance refresh. (#1872)

  • The platform interrogation agent appears under Discovery agents on Discovery → Sensors & Agents, using its existing system-sensor identity and health status. It remains platform-managed and cannot be deleted. (#1864)

  • A crypto configuration's risk score could go up but never down to clean. Ingest wrote crypto_implementations.risk_score only when the computed score was above zero, to keep a persisted 0 from reading as "assessed and safe" when nobody had looked. The column is a last-write, not an accumulator, so the guard also meant a configuration first seen negotiating TLS 1.0 kept that score for ever: every later observation that resolved to a clean set computed 0, and the 0 was never written. Remediation was invisible in the number, and the stale score went on feeding the finding, the asset roll-up and the severity band. The write is now gated on whether the configuration was ASSESSED rather than on the arithmetic, so a re-observation can lower the score, including to zero; a pass that recognised nothing still writes nothing and leaves an earlier verdict intact. The honest-zero distinction is kept where it already lived: a configuration is assessed when it has at least one catalogue component linked, which is the same predicate the crypto producer reads.

  • Two approval tests deadlocked intermittently under the parallel integration runner. TestIntegration_AssetIngestionPendingApproval and TestIntegration_ApproveAssets failed with pq: deadlock detected against a neighbouring package binary applying scripts/database/schema.sql — a harness race with nothing to do with approvals, reported as a failure of the approval logic. The exposure belongs to the shared getTestDBAndTenant fixture rather than to the approval tests, so every test in both files that use it — the approval tests and the network-space tests — now holds the same shared schema advisory lock, and two source-level guards fail if one is added without it or if a third file starts using the fixture. shared/query's three DB-backed tests took the same cure, for the same deadlock reported as "Postgres refused the generated clause". Test-only.

  • A network device running Cisco IOS could be exported to a SIEM as an Apple handset. Core. The OCSF export maps an operating-system name onto OCSF's os.type_id, and it treated a bare "iOS" or "iOS 15.2" as Apple's. show version on a Catalyst prints exactly "IOS 15.2(4)E10" with no vendor word in it, and Cisco IOS 12.x–15.x overlaps iOS numerically, so name-only the two are identical. The mapping now requires an Apple signal — iPhone, iPad, iPadOS or an Apple hardware vendor beside it — and answers Unknown without one, which for a SIEM correlating on platform is the difference between "not identified" and a false assertion about a core switch.

  • A second, different class disagreement about the same asset was silently dropped. Core. When the classification rules contradict each other the platform proposes no class and asks a reviewer which is right. The index that stops the same question being re-asked on every poll keyed those proposals on the proposed class — which a conflict does not have — so every conflict about one asset collapsed onto one row. An asset the catalogue argued over twice showed the first disagreement and swallowed the second for as long as the first stayed unanswered. The key now includes which classes disagreed. The Approvals queue's own read also gained the index it never had, so paging it no longer scans the whole history table.

  • The query language's spec fixtures accepted predicates the product refused. Core. The static §4.3 catalogue the conformance fixtures resolve against had drifted from the registry-derived one the running validator uses, in eleven places: attr.os_version typed as a number against a column holding "22.04.3 LTS", protocol five OT values short so protocol:S7 was invalid in the fixtures and stored in the database, strength with no value set so strength:strng validated and matched nothing, identifier:(kind:mac) offering a value the column never holds, network.type at two values instead of four, and keys (attr.managed, fact.cve.max_cvss, fact.eol.software.date) that no registry declares. All resolved in the registry's favour, with a parity test that refuses a twelfth.

  • An alert's severity only ever went up. Core. A raise at the same or a lower severity was deduped into a silent touch, so an alert that opened critical stayed critical until the condition vanished entirely: a package downgraded from CVSS 9.8 to 5.1 by a partial fix kept a critical badge, and an asset whose worst end-of-life deadline was dealt with kept the grade of the deadline that was gone. The Alerts page is triaged top-down by severity, so this put stale worst-cases at the top of the list. The findings-driven detectors now lower an open alert to the rung its findings actually reach. The row is never deleted and never re-opened — the severity changes on the alert that is already there, the move is appended to its evidence timeline with its direction and reason, and nothing is notified: a pager that fires to report good news is a pager that gets muted. Escalation is unchanged. The evidence timeline draws a lowered severity with a downward arrow labelled "Severity lowered" — it drew every severity change with an upward arrow, which on the one row a person reads to learn which way it went said the opposite of what happened.

  • Billing webhook audit events were filed under system. Enterprise. The Stripe webhook publisher named no event_category on the NATS path, so audit-service's ingest fallback filed every billing.* event under the platform's own catch-all — while the same event sent over the HTTP fallback path was filed under tenant, so the category depended on whether NATS happened to be up. Both paths now build one envelope, categorised tenant. Existing rows are not rewritten.

  • The Findings page's search box searched a prefix of the list, not the list. It narrowed the rows the browser already held, and the page fetches at most five pages of 200 — so on a tenant with more than a thousand findings a term matching only the 1,200th one answered "no findings match", which on screen is indistinguishable from a clean estate. The software surfaces link here with ?q=<product> for any product in the catalogue, so this was reachable in one click. GET /findings now accepts q, matched server-side across the finding's summary, its subject label, its kind as it is displayed (end of life finds software_end_of_life) and the host the row names underneath it (web-01 finds every finding on web-01); % and _ are literal characters rather than wildcards. The term narrows the rows, the total and the per-producer facet counts under one predicate, so none of them can disagree.

  • The topology view's "cross-segment links" headline reported the size of the picture as the size of the estate. It counted the edges DRAWN, which is the same number as the real total only until an estate is big enough to truncate — a tenant with 900 cross-segment links and a cap of 200 read "200" in 24-point type. It now reads the server's own total_edges and says how many were drawn when the two differ.

  • Two relationships between the same pair of assets were drawn as one line on the map. An application that both runs_on and connects_to its host had its second edge hidden underneath the first, with the label overprinted and no way to hover it — so that edge's provenance, confidence and observation count were unreachable, and the map silently under-reported how two things are related. Parallel edges are now spread apart and each is separately hoverable.

  • The map's Export menu could not be closed by a keyboard user. It closed on mouseleave and nothing else: Escape did nothing, tabbing away left it open over the graph, a click on the canvas left it open, and on a touch device (where there is no mouseleave) it never closed at all. It now closes on Escape, on an outside click and after choosing an item, returns focus to the button, and carries aria-haspopup / aria-expanded.

  • An end-of-life or vulnerability finding on a package showed the machine's name, not the package's. Every such finding on one host rendered with an identical label, so nine end-of-life packages read as nine identical rows. The Findings list and drawer now name the package and carry the host beside it as context; search still matches either.

  • Orphan-relationship findings were invisible from the assets they concern. A relationship edge pointing at a missing asset was listed on Risk & Compliance → Findings and nowhere else — not on either asset's Findings tab, not in the has_findings filter, not behind a finding:(…) query — which is every surface a person would actually fix it from. An edge is now reachable from either of its ends.

  • An expired fact was read as "the problem went away". asset_facts.expires_at says when a collected answer stops being current. The end-of-life and configuration producers ignored it, and once it was honoured naively an expired fact would have looked like an absent one — making the producer stop asserting its finding, which resolves it. Both now treat an expired fact as not evaluated: no new finding, and the existing finding is left exactly where it is rather than being marked "no longer detected" by a pass that measured nothing. A fact that is genuinely gone still resolves, as it always did.

  • A finding's evidence can no longer grow without bound. A certificate-issuer finding on a host presenting hundreds of certificates wrote every one of them into the finding's evidence. Long lists are now truncated with an explicit marker saying how many were omitted — never silently — and an oversized document drops its largest entries, naming them, while keeping everything the finding needs to stay matchable and navigable.

  • The AI query seam sent an asset's full record to the model provider on a get_asset follow-up. The page of rows crossing the provider boundary has always been projected onto an explicit field allowlist, so the tenant's owner_email, description, tags, attributes, metadata and tenant_id never left the platform. A follow-up "tell me more about that one", however, forwarded inventory-service's full asset envelope verbatim — every one of those columns, plus the asset's identifiers, endpoints, crypto configurations and certificates. A tenant asking their inventory a question in prose was sending their colleagues' addresses and their own free text to a third-party provider. Follow-up detail now crosses on the SAME allowlist the rows do, and an unrecognised envelope crosses as nothing rather than as itself. Faceting by owner_email (or owner) is refused before the tool runs, for the same reason: the facet's values are the people.

  • Every request the audit middleware recorded was categorised system. The global request-logging middleware, which runs in every service, derived event_category from the request path by reading the second path segment as the service name — and for /api/v1/inventory-service/assets that segment is v1. Nothing matched, so for as long as the /api/v1 prefix has existed every row it wrote landed as system whatever it was about, with an event type naming the service (system.inventory-service.create) instead of the resource. Handlers that pass their category explicitly were unaffected. The service segment is now found whether or not the /api/vN prefix is present, the category comes from an explicit per-service table covering every registry service (a test fails if a service is added without a decision), and the event type names the resource (asset.assets.create, tenant.tenants.delete).

Existing rows are not rewritten — they stay system, so anything that reads event_category shows a step at the deploy: on the platform admin Security dashboard the "Events by category" panel and the compliance report's events-by-category summary show system shrinking while asset, discovery, compliance, user and authentication appear; the compliance-gap analysis's covered categories widen from that point; and the compliance tags audit-service assigns from the category (soc2, iso27001, pci_dss, …) attach to these rows from now on, having never attached before. An audit alert rule or SIEM filter written against event_category = system, or an event type of the form system.<service>.<action>, matches only the old rows and needs rewriting. The activity page's category chips are built from the rows on screen and widen on their own.

  • Billing audit events from Stripe webhooks were discarded on INSERT. The NATS ingest path in audit-service defaulted a missing event_category to api, which the audit.activity_logs CHECK rejects, and the billing webhook processor is the one publisher that sends no category — so every billing.* audit event it recorded was refused by the database with nothing visible to the publisher. The default is now system, which the CHECK accepts. The billing publisher still names no category of its own; tenant would be the accurate one and is a follow-up.

  • A framework could report PASS for controls nothing had assessed — the materialized compliance score's "is anything in scope?" probe was one tenant-wide question ("does this tenant have any crypto configuration or certificate?"), written when every measurement read one of those two tables. The registry-driven measurements added three more shapes (asset, fact, finding) and a single TLS endpoint satisfied the old probe for all of them. Two customer-visible consequences, both on the Posture page, the framework card and the dashboard's Inventory health hero:

  • Lifecycle scored 100 on an estate the end-of-life catalogue had never resolved a date for. The live evaluator correctly reported NOT ASSESSED while the stored rollup — which is what those three surfaces read — reported four passing controls out of four.

  • Inventory Hygiene's IH-005 and IH-006 read PASS wherever the hygiene producer had never run, so the score went UP for not looking.

The probe is now per measurement shape, each mirroring its shape's own FROM/WHERE, with the fact and finding shapes probing the specific fact key or producer the control measures rather than "any fact at all". Nothing that genuinely has data to read changes status.

  • Cryptography findings had no evidence panel. The crypto producer writes the whole derivation of its score — the two numbers it takes the worse of, and the catalogue components that produced them — and the Findings inspector fell through to the generic "raised by the Crypto producer" card, answering "why this score?" for the five other producers and not for the one whose entire output is a score. Opening a cryptography finding now shows the score, its components worst-first with each one's catalogue rating, and — when the catalogue's number and the number recorded at observation disagree — both, with which one won. The customer documentation already described this.

  • scripts/lint-go.sh shared golangci-lint's cache across every git worktree of this repo on a host. The cache keys entries by file path, so a worktree that had since been deleted could still serve a stale result to a sibling worktree resolving the same path — leaving a //nolint directive unread and make standards-check reporting a false lint failure with no repro under a hand-run golangci-lint run. GOLANGCI_LINT_CACHE is now derived per worktree from git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir (scripts/lib/golangci-cache.sh), unless a caller already set it.

  • API server WriteTimeout was shorter than every generative seam's own per-call timeout in inventory-service, compliance-engine and cbom-service (15s vs. 20s–90s), so a slow /ask, /remediation/draft, /draft-controls or /cbom/compare request could lose its response to a dropped connection with no body. All three API servers (never the plaintext /health server) now read the new seams.GenerativeWriteTimeout constant, sized above the slowest configured seam call.

  • tenant_frameworks.description (custom policies) was nullable but scanned into a plain string in two readers. TenantFrameworkService.ListTenantFrameworks and .GetTenantFramework failed the whole read (converting NULL to string is unsupported) for a custom policy whose description is SQL NULL — the same defect #1680 fixed for platform_frameworks.description/.organization, on the tenant_frameworks sibling that was left standing. Both queries now COALESCE(description, ''). A DB-integration test seeds a NULL-description tenant framework and reads it through both fixed readers plus a regression guard on the evaluation path's existing COALESCE.

  • shared/discovery's SSH banner was unbounded, unredacted free text from the remote device, unlike the structurally identical LLDP/CDP banner in shared/hostobs (redact then truncate). Both capture sites (the full-handshake path and the plain-read fallback) now route through boundSSHBanner, which strips an embedded PEM block before capping the result at 256 bytes — redacting before truncating, so a PEM straddling the cut is still caught. ProbeResult.SSHBanner and Metadata["banner"]/Metadata["ssh_banner"] all inherit the bound from the same source value.

  • The in-cluster Platform Sensor kept its own SSH prober, and it still stored the raw banner. services/cluster-sensor-service's ssh_prober.go was an independent copy of the handshake shared/discovery runs for the standalone sensor — the parallel-copy drift the shared-source rule exists to prevent — so the bound above never reached it: both its handshake path and its banner-only fallback wrote the unredacted, unbounded banner into the finding. It now delegates to the shared prober, the way tls_prober.go already does, and inherits boundSSHBanner. Reconciling the two also fixed the shared fallback, which read from the connection ssh.NewClientConn had already closed on error and so could never return a banner (a device that announced itself was recorded as a probe failure); it now re-dials, as the in-cluster copy did, and is skipped once a host key has been captured rather than discarding it for a version string. The banner-only result no longer manufactures ssh_key_types = [""].

  • crypto:(…) and cert:(…) could not see a configuration with no endpoint. crypto_implementations.endpoint_id is NULL by design for a configuration that is not tied to one socket — an at-rest cloud resource, disk or database encryption — and asset_id is the roll-up target. The query language's asset/crypto and asset/cert shapes inner-joined the endpoint, so every such configuration, and every certificate reachable only through one, was missing from crypto:(…) and cert:(…) over an asset: the Inventory facet rail, saved views, the ask seam and any compliance measurement over the asset shape all returned a narrower set than the language defines, with no error and nothing empty to notice. The two reverse shapes (crypto_configuration/asset, certificate/asset) made the same assumption, so such a configuration could not name its own asset either.

The endpoint stays authoritative where there is one — a configuration whose endpoint moves to another asset follows the endpoint — and the fallback applies only where the walk has no endpoint to follow. This is the same rule, spelled the same way, as shared/findings.AssetSubjects, which finding:(…) and the has_findings facet resolve through; a new unit test holds the two definitions to the same text, and an integration test drives both over the same rows. crypto:(…) from an endpoint deliberately does not fall back: a configuration measured at no socket belongs to no socket.

  • shared/redact now recognises SNMP community strings. A v1/v2c community string IS the credential — an SNMP GET authenticates with nothing else — and the interrogators carry one as Credentials.Custom["community"], where the name-based redactor did not recognise it. Matched as a name suffix (community, snmp_community, read_community, trap_community) plus both spellings of community_string; deliberately not a bare community fragment, which would redact Azure's communityGalleryImageId. Both polarities are in the provider-boundary field table.

  • The tenant AI kill switch is now enforceable on POST /ask and on the remediation-draft route, and tested. Both handlers read tenant_admin_settings and answer 403, and both blocks could be deleted outright with every suite staying green — the contract harnesses construct the handlers with no database, so the read, the refusal and the context stamp that carries the question-recording opt-in were never executed. A tenant that turned the assistant off in Settings was protected only by the web UI declining to render the control; an API token, the vistaplatform_ask MCP tool or a script would still have had the question translated, or the finding's evidence projected, and sent to the model provider. No behaviour changed: what changed is that deleting either block now goes red.

  • Settings → AI assistant no longer reports the matcher as "Not yet built". Its learned scorer has been the seam's default in every deployment, Core included, since the matcher workstream, with merge-candidate ranking and the model id on Settings → Identification rules as its consumers. The seam catalogue row is corrected, and a new guard makes the classical half structural rather than hand-maintained.

  • go test -tags ee ./... is green in auth-service again. A contract test asserting a Core-build property lived in an untagged file, so the suite of the build the commercial images come from failed on it. Split per polarity, with the Enterprise half — which did not exist — now covering what a build with the providers linked and no AI_PROVIDER configured reports.

  • The public tree's go test ./... is green under shared/ai/seams. The invoker-ownership guard ships to the Core export and hard-failed there, on a rule about ee/ directories that the export removes by construction. It now identifies the export positively and skips, while still failing on a checkout that has lost its Enterprise trees some other way.

  • Four collector guards that could not fail (asset-inventory gate 2). A mutation sweep over every projection phase 2 widened found three tests that stayed green with the thing they guard deleted, and one row whose provenance nothing checked.

The F5 sys/version projection was unguarded. Its only test drove the interrogator through Registry.Get, so the name-based redaction backstop scrubbed the fixture's adminPassphrase and sslPrivateKey and the test passed with the projection removed. The backstop matches NAMES, so a vendor field that is sensitive without being named like one — a licence key under Title, a support-contract id — reached DeviceInfo on every F5 interrogation with nothing failing. There is now a test that reads the projection's output directly, before any redaction.

The host agent's TestProjections_DoNotForwardPoison asserted the absence of a string that was never in its inputs. All four projections could have been replaced with a whole-struct copy without it noticing.

shared/hostobs redacts free text before it truncates it, and the ordering was unpinned. Cutting a PEM block in half first leaves a fragment with no END line, which the scrubber's regex cannot match, so the fragment ships. The two orderings agree on every input except that one, and the existing tests' banners all fit inside the 256-byte bound — so swapping the two lines left the suite green while any LLDP or CDP system description over the bound with a key straddling the cut would have carried key material into a device's banner.

Cloud containment edges were written with provenance nothing asserted. source_kind is the field a reviewer uses to decide whether to believe an edge — "the provider's API stated this" is a different claim from "something proposed it" — and source_ref is what lets a pass sweep the edges it drew.

  • The Ask endpoint's own tenant-kill-switch read had no test. Ask consults ai.TenantAIControls directly (fail closed to 503 if the read errors, 403 if the tenant switched the assistant off) whenever it holds a database handle, but the existing harness always builds AskHandlers with a nil pool, so neither branch was ever driven — only the boundary's SECOND enforcement of the same switch (stamped onto the context directly) was tested. Added DB-integration tests that seed a real tenant_admin_settings row and drive both branches through a real *sql.DB. Mutation-tested: made the unreadable-settings branch fail open (return without a 503) and confirmed the new test catches it.

  • Removed shared/ai/seams.StripPlanCitations, a stripping helper with a doc comment and a test but no caller. Unlike its row-grammar sibling StripCitations (which the CBOM comparison narrator genuinely needs, for a plain-prose summary alongside the raw chip-rendered text), the plan grammar's one caller — the Enterprise remediator's renderPlanNotes — deliberately keeps the [ev:…]/[guide] markers in an accepted plan's notes, because the markers are the checkable part of an auditable step. No code path wanted a stripped plan step, so the helper is gone rather than left unreachable "just in case."

  • A generative call from a Core handler could not be attributed, so every question would have been refused. The grounded query seam held its own private invoker context key, which meant the only code able to attribute a call was the Enterprise package itself — while its caller is, by construction, a Core HTTP handler that may not import an Enterprise tree. Every request would have reached the audit boundary unattributed and been rejected, reporting a perfectly healthy model provider as unavailable, with the cause visible only in a log line. The same bug the enricher had; caught this time by landing the caller. (asset-inventory workstream 4.4b)

  • Findings on an endpoint-less crypto configuration were invisible to their asset. findings.AssetSubjects — the one definition shared by the query language's finding:(…), the has_findings facet and the per-asset findings read — walked crypto_implementations.endpoint_id with an inner join. That column is nullable by design (an at-rest cloud resource has no socket; asset_id is the documented roll-up target), so every such configuration's findings, and every certificate reachable only through one, were unreachable from the asset with no error anywhere. The path now falls back to asset_id where there is no endpoint.

  • A control alert stayed open after every finding behind it was resolved. The control_noncompliant detector read its findings with its own near-miss of the open-finding predicate — detection_state = 'ACTIVE' AND workflow_status <> 'SUPPRESSED' — which agrees with the registry's one definition on three of the four workflow values and disagrees on RESOLVED. A tenant who worked every finding on a control and marked them resolved kept the alert: Remediation → Alerts still said the control was noncompliant, with nothing open behind it, and the only way to clear it was to suppress findings they had genuinely fixed. It now compiles shared/findings.OpenSQL, the same generated definition the query language and the has_findings facet use (ADR-0005 D3).

  • control_noncompliant re-raised every noncompliant control on every scan pass, even when nothing about it had changed. Unlike the findings-driven alert jobs in the same package, this detector called Raise unconditionally for every control its query matched — and a noncompliant control matches that query on every 30-minute pass until its findings clear. The alert engine dedupes a same-severity re-raise into a silent touch, so this never duplicated an alert, but it still moved updated_at/last_event_at (and issued a needless write) every interval for every noncompliant control a tenant had. It now mirrors FindingsAlertScanJob's raise-on-change guard: Raise is called only when the alert is new or the control's baseline severity has risen above the open alert's.

  • Silencing one score-drop alert type auto-closed the alerts it already had. Splitting hygiene_score_drop out of compliance_score_drop made one detector serve two types, so a disabled type no longer returned before the auto-resolve sweep — and the sweep closed that type's open alerts under the observation "framework no longer active or scored", which was not what had happened: the framework was still activated and still scored. Turning an alert type off in Settings → Notifications & Alerts → Alert Rules now leaves its open alerts alone, as it did when the job served one type.

  • A framework with no organization recorded could blank the Frameworks page. platform_frameworks.description and .organization are nullable but are read into plain Go strings, and a NULL fails the scan — which aborts the whole read, so one such row returned an error instead of one degraded entry for every licensed, available and default-framework list. Both columns are now COALESCEd at every read, reporting "no organization" as an empty string.

  • The same NULL-organization defect broke every other reader of platform_frameworks, not just framework_license_service.go. PlatformFrameworkService.ListFrameworks / GetFramework / GetPlatformDefaultFramework, TenantFrameworkService.ListPublishedFrameworks / ListPublishedFrameworksWithLicense / ViewFramework, FrameworkContextService's batch-evaluate framework lookup, and EvaluationService.GetFrameworkStatus / GetComplianceScore all scanned the same nullable description/organization columns into plain Go strings. Worse than the Frameworks-page defect above: EvaluateFramework — the core evaluation function every score, control-status and finding view goes through — also scanned an uncoalesced description for both platform and tenant (custom-policy) frameworks, so a NULL there surfaced as "framework not found" for a real, published, licensed framework, and GetFrameworkStatus's per-row error tolerance meant the framework simply vanished from a tenant's Frameworks status with no error at all — a real "not assessed" rendered as "does not exist". All of the above are now COALESCEd the same way.

  • Risk & Compliance → Findings: the search box now filters the findings. It narrowed only the inventory-service crypto-risk stream, so on every findings-shaped lens — the producer lens included — typing in it did nothing while looking exactly like an applied filter. That is the failure the page already refuses for its producer chips, pointed the other way. It now matches what the row SHOWS — summary, target label, subject label, joined hostname — and deliberately not kind or producer: searching a field nobody can see makes a hit unexplainable.

  • A discovered certificate could be invisible from the asset serving it. A crypto configuration's leaf certificate is recorded twice — as crypto_implementations.certificate_id (a denormalisation a few reads use directly) and as a row in the crypto_implementation_certificates junction. Everything that walks DOWN from an asset to its certificates reads only the junction: the certificate path in shared/findings.AssetSubjects (behind the asset page's Findings tab, finding:(…) and the has_findings facet), the query language's cert:(…) sub-predicate from an asset, an endpoint or a configuration, certificate/asset traversal, the location roll-up's certificate and expiry counts, and the certificate-expiry bands on the crypto risk list.

The two were written by different statements in different transactions — the column by ingest, the junction row by a later best-effort call that only logged on failure — so they could diverge, and did: the original valid_certificate_role CHECK rejected the literal leaf, so on every sensor-discovered certificate the column landed, the junction insert was refused, and ingest reported success. The certificate existed and carried its risk while being unreachable from, and unsearchable by, the asset it was served on.

Ingest now writes both halves in one transaction, deriving the junction row from the row's own certificate_id so the two cannot name different certificates, on both the insert and the re-observation path. Configurations written before that — and the demo/QA fixtures that set only the column — are converged by an idempotent backfill in the schema's POST-MIGRATIONS block, so an existing database repairs itself on the next apply.

  • A failed history append aborted a finding producer's whole run. producer.Writer treats the history trail as best-effort, but ignoring an error inside a transaction does not undo it: Postgres aborts the transaction on any failed statement, so every later Upsert in the pass came back current transaction is aborted, naming a statement unrelated to the cause. The append now runs in a SAVEPOINT, so "best-effort" is a property of the code rather than a comment above it.

  • An SBOM upload could return 500 for data it had already stored. The post-commit hook that triggers the finding producers ran in the request path unguarded; a failure in it unwound through the handler after the commit, and the user's retry swept and rewrote everything the first upload landed.

  • Inventory Hygiene and Lifecycle were unreachable on a 0-cap tier (asset-inventory workstream 3.6, the recurring CMP-6 class). Both frameworks were added to scripts/database/seed.sql and to scripts/audit-edition-boundary.mjs's FREE_FRAMEWORKS list, but not to shared/services.FreeFrameworkCodes — the list that actually exempts a framework from the compliance_frameworks_max cap. On the community, free and starter tiers (cap 0) a tenant could not activate either one. Both codes are now in FreeFrameworkCodes (and in the same list's second copy, services/compliance-engine/ee/content.FreeFrameworkCodes, now pinned against the shared one by its own test so the two cannot drift again). The parity test that is supposed to catch exactly this kind of drift, TestFreeFrameworkCodesMatchTheEditionBoundaryAudit, was also failing on main for an unrelated reason: an apostrophe in a comment the same PR added next to the two new codes ("the inventory's own two") broke its quote-matching regex, which read the apostrophe as a string delimiter and manufactured a bogus multi-line "code" out of the prose in between. The test now scans the array literal character-by-character with real string/comment state instead of a bare regex pair, so a comment's punctuation can no longer corrupt what it extracts.

  • tls_compression_enabled could not report enabled (asset-inventory workstream 3.6). The measurement answered false for every configuration that has ever existed: it uppercased the probe record and then searched the result for a lowercase literal, and the stored JSON renders a space the search did not expect — two independent reasons the check could not fire, in four lines. It now reads the value out of the probe record, and reports not assessed when the probe recorded nothing about compression. No shipped control targets this measurement type, so no compliance score moves.

  • A replayed PCAP and a live sensor now grade the same host the same way. pcap-processor wrote a flat confidence of 0.85 on every row it produced, while the sensor graded host observations 0.60–0.95 by how directly the device stated its own identity. So an LLDP advertisement worth 0.95 live arrived as 0.85 from a replay of the same capture, and a DNS answer worth 0.60 arrived as 0.85 as well — an auto-approval rule reading confidence >= 0.8 fired on a DNS answer it was never meant to. One ladder now, in shared/hostobs, called by both.

  • A large mDNS announcement is no longer reported as a malformed frame. The sensor caps captured payloads at 2 KB, and a printer advertising a dozen service types goes past that routinely; the reader refused the whole message and counted it as a parse fault, discarding the records that HAD parsed. It now keeps what parsed before the cut. A message that contradicts itself — a forward or self-referential compression pointer, a reserved label type — is still refused whole, because that is a different fact about the segment.

  • A clock step no longer stalls a sensor's host observations. The coalescer compared a wall-clock tick against a capture timestamp, so the length of its window depended on the drift between two clocks: an NTP step backwards froze expiry until the clock caught up, with subjects piling up and nothing anywhere saying why. Both ends read the same clock now, which also means the monotonic reading is present on both and a step in either direction cannot affect it.

  • The NetBIOS name reader bounds compression-pointer chains, as the DNS reader in the same package always has. Not exploitable at the sensor's payload cap; two parsers of one construct that disagree about what they refuse is how one of them turns out to be the wrong one.

  • Two nav items were drawing a question mark instead of their icon. The tenant UI's icon set is an explicit name → glyph map (a full-icon-library import once put ~935 kB in the bundle), and a name missing from it renders a neutral placeholder rather than failing — which is right in production and is exactly why nothing noticed that Inventory → Software and Inventory → Map both named icons that were never added. A test now walks the lens registry and asserts every icon it names can actually be drawn. A wider sweep found 24 more such names elsewhere in the UI; those are tracked separately.

  • An inferred relationship no longer became fact because an unrelated asset was approved. Approving an asset activates the pending relationships attached to it, on the principle that approving an asset approves what was observed about it. That reasoning covers measured and imported relationships; it does not cover ones the platform inferred, which are conclusions rather than observations and are supposed to appear in Approvals for a person to decide. They were being activated along with the rest, so a guess drawn while either end was still pending silently became a confirmed relationship that then counted in impact analysis — with nobody ever asked.

  • "What breaks if this dies" answered nothing for controllers and networks. Impact analysis followed every relationship the same way round — backwards, from the thing that depends on something to the thing it depends on. That is right for most of the vocabulary and exactly wrong for the two types that point the other way: a controller manages its access points and a virtual network contains its subnets, so asking what breaks when one of those dies returned an empty answer, while asking it of an access point returned the controller. It was backwards for precisely the kind of asset the question is usually about. Each relationship type now declares which way it is followed, and "what this depends on" is the exact mirror of "what depends on this".

  • A business service you declared was left out of the blast radius. Recording that an asset impacts a business service had no effect on impact analysis — the relationship was skipped, because the platform reserved that type for a conclusion of its own. Your own assertion now counts. The answer includes the service and stops there, rather than continuing into everything else the service touches.

  • Asking for zero hops quietly gave you two. depth=0 on the neighbourhood and impact reads fell through to the default instead of being refused, so a caller got a graph it had not asked for with nothing to indicate it. Out of range is now refused at both ends of the range, as it always was at the top.

  • A relationship could be confirmed against an asset nobody had approved. Accepting a proposed relationship only checked that the relationship itself was still undecided, not that both of the assets it joins had been admitted to the inventory. The Approvals queue never offers such a relationship, but the asset page's Relationships tab did: from an unapproved asset's own page the only other end it can see is the approved one, so Accept looked available and worked — producing a confirmed relationship to an asset nobody had let in, which then counted in impact analysis. Accepting now requires both ends to be approved and says which asset to approve first; rejecting is unaffected, since "this claim is wrong" is answerable whatever the assets are doing.

  • ServiceHints was outside the interrogation redaction backstop. deviceinterrogation.Sanitize masked PEM blocks in the device identity and in peer references but not in an asset's service_name / service_version, which the HTTP and TLS probers fill from a server banner and host inventory fills from the process holding a socket — free text whose origin is outside our control. Found by the host-inventory boundary test; the same redact.TextPEM rule now applies there.

  • Gate 1 review of the asset-inventory phase-1 stack. Nine review passes over the integrated branch — reads, identity wiring, frontend, device-interrogation, schema and RLS, removed-table residue, other services' readers, contracts and docs, and test adequacy — before any of it ships in core-v1.0.0. What they found, by theme:

  • A contested identity erased the proposal it told you to go read. Three intake paths returned the "these might be the same thing" outcome as an error from inside RunInTx, so the transaction rolled back and took the merge proposal with it — while the message said to review it in Approvals. The contested outcome now commits the proposal and is mapped to a 409 outside the transaction. A batch of discoveries no longer aborts on one contested finding either; the rest of the batch lands and the held one is counted.

  • A second sighting of an application could never match the first, so every poll INSERTed another merge proposal for the same question. OpenMergeProposal is idempotent now, and an application observed with its host resolves dependently against that host.
  • Every S3 bucket was inventoried as an application and every RDS instance as a server. Two tables answered "what class is this cloud resource" and neither knew the strings the collectors actually write. One table now, in shared/assetclass, with a guard that scans for those literals — an unrecognised resource type is a plain cloud_resource, because coarse and true beats a guessed leaf.
  • A merge moved one of the eight columns that point at an asset or an endpoint.
