The other seven are ON DELETE SET NULL, so nothing errored: the survivor simply showed no SSH host keys, no external connections, no interrogation jobs and no disk-encryption state for hardware it had just absorbed. The lists are data now, and a test reads the foreign keys out of schema.sql and fails in both directions.
  • PUT /infrastructure-assets/{id} accepted an identifiers array and dropped it, while rewriting hostname and address by raw SQL — so a renamed host kept its old identifiers, gained none for the new name, and was duplicated by the next sighting. Identifier edits go through the engine; a person may retire only what a person declared, and the response reports what was KEPT. The form shows collector-minted identifiers locked rather than hiding them.
  • A schema file that was fine on a fresh database could wedge an upgrade. A trigger's WHEN clause named a column added three thousand lines later in POST-MIGRATIONS; on any database still carrying the previous shape the file aborted with the DROP TRIGGER already committed. Invisible to a double-apply, whose two passes both build today's shape — so the new test builds the OLD shape deliberately and applies the file over it.
  • Several honest-looking empties were failed requests. A facet level that 500s no longer renders as "No sites recorded."; a failed merge-proposal read no longer renders as "Nothing awaiting review"; a failed saved-views read no longer invites you to create the views you already have. Each now says it could not load, and offers a retry.
  • The import wizard guessed an IP identifier out of any column with "ip" in the middle of a word — "Description", "Equipment", "Email Address". An identifier is not a mis-filed value: it is what the engine matches on. Identifier columns are matched on whole words only.
  • Counts and links that did not mean what they said: the merge queue reported its page size (50) as its total; the dashboard's "High-risk assets" and "Unscored assets" tiles linked to the unfiltered list; an asset nobody had assessed wore the same chip as one assessed and found clean; ⌘K advertised two retired lenses and none of the new ones.
  • The removed-table audit is strict and reads the SQL. It was advisory and Go-only, which left a hole the shape of the defect it exists to catch: a seed file filtering on the dropped asset_type column, inside a DO block with no exception handler, would have rolled back an entire demo load.

The parity ledger's phase-1 column is filled from the automated suites, with the tests named per journey and a note saying what that evidence does not cover: the fresh install on our own development cluster and the soak are still owed. One journey — elevating an external connection to an owned asset — stays unverified, because it has no test at any layer.

  • make lint and make standards-check now actually lint the Go code. Both ran golangci-lint from the repository root, which a go.work workspace with no root module cannot load: golangci-lint printed a typechecking error next to 0 issues. — a red make lint on 2.x, a false green on older releases — and the standards gate skipped the step whenever the tool was absent. Neither had ever linted a package. scripts/lint-go.sh now runs golangci-lint from inside every module go.work declares, with --max-same-issues=0 --max-issues-per-linter=0 so findings are never silently truncated, and treats a typecheck error as a failure whatever the exit status. Making the guard real surfaced 20 findings the diff-scoped CI gate had never seen — the device agent's audit logger dropped write and fsync errors (a lost audit event was invisible), five unchecked Body.Close calls, ten WriteString(fmt.Sprintf(...)), and a deprecated go-redis SetEx in the token-revocation path — all fixed.

  • ai.Redact was not idempotent, and the second pass corrupted the text. The redaction marker [redacted] ends in ], which the value grammar lists as a terminator, so redacting an already-redacted string read the value one byte short, wrote a fresh marker, and left the old bracket behind — [redacted]], then ]], growing by a byte on every pass. Two things were wrong with that: the audit digest of a prompt that had been through the boundary twice differed from the same prompt seen once, which is precisely what ADR-0008 D4.7's prompt hash exists to make answerable; and a caller that scrubbed early and indexed into the result — ai.Redact is exported so it can — found every offset shifted. redactText now recognises its own output and copies it through. (#1639)

  • CBOM comparison results are now returned in a deterministic order. The diff engine built its change list by iterating Go maps, so the change set was stable across recomputations and the order was not — contradicting the "compare the same pair tomorrow and get the same result" property the feature is documented on. Invisible while the client re-sorted anyway; load-bearing now that a narrative cites rows by position.

  • A comparison whose changes are all non-semantic no longer renders a summary with an empty breakdown. "Mixed posture change between …: ." — the neutral count was suppressed unless some other category was also present. It now reads "No posture change between …: 2 neutral."

  • A rack spare no longer produces a merge proposal on every scheduled import. A NetBox device with a serial, no address and a free-text name maps to no role, so it arrives as an unknown host — a class that did not recognise a serial. The first import created it and every import after it asked you whether the same untouched chassis was the asset it had just made. An unknown host now identifies by its serial number, so such a device is imported once and matched thereafter. assets_skipped no longer counts it, and it no longer appears in the drift view as "in NetBox, not in your inventory" — because it is in your inventory. To give it a real class, map its role under Settings → Integrations → your NetBox connection → Device-role mapping.

  • A device an asset class still cannot match on is not imported. One with no serial, no address and no DNS-shaped name, or one whose device-role mapping points at a class that does not identify by anything NetBox holds for it (a virtual machine or a cloud resource never identifies by serial). Those are skipped and counted, and show up in the drift view instead, where they belong.

  • testdb.NewTenant was the one un-retried write in the DB-integration harness. The schema-apply helpers (ApplySchema*) already wrap their work in RetryTransient (added for a nightly flake), but NewTenant's INSERT was a bare db.Exec: when another integration leg applied schema.sql concurrently (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on tenants), Postgres's 40P01 deadlock detected failed the calling test outright instead of retrying — observed on admin-service/ee/msp under a concurrent make test-integration-db run, passing in isolation. Both the INSERT and the cleanup DELETE now go through RetryTransient.

  • A healthy 256-bit EC certificate counted as a crypto-risk "certificate issue." GetSummary's certificate-issue counter used a bare public_key_size < 2048, the RSA/finite-field floor, against every key family — while the crypto finding producer raised no weak_certificate finding for the same certificate. It now uses anyWeakKeySizeSQL (services/inventory-service/internal/services/crypto_risks_service.go), the same family-aware classifier the crypto_implementations key-size counter already used.

  • One asset was reported as assessed and clean while its finding was filed under another. crypto_implementations carries both an asset_id (the roll-up target written at ingest) and a nullable endpoint_id, and an endpoint can be re-homed to a different host without the configuration's asset_id being rewritten. The reader that answers "what is wrong with this asset" resolves the endpoint's asset first; the crypto producer read the bare asset_id. So for a moved endpoint, one producer pass recorded coverage of the OLD host — which then read as "assessed by crypto, nothing scored" — while the weak-configuration or quantum-vulnerability finding it raised was reachable only from the new one. Both sides now share a single definition of which asset a configuration belongs to, for configurations, certificates and keys alike.

  • Inventory → Software's "N vulnerabilities" and "end of life" links opened the wrong list. They carried the install (or the product) as a filter and landed on the Findings page's crypto-risk lenses, which read a different data set and ignore that filter — so the page showed an unfiltered crypto list under a banner claiming it was narrowed to one software install. The same defect was fixed for the Alerts page earlier in this cycle; these two were missed.

  • A finding on a cryptographic key or on a relationship between assets had no word for itself. The asset page's Findings tab printed the raw subject type ("crypto · key") and a remediation plan item printed only "finding", months after both became real subjects. Both now name every subject type the finding registry defines, and a test reads that registry so a new subject type cannot ship without a word for it.

  • Every Enterprise-only operation in the admin, auth and audit API specs is now marked as such. 97 operations documented routes that only an Enterprise build registers — the whole MSP tenant-lifecycle and self-service billing surface, SSO configuration, SIEM export — so the Core edition shipped documentation for capabilities it has no handler for. Four services now check their spec against their routes on every build, in both directions.

  • The published Core copy of the auth API spec was invalid YAML. A description that ended on a line beginning with # was mangled when internal issue references are stripped for publication, leaving a stray . that no parser would accept. Nothing had ever parsed the published specs; something does now.

  • The health endpoint of a service whose whole API is admin-plane now answers through the edge. GET /api/v1/tenant-health-service/health returned 404 on both the tenant host and the admin host on any Kubernetes install with an admin host configured: tenant-health-service is declared in the service registry's admin plane as a whole service, so the admin-plane routes (priority 900) also matched its /health path and outranked the per-service health carve-out (priority 150) — the request was denied on the tenant host and reached the backend with an un-rewritten path on the admin host. The carve-out is now generated above the admin plane, on both hosts, for every backend. Health carries no tenant data, so this is the same posture every other service already had. Pre-existing; also present in 0.12.x.

  • Actively enriched and PCAP-uploaded discoveries now auto-approve. The sensor's TLS enricher stamps its results active_enrichment and pcap-processor stamps pcap_upload; the approval evaluator's source mapping recognised neither, so every source:sensor segment rule silently skipped exactly the discoveries that carry the certificate chain and the measured protocol version, and every discovery from an uploaded capture — they piled up in Approvals on segments set to auto-approve. Both now map to sensor, each with a mutation-checked test alongside the earlier passive_host_observation one. Every other consumer of these values already handled both spellings; the approval evaluator was the one that did not.

  • The Dashboard's "Critical findings" tile counts every producer. It read /findings/statistics.severity_counts, which is scoped to the compliance producer — failed controls on activated frameworks — while labelling itself "across all assets" and linking at the By Framework lens. An organization whose only Critical findings were end-of-life or vulnerability ones read "0 critical findings" on the Dashboard and saw them on Risk & Compliance → Findings: the same Dashboard-vs-Findings divergence closed once before (H-2), recurring one producer later. /findings/statistics now also returns all_producer_severity_counts, built from findingListWhere — literally the WHERE behind GET /findings — so the tile and the page it links to (now By Producer) read one row universe by construction rather than by two hand-written expressions agreeing. The compliance-scoped rollup stays for the surfaces that are about framework compliance, and the framework licence gate still applies to compliance rows inside the wider one, so an unactivated framework's findings remain off the Dashboard. Two things the number is not, documented on the tile and in docsv4/core/features/findings.md rather than left to be discovered: it is the Critical rung only, so the page lists more rows than the tile counts, and it includes suppressed and resolved findings that the Findings page's default Open filter hides. Pinned by a cross-layer guard that fails if either rollup's producer scope changes without the tile's caption changing with it, and by a registry-driven count that requires one Critical per producer in standards/findings-registry.yaml.

  • An RSA certificate is no longer scored as static RSA key transport. The crypto finding producer resolved a certificate's public_key_algorithm — the bare string RSA — against the catalogue row of that exact code, which is RSA key transport (static): the TLS key-exchange assessment (weak, deprecated, risk 70). Every RSA certificate therefore raised a High weak_certificate finding whatever its modulus, an RSA-4096 root CA included, and because every host chains to its CA, every host in an estate rolled up to High — the RC-verification dataset reported 20/20 assets High with 18 of them carrying nothing above Low in their own configurations. A finite-field public key now resolves through its sized catalogue row (RSA-2048, RSA-4096, …), the same rule the key inventory already used. A size the catalogue does not carry gets no catalogue verdict for its key rather than borrowing the key-transport row (the SP 800-131A floor still reports a below-floor modulus); a family the catalogue does not size at all keeps its bare row, so a DSA certificate is still scored — and still reported as quantum-vulnerable — by the DSA row at every modulus. Five mutation-checked integration tests pin it. Existing installs re-score on the producer's next pass; the change is visible as assets moving from High to the band their own configurations earn.

  • The Dashboard's "Critical findings" tile and the page it opens now describe the same set. #1742 widened the tile's number to every producer but left two axes disagreeing with its destination, both documented at the time as caveats. Both are closed.

The tile counted every ACTIVE finding whatever its workflow status, so a Critical you had suppressed with a reason ("accepted, compensating control") stayed on an attention tile forever — and the Findings page opens on its Open filter, which hides exactly those rows, so the one finding driving the count was the one finding the destination would not show. The rollup now excludes Resolved and Suppressed, spliced from the findings registry's own definition of open (shared/findings.WorkflowOpenSQL) rather than a second hand-written predicate, so the count and the page's Open chip cannot drift apart. A finding you suppressed is off the tile, not out of the product: the Findings page has no separate Suppressed filter, so switching its Open chip to Critical + High brings it back with its status on the row.

The tile counts the Critical rung while the page listed every severity and had no severity URL parameter, so clicking "40 critical findings" opened a list of several hundred rows with nothing saying which forty were meant — the failure dashboard-metrics.ts already names for the High-risk assets tile ("a tile that counts a subset must link to that subset"). The Findings page now reads ?severity=critical|high|medium|low, applies it on the server (the page caps at five pages of 200, so a client-side narrowing would under-report a large tenant), and renders it as a clearable banner, because a filter arriving from a link is one the reader never chose. The page's own Critical + High chip and the URL filter are one axis, so picking the chip clears the parameter instead of intersecting with it.

Guards on both halves, mutation-tested in both polarities: TestDashboardCriticalTile_RouteCarriesItsNarrowings fails if the route stops naming the rung the tile reads, and TestSeverityRollupScopes_AreWhatTheirNamesSay fails if the rollup starts counting suppressed rows again.

  • /findings/statistics.severity_counts is recorded as contract-only. The Dashboard was its only consumer and moved to all_producer_severity_counts; the field stays in the published contract (removing it would be breaking) but is now documented as unverified by any screen.
  • ECDSA certificates and keys are classified for post-quantum migration. A certificate's public-key algorithm is the bare family name crypto/x509 reports — "RSA", "ECDSA", "Ed25519" — and the crypto producer resolves it against the algorithm catalogue to decide whether the key is Shor-breakable. The catalogue had no bare ECDSA row (only the ECDSA-with-hash pairings and the SSH host-key names, neither of which assesses an EC public key as such), so an ECDSA certificate resolved to nothing, was left unclassified and raised no crypto/pqc_vulnerable finding: on one tenant 16 RSA certificates raised 16 findings beside 6 ECDSA certificates raising none, while NIST IR 8547 puts both on the same deprecation clock. The same six keys sat in the Keys lens with no algorithm, because the key producer asks the catalogue for the same code. The catalogue now carries ECDSA as a bare signature row (strong, current, risk 15, the counterpart of DSA), the seed backfills the algorithm onto EC keys already recorded without one, and the signature component of every TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_* suite — previously "ambiguous" and left unlinked — links to it. ECDSA certificates also pick up the row's catalogue verdict as a Low weak_certificate finding, exactly as RSA-4096 ones already did.
  • One Ed25519 catalogue row, not two. Ed25519 and ED25519 both existed, with different risk scores; the code column is unique only case-sensitively while every lookup is case-insensitive, so which row rated an Ed25519 certificate depended on scan order. Ed25519 (the RFC 8410 / crypto/x509 spelling) is kept and takes over the retired row's OID and guidance; the seed re-points every reference before deleting the duplicate, so an upgrade of a database that linked it does not trip a foreign key. The catalogue consistency test now fails on any pair of codes that fold to one.

  • A key the catalogue cannot size or spell is still classified for post-quantum migration. Whether a key is Shor-breakable is a property of its FAMILY — true of RSA at every modulus and of ECDSA on every curve — while the catalogue row a key resolves to answers a different question, how risky its SIZE is. Deriving both from the one row meant a key dropped out of the migration queue whenever no row matched it: an RSA certificate at a modulus the catalogue does not carry (RSA-1536, RSA-8192) raised no crypto/pqc_vulnerable finding, and neither did a key in the Keys lens whose size could not be read at all. The producer now resolves the family taxonomy the catalogue already carries (algorithm_family + primitive) alongside the row, and falls back to it for the public key alone when no row of its own answered. It remains the same NIST IR 8547 denylist of Shor-breakable primitives, applied to a family instead of a row — a family the catalogue does not know stays UNCLASSIFIED rather than being assumed safe, and symmetric and post-quantum families (AES, SHA-2, ML-DSA, ML-KEM) are untouched. A family verdict is deliberately not a measurement: it never scores a certificate, because knowing a key is RSA is not knowing what its modulus is worth.

  • Self-signup returned HTTP 500 for most real company names. The tenant slug replaced spaces and nothing else, so any name carrying a character outside [a-z0-9 -] produced a value the database's CHECK (slug ~ '^[a-z0-9-]+$') rejected — and signup is the only way into a Core install. Acme, Inc., O'Brien Ltd and Müller GmbH all failed. The derivation now folds any run of other characters into a single dash, trims the ends, and appends a block of the tenant's UUID so the two constraints the old code never considered — UNIQUE and varchar(100) — are guaranteed rather than hoped for: two tenants may legitimately share a display name, and a name that slugifies to nothing (日本, !!!) still yields a valid slug instead of a 500. Found by rc-verify, whose own per-release tenant is named after the version it is verifying.

  • A blank entitlement value no longer means "unlimited". Every entitlement value — a catalogue default, a tier's composition, or a per-tenant exception — is now validated against its item's kind before it is written: a boolean gate is {"enabled": true|false}, a capacity is {"quantity": N} with N a whole number ≥ 0 or an explicit null for unlimited, a choice is a non-empty string. An omitted or empty value used to be stored as {}, which the resolver treated as a present value and the quantity reader parsed as unlimited — so a composer cell left blank, or a request that left the value out, granted unlimited capacity from whichever layer outranked the tenant's real plan. The same item named twice in one composition is now a 400 naming the key instead of a swallowed database error, the admin forms refuse the inputs the API refuses (abc used to become null and therefore unlimited), and a pre-existing malformed row now fails closed rather than open. (#1775)

  • Platform collectors no longer consume the tenant's sensor cap. Every tenant is provisioned two platform-managed collectors at creation. The sensor cap counted them while the Usage & Limits page never did, so the gate charged two slots the meter did not show — and on a plan allowing one sensor the tenant could never register a real one. Registration now counts only sensors the tenant registered, as the page always has. (#1776)

  • A connector import no longer proceeds when the plan check itself fails. NetBox import and CMDB pull treated an error from the asset-cap check as permission and carried on past the plan limit; both now stop and report the error, as manual creation and spreadsheet import already did. Restoring a soft-deleted asset and elevating a third-party connection into a managed asset — both of which raise the enforced count exactly as a create does — now go through the same cap. (#1776)

  • Two views stopped describing a plan by columns nothing writes. The feature-availability endpoint and the plan impact analysis both read the legacy per-plan limit columns, which the plan editor never updates, so for any operator-authored plan the analysis reported "no change, no tenant affected" whatever the composition did. Both now read what the plan actually grants — the same resolved entitlements that gate the tenants — and the analysis counts usage the way the gates do: pending invitations hold a seat, platform collectors are not the tenant's sensors. (#1777)

  • The MSP tenant-settings endpoint now works at all. Its optimistic-locking WHERE clause left Postgres unable to infer the type of one parameter, so every real call failed at query-parse time with a 500 — whether or not a version was supplied. Nothing called the endpoint, which is why a fault this total went unnoticed; it is fixed with an explicit cast, and the new tenant Settings tab above is its first working caller.

  • Retired the MSP tenant-settings frameworkId field. It wrote a "default compliance framework" key into the shared tenant settings document that no code anywhere read back — the authoritative default framework has lived on the tenant's framework licences in compliance-engine since the evaluation rework. Existing stored values are left in place, unread; the GET no longer returns the field and the PUT no longer accepts it.

  • The MSP tenant-settings save no longer wipes a tenant's other settings. admin-service's MSP PUT .../tenants/:id/settings replaced the entire tenant_admin_settings.config document with just the fields the MSP form itself owns (frameworkId, email_verification_required, onboarding_required) — so a platform admin saving any one of those silently deleted the tenant's discovery_auto_scan policy, drift baseline window and identity auto-accept threshold, each owned and written by a different service. The audit trigger recorded the wipe but nothing prevented it. The save is now a top-level jsonb merge (config || EXCLUDED.config) that only ever touches the keys the request actually sets — an absent field leaves the stored value untouched rather than nulling it out. See services/admin-service/ee/msp/tenant_settings.go.

  • cluster-sensor-service could not read back a discovery job the platform created on its own initiative (created_by IS NULL — every HMAC service-auth caller, including the automatic active-scan sweep), nor one that named a sensor, nor list jobs at all, so such jobs would have sat in queued forever with the stuck-job sweep republishing them to the same failure every 30 seconds. All three reads are fixed. (#1839)

  • Risk, cryptographic strength, compliance, health and confidence now retain their own units and shared definitions. Crypto findings inspect every relevant component instead of treating a high catalogue score as proof of weakness; unscored CVEs and unresolved evidence remain visible. Compliance/hygiene colours retain their existing thresholds. External strengths use a nullable canonical vocabulary with preserved historical values, control writes use lowercase severities, and new catalogue rows require explicit scores. See the rating upgrade guide for coordinated schema/client changes, reassessment and evidence limitations.

  • A denied asset's last-seen no longer freezes the moment it is denied. Re-observation ingest hard-filtered a denied asset BEFORE the observation ever reached the identification engine, so its last_seen_at (and every operational surface ordered by it) never moved again however many times a sensor kept reporting it — even though the same re-observation correctly keeps archived assets' last-seen current. A denied asset still stays denied and its crypto is still never (re-)materialized; it now also still advances its last-seen, via a minimal touch that deliberately does not run the full identity resolve — a denied asset gains no new identifiers, no new endpoints and no reclassified ownership, only the honest fact that it is still being seen.

  • sensor_discoveries.approval_status no longer says "pending" forever on rows no human will ever act on. Two classes of processed row sat pending indefinitely: host observations (identity evidence, never a crypto finding awaiting approval) and findings that matched an asset already archived or denied (nothing is materialized for either, and no approval decision follows). Both now land on a terminal value — observed and suppressed respectively — set at write time going forward and backfilled for existing rows on upgrade. cluster-sensor-service's per-job materialization summary no longer counts either as "awaiting approval" (previously approval_status <> 'auto_approved', now = 'pending'), and the Discover wizard states suppressed findings ("N on denied or archived assets — not shown in Approvals") instead of silently folding them into "awaiting approval" or a shortfall nobody could explain.

  • Reverse-DNS hostname resolution for a sensor discovery now only runs against a public destination address. For a private/LAN address the cluster's own resolver is either unreachable for that address or answers a different network's idea of it — and is weaker evidence than the sensor's own passive mDNS/NBNS/LLDP observations besides, for exactly the population (LAN hosts) this affected most. The fabricated-cluster-answer rejection (#1804) is unchanged and still applies to the public case; sensor-side passive DNS capture is a separate code path and is unaffected.

  • A partially observed crypto configuration is now completed by the full observation instead of sitting beside it. A passive sensor that decodes only the protocol of a handshake wrote a configuration with every component empty; the active probe that followed measured the full handshake and, because the two fingerprints differed, added a second configuration for the same endpoint that never superseded the first. The asset page listed both, the inventory's configuration count included both, and the CBOM shipped an empty component beside the real one. Ingest now recognises a live configuration whose measured components all agree with a fuller observation as the same configuration seen less completely, fills it in place (keeping its first-seen date, certificate and links) and re-scores it exactly as a fresh one; a less complete re-observation of a configuration already held is treated as a re-observation, never a new row. A genuinely conflicting pair — TLS 1.2 seen passively, TLS 1.3 seen actively — stays two configurations. Each configuration now records every discovery method that contributed to it (discovery_methods, shown as provenance chips on the asset page's Cryptography tab), and the schema reconciles pairs written before this fix on upgrade: the partial row is retired (soft-deleted), its certificate and algorithm links and tickets move to the complete row, and the complete row inherits the earlier first-seen date.

  • A floating address no longer proposes merging the service at it with the node announcing it. MetalLB in L2 mode, kube-vip, keepalived, Windows NLB, VRRP, HSRP and CARP all announce a virtual address by gratuitous ARP from whichever node currently holds it. The sensor decoded that correctly — the node's MAC at the floating address — and the identification engine, finding the MAC on the node's asset and the address on the service's, called it a cross-kind conflict and opened a merge proposal (scored 0.84, because a MAC is a strong identifier), again after every "keep separate". Three changes, one rule each: (1) an observation that is only a measured MAC-to-address binding — no name, host key, serial, agent or cloud id — whose MAC and address resolve to two different assets is now resolved to the address's asset with the MAC deliberately left unattached, recorded as a hosted_on relationship (service → node) carrying the evidence, and opens no proposal; an observation carrying the node's MAC plus a name or stronger identifier of the other asset is still the genuine conflict it always was. (2) A reviewer's "keep separate" is now read back: a conflict between assets a reviewer already kept apart, on the same kinds of evidence, is resolved without re-asking (to the earlier proposal's own observation asset when it had one, otherwise to the asset the weaker evidence names), the history entry names the honoured proposal, and the ingest log says "kept separate on "; new evidence of a kind the reviewer never saw reopens the question. A question already pending is also no longer re-noted in history on every observation that re-asks it. (3) VRRP/CARP (00:00:5e:00:01:xx, 00:00:5e:00:02:xx), HSRP (00:00:0c:07:ac:xx, 00:00:0c:9f:fx:xx) and GLBP (00:07:b4:xx:xx:xx) virtual router MACs — which move between routers with the address — are no longer used as identifiers, like locally-administered MACs; the protocol is kept as an attribute.
  • MCP OAuth discovery now points somewhere. The MCP endpoint's 401 answered WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="" — an empty pointer, from which a client learns nothing and abandons the flow — and /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource was not routed at all, so it fell through to the web-UI catch-all and returned the app's index.html with HTTP
  • A client following the chain received HTML where it expects JSON, with a success status hiding it. mcp-service now serves RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata at both the well-known root and the RFC 9728 §3.1 path-suffixed URI, the chart routes those paths to it ahead of the UI catch-all, and the 401 carries the document's absolute URL. Note this is necessary but not sufficient for hosted clients: Vista's authorization server still does not implement RFC 7591 dynamic client registration, so Claude.ai, ChatGPT and Claude Code cannot complete automatic sign-in and must use a Personal Access Token.
  • The sensor's heartbeat now reports config_running — the effective values of every control-plane-managed setting (active_probing, network_discovery, host_observation, host_observation_window_seconds, host_observation_dns, dedup_ttl_minutes, reporting_interval_seconds, log_level) seeded from its own configuration file. Without it, sensor-manager's platform bootstrap had nothing to adopt on a sensor's first report, so a sensor with locally customised settings would be silently reset to built-in defaults on its next beat.
  • An agent's first heartbeat no longer switches off what its configuration file turned on. Control-plane-managed settings (#1785) resolved to their built-in defaults for any device nobody had configured, so an agent started with HOST_INVENTORY_ENABLED=true was handed false about a minute later and stopped collecting for good; poll and heartbeat cadences reset the same way. A device now reports the settings it is running, and the first report — that one only — is adopted as its own override where nothing else is set and the value differs from the built-in default. The revision it receives therefore describes what it is already doing, an operator sees the real starting position in the console instead of a default nobody chose, and a device running the defaults still inherits any fleet default set later. Recorded in the audit trail under its own bootstrap scope with no acting user, because nobody made the change.
  • External connections no longer count certificate-hygiene observations (a missing Signed Certificate Timestamp, an untrusted or self-issued/pinned CA, an incomplete chain, a missing Subject DN) as cryptographic weakness. A TLS 1.3 / AES-256-GCM connection to a trusted endpoint could previously be flagged "weak crypto" on the dashboard's External Exposure panel for no reason other than a missing SCT. Those observations are now recorded separately (cert_hygiene_flags) instead of folding into weak_reasons/ crypto_strength. Also extends Signed Certificate Timestamp detection to all three RFC 6962 delivery routes (embedded, TLS extension, OCSP) via a new cert_sct_source field on both external_connections and certificates, where previously only the embedded route was checked.

  • Actively probed SSH servers now report their key exchange, cipher, MAC and host-key algorithms. The active probe completed a key exchange with a library that exposes no algorithm names, so an SSH crypto configuration reached the inventory with only a banner and a host key type: key_exchange_algorithm, symmetric_encryption and hash_algorithm stayed NULL, nothing resolved against the algorithm catalogue, and every SSH asset scored 0 — which the product means as "not assessed" — however it was configured. The shared prober now reads the server's SSH_MSG_KEXINIT in cleartext before any key exchange, records the offered name-lists verbatim and derives the negotiated algorithm per RFC 4253 §7.1. Weak offers (diffie-hellman-group1-sha1, CBC and 3DES ciphers, hmac-md5, SHA-1 ssh-rsa host keys) are linked as inferred, so worst-component-wins scoring reports what a server will agree to rather than only what it agreed with us. Reading KEXINIT needs no algorithm in common, so a legacy-only appliance — previously reduced to a banner — is now inventoried in full. The standalone sensor and the in-cluster Platform Sensor share the probe and both carry the result.

  • SSH banners no longer carry a binary packet. The banner-only fallback read a fixed-size blob rather than the identification line, and an SSH server sends its SSH_MSG_KEXINIT immediately behind that line — usually in the same TCP segment — so algorithm name-lists, a cookie and random padding were stored as the device's banner and shown in the UI. The read now stops at the line terminator RFC 4253 §4.2 defines.

  • Algorithm catalogue: five SSH names a current sshd offers. Added sntrup761x25519-sha512 (the standardised spelling OpenSSH offers from 9.9), mlkem768nistp256-sha256 (post-quantum hybrid, flagged is_pqc), curve448-sha512, hmac-sha1-96-etm@openssh.com and hmac-md5-etm@openssh.com. Without a catalogue row these resolved to nothing and the component was recorded as unassessed.

  • An active-scan target that was an IP literal duplicated the endpoint. When an intake path did not know a listener's name it could write the scan target into fqdn even when the target was an address — it has dots, so it passed a naive "contains a dot" check — producing a second asset_endpoints row for a listener already recorded with fqdn NULL, each with its own crypto configuration and findings. An IP is never a name: it is now dropped from fqdn at the source (the active-scan finding builder) and at the funnel (identity.EndpointObservation.Sanitized), and an address-bearing endpoint is now matched on (address, port, transport) rather than the full tuple including fqdn, so a differently-named re-observation of the same listener updates the existing row instead of inserting a second one. Existing duplicate rows on upgraded installs are merged by a one-time reconcile, keeping the oldest row and re-pointing its crypto configurations, external connections and SSH keys. The reconcile never keeps an IP literal as the survivor's name: the losing rows the defect wrote usually hold the address spelled as text, so backfilling one would have re-created the very value this release stops writing — permanently, because a name is only ever filled onto a row that has none. A real name among the duplicates wins, a survivor carrying the literal itself is corrected, and a lone row that has only the literal is cleared.
  • discovery-processor-service's reverse-DNS enrichment ran from inside a cluster pod, whose resolver synthesises PTR answers for in-cluster IPs (<a>-<b>-<c>-<d>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local and similar) — a customer host's real address could come back as a Kubernetes-internal name nothing on the customer's network ever answers to. reverseDNSLookup now rejects cluster-internal answers and returns "" instead, so the asset keeps its address as its display name until a real name arrives.
  • Several device-interrogation collectors (UniFi managed devices and VPN networks, Fortinet IPSec tunnels and SSL VPN, PAN-OS SSL-decrypt profiles and security rules, F5 virtual servers, SNMP sysName) copied a vendor display/config label straight into the asset's hostname field. A label like "U6+ Living Room" or "Back Porch #1" is not a DNS name, so the identity layer rejected it as an invalid hostname identifier on every run — losing the identifier and flooding the log with the same reject. Collectors now keep the raw label in asset metadata for display and only promote it to hostname when it is a valid DNS name.
  • Third-party TLS connections with no reverse-DNS record (most cloud/CDN IPs) now show the hostname the client's TLS ClientHello actually requested (SNI) instead of a bare IP:port in Inventory → 3rd Party — sensor-manager and discovery-processor now fall back to the captured SNI before reverse DNS, and external_connections.dest_hostname fills from a later observation without ever being blanked by one that carries no hostname.
  • Ingest now defers a finding's certificates and crypto configuration on the status the matched asset has, not the one the batch asked for. A discovery row that matched no auto-approval rule — the same host seen on an address in no registered segment, a TLS endpoint reported by device interrogation — arrives pending_approval, and when it landed on an asset already monitoring its crypto was parked in assets.metadata->'deferred_findings', which only an approval of a pending asset ever replays. It is materialized immediately instead, and the import response reports the effective status per finding so discovery-processor stamps those sensor_discoveries rows auto_approved rather than leaving them pending where nothing surfaces them.
  • A discovery no longer un-archives an asset. A device the tenant archived and that later reappeared on a segment carrying an auto-approval rule was promoted back to monitoring — with an approved history entry naming no person — and its certificates and crypto configuration written into the live inventory. Archiving is now respected the way denied always was: the status is left alone and the finding is neither materialized nor deferred.
  • Sensor heartbeat discoveries_made and errors_count were not trustworthy. discoveries_made read the length of the in-memory batch buffer, which drains every report interval — a sensor that had accepted hundreds of discoveries over its lifetime reported discoveries_made: 0 on every heartbeat after its first successful submission, making an active sensor look idle on the sensor detail drawer. errors_count was hardcoded to 0. Both are now cumulative, process-lifetime counters: discoveries_made increments when a discovery is accepted into a submit batch (not on successful upload, so outages don't hide capture activity), and errors_count increments at the sensor's existing capture/submission/heartbeat/registration failure log sites.
  • Reflected mDNS no longer inventories the gateway as every host on every other VLAN. The sensor attributed every mDNS response to the frame's sender MAC, and a router running an mDNS reflector (UniFi, Avahi, Bonjour gateways) re-originates other hosts' announcements from its own MAC. A response now counts as the sender's only when an A/AAAA record names the frame's source address; otherwise it is hearsay about the named host, carries no MAC, and is graded like a DNS answer. The consumer files .local names as segment-scoped hostnames rather than globally unique FQDNs, so a reflected copy of a name can no longer absorb the host itself from another segment.
  • A platform-sensor scan that asked for TLS and SSH no longer records "SSH on 443" with TLS data. A finding created for one requested protocol only receives that protocol's probe, and a protocol refuted by its own probe on a port it is not known on records no finding instead of an empty crypto configuration.
  • A host inventory the platform could not materialise no longer reads as a success. The Job Logs line leads with the consumer's error instead of the listener count it never wrote, and the agent card's "Last host inventory" ignores failed runs.
  • A name typed on the Devices page is now the asset's display label. Registering a device that the sensor had already observed kept the sensor's measured name as the label; the declared name now wins, while an address typed into the same field still only fills an empty label.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• measurement_types.extraction_query (asset-inventory workstream 3.6, ADR-0005 D5). The column stored the SQL a measurement type "runs". Nothing ever executed it, and what a measurement type reads is now declared in standards/measurement-types.yaml. A seeded query is an injection hazard and an upgrade hazard at once, and a column holding SQL that nothing runs is a standing invitation for something to start running it. Dropped from the schema, the API and the generated client.

  • compliance_findings is dropped. There is one findings table, and every producer writes to it. Asset-inventory workstream 3.1 (ADR-0005 D3): the compliance producer's rows now carry producer = 'compliance' and kind = 'control_noncompliant' in the unified table alongside the crypto, end-of-life, vulnerability, configuration, hygiene and drift producers that follow it. No view, no backfill, no dual-write — ADR-0007's no-migration decision applies, the old table is dropped in POST-MIGRATIONS with DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ... CASCADE, and scripts/audit-removed-tables.mjs fails make audit on any Go or SQL that still names it.

What changed in the shape, and why each one had to:

  • Subject, not asset. (asset_id, asset_type) and its three-value CHECK become (subject_id, subject_type) from the registry's vocabulary, and the three values map onto two: network_asset → asset, crypto_implementation → asset, certificate → certificate. The old asset_type named the measurement KIND, not the type of the id beside it — asset_id was always the asset's for the first two, because a cryptographic configuration measurement is scoped and selected per asset. On live data about three in four of those ids were a certificate's, which is why the old name described the minority case, why the posture grid dropped three findings in four into an "unattributed" row, and why a certificate finding rendered a raw UUID where a hostname belonged.

    The configurations a measurement was taken over are not lost: they are listed on the finding as evidence.crypto_implementation_ids, which is what the inspector links through and what a ticket copies into crypto_implementation_id when there is exactly one. crypto_configuration remains a valid finding subject, reserved for the configuration producer that measures one at a time. - Severity is the registry's lowercase ladder (info/low/medium/ high/critical), not Low/Med/High/Critical. Med had no spelling anything else in the product used. Control authors still type High, so the writer normalizes and the database holds one vocabulary. - Identity gained control_id, with NULLS NOT DISTINCT: a compliance finding is one per (control, subject) pair, so two controls failing on one server are two things to triage. Without it the second control's write reaches the first's row through ON CONFLICT and overwrites it — a lost violation with no error. NULLS NOT DISTINCT keeps the dedup on for the six producers that leave control_id NULL, which Postgres would otherwise treat as always-distinct. - The workflow columns came with it — assignment, remediation notes, resurfaced-at, staleness. None is compliance-shaped; they are the finding LIFECYCLE, which is the half of the old table that generalised. - compliance_finding_history, remediation_plan_items and tickets keep their finding_id, re-pointed at findings(id). A ticket whose finding is gone survives with the link cleared, because the ticket is the user's work.

  • The port-as-asset tables, and the asset_type enum, are dropped — with no migration and no compatibility view. network_assets (the view, the partitioned parent and its eight partitions), devices, and the four-value asset_type enum are removed from the schema body and dropped in POST-MIGRATIONS with DROP TABLE / DROP TYPE IF EXISTS ... CASCADE. Links are re-parented rather than bridged: crypto_implementations.endpoint_id, external_connections.source_endpoint_id and ssh_keys.endpoint_id now point at the endpoint, while device_jobs and database_encryption_states point at the asset.

The owner established (2026-09-11) that there are no installs of the current line to carry forward — the public repository has no released version on this model, and our own development cluster is rebuilt from the published chart — so a compatibility view would have been a layer maintained for nobody, and every reader was rewritten in place instead. make audit runs scripts/audit-removed-tables.mjs --strict unconditionally so a query naming one of these cannot reach main: a dropped relation does not fail to build, it fails at runtime, per query, and this codebase has form for swallowing exactly that error behind a 200.

The scopes and auto-approval-rule JSON predicate columns go the same way, replaced by a query text column holding a query-language string.

  • The legacy per-field asset filters are gone from the MCP tool surface, with no deprecation window: query_assets takes a query string, and sending one of the old filters is a schema violation refused before any backend call. The REST API keeps them for one release, translated into the language server-side.

  • GET and PUT /api/v1/inventory-service/discovery/capabilities (and their /api/v2 twins), together with the capability_policy key they wrote into tenant settings. They served the retired web-ui discovery wizard; no current UI, MCP tool or QA tool called them, and no discovery path enforced the key. The two real switches are unchanged: Settings → Discovery → Active Scanning for automatic scans, and the per-job active_scanning option a discovery job carries. The MSP tenant-settings endpoints in admin-service no longer echo or accept capability_policy.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• npm: uuid pinned to ≥ 11.1.1 through a root overrides entry (GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq, missing buffer bounds check in v3/v5/v6). It reaches the tree only as exceljs's dependency and exceljs calls v4 without a buffer, so shipped behaviour is unchanged; the lockfile no longer carries the vulnerable version.

  • The AI provider transport followed a redirect off its own origin, re-sending the prompt. A model endpoint that is compromised, misconfigured, or reached through a poisoned resolver could answer 307/308 with a Location anywhere; Go re-sends the POST body, so the whole prompt — system prompt, question, and the grounding rows the redaction boundary had just decided were safe to send to THAT provider — was delivered to a host the endpoint chose, with the call still succeeding. Under AI_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS (a self-hosted model, the flag's whole purpose) the client has no dial guard at all, so the target could be the cloud metadata endpoint. The transport now refuses any redirect that leaves the configured endpoint's scheme+host, the same decision the NetBox connector already made for itself; a same-origin redirect is still followed, because a reverse proxy normalising a path is legitimate.

  • Every upload cap in the platform was preceded by an unbounded read. The audit middleware, which runs ahead of every handler in all sixteen services, read each request body into a buffer and never used the bytes. The SBOM upload's 32 MiB ceiling and the host-inventory intake's were therefore applied to a body that was already resident, so an authenticated caller ignoring them could make any service hold whatever the edge forwards, per concurrent request, before a handler line ran. The read is gone; both caps now bind.

  • POST /ask and POST …/draft-controls decoded unbounded bodies before applying their published caps. Both checked their limit — 4096 characters for a question, 64 KiB for a pasted standard — on a string the JSON decoder had already built, so the cap chose which error the caller got and said nothing about the allocation. Both now bound the body first and answer 413 naming the published cap, with headroom for JSON escaping so a legal request never meets the transport bound. The drafting endpoint's published 64 KiB cap was also a property of one Author implementation rather than of the endpoint — it lived inside the Enterprise drafter, so any other seam (the null one, a future local model) received whatever got past the transport bound, eight times the number the error message names. It is now checked at the seam, before dispatch.

  • passcode and a bare pin are credentials the redactor did not recognise. Neither matched a fragment nor ended in "key". Added, with snmp_version, pinning and pinned_certificate pinned as must-survive so the fix cannot become the over-strict version of the same bug. (This finding also covered SNMP community strings, which gate 4 closed independently and better, with a suffix rule rather than the bare fragment X.5 proposed — communityGalleryImageId is an Azure image id and is posture.)

  • The resource-tracking middleware drained every request body too, so the fix above did not bind. Six services — auth, admin, cbom, compliance-engine, inventory-service and sensor-manager — register resourcetracking.Middleware BEFORE the audit middleware, and it read each body into a buffer for the same stated reason and threw the bytes away the same way. Removing the audit read alone therefore changed nothing for the SBOM upload's 32 MiB cap, the catalogue bundle's, /ask's or draft-controls'. It now counts the bytes the handler reads through a transparent wrapper instead of buffering them, so the usage meter reports the same number and every downstream MaxBytesReader finally binds.

  • Two settings on one page asked for two different permissions. PUT /settings/identification (the auto-merge threshold) was gated on assets.update while its sibling card on the same Settings page, the drift baseline, was gated on settings.update — so a role granted one and not the other could edit half a page, with nothing on screen saying why. The threshold now requires both: settings.update because it is a settings page, and assets.update because the threshold authorises the platform to merge two of your assets without asking, which is the same act as accepting a merge proposal by hand. Swapping one for the other would have let settings.update alone authorise asset rewriting.

  • Owner email addresses no longer cross the AI provider boundary. owner_email was on the allowlist of asset-row fields sent to a model for the narration turn. The redactor does not touch it — an address is not secret-shaped — so the allowlist WAS the decision, and it was one a field list implied rather than stated. It is projected out, and the ai-assistant page now says in so many words what an asset row carries when it is sent. The capability is unaffected: exists(owner_email) is a predicate and runs in Postgres, so "which production servers have no owner?" is still answered — what the model no longer sees is the address it could only have repeated back.

  • Accepting a drafted remediation plan now records the server's provenance, and bounds the plan. POST /findings/:id/remediation/accept stamped the row inferred with a source_ref built from the model id in the REQUEST BODY, so the one piece of provenance the server could have stood behind was a caller assertion — any client could claim any model, of any length. The row now names the model this deployment is configured with, or remediator:model when it pins none. steps and summary were also unbounded, and are rendered into the plan item's notes; they are now held to the same limits that bound what the drafter may propose (12 steps, 600 characters each), refused rather than truncated. A plan this platform drafted always fits.

  • A human's decision on a merge, class or relationship proposal is now audited by name. The accept and reject routes carried no explicit audit entry, so the record said "POST /approvals/classes//accept, 200" and not which class was applied to which asset. Note the asymmetry that made it worth closing: the MACHINE path (an auto-accepted merge) writes a rich record — score, model, candidates, reason — precisely because nobody is there to ask, while the path with a person behind it wrote less.

  • Three audit events in this build were being discarded by the database. audit.activity_logs.event_category carries a CHECK constraint, and data_modification (the auto-accepted merge) and configuration (both tenant settings handlers, and the algorithm-catalogue writes) are not in it — so every one of those entries was rejected on INSERT with nothing visible to the caller: the helper discards the error, the write is batched, and the flush is a background goroutine talking to another service. Two of the shared audit package's own published category constants were values the database rejects, which is where configuration came from. The constants are corrected, the call sites use them, LogActivity now refuses an unstorable category loudly instead of letting it vanish, and two tests hold the line: one derives the valid set from the CHECK in schema.sql, the other scans inventory-service's own call sites.

  • A statement ceiling on every read that runs a tenant's own query. The asset list, the facet rail and the stale list splice a caller's query-language predicate into their WHERE clause, and no deployment set a statement_timeout; context cancellation was the only backstop, which sends a cancel request on a second connection and leaves the statement running until the backend notices. Those reads now open their transaction with SET LOCAL statement_timeout, five seconds, reverting with the transaction so it cannot leak onto a pooled connection.

    • Honest about what prompted it: the review expected a catastrophic regex ((a+)+) to be the way in, and that was measured and does not reproduce — PostgreSQL's ARE is a hybrid DFA and returned in under a millisecond on every pattern tried. The ceiling is kept as a general bound on a predicate a tenant controls, not as a fix for a demonstrated blow-up, and the tests say so.

    • The findings evidence rail has a redaction backstop. Writer.Upsert wrote Finding.Evidence verbatim into findings.evidence, a jsonb the UI renders and the remediation drafter reads, for every producer. Every other rail in the platform has a backstop and this one — the single chokepoint for six producers — had none. Nothing leaks through it today; the point is the next producer. A key the redactor has explicitly NAMED as a credential is now masked, and PEM private-key blocks are masked inside string values wherever they appear. Deliberately NOT the ordinary redactor: its catch-all treats anything ending in "key" as material, and the drift producer's observation_key is the finding's own identity. Masking that would have broken a producer silently, which is the same bug pointed the other way.

    These twelve come from the general asset inventory's cross-cutting security review (BUILD_PLAN X.5), whose full findings — including what was reported for the owner rather than fixed — are in docsv4/internal/developer/design/asset-inventory/SECURITY_REVIEW_X5.md.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Added a Concepts page (docsv4/core/concepts.md) defining the vocabulary the platform is adopting as it grows from a cryptographic inventory into a general asset inventory: asset, endpoint, class, identifier, relationship, fact, finding, risk, alert, provenance, approval, query, scope, and snapshot. Linked from the Platform Overview and the customer docs index. First deliverable of the general asset inventory initiative's Phase 0 (workstream 0.7); no product behavior changed.

  • Audit logging guide gains an "Upgrading" note (docsv4/core/guides/audit-logging.md) explaining that rows recorded before the #1699 event-category fix keep event_category = system and an event type of the form system.<service>.<action> — an alert rule or SIEM filter written against either shape matches only the old rows going forward.

  • Product-descriptor docs corrected to the current nav label. CBOM generation moved from "Risk & Compliance → CBOM" to "Risk & Compliance → Bills of Materials" when the artifact pipeline gained kinds (ADR-0005 D6); the route stays /risk-compliance/cbom. Fixed in docsv4/internal/product-descriptors/scopes-and-reproducible-boundaries.md, docsv4/internal/product-descriptors/cbom-as-audit-evidence.md, and docsv4/internal/developer/standards/features/post-design-permission-families.md.

  • The upstream data sources' attribution is now stated, and travels with the data. NOTICE gains a "Third-party data" section: this product uses data from the NVD API but is not endorsed or certified by the NVD; OSV's aggregated database is CC-BY-4.0, attributed to OSV (https://osv.dev) and to the upstream database named on each record; endoflife.date is mirrored under its published API terms. Every offline catalogue bundle built by make build-catalog-bundle now carries the same wording as an ATTRIBUTION.md member inside the tarball, so the obligations reach whoever ends up holding the file rather than staying behind in the repository. The operator guidance in "Attribution and terms" (catalogue docs) says so, and no longer describes the review of these terms as pending.

  • The minimum supported Windows version is documented: Windows Server 2019 or later (or Windows 10 1809 and later), for the host the device agent runs on and for any Windows host it collects from in remote mode. That is where the OpenSSH Server feature is available, which is what PowerShell-over-SSH remote collection needs. WinRM remains unsupported.

  • The README, the edition matrix and the Usage & Limits page now say what the code does. The README claimed six free frameworks (there are eight), nine inventory lenses (eleven, two of the named ones do not exist) and grouped plan authoring with billing as MSP-only, while the shipping Core build mounts plan authoring and billing is an Enterprise capability; the generated edition matrix said only MSP could author plans. All three now agree, the README gained rows for the NetBox connector and the AI assistants, and the tenant Usage & Limits page shows Storage as not metered instead of rendering the unmeasured value as "0.0 GB used" against the plan's quota. (#1778)

docs.title: Internal
docs.text:
• make test-integration-db now applies seed.sql, matching the nightly test-backend CI job, which has always applied schema + seed before running any test binary. The local runner previously stopped at schema.sql, so a test relying only on testdb.Connect(t) (never calling testdb.ApplySchemaAndSeed/ApplySeed itself) saw an unseeded database locally and a seeded one nightly — passing locally and failing nightly on a real collision with a seeded row, not a flake (#1672).

  • TestContract_EverySpecPathHasARoute (inventory-service) is now edition-aware. A spec operation whose handler lives under an ee/ tree is marked x-edition: enterprise in api/openapi/inventory-service.openapi.yaml (see api/README.md for the convention) and is expected to have no route in a Core export (ee/ absent) while still being required to have one in a full/Enterprise checkout — both directions are pinned by tests in spec_route_table_contract_test.go. Previously this test hard-failed in a Core export because the NetBox and CMDB-sync connector routes (registered under ee/connectors/netbox and ee/cmdbsync) genuinely have no matching route once ee/ is stripped.

Nothing in this section changes anything a customer sees or runs — it is the test harness only.

  • The parallel DB-integration test run is deterministic again. Nightly test-backend failed on two consecutive nights and roughly half of local make test-integration-db runs failed, always in a different test, always one that passed alone. The cause was not any of those tests: shared/testdb's ~200 ApplySchemaAndSeed call sites each re-applied the whole 30,000-line schema.sql and seed.sql from inside a run whose package binaries are parallel, so an apply held ACCESS EXCLUSIVE across every table while other packages were mid-transaction and Postgres broke the cycle by killing one side (40P01 deadlock detected). The seed half had the mirror problem — its tenant-scoped inserts select from tenants, and a throwaway tenant being CASCADE-deleted mid-statement failed their foreign-key check, exhausting the applier's retries and failing a whole package at setup.

Both files are now applied once per database: their sha256 is recorded in testdb_meta.applied_sql by the local runner and by nightly, and the harness reads that marker while holding the same exclusive advisory lock the apply takes, so two binaries cannot both decide to apply. A test whose subject is the re-apply calls the new testdb.ForceApplySchema / ForceApplySeed. The role and grant re-assertions behind ConnectAsAppRole (a GRANT … ON ALL TABLES per call, which rewrites a pg_class row per table) are cached the same way. Ten consecutive full parallel runs are clean, with zero genuine transient-race retries where the same tree previously logged fourteen.

Locking the tenant lifecycle against the applier — the other obvious fix for the seed half — was tried and reverted: it hangs the suite, because a shared advisory request queues behind a waiting exclusive one, so a test holding a row lock and then wanting a tenant waits on an applier waiting on that row lock. Ten packages sat at the timeout under nightly's own whole-module command. The seed re-applies simply stop happening instead, which leaves the two deliberate re-appliers to the foreign-key retry that exists for them. NewTenant carries a comment saying not to try it again.

  • Test fixtures that bind a well-known port get their own loopback address. cluster-sensor-service's UDP-dispatch suite bound 127.0.0.1:44818 and :47808, the same sockets sensor/internal/discovery's sweep suite needs — packages make test-parallel runs at the same time. The sensor suite had already moved to 127.0.0.2 and said why in a comment; the comment was not a check, so the other suite stayed put. It is now on 127.0.0.3, and a guard fails any test file that binds a fixed well-known port on 127.0.0.1.

  • Two edition-gate tests no longer write to seeded reference rows. Applying the seed once removed a mask: the enforcement-layer test that proves a hand-edited tier cannot unlock a paid capability was writing that grant onto the seeded enterprise tier and never putting it back, while a test in another package — running in parallel against the same database — asserts that no active tier grants an edition-gated capability. Both used to be rescued by seed.sql's corrective UPDATE running a couple of hundred times per run. Each test now uses a tier of its own and cleans it up, and the enforcement test asserts its premise (the tier row really does grant the capability) so it cannot pass by granting nothing.

  • Every Core release is now published as a release candidate first. Owner decision: core-vX.Y.Z-rc.N goes through the real pipeline — export, public tag, release-core.yml, signed images and chart at ghcr — is installed on the dev cluster from the published chart, and is smoke-tested; only then is core-vX.Y.Z cut, from the same commit. The pipeline support is the smallest set of changes that makes an RC correct rather than merely accepted: the GitHub Release is created --prerelease --latest=false, the images job does not move any :latest tag for a prerelease, release notes come from the base version's CHANGELOG section (an RC has none of its own, by rule) and the public export carries that section relabelled under the RC heading without duplicating it. publish-public-tree.yml warns — deliberately not fails — when a final tag has no matching -rc.* tag at the same commit. New: scripts/rc-smoke.sh, a curl/jq smoke run over a live install (every backend's health through the gateway with the service list derived from the registry, both UIs, both login planes, the tenant reads, the Core-vs-regulated framework partition, a real CBOM generation, and the version every pod reports). Procedure: RELEASE_PROCESS.md § Release candidates.

  • make audit now guards CHANGELOG.md against the release-prep merge bug that hit three times in one day. A branch that merged origin/main after [Unreleased] was consolidated into a new ## [X.Y.Z] section replayed a stale diff and re-inserted bullets git had already moved, so the shipped release section carried the same bullet twice and duplicate ### Added / ### Fixed headings. scripts/audit-changelog.mjs now checks: no bullet's first line repeats anywhere in the file; no ### Heading repeats within [Unreleased] or the release section right after it (older, already-frozen sections that legitimately repeat headings are left alone); exactly one leading ## [Unreleased]; every other ## [...] heading carries a - YYYY-MM-DD date; and [Unreleased]'s own headings are drawn from the file's existing heading vocabulary. Mutation-tested both polarities in scripts/audit-changelog.test.mjs.

  • This release's own notes are published from a lead, not from the whole entry. The entry you are reading ran to roughly 200 KB — a reference document, and well past the 125,000-character limit GitHub answers 422 to, which would have failed the release at its very last step with every image already built and signed. So the detail moved here, CHANGELOG.md's ## [1.0.0] section carries a hand-written lead (Highlights, Breaking / Upgrading, Editions, Verify) plus a link to this page, and the lead ends with a <!-- release-notes-end --> marker that release-core.yml lifts the GitHub Release body from. A section with no marker is still published whole, so nothing changes for the releases already recorded below this one, and the byte cap stays behind the lift as the belt. The changelog audit's duplicate-bullet check follows the bullets across both files, and the export strips issue references from this document the same way it already strips them from the carried changelog — they address a repository a public reader cannot open.

  • scripts/rc-smoke.sh now drives the platform-admin plane against the admin host rather than the tenant host, where deny-admin-plane answers 404 by design — so the platform-admin rows failed on a correctly configured two-host install and would have passed on a misconfigured single-host one. The session row is now the Core-served GET /admin/auth/me, and the Enterprise-only tenants list is asserted against the build's own edition read-out (GET /admin/platform/edition) instead of being expected to answer on Core. scripts/test-rc-smoke.mjs pins that no admin-plane path is ever requested against the tenant host, and runs the unreachable-host rehearsal.

  • The schema upgrade-path tripwire no longer fires on release candidates. It matched core-v1.*, which core-v1.0.0-rc.1 satisfies, so the unit suite went red on main telling us to re-arm a test for which no prior release exists — a candidate is installed, looked at and thrown away, never upgraded from. CI never saw it because its checkout has no tags. It now matches a final core-v1.Y.Z only, and the tag filter is unit-tested in both polarities so the guard still fires the day 1.0.0 ships.

  • rc-verify waits for the ingress, not just the pods. kubectl rollout status proves every pod is Ready; it does not prove Traefik is routing to them, and for a few seconds after a rollout the public URL can refuse the connection outright. Everything after the install talks to that URL, so the gap bit three separate steps in three disguises: the smoke tenant got HTTP 000 — registering and failed core-v1.0.0-rc.7, Playwright's globalSetup timed out on the login form, and the first framework-score reads come back mid-convergence. One bounded wait now covers all of them. It WARNs rather than fails if the edge never answers — the steps below report the real problem with better messages, and a readiness probe that can end a run adds a failure mode instead of removing one. step grew a printed WARN level for it, because a level that is recorded and never shown is how a check becomes invisible.

  • rc-verify stops waiting for a chart that is never coming. A chart that has not been published YET and one whose build already failed look identical from the registry, so the wait loop reported "not published yet — retrying" either way. On core-v1.0.0-rc.7 that cost 27 minutes: Release Core had failed three minutes in, when one of eighteen image jobs hit a transient reset pulling its base image, and the verifier went on hoping until its deadline. It now asks the run that is supposed to publish the chart whether it is still trying, and fails immediately — naming the conclusion and linking the run — when that run has finished without succeeding. Deliberately one-directional: a missing run, an in-flight run, a rate limit, no network or no jq all stay silent and leave the existing deadline in charge, because a diagnostic that can itself fail a release is worse than the wait it replaces.

  • rc-verify's score deadline raised to 10 minutes, from measurement. A tenant seeing the golden dataset for the FIRST time needs ~3 minutes for the compliance reconcile worker to settle — early reads legitimately show cert-expiry-not-expired at 100 and best-practices at 33 before the producers finish and the scores converge to what expected.json pins. Now that every automatic run uses a fresh tenant, every run pays that cost, while the same cluster finishes rolling eighteen services. Five minutes left two minutes of slack; that is not margin for a gate. HTTPTotal follows, because a whole-run cap below the sum of the per-check deadlines turns a slow check into a confusing timeout instead of a named failure.

  • The Findings page now has a browser journey. It had none, while Posture and Bills of Materials did — backwards, since Findings is where a compliance failure becomes something a person can act on, and it is the page that has silently omitted a whole producer before (it read compliance-only for a while after the eol and vulnerability producers shipped). The journey asserts the property the API contract names as the hazard: per-producer facet counts come from producer_counts, computed under the same filters minus the producer one, "so a facet's number and the list it leads to describe the same set". Labels come from the GENERATED FINDING_PRODUCERS registry the page itself renders from, so a new producer is covered the day it is added and a page that disagrees with the registry fails here rather than dropping that producer's findings quietly.

  • rc-verify now asserts what the frameworks SCORE, not merely that they scored. The previous check was satisfied by any non-null number, which cannot see a change to the scoring MODEL. A score is severity-weighted over CONTROLS and a control fails if it has one active finding anywhere in the tenant (the XCCDF model, #1369) — it is not a percentage of compliant subjects, which is why 19 of 20 valid certificates still leave cert-expiry-not-expired at 0. That is correct and surprising enough that expected.json already warned against re-investigating it; the numbers are now pinned so the model cannot be changed by accident (flip it to per-subject and the score reads 95 and the gate fails). The dataset deliberately earns one partial score (inventory-hygiene = 71) and the suite asserts that at least one framework is strictly between 0 and 100, so a scorer collapsed to the two extremes cannot pass. Polls, because scores converge downward as producers finish. Mutation-tested with score_drift.

  • rc-verify's UI leg could fail before running a single journey. retries in the Playwright config covers tests, not globalSetup, so one slow first paint took the whole leg down — which is what happened on core-v1.0.0-rc.4: the browser starts the moment the data path returns, ~90s after a helm upgrade has restarted all 18 services, and the login form had not rendered inside the timeout. An identical run minutes later passed 9/9. globalSetup now waits for the platform to answer (auth-service health and the login page — separate pods, independent failures) before launching a browser, and retries a login that never got off the ground. It deliberately does NOT retry a login the form rejected: "Rate limit exceeded" and a wrong password are answers, not flakes, and hammering either makes the report worse. Its failure screenshots are now collected into the run artifact — the one artefact that would have named rc.4's cause was never captured — written to a directory that holds no session state, because .auth/tenant.json is a live login and must never reach a downloadable artifact.

  • rc-verify counted the dataset's outbound SaaS observations as expected assets. The golden dataset names six public destinations — GitHub, Stripe, Datadog, Okta, S3, Slack — which the platform routes to external_connections, the third-party lens, and never turns into managed assets; the generator says so in as many words. The data path counted every destination it generated, so on core-v1.0.0-rc.3 it sat at "20 of 26 assets exist" for five minutes and failed the release gate on correct behaviour, on a fresh tenant as well as a reused one. The expectation now splits the two populations the way the platform does, from the address, and the external half is asserted against /external-connections rather than going uncounted — it had been covered by nothing, which is how the asset count came to be wrong about it.

  • rc-verify also counted host observations as endpoints. A host observation is the host naming itself over ARP/DHCP/mDNS — it is what CREATES an asset, not a service listening on one, and the platform writes no asset_endpoints row for it. The data path counted one per host anyway, deriving 62 endpoints against a platform that stores 42. This was invisible on core-v1.0.0-rc.3 only because the asset miscount above failed the run three checks earlier; fixing that one uncovered this one. The derivation now decides it the way the platform does (discovery_type == "host_observation"), the fake platform in the tests models the same thing, and the golden profile's derived numbers (20 assets, 6 external connections, 42 endpoints, 22 TLS) are pinned against what a live tenant on the dev cluster actually holds.

  • The README is now audited against source. It was the only edition surface with no drift guard, which is how "six frameworks" and "nine lenses" survived for weeks after both had grown. make audit now checks its framework and lens counts against the code that defines them and asserts every edition-gated capability has a paid-only row; the check fails if it reads nothing, so an emptied pattern cannot pass vacuously. (#1778)

docs.title: Vista Platform 4.1.0 — full list of changes
docs.text: Released 2026-09-30. The release summary — highlights, what to do before upgrading, what each edition includes, and how to verify the signatures — is in the CHANGELOG published with that release. This page is the complete, per-change record behind it.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• CMDB schedules run. A CMDB profile set to Hourly, Daily or Weekly is now synced on that schedule (Enterprise). Before, the schedule was saved and shown and nothing ran it. A scheduled run follows the platform's direction — pull for SolarWinds, pull then push for ServiceNow, Device42 and Oomnitza — and is skipped for disabled profiles, suspended or canceled tenants and tenants without CMDB sync. One run per profile at a time across replicas: Sync or Pull during a run answers 409 "a sync for this profile is already running". Runs are limited to 60 minutes, and a run cut short by a restart is closed as failed ("interrupted (service restarted)"). Pulls are now recorded in the sync history too.
  • CMDB field mapping, incremental sync and retirement (Enterprise; Oomnitza first). Each CMDB platform now ships a default field mapping that a profile can override through GET/PUT /cmdb/profiles/{id}/mapping. A mapping is checked on save, before every run and at every start; one that no longer checks out pauses the profile ("Mapping invalid" on its card) instead of syncing wrongly. Runs send and write only what changed (full re-sync daily, or with ?full=true); a record retired or removed in the CMDB marks the asset absent from that source instead of being deleted; records Vista pushed are recognised when a pull reads them back, so they are neither duplicated nor bounced back. A pull reads only mapped fields, and mapped personal data is recorded on the asset for data-subject requests.
  • ServiceNow sync works the way a ServiceNow CMDB expects (Enterprise).
