Pushes go through ServiceNow's Identification and Reconciliation API under a discovery source you name, so a server its own Discovery already found is updated rather than duplicated, its classification is kept, and your reconciliation rules decide which source owns which field. Hardware is sent as its standard CI class (servers, computers, PCs, switches, routers, firewalls, load balancers, access points, storage, printers). Approved relationships between synced CIs are sent as standard ServiceNow relationships. An asset archived in Vista retires its CI (install status Retired). A pull reads every page of every class it covers — Linux, Windows and other servers, PCs, network gear, VMs, applications and business services — classifies each by its ServiceNow class, reads only mapped fields, and fetches only what changed since the last pull.

  • CMDB profiles can reach an on-premises CMDB. New per-profile settings: "CMDB is on our own network" (private addresses, by opt-in, audit-logged) and a CA bundle for a CMDB behind an internal CA. Both are checked on save. Redirects to another host are refused, since credentials travel with them.

  • NetBox connections accept a custom CA certificate. A NetBox whose HTTPS certificate your own CA issued can now be reached by pasting that CA's certificate (PEM) into the connection. It is added to the trust store for that connection only; it is checked on save, and a pasted private key is refused. There is deliberately no "skip verification" option.

  • SIEM export shows delivery health and reaches on-premises receivers (Enterprise). Each integration in Security & Trust → SIEM Export now shows its status, last success, last error, and events sent / failed. An integration can opt in to a private-network receiver and carry a custom CA bundle, and Send test event reports the receiver's own status and message on failure.

  • Generic webhooks can authenticate and are signed. The connection form now offers none / bearer token / basic / one custom header, and every delivery carries X-Vista-Event-Id (identical across retries — an idempotency key), X-Vista-Timestamp and, when the channel has a signing secret, X-Vista-Signature: sha256=<HMAC-SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + body)>. A new webhook gets a generated signing secret, shown once; rotate it by entering a new one. Verification recipes are in the notification-provider guide.

  • The Email connection card says when email can't be sent. A new GET /tenant/delivery-status reports whether an SMTP host is configured.
  • A dedicated integration service (Enterprise). A new backend that owns every exchange with a third-party system of record. SIEM export runs in it from this release (see Changed); NetBox and CMDB sync follow. It deploys with the commercial chart only (Deployment, Service, service-mesh certificate, gateway routes) and reports its version and edition to an authenticated caller. The commercial image set grows to 19. Core installs are unchanged — the service does not exist there, and the Core admin console no longer offers what it serves.
  • Identity: two records the rules are sure are one device are merged for you (default on, turn it off under Settings → Policies → Identification rules). The same MAC address or serial number seen directly on the device (or reported by a controller that manages it), both records on the same network segment, nothing contradicting it and neither ever marked keep separate — never an address alone, never a generic or synthetic name. A record you typed in is the survivor and keeps your values. Each merge is listed under Discovery → Approvals → Merged automatically as Merged by rule, with its evidence. Turned off, the same cases become ordinary merge proposals.
  • Identity: a MAC worked out rather than seen. A device whose IPv6 address is built from its network card's MAC (EUI-64), or whose 12-hex-digit serial number is its MAC, now carries that MAC as an inferred identifier, so it matches the record a sensor or controller built from the MAC. Inferred identifiers vote only after a stated one of the same kind.
  • Identity: DHCP is understood per network segment. A network segment's DHCP setting (Settings → Network segments) can be set by an operator, measured by a controller that answered, or inferred from DHCP traffic; a lower source never overwrites a higher one. On a DHCP segment the address follows the MAC that now holds it, and an address alone no longer creates a provisional record.
  • Identity: generic names never decide. A host name many unrelated devices carry (iphone, android, localhost, printer, or any name three or more live assets already hold) is still recorded, but it is never the reason two records match, and a record that matched only on such a name is not offered as a merge candidate.
  • Merge proposals show how alike the two records are. The Approvals card adds "The two records themselves score N%", and an identifier with more than one value (a second MAC) now matches when any value agrees.
  • Exports say when an asset was never assessed. The inventory CycloneDX xBOM carries vista:asset:risk_assessed and omits vista:asset:risk_score for an asset nobody has assessed; OCSF omits device.risk_score; the CSV cell is blank.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The NetBox connector runs in the integration service (Enterprise). It moved out of the inventory service; connections, tokens, schedules and run history carry over, and an import produces the same segments, assets and counts. The connector now writes the inventory only through the inventory service's identity engine, approval rules and plan limits, over an internal service-to-service API — never its tables.
  • ServiceNow profiles: API token removed; certificates and keys are no longer pushed (Enterprise). ServiceNow's APIs take a username and password or OAuth client credentials; the "API token" option could never authenticate, and a profile saved with it now has to be edited to one of the two. Test now reads one CI instead of an admin-only table, so a least-privilege integration user passes. Certificates, keys and crypto configurations are no longer sent as ServiceNow CIs (they went to classes a standard instance does not have); the crypto posture stays on each asset's description. Records a previous version created in those classes are left as they are. Pushes now need a discovery source value on the instance — see the ServiceNow section of the CMDB guide.
  • SIEM export no longer loses events when a pod dies (Enterprise). It moved from the audit service into the integration service, and it no longer buffers events in memory: each integration reads the stored audit log forward from its own position, kept in the database, and moves that position only after its receiver accepts a batch. Delivery is now at-least-once across pod loss (was at-most-once): a batch in flight when a pod dies is re-sent, so receivers should de-duplicate on the event id. A receiver that is down, or that refuses events outright (a bad token, an untrusted certificate), now holds the integration's position instead of dropping events, and delivery catches up once it is fixed; the 10,000-event buffer and its drop-oldest overflow are gone. Events refused for their content (an Elasticsearch mapping conflict) are still passed over, and are now shown as Refused. One replica delivers a given integration at a time. The list shows Delivered through — how far each integration has got.
  • A new integration starts at "now" and never floods its receiver with the retained trail; Start from sends up to 168 hours of recent history first. Re-enabling a disabled integration starts it at "now" again.
  • The SIEM API moved to the integration service's own route prefix (only the admin console calls it; no compatibility route).
  • Events reach the SIEM about five seconds after they are stored.
  • The SIEM API is denied on the tenant (web-UI) host; the admin console reaches it on the admin host. And, like the NetBox and CMDB connectors, the integration service's dial guard is given the cluster's own pod and Service ranges (networkPolicy.clusterInternalCIDRs), so a destination allowed onto a private network still cannot reach in-cluster addresses.
  • The Core admin console no longer shows SIEM Export. SIEM export is an Enterprise capability served by a service Core does not have, so the entry is gone rather than showing an upgrade notice.
  • The audit service stamps each event's created_at with the database clock, and serves an internal, service-to-service feed of stored events (HMAC-signed calls only; denied at the edge on every host).
  • Channel Test reports the real reason. A channel that did not deliver now answers 422 with a sanitized reason instead of a generic 500 ("Test failed"), covering every channel type including refusals of internal addresses. The reason is drawn from a fixed vocabulary and never contains the URL, query string, headers or tokens. The same reason is stored in Delivery History.
  • Email with no SMTP configured is an explicit, permanent outcome. It used to fall back to localhost:587 and retry every alert five times. It now fails once, with "Email delivery isn't configured by the platform operator", and is not retried. An explicit SMTP_HOST (dev/compose) still works.
  • PagerDuty events carry a stable dedup_key (from the alert id, else the event id), the alert engine's auto-resolve is sent as a resolve, and Test triggers and immediately resolves a throwaway incident instead of leaving one open.
  • Routing-rule Alert source now offers discovery, ticketing, remediation_plans and billing, and a test fails if a producer publishes a source the list lacks.
  • Slack messages escape &, < and >; email subjects use the alert's title and bodies list readable fields instead of a JSON dump; GET /platform/channels masks credentials like the tenant endpoints; digest-only rows in Delivery History read "queued for digest".
  • Platform integrations of type Slack, PagerDuty, Datadog and Splunk are refused. Creating, editing or testing one through the admin API now answers 400 and names where the job is done (notification channels, or the SIEM export page). Nothing ever acted on these rows, and their "test" only checked that a credential field was filled in before reporting success.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The connector catalogue says only what the code does. Settings → Integrations → Available connectors is generated from the connector registry, and the registry had drifted from the platform (integrations review M32–M35). Cloud: no provider claims serverless functions any more (no Lambda, Azure Functions or Cloud Functions collector exists), and each lists the classes its collectors really produce, including CDN distributions, API gateways, key stores, virtual networks and subnets. Notifications: Slack and PagerDuty are listed where they are delivered (notification channels), joined by email, generic webhook and the in-app bell; Microsoft Teams stays absent. SIEM: Splunk, Datadog, Elasticsearch and the generic webhook are shown as Enterprise and Configured by your platform operator, with no Add button for a tenant. SBOM upload is live (CycloneDX 1.4–1.7 and SPDX 2.2/2.3; with no target asset it creates an application that waits in Approvals). The custom type, which nothing reads, is no longer a card that points at the wrong form: it is listed as not yet available. CMDB and NetBox entries state the classes their pulls can create (taken from each platform's mapping template; NetBox lists every class its role table yields) and the real conflict rule for NetBox. New tests derive those class lists from the collectors, the CMDB mapping templates and the NetBox role table, so they cannot drift again; the schema check now covers the notification-channel and SIEM tables and every value each CHECK accepts.
  • Oomnitza pulls classify assets and keep numeric ids. Every pulled Oomnitza asset became a server; it is now classified from its type (a Laptop is a laptop, an unknown type is generic hardware), and an equipment_id returned as a number is no longer dropped.
  • Device42 sync sends devices, correctly, and never by name alone (Enterprise). Certificates, keys and crypto configurations are no longer pushed into Device42 as devices (one bogus "TLS 1.2" device per host, and Device42 matched them by name, so they collapsed into one). Only approved infrastructure assets are sent, with the calls Device42 documents (form-encoded POST/PUT /api/1.0/device/; the old JSON POST to /devices/ was not the create endpoint). A device is matched by its Device42 id, then its serial number; a record with neither whose name Device42 already uses is skipped with the reason instead of overwriting that device. Device42 owns a device's name, serial number, UUID, hardware and OS after creation; Vista rewrites only the Notes. Pull reads every device in pages of 1000 (it stopped at 1000), classified by Device42 type. Sign-in is Username & password: the "API token" option sent a Bearer token Device42 does not accept, and a profile saved with it (or an API key, or OAuth2) is now refused at save.
  • SolarWinds is pull only for real, and pulls every node. The push code that wrote certificates, keys and configurations into Orion as nodes is gone. Pull reads all of Orion.Nodes (it stopped at 1000) and classifies each node from its MachineType / description (a switch is a switch, not a server); unrecognised nodes are generic hardware. Sign-in is Username & password — the "API key" option sent a Bearer header SWIS rejects; saving one is now refused. Orion's self-signed certificate is trusted with the profile's CA bundle.
  • Oomnitza pulls every asset and no longer receives certificates and keys. The pull stopped at the first 1000 assets; it now pages (limit/skip). Only infrastructure assets are pushed; certificates, keys, crypto configurations and libraries are not assets in an asset register (assets already created that way stay in Oomnitza).
  • Scheduled cloud discovery delivers buckets, databases and key stores. A scheduled run dropped every S3 bucket, RDS instance, Azure storage account and SQL database, GCP bucket and Cloud SQL instance, and KMS key store, and the rows it did write lacked the provider resource id, certificate quality flags, OCSP and region. Scheduled runs now write exactly what a clicked Discover run writes, report their counts from what landed, and complete (or fail) the identity refreshes they serve — partial runs included.
  • Azure and GCP Test Connection contacts the provider. Azure's test reported "validated" for any three strings and GCP's only parsed the key. Azure now obtains a token and reads the subscription from Resource Manager; GCP exchanges the key and reads the project. Failures show the provider's own error (AADSTS…, AuthorizationFailed, invalid_grant, PERMISSION_DENIED). A GCP key whose token_uri is not Google's OAuth endpoint is refused.
  • Azure and GCP runs report each resource type. One refused collector used to abort the whole run (load balancers, proxies) or read as "success, 0 found" (Key Vault, storage, SQL, KMS, Cloud SQL). Every type is now collected independently and its outcome, with the provider's error code, is on the job.
  • Azure Key Vault, storage and SQL, and GCP Cloud KMS, storage and Cloud SQL can be chosen in the Discover dialog, and scheduled runs collect them.
  • A refused ec2:Describe* call in a region is shown on the job rather than reading as a region with no instances.
  • The cloud integration's Enabled switch works: runs of a disabled integration are refused. Jobs queued before a tenant was suspended no longer run.
  • A credential saved under a retired encryption key says "re-enter it" in Test Connection instead of being sent to the provider, and editing an integration no longer re-encrypts such a credential into a usable-looking but wrong value.
  • One list of cloud secret keys. Platform-shared cloud integrations created through admin-service now encrypt the AWS external ID, Azure client ID and GCP service-account key, and the legacy device-credential job payload no longer hands the agent an encrypted username.
  • CMDB push sends only configuration items. Assets pending approval, denied, archived (including from the Stale lens), merged away or deleted were pushed to the customer's CMDB, along with certificates, keys and crypto configurations not in use on any approved asset and destroyed certificates and keys. A push now sends approved assets and what is in use on them.
  • SolarWinds is pull-only. Sync is no longer offered for SolarWinds and the API refuses it: it pushed certificates, keys and crypto configurations into Orion as nodes.
  • CMDB Test, Sync and Pull say why they failed. Test used to answer "Connection test failed" and Sync "Invalid request" whatever went wrong; both now give the sanitized reason (private address, untrusted certificate, rejected credentials, disabled profile, pull-only platform, …) without URLs, headers or response bodies. Pull no longer echoes the raw error. The sync history shows each item the CMDB refused, and the Pull message counts failed and held-for-review records.
  • CMDB push honours the batch size, and records each batch before sending the next, so a push that stops part-way does not create the same CIs again on the next run. batch_size (1–1000) and schedule are validated on save.

  • The CMDB sync history (GET …/cmdb/profiles/{id}/jobs) now requires View Settings, like the profile reads. Deleting an unknown CMDB profile answers 404 instead of 500. A disabled CMDB profile can no longer be pulled from.

  • NetBox connector: seven smaller defects. The same prefix in two VRFs is imported once and the second copy is reported as skipped (with both VRF names) instead of counted as matched. The connection card shows the last error and Drift shows the reason a comparison failed, rather than a generic message. The Import response carries the run's real start time. A run left in_progress by a service restart is closed as failed ("interrupted (service restarted)"). Only one import of a connection runs at a time across replicas; pressing Import during one answers 409. New connections default to a manual schedule. A sensor-discovered asset that NetBox matches keeps its original discovery source.

  • SIEM export integrations are saved and survive restarts (Enterprise). They were held in memory only: every restart or helm upgrade lost them, and with more than one audit-service replica each pod had its own list. They are now stored in the database with credentials encrypted and write-only, every replica picks up a change within 10 seconds, failed deliveries are retried with backoff, batch_size and flush_interval_sec are honoured, and a graceful shutdown flushes buffered events. (Delivery was then made durable in this same release — see "SIEM export no longer loses events when a pod dies" under Changed.)

  • SIEM export sends what each destination actually accepts (Enterprise). Splunk now receives HEC event objects with Authorization: Splunk <token> and the event's own epoch time (it was sent a JSON array with a Bearer token); Datadog receives Logs API v2 logs with DD-API-KEY at the intake for the chosen site, split to Datadog's per-request limits; Elasticsearch receives _bulk NDJSON create actions (index or data stream) with API-key or basic auth, and a 200 with per-document errors is counted per document, retrying only the documents Elasticsearch deferred; the generic webhook receives a JSON array with none / bearer / basic / custom-header auth and the same HMAC signature as notification webhooks. Splunk and Elasticsearch are verified end to end against the real products; Datadog is checked against its documented API only. The form shows only what is implemented — the LEEF and CEF format choices and the unimplemented "Basic Auth" option are gone, and the API refuses them. Audit events arriving over the message bus (including batched entries) are now forwarded too; only directly-posted ones were before.

  • Enterprise and MSP service images no longer crash under load. The commercial backend images were obfuscated with garble's -tiny option, which hides function names the Go runtime relies on to decide when it may safely interrupt a running goroutine. Under heavy work (large host-observation imports in inventory-service, the startup re-evaluation sweep in compliance-engine) a service could corrupt its own scheduler and exit with code 2, printing nothing — and an import in flight when it did could be dropped after its retries ran out. All commercial images now build without -tiny; obfuscation of names and string literals is unchanged. Core images were never affected.

  • Cloud storage, databases and key stores now become assets when identity admission is enforced — the default for new tenants. S3 buckets, RDS, Azure storage and SQL, GCP storage and Cloud SQL, and KMS / Key Vault keys stayed in Discovery → Observations as "a name was observed without a confirmed device or address binding" and never reached Inventory. A resource listed by the platform's cloud collector is now admitted on the provider's resource id and matched on it by the next run; observations parked by earlier runs are linked by the next discovery run, with no data migration. A name reported by anything else is still not enough.
  • Outbound integrations work behind an egress proxy. With HTTPS_PROXY set, the SSRF guard judged the proxy's address instead of the destination, so a proxy on a private address made every webhook, Slack, PagerDuty, SIEM, NetBox and CMDB call fail with "refusing to connect to internal address". The guard now judges each request's destination (every redirect hop included) and trusts the configured proxy; loopback, link-local/metadata and the platform's own cluster ranges stay refused. See Outbound connections for what the guard can and cannot see behind a proxy.
  • networkPolicy.egressEnabled=true no longer cuts off the Enterprise integrations. inventory-service (NetBox and CMDB connectors) and the integration service (SIEM export) are now in networkPolicy.externalEgressBackends; audit-service stays there for S3 archival. So are compliance-engine (framework authoring, remediation drafts) and cbom-service (the comparison narrative), which call the configured ai.provider endpoint.
  • Suspended, canceled and deleted organizations are no longer notified.
  • device-interrogation-service's HTTP fallback to notification-service now presents its client certificate under mTLS.

  • Security-incident notifications now reach someone. monitoring-service raised incidents from log patterns (PII in a log line, a critical security event, an authentication-failure pattern) and tried to tell operators through a channel table nothing ever populated, so they went nowhere. They are now published to the notification service as platform notifications (monitoring / security_incident) and delivered through the platform channels and rules under Settings → Notification Delivery — including the default pack on a fresh install. They are platform-scoped: a tenant's own rules never see them, even when the log line belonged to that tenant.

  • Sensor and device-agent install steps point at downloads that exist. Discovery → Sensors & Agents → Register used to send operators to a download "from the platform" that the platform does not have, and to an install-sensor.sh that releases do not ship. The steps now fetch the binary and installer from the public release matching the running platform version (the version shown on the About page; on a development build with no release version they link the releases page instead of guessing). Serving binaries from the platform for air-gapped installs remains out of scope.

  • Partial delivery is recorded as partial. A notification delivered in-app but not by email used to be written to Delivery History as sent, and a retry that finally worked or was abandoned changed nothing the tenant could see. Status is now sent, partial or failed from the per-channel outcome, the retry worker updates the row when a retry finishes, and the page lists each channel's result ("in_app ✓, email ✗ (retrying)"). A row whose rule matched but whose channels all failed no longer reads "no rule matched". Error text is deliberately not stored — a transport error can carry a webhook URL, which is a credential.
  • Azure cloud integrations run. Every Azure integration saved through the UI stored its tenant and subscription ids in a form the client could not read, so every run failed with failed to decrypt subscription_id. Existing integrations work unchanged, with no re-entry. GCP key names (service_account_key, credentials_json) are now recognised as secrets (see Security).
  • Scheduled cloud runs collect what a clicked Discover run collects. A schedule created in the UI named no resource types, so every scheduled run refreshed only compute enumeration and still reported success. A schedule with no resource types now uses the same set a manual run pre-selects for that provider; a source-refresh run is never widened.
  • Two tenants can name a cloud integration the same. The uniqueness rule covered every tenant, so when one tenant called an AWS integration "Production" no other tenant could, and the dialog said only "Failed to create integration". The name is now unique per tenant (and among platform-shared integrations), a clash answers 409 An integration named "X" already exists, and the dialog shows it.
  • NetBox imports read every record. The connector stopped as soon as a page came back with fewer than 250 records; NetBox clamps the page size to its own maximum, so with a cap of 100 every import read 100 records per kind and reported success. It now follows the response's next link, and an empty page that links onward is an error, not a silent truncation.
  • A long NetBox import no longer reports "failed" while it succeeds. Run now and Drift can take minutes, and the server dropped the connection at its two-minute write timeout, so the browser saw a 502 for an import that finished. Both now extend their own write deadline.
  • NetBox scheduled imports skip tenants that cannot use them. Suspended, canceled and deleted tenants, and tenants that lost the NetBox entitlement, were still imported on schedule — and could not even disable the connection, because every route answered 402. A reactivated tenant's overdue connections run on the next tick.
  • A deleted NetBox connection or CMDB profile name can be used again. The uniqueness rule also counted soft-deleted rows, so re-creating a deleted name answered 500. It now applies to live rows only and a genuine clash answers 409 with the name.
  • CMDB profiles can be created and edited. The Settings → Integrations dialog never sent the two mapping fields, the server bound them as SQL NULL, and every create and edit failed with 500. Omitted mappings are stored as empty on create and kept on update.
  • CMDB sync jobs finish. Completing a job failed on an untyped SQL parameter and the error was thrown away, so every job stayed in_progress forever. Jobs now complete or fail with a recorded reason, per-item errors reach the job summary (first 50, each cut to 500 characters, with totals), a profile's sync_error reads "N of M items failed; first error: …", and the profile card shows it as a tooltip. An invalid platform_type, blank or over-long name or malformed connection settings answers 400, and an unknown id answers 404 instead of 500 (or a panic on Pull).
  • ServiceNow OAuth2 sign-in works. The connector sent the client secret as a bearer token and never exchanged it. It now requests an access token from /oauth_token.do, caches it until shortly before it expires, and exchanges once more on a 401.
  • Audit alert rules validate their input. Creating or editing a rule with a missing or unknown rule_type or severity reached the database constraint and answered 500; it now answers 400 naming the field.
  • Exports stop reporting "never assessed" as risk 0. risk_score 0 in the database means both "assessed clean" and "never assessed"; three exports and two CSVs asserted the first. The inventory CSV, the inventory CycloneDX xBOM and OCSF now carry no risk score for an unassessed asset (the xBOM adds vista:asset:risk_assessed = false), the Data Protection CSV leaves the cell blank when the drawer says "not assessed", and the map's GraphML and Cytoscape exports omit it — for which the neighbourhood and impact nodes now carry risk_assessed. An asset assessed at 0 still exports 0.
  • Core CBOM comparison answers 402. Core mounted no comparison routes, so /cbom/compare answered a bare 404 and an AI assistant could conclude the artifacts did not exist. It now answers 402 "not included in your subscription", and the MCP compare tool reports available: false with reason edition.
  • A compliance summary for a framework you have not activated is an answer, not a 500. The API returns 403 framework_not_activated, and the MCP tool reports it as unavailable rather than as a tool error.
  • An SBOM uploaded to a merged-away asset lands on the survivor. The upload stored software on the archived tombstone, where nothing shows it. It now follows the merge to the surviving asset (bounded at 8 hops) and says so in a warning.
  • Merge proposals stay tidy. Merging left the proposal that launched it pending; a proposal whose live candidates collapse to one is now resolved; a single owner of every identifier is a supporting sighting, not a question; a link made on an address alone carries no device; and there is one pending proposal per pair, with new evidence folded in.
  • Identical evidence that now resolves to a different asset no longer fails ingest. After a segment was switched to DHCP, the same sighting could resolve to a different asset than before and the observation link was refused, rolling back the whole ingest for that finding on every recurrence. The observation is now split instead.
  • Personal API tokens are for AI assistants (MCP) only. Nothing about how a token behaves changed; what the product told you did. Only the MCP server exchanges a token for a session; the inventory and audit APIs answer 401 to one, so the SBOM-upload-from-CI and scripted audit-export examples are gone, and the documented Claude.ai / ChatGPT / Gemini "paste the URL and sign in" flow is withdrawn until hosted assistants can register (they cannot complete sign-in yet). My Profile → API Tokens now offers only the scopes an MCP tool uses (assets.read, compliance.read, reports.read); existing tokens keep working. Header-capable MCP clients (Claude Code, scripts) connect with Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  • Tenant notification channels no longer show their credentials. Every channel response masks them — a URL keeps its scheme and host (https://hooks.example.test/••••), other secrets keep their last four characters — and the edit dialog shows a blank field with a "Leave blank to keep the current value" hint. On update a credential that is absent, blank or the masked form we sent keeps the stored value; an omitted header is a deleted header. Delivery and Test use the stored values. See Security.
  • Dependency updates. Docker base images, github/codeql-action/upload-sarif 4.38.1 → 4.38.2, the npm minor/patch group (8 updates across 3 directories), the Go modules group (5 updates across 2 directories), and brace-expansion 2.1.4 → 2.1.7 (two directories).
  • Build. The Go toolchain guard now dry-runs a dist image target and asserts it is built with the exact go.work patch release, not a floating minor tag.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• The CMDB profile's On conflict setting (platform wins / CMDB wins / skip). Nothing read it: every push upserts. The documented Vault credential references (api_token_ref, client_secret_ref) and "Sync Deletions" option are removed from the docs; nothing implemented them.

  • The Audit alert rules list and enable/disable toggle under Settings → Alert Rules. Nothing evaluated those rows, so the toggle did nothing; the alert catalog on that page is unchanged.

  • The SMS option in the admin console's channel form (there is no SMS sender).
  • monitoring-service's own notification delivery (Slack, webhook, PagerDuty and email senders reading monitoring_notification_channels) and the unused email plumbing in cluster-sensor-service's alert service. Alerts from both go out through the notification service. The monitoring_notification_channels table is no longer created, and is dropped on upgrade when it is empty; a table an operator filled by hand is left in place, unread.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Any signed-in tenant member could read notification-channel credentials. GET /tenant/channels and /tenant/channels/{id} had no permission gate and the service decrypted the configuration into the response: the Slack webhook URL (the URL is the secret), the PagerDuty routing key, and webhook tokens, passwords and header values. Both reads now need settings.read, and — because the seeded viewer role holds it — every channel response is masked regardless (see Changed). Rotate any credential that mattered.
  • Any signed-in tenant member could read CMDB profile credentials. GET /cmdb/profiles and /cmdb/profiles/{id} had only the entitlement gate and returned password, api_token and client_secret in plaintext, to viewers, billing admins and read-only tokens alike. Both reads now need settings.read, no response carries a secret value (has_password, has_api_token and has_client_secret say whether one is stored; extra_headers values are blank), and an update with an omitted or empty secret keeps the stored one. Rotate any CMDB credential that mattered.
  • GCP service-account keys were stored unencrypted. The cloud-integration handler encrypted a fixed list of keys that did not include service_account_key or credentials_json, though the client decrypted them. The list now comes from one place per provider, so it cannot drift from what the client reads. The upgrade does not rewrite keys already saved — rotate the key and save the integration with the new one.
  • A NetBox URL could reach the cluster's own pods and Services. The NetBox connector's private-endpoint opt-in defaults on, but the guard that refuses the platform's pod and Service ranges was configured only for device interrogation, so a tenant could reach in-cluster addresses, and Test's distinct errors ("refused" versus timeout versus "not NetBox") worked as a port scanner. The chart now gives inventory-service the same networkPolicy.clusterInternalCIDRs (and refuses an extraEnv override of them), as it already did for device interrogation.
  • The SIEM API is denied on the tenant host, and the audit service's new internal event feed answers only HMAC-signed service calls and is denied at the edge on every host.

docs.title: Vista Platform 4.2.0 — full list of changes
docs.text: Released 2026-09-30. The release summary — highlights, what to do before upgrading, what each edition includes, and how to verify the signatures — is in the CHANGELOG published with that release. This page is the complete, per-change record behind it.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Per-connection scan consent (Enterprise). CMDB profiles gain Assets from this source may be actively scanned and NetBox connections Devices from this source may be actively scanned, both off by default. Off: an asset Vista knows only from that connection's pulls or imports is left out of auto-scan; Settings → Auto-scan → Not scanned counts them as Imported, not cleared for scanning. On: they become auto-scan candidates, still subject to owned networks, exclusions and sensitive assets — the setting never makes a public address scannable. Scanning them yourself in Active Scan, any asset a sensor, agent or device interrogation has also seen, and assets uploaded or listed in a spreadsheet are unaffected. The choice is recorded with the profile or connection (a save that cannot record it is refused, 502, nothing stored); deleting the connection withdraws it; each change is audit-logged. Needs Update Settings.
  • CMDB dry run, confirmed first sync, run changes and undo (Enterprise). A CMDB profile's card has Dry run: what the next push or pull would create, update and retire, with examples, writing nothing in Vista or in the CMDB; Confirm runs it. A new profile's first sync can only be made that way — until then its card says Not synced yet, Sync and Pull open the dry run, and scheduled runs wait. Sync history shows what each run created or changed on each side (kept 90 days; each asset a pull created or wrote to also names the run on its timeline), and Undo this run… — confirmed first — archives the assets the run created in Vista (never deletes; an asset another source has also reported is kept) and lists what it wrote in the CMDB without changing anything there. Undo never deletes or edits anything in your CMDB. Undo is audit-logged. Dry run and undo need Manage Assets; the changes list, View Settings. New endpoints: the dry-run, changes-list and undo routes named above, and ?plan= on Sync / Pull.
  • CMDB field-mapping editor (Enterprise). Each CMDB profile's card and edit dialog open an editor for how the CMDB's records and Vista's inventory translate: class rules, field rules (with per-field authority — which side wins — and the value-map / default / constant / join / conversion transforms; no scripting), value maps and identity rules. Vista's side is picked from the canonical vocabulary; the CMDB's fields and types are listed from its own schema where it has one (ServiceNow's dictionary and class list, SolarWinds' Orion.Nodes metadata) or from a sample of 25 of your records (Device42, Oomnitza), and the editor says which. Personal-data fields are marked. Preview maps up to ten live records — pulled from the CMDB or about to be pushed — through the mapping as it stands in the editor, saved or not, and shows the result and whether the mapping is valid; it writes nothing on either side. The editor stores only the profile's changes to the default mapping, and a save that does not validate is refused with the entry to fix. Reading the mapping needs Read Settings; listing the CMDB's fields, previewing and saving need Update Settings. New endpoints: the vocabulary, schema and preview routes named above.
  • Device42 custom fields can be mapped as custom_fields.<name>.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• CMDB sync runs in the integration service (Enterprise). The ServiceNow, Device42, SolarWinds and Oomnitza connectors, their field mappings and the sync engine moved out of the inventory service. Nothing changes on Settings → Integrations: profiles, credentials, schedules, field-mapping overrides, links to CMDB records and sync history carry over as they are, and a push or a pull sends and writes what it did before. What changed is underneath: a push reads the inventory only through the inventory service's new internal CI export, and a pull writes it only through the inventory service's identity engine, approval rules and plan limits (the internal source-import API NetBox already uses) — never its tables.
  • The CMDB API moved to the integration service's own route prefix (the exact path is in the Enterprise edition of these notes; only the tenant UI calls it, with no compatibility route), and it now answers a tenant session only — a platform-admin token or a service call gets 403. The old /api/v2/inventory-service/cmdb/profiles* paths are gone from every edition.
  • The inventory service serves an internal CI export (/api/v1/inventory-service/internal/ci-export/*): the configuration items in push scope, per-asset detail through a field allowlist, and approved relationships. Its source-import API gained link and presence writes. All are HMAC-signed service calls only, each naming one tenant in a signed header; refused with any user token and denied at the edge on every host.
  • Core's Integrations page shows the CMDB section as an Enterprise upgrade from the connector catalogue and the feature flag, without a request.
  • Connector egress is now only where connectors run. With the SIEM, NetBox and CMDB connectors all in the integration service, the inventory service is off the chart's private-network dialer list (VISTA_PLATFORM_INTERNAL_CIDRS is no longer injected into it; its only outbound call, the configured ai.provider endpoint, never used it), and the audit service no longer carries an ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY — the SIEM credential store that key guarded lives in the integration service. Both services stay in networkPolicy.externalEgressBackends, for the model provider and S3 archival respectively and nothing else. The chart egress test now fails if either returns to the connector or private-dialer set.
  • The CMDB guide and glossary are Enterprise documentation. They moved out of the Core feature guides into the Enterprise integrations guides, next to the NetBox guide; Core pages link to them only from Enterprise sections.
  • The Core export gate builds and tests both web consoles. Before a Core release is published, the exported source tree is installed clean and both the tenant and admin consoles are type-checked and built exactly as their production images build them, then their unit-test suites, and the shared primitives' suite, are run. A failure stops the release and names the failing build or test. Until now the gate built only the Go modules, so a build break that exists only in the Core source tree could be found first by the public image build.
  • Go lint is a hard gate in CI and runs over the whole tree nightly. In CI, a missing golangci-lint now fails the standards check instead of skipping it (locally it still finds the tool in the Go bin directory, and says loudly when it cannot). The pull-request lint step sees only new issues, so a new nightly job lints every Go module in full and reports findings a dependency bump or a removed caller creates.
  • Go lint findings on main are cleared (11 across four modules): two unused test helpers removed, and the AWS SDK's deprecation notices for the S3 transfer manager and ACM's certificate-transparency option annotated with their reasons rather than migrated — the replacement is a new pre-1.0 module and needs its own change with S3 coverage.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Backends no longer start before an upgrade's schema migration finishes. Each backend's wait-for-schema init container waited only for the tenants table, which exists on every upgrade, so new pods started while the schema-migration Job was still adding columns and a first query could fail with SQLSTATE 42703 (undefined column) until the Job caught up. The gate now waits for the Job's completion marker for the chart's own schema hash — the same check the seed Job already made. It applies to all 16 backends that use Postgres. With schemaMigration.enabled=false it checks only that a schema exists, and it gives up after ~10 minutes with the reason in its log (kubelet then retries) instead of waiting silently. On a fresh install, backends now wait for the whole schema rather than its first table.
  • The integration service tolerates an in-flight schema migration at start-up (Enterprise). During the 4.1.0 upgrade its first SIEM configuration load ran before the migration had added a column, logged a warning and recovered ten seconds later. A missing column or table is now recognised as "schema not ready": logged at INFO ("waiting for the database schema migration"), retried after 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds (never longer than the normal poll interval) and back to normal once a read succeeds. Any other error still logs a warning. This stays useful where the chart gate does not apply, such as an external database with schemaMigration.enabled=false.
  • The connector-registry check for Enterprise implementations was silently skipping them. It decided it was looking at a Core checkout by the absence of services/inventory-service/ee, which the CMDB move deleted, so a renamed or removed connector package would have passed. It now probes any services/*/ee tree and the probe has its own test.
  • A test-only wall-clock flake is fixed. The identity-enrichment replay test failed every time it ran between 23:40 and 00:00 UTC, because its clock crossed the day boundary that legitimately starts a new rescan cycle. The test clock now starts inside a cycle and the test also asserts that the same evidence in the next cycle does dispatch. No production behaviour changed.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
• An upgrade that changes the schema now waits for the migration. New backend pods sit in Init until schema-migration has applied the new schema; under the default rolling update the old pods keep serving, while a backend on strategy: Recreate is down for the whole migration. helm upgrade --wait now includes the migration time, and Helm's default --timeout is 5 minutes: give it a --timeout that covers the migration plus the rollout. A release that doesn't change the schema passes the wait at once. On a single-node cluster, new pods hold their CPU requests while they wait, so the surge lasts for the whole migration. With schemaMigration.enabled=false the old wait (a schema exists) still applies.
  • Auto-scan no longer scans imported-only assets until their connection allows it (Enterprise). Scan consent is off for every existing CMDB profile and NetBox connection after the upgrade; nothing is migrated. An asset that exists only because a CMDB pull or NetBox import created it — no sensor, agent or device interrogation has seen it, and no spreadsheet upload has listed it — and that auto-scan was scanning because its address is private stops being scanned automatically. Assets from spreadsheet uploads and SBOM uploads are not affected. To keep scanning them, turn on Assets / Devices from this source may be actively scanned on the connection. Assets a sensor or agent has observed are unaffected, as is Active Scan. The schema gains source_scan_consents (RLS; no row = no consent) and the inventory service a signed internal route, PUT /internal/sources/scan-consent, used only by the integration service and denied at the edge like the other source routes.
  • CMDB (Enterprise): a never-synced profile needs a confirmed dry run first. A profile that has never written anything has its scheduled runs skipped, and its Sync and Pull open the dry run, until that first run is confirmed. A profile that has linked a record or pushed or created anything counts as already synced, so its schedule and its Sync / Pull buttons work as they did.
  • CMDB (Enterprise): run provenance table. The schema gains cmdb_sync_job_items (one row per record a run created or changed; RLS; pruned after 90 days by the integration service). Nothing is backfilled: runs before the upgrade have no recorded changes and cannot be undone. A plan made by a dry run is valid for an hour and only for the mapping it was made with.
  • The inventory service gains two more internal source routes used only by the integration service — /internal/sources/assets/runs (tag assets with a run) and /internal/sources/assets/archive (undo a run: archive what it created) — HMAC-signed service calls only, one signed tenant per call, denied at the edge like the other source routes.
  • CMDB (Enterprise): a sync running during the upgrade is cut off and closed. A push or pull the old inventory-service pod was running when it was replaced is left "in progress" and closed as failed with "interrupted (service restarted)" by the integration service about an hour after it started (the run budget plus a margin); scheduled profiles then run at their next due time, and Sync / Pull re-run a manual one straight away. The old and the new pods share one run lock per profile, so a profile is never synced twice at once during the rollout. No data is migrated: the profiles, jobs and entity-mapping tables are adopted as they are.
  • CMDB operator settings move to the integration service. An HTTPS_PROXY / NO_PROXY or CONNECTOR_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS set on inventory-service for the CMDB connectors must be set on the integration service now, and the integration service must run with the same ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY as the inventory service. The exact values key is in the Enterprise edition of these notes.
  • Egress exceptions for the connectors are no longer needed on the inventory or audit service. If you added a NetworkPolicy exception, proxy bypass or NO_PROXY entry on inventory-service for NetBox / CMDB, or on audit-service for SIEM collectors, it can be removed; the destinations are dialled from the integration service now. inventory-service no longer receives VISTA_PLATFORM_INTERNAL_CIDRS, and audit-service no longer receives ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY by default.
  • CMDB mapping editor: ServiceNow schema access is optional. To list ServiceNow's fields and classes in the editor, the integration user needs read access to sys_db_object and sys_dictionary (the base itil role does not give it). Without it the editor lists the default mapping's fields and says why; sync, pull and preview are unaffected. Existing mappings are unchanged: the editor reads and writes the same stored overrides.

docs.title: Vista Platform 4.4.0 — full list of changes
docs.text: Released 2026-10-05. The release summary — highlights, what to do before upgrading, what each edition includes, and how to verify the signatures — is in the CHANGELOG published with that release. This page is the complete, per-change record behind it.

docs.title: Identity: one intake for every observation
docs.text: Every way Vista learns about a device — a sensor's scan or capture, a host agent's inventory, a device you add by hand, a firewall's neighbour table, a CMDB link, a DNS lookup — now decides which asset this is in the same place, by the same rules. Before, about ten code paths each made their own call, so the same device seen the same way could land as an existing asset on one path and a second asset on another. What you will notice:

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Static addresses can be pinned. On a network flagged DHCP, an address its asset holds pinned still identifies that asset, and only that asset, so a plain port scan of a router's own LAN address updates the router instead of waiting in Observations. An address is pinned when you add it to an asset (the asset form, or Add device / Edit device), when you tick Pin next to a recorded address, or when the host's own agent reports it as statically configured. The asset's Identifiers list shows static. The network keeps its DHCP setting. See Asset identity and discovery evidence.
  • Link to the asset that already owns an observation. An observation whose address (or another identifier) one existing asset already owns is no longer offered as Ready to confirm; it reads Matches an asset and suggests Link to that asset, and the bulk bar's Link to existing links a selection of such rows, each to its own owner. When several assets own identifiers of it, it reads Several match and leaves the decision to you.
  • A changed host key or address is explained, not just accepted. When a sighting matches an asset but its identifiers differ, the platform decides whether an SSH host key was rotated, the device moved to a new address, it was reimaged, or a different device now answers. The asset's History tab says which, with the old and new values, and a notification (asset_identity_drift) can be routed. A different device still opens a merge proposal; an address-only key change with nothing else to go on is kept and flagged for review. See When a device's identifiers change.
  • Host agents report every interface address. Host inventory records each real interface address under its own network segment, with whether the operating system says it is static or a DHCP lease. See Host inventory.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Endpoints are written where an identity decision attaches them. A sighting that only supports an asset you already have (for example a scan of an address in none of your network segments) updates its last-seen time but no longer adds endpoints, identified services or crypto configurations to it; the ports wait on the observation, and Link, Confirm or Attach endpoints… attaches them. Confirming several observations of one address gives one asset with all of their endpoints. Endpoints already on an asset are never deleted.
  • Add device recognises a device Vista already knows. A device added after Identify is matched by the MAC address and SSH host key the probe read, so it no longer becomes a second asset beside the one a sensor found. A hostname, address or serial typed onto a device that another asset already owns is refused with a merge proposal in Approvals rather than silently skipped.
  • Names and MAC addresses are filed the same way on every path. A name whose address is in no registered network reaches its domain segment; a .local name in a scan no longer matches hosts on other VLANs; randomised MAC addresses from scan findings or a controller's client list no longer become identifiers; and a network you marked static stays static for identity even when a controller reports DHCP on it.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Bulk Confirm no longer fails on every row of a DHCP network. Rows offered as Ready to confirm whose address an asset already owned were all refused as "changed since you looked"; they now offer Link instead.
  • A scan or interrogation is no longer counted as a passive sighting. The sensor converter overwrote the source of every row, so active measurements ranked as passive observations.
  • Evidence that matches exactly one known asset is another sighting of it, on every path, and a sighting under a pending merge proposal is not silently linked to one side before you decide.

docs.title: Discovery, scanning, inventory and everything else
Deprecated
docs.text: • POST /infrastructure-assets/stale/rescan, /stale/archive and /revalidate (and their v1 /assets/… forms). Inventory's bulk actions replaced them in the UI. They still work; each response now carries a Deprecation header and a Link to its successor — POST /infrastructure-assets/scan for rescan and revalidate, POST /infrastructure-assets/bulk-actions/archive for archive. (#2272)

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Select many assets in Inventory and act on them at once. All assets and Stale have a checkbox on every row; tick rows across pages, or tick the page and choose Select all N matching for every asset the query matches. A bar above the list then offers Scan (with Run from), Edit (owner email, environment, business unit, support group, add or remove tags), Archive, Restore, Delete and Export (CSV), each shown only to people with the permission it needs. A selection of all matching assets is sent as the query and the count you confirmed, and is refused without changing anything if the query now matches more. Up to 5,000 assets, or 1,000 for a scan. Every change is recorded in each asset's history under your name and once in the audit log. API: POST /infrastructure-assets/bulk-actions/ {archive,restore,update,delete}, and POST /infrastructure-assets/scan accepts the same query + expected_count selection. (#2272)

  • One Helm value keeps the database server's own JIT setting. The platform asks PostgreSQL for jit=off on every connection. Keeping the server's own setting used to mean a DB_JIT entry in each backend's extraEnv, one service at a time. Set appConfig.dbJit: true instead and every backend gets it; a DB_JIT under backends.<service>.extraEnv still overrides it for that service. Left empty, nothing changes. An unrecognised value is refused at install time rather than silently ignored. The behaviour behind PgBouncer or a managed database proxy is documented but not tested.

  • Networks show their gateway. After a router is interrogated, Inventory → Map names the gateway on each network it routes instead of "gateway not recorded", the router's asset page gains a Networks routed section (its address, VLAN, DHCP or static, host count and sensor coverage per network), a host's page shows via beside its network, and Settings → Network Segments has Gateway and Coverage columns. A network no sensor reaches says so. Nothing is entered by hand; a network whose router has not been interrogated still reads "gateway not recorded". (#2242, #2246)

  • Add a device that only a device agent can reach. When your organization has device agents, Discovery → Devices → Add device shows Reach it from. Choosing an agent queues the identification on that agent; the attempt appears in the table as Discovering…, then becomes the device, or shows Discovery failed with the reason and Retry, Not picked up if the agent never collected it, or Held for review. Adding from the platform is unchanged and still answers immediately. Needs a device agent from this release. (#2236)

  • Let the platform re-check a device on its own. Add / Edit device has a new option, Allow the platform to re-check this device automatically (off by default). With it on, identity enrichment may run that device's interrogation again when it needs fresh evidence; observations that were waiting on it are retried on the next cycle, and their explanation now names the setting. (#2232)

  • A gateway is recorded for each network it routes. Interrogating a router now records its own address on every network it reports and the network's gateway, with no manual entry; network and asset reads return them. An address a provisional or address-only record held moves to the gateway; anything stronger keeps it and a merge proposal opens. Devices an interrogation reports are approved automatically on networks set to auto-approve. The screens that show the gateway follow. (#2234, #2239)

  • A model provider can be set from the product, not only at install. Until now the AI assistant's model provider could only be named in the chart's ai.* values, which meant a Helm upgrade and a restart of every service. Two new routes, both Enterprise:

  • A default for every organization, in the admin console under Settings → AI assistant: choose Anthropic or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Test connection, Save. It takes effect on the next request and overrides the one set at install; the page shows both and says which is in effect.
  • An organization's own, on its Settings → AI assistant page: the Model provider row now says whose provider answers (Provided by this deployment or Connected by your organization) and, where the organization is allowed to, opens a form to connect, test and disconnect one. An organization's own provider answers for that organization only. On Enterprise every organization may; on MSP a plan decides (the new Own AI Model Provider entitlement, off in every plan by default), so a service provider can include a model in a plan or let customers bring theirs. A platform administrator can also switch organizations' own providers off entirely.

    • API keys are stored encrypted and never shown again (the pages show the last four characters). An organization can only use a public address unless the platform administrator allows private ones. The organization's Use the AI assistant switch still turns everything off, its own provider included. Platform features that belong to no organization (the catalogue's "Propose with AI", drafting into the shared framework catalogue) use the default and never an organization's provider. The install-time ai.* values still work unchanged. See Connecting a model provider. (#2219)

    • The observations API says what each observation needs, in names, and decides many at once. GET /discovery/observations now returns, on every item, the network's and the collector's names instead of only their ids, a "needs" category (ready to confirm, needs a network, needs a sensor, likely noise) with a suggested action, an explanation code and a proposed reason sentence, and the identifiers in readable form. It filters by needs, network, source and free text, sorts by last seen, host, network or needs, and reports per-category counts for the review table's chips. A new POST /discovery/observations/bulk confirms or dismisses up to 200 observations with one reason, reporting each one's outcome — an allowance reached or a changed observation fails that row only — and bulk confirm accepts only observations that are ready to confirm. Every decision is audited with a shared batch id. (#2200)

    • Scans by depth run from your own sensors, host by host. A discovery job with a scan depth can now run from one of your sensors — the only way to reach most private and plant networks. The sensor scans with the same engine as the platform sensor and reports each host as soon as it is done, so the job's progress, coverage and results by host fill in while it runs and each host's findings reach inventory right away; nothing is held back for the end. Such a scan has no time limit — it runs as long as the sensor keeps checking in, and is marked failed only after 15 minutes of silence, keeping every host already finished; a Retry then scans only the hosts not done. Cancel now reaches the sensor: it stops at its next report or heartbeat, and a scan still waiting on it is dropped. The sensor never contacts an address its own rules forbid — loopback, link-local, multicast, a range you excluded from probing, anything outside your networks — and reports it as not scanned, with the reason. Requires this release's sensor; older sensors keep running protocols × ports jobs and are not handed these. (#2170)

    • Discovery → Discovery Jobs shows a long scan as it runs. A scan described by depth shows a progress bar on its row with a live line ("112 of 254 hosts · 31 responded · 9 open ports"), where it runs and its depth, and the page refreshes itself while anything is unfinished. Its detail refreshes until the scan ends and shows what the scan does and why (depth, pace, targets, where it ran, and every target scanned less deeply than asked, with the reason); coverage that says no answer — never "down" — with reachability guidance when nothing answered and where and why a scan that ended early stopped; results grouped by host, a page at a time, with an open port nothing could name shown as open, unidentified and a host that answers on every port collapsed to one line; and where the findings went, with a link to Approvals. A failed or queued scan has Resume scan, which runs again only the hosts it had not finished and keeps the rest; a refused Resume or Cancel shows the server's reason (Cancel used to fail silently on the list). GET /discovery/jobs now carries each such scan's plan, and its progress and coverage while it has not ended; ?job=<id> on the page opens that job. (#2170)

    • Scans described by depth run host by host, with real progress and an honest coverage summary. A job sent with scan_depth and run from the platform sensor is split into one durable unit per address. Every address is checked against your registered networks and exclusions before anything is sent to it — even the "is anything there?" probe — so a range marked sensitive after the job was queued is never touched. Each host's results are stored and sent on to inventory as soon as that host is done; a cancel keeps what was found, and a Retry or a restart resumes only the hosts not finished, without storing anything twice. An open port nothing can name is recorded as an open, unidentified port on the host instead of being dropped, a host that seems to accept every port is reported once rather than tens of thousands of times, and a silent UDP port is never reported as found. GET /discovery/jobs/{id} now reports progress per host for such a job and a coverage summary — addresses that responded, gave no answer (never "down"), could not be scanned and why, ports open / closed / filtered / not probed — with warnings such as "0 of 254 scanned addresses responded — the platform sensor may not be able to reach this network". (#2170)

    • Scans by depth share the platform sensor fairly, and results can be read by host. A long scan no longer holds up every other scan on the same platform sensor replica: each replica scans at most 16 hosts at once and any one organization at most 4 (chart values discovery.maxConcurrentUnits and discovery.maxConcurrentUnitsPerTenant). UDP probes of one host now wait for replies in parallel while still sending no faster than the host's packet rate, so a wide custom UDP range takes minutes instead of hours; industrial (OT/ICS) UDP ports are still probed one at a time. GET /discovery/jobs/{id}/results?group=host returns each host with all its ports, paged by host. (#2170)

    • Sensors: "Additional TLS ports" is a setting in the console. A port where your organization runs TLS on a non-standard port (for example 9443) can now be listed on one sensor (Discovery → Sensors & Agents → a sensor → Control) or for every sensor (Sensor defaults), instead of only in the sensor's own configuration file. Sensors decode TLS handshakes seen on the listed ports; a port the sensor already watches is accepted and labelled with what it is already monitored as, and an entry that is not a port is refused by name. The list shapes the capture filter, so it shows Pending restart until the sensor restarts and reports it in effect. Exposed through the desired-config API as extra_tls_ports, a port_list setting carried as a comma-separated string. A sensor older than this release cannot apply it: while the list is left empty that sensor is not shown as failed (it already watches no extra ports); once ports are set, it shows Failed with "upgrade the sensor to apply it". (#2170)

    • Quick Start guide. A single walkthrough from first sign-in to a populated inventory: registering a sensor (with download links), adding a network device, connecting a cloud account, approving what was found, and where to look first. It is in the user docs (docsv4/core/quick-start.md) and at the root of the Core repository as QUICKSTART.md.

    • Discovery jobs can be described by scan depth. POST /discovery/jobs accepts a second request shape — scan_depth (quick, standard — the default —, thorough, custom with tcp_ports/udp_ports ranges such as 22,8000-8100), pace and run_from (auto, platform, sensor) in place of protocols and ports — and the server-side plan behind it: per target, whether it is private, inside a registered network segment (and which one) or external, and the depth it gets (a target outside your registered networks at Standard at most, each downgrade listed with the reason; a guardrail for unclaimed targets, which registering the range lifts); Run from Auto choosing one of your sensors only when one online sensor serves every target; and a probe budget (addresses × ports, default 25,000,000, chart value discovery.maxJobProbes, refusals 422 scan_budget_exceeded). The Discover wizard sends this shape (see Changed). The proxy now forwards ot_probe_protocols, the explicit OT opt-in it used to drop. The legacy protocols/ports request is unchanged. (#2170)

    • Preview a scan before starting it (API). A scan-depth request to POST /discovery/jobs with "dry_run": true answers 200 with the plan the server would store, an estimate (probes, addresses, and a duration as a range with the assumptions it rests on), whether targets outside your registered networks still need confirming, and which. It runs the same checks as a real create — validation, target authorization, the Standard cap on external targets, Run from Auto, the budget — and is refused the same way, but creates no job, sends nothing to a sensor and uses none of your scan allowance. The Discover wizard shows it before every scan (see Changed). (#2170)

    • Claim a public range learned from one of your devices. A firewall's public networks become segments when you interrogate it, but they are not treated as yours, because a device cannot show whether a public network is your DMZ or your internet provider's link. Settings → Infrastructure → Network Segments now offers Claim as mine on such a row (needs settings.update): after you confirm, the range is treated like a public segment you created — scannable when someone asks, never automatically, and treated as yours by sensors — still subject to the /8 (IPv4) and /16 (IPv6) limit and to sensitive or probes-disabled exclusions. The claim is your own statement, not verified; each claim and Revoke claim is audit-logged (network_segment.claimed, network_segment.claim_revoked). API: POST / DELETE /api/v2/inventory-service/network-segments/{id}/claim. A segment's learned provenance and claim can no longer be set or removed by editing its metadata; before, an edit that omitted source turned a learned segment into a declared one. (#2170)

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The Dashboard's "Inventory Health" panel is now "Assets Monitored". The big number was never a health measure: it is the count of assets under monitoring, with assets still waiting for approval counted separately beside it. Only the heading changed; the numbers and links are as before.

  • Discovery → Active Scan is now a view of Inventory. Its list is Views → Never scanned on All assets, and scanning is the bulk bar's Scan; the page's entry is gone from the Discovery menu and a bookmark to it opens the view. Scans started here, under the bar, names every asset a scan did not reach and why, rather than a count and the first reason. The Active Scan button on an asset now opens the same dialog, so a single scan can also choose where it runs. On Stale, the per-row Rescan/Archive buttons and the whole-page Revalidate all/Archive all bar are replaced by the same checkboxes and bar. (#2272)

  • Clicking a row in Inventory → All assets now opens the asset drawer, and the asset page has an Active Scan button. The drawer is the quick look that keeps your place in the list; its Open full page button goes to the asset page. Ctrl/cmd-click or middle-click an asset's name to open the page in a new tab. The asset page now carries the same Active Scan button as the drawer, for people who can edit assets, and shows "Scanning…" until the scan finishes.

  • Finding the assets behind a scan's addresses no longer reads the tenant's whole asset table. Looking an asset up by its address compared a text value with the address of every live asset in the tenant, which on a large estate made adopting a completed automatic scan's job a full scan of the tenant's assets. The database now keeps an index on that address text, added by the schema on the next upgrade. The planner starts using it once PostgreSQL next analyses the assets table, which autovacuum does as the table changes.

  • Import-only assets in a network you registered are scanned automatically without connection consent. An asset known only from a CMDB or NetBox connection is still withheld from automatic scans until that connection allows active scanning, but only when its address is in private space you have not declared. A network segment a person registered vouches for the addresses in it; a segment learned from a device or imported by a connection does not. When two assets are merged, the result is import-only only if both were. (#2268)

  • Automatic scans, identity checks and Active Scan now run on the same scan engine as Discover assets. Each checks its ports first and identifies the service from what answers, so a host that drops packets finishes in seconds instead of minutes. The Protocols checkboxes are gone from Settings → Active Scanning: services are identified from what answers on the ports you list. The protocols field of the create-scan API (POST /discovery/jobs) is deprecated and ignored; a request naming protocols and ports is scanned on exactly those ports. Sensors older than this release keep working, are marked Needs upgrading to run scans on the current engine on Discovery → Sensors & Agents, and should be upgraded.

  • Every scan now runs on that one engine, including OT-only API requests. A create-scan request that names only ot_probe_protocols is scanned on exactly those protocols' standard ports (Modbus TCP 502, OPC UA TCP 4840, EtherNet/IP UDP 44818, BACnet UDP 47808) and probed there, with the same opt-in, operator switch and audit record as before. One naming only OT probes that the operator has switched off is now refused instead of creating a scan of nothing. The older protocols × ports scanners are removed from the platform and from the sensor. A sensor from this release refuses a protocols × ports job and asks for the platform to be upgraded; a job of that shape created for a sensor before it was upgraded fails with a reason, and running the scan again plans it. Older sensors are still sent that shape until they are upgraded.

  • compliance-engine now needs the deployment's encryption key. It opens the stored API key of a model provider configured in Settings (above) to draft controls and remediation plans. The chart, the compose files and the service registry pass ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY to it, as they already do for the other services; a hand-maintained deployment must do the same or drafting reports no provider for organizations that connected one. (#2219)

  • Discovery → Observations is a review table you can work through. It opens on Ready to confirm, with chips and counts for Needs a network, Needs a sensor, Likely noise and All (where the state control still reaches linked, dismissed, expired and conflict observations). Each row is one line — host and services, the network's and the sensor's names, last seen, and what it needs — and opens to its evidence beside a plain What this needs: why the platform did not create an asset itself, what will fix it (add a network, add a sensor, or — for a DHCP network whose addresses do not move — a shortcut to its DHCP setting), and the alternatives. Tick rows to confirm or dismiss many at once with one prefilled, editable reason; bulk Confirm is offered only when every selected row is ready to confirm, and a row that fails stays in the table with its reason. Single-row decisions now start with the proposed reason filled in too. (#2200)

  • Discover assets finds everything on a host or a network. The dialog (Discovery → Discover assets) no longer asks which protocols and ports to probe. You choose a scan depth — Quick, Standard (the default), Thorough, or Custom — and services are identified from what answers. Run from offers Auto, the platform sensor or one of your sensors by name, as Active Scan does; the old "Cloud — platform sensor" option is gone. Advanced, closed by default, holds Custom's TCP and UDP ports (a range such as 8000-8100 now means the whole range — the old Ports box quietly read it as 8000 — and a mistake is shown in the platform's own words before you start), the scan's pace, and an unchecked Probe industrial (OT/ICS) devices opt-in with its acknowledgement, shown only while OT probing is switched on for your organization. Before you start, a preview shows the size of the scan, a duration range and what it assumes, where it will run and why, which targets will be scanned at less depth (targets outside your registered networks are scanned at Standard at most), and any refusal — too large, over the installation's budget, an offline sensor, a sensor whose software cannot scan by depth (with a one-click switch to the platform sensor) — in the server's words; a preview that cannot be worked out never stops you starting. Start says what started and links straight to that scan on Discovery → Discovery Jobs, where the scan's progress, results and Cancel live: the dialog no longer follows the scan or lists findings, and can be closed at any moment. (#2170)

  • OT/ICS active probing is now part of Core, and on by default. It was an Enterprise capability. The ot_active_probing switch now ships enabled on every plan, and an operator can still turn it off for a whole plan (Plans & Pricing) or for one tenant (a plan exception), which keeps winning over the plan. OT probes still run only when a person asks for them on a scan, through the Discover wizard's Advanced opt-in or the discovery job API; automatic scanning never runs them. The catalogue item stays, priced at $0. On upgrade, existing plans that had it off are switched on once; a tenant that was turned off by an exception stays off, and a later choice to turn it off is never undone by a subsequent upgrade. The OT inventory lens (ot_primary_lens) is unchanged and remains Enterprise.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• "Scan anyway" no longer scans assets a second time. When some assets in a scan were outside your registered networks, confirming resent every asset in the request — including ones that had already been dispatched. It now sends only the assets it asked about. (#2272)

  • A stopped sensor no longer strands every host it has seen. When the sensor that last observed a host is offline, automatic scans and Active Scan under Auto now run that host from another of your sensors that is online and on the same network. Only when there is no such sensor is the host skipped for the pass, as before. A host your sensors have observed is still never moved to the platform sensor because its sensor went away.

  • Identity enrichment can probe a device through a sensor other than the one that saw it. When a sensor on one network sees evidence about a device on another network, enrichment hands the probe to a sensor that has an interface on the device's network. The dispatch check refused every such probe, logging "probe source or scope changed" and retrying, because it still required the probing sensor to be the one that observed the evidence. It now checks the two separately: the observing sensor must be a current sensor of the same tenant, and the probing sensor must be live with an interface on the device's network. What may be probed is unchanged: the target must be inside the observation's network and not excluded, the evidence must still be a sensor's own measurement, and neither sensor's own addresses are probed. Platform-managed sensors are never accepted as either.

  • The automatic scan no longer re-queues the whole estate on every pass. On an install whose asset timeline had grown, creating an automatic-scan job took minutes instead of seconds; the request timed out, the assets were never marked as scanned, and the next pass queued them all again. Three things change. Platform database connections now turn off PostgreSQL's JIT compiler, which was spending 20 to 40 seconds compiling a query that runs in a tenth of a second (DB_JIT=on keeps the server's own setting, which on the Helm chart is the one value appConfig.dbJit: true; a connection pooler such as PgBouncer must be told to ignore the jit start-up parameter). A job whose creation call timed out but which was created anyway is now recognised as dispatched. And the check that withholds import-only assets no longer reads the asset timeline: a whole job is authorised in a handful of queries whatever its size. (#2268)

  • The asset timeline no longer gets an "updated" entry every time a device is seen again. An entry is written only when an observation changes something about the asset: a new identifier or service, a better name, a moved address, or the first time a condition is noticed. Last-seen times still update on every sighting. On one 80-asset install the timeline had reached 424,000 entries in two days, 97% of them exact repeats. Existing entries are not removed. (#2268)

  • One interrogation of a network controller no longer identifies each device hundreds of times, and a held run is no longer replayed for ever.
