  • Two internal services set HTTP timeouts. The health and fallback servers of discovery-processor-service and resource-tracker-service now have read, write and idle timeouts (5, 10, 15 and 60 seconds, as other services use). (#2325)

  • A sensor registration key is no longer written to the logs. The key is masked when a sensor registers. (#2319)

  • Database interrogation redacts through every entry point. The connection variants of the database interrogators skipped the settings redaction the registry applies; they no longer do, so no configuration secret reaches stored results. (#2319)

  • Only http and https addresses are rendered as links from stored data. A catalogue or classification-rule URL with another scheme (javascript:, for instance) shows as text in both user interfaces. (#2319)

  • A service that verifies internal requests refuses all of them when started without its secret. device-interrogation-service's verifier admitted every request if its secret was empty. (#2316)

  • Chart guard. A test now renders the chart with its defaults and fails if agentMtls.enabled is not true. (#2319)

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Every manufacturer the IEEE registry knows is now recognised from a MAC, and the sensor no longer does the lookup. The platform resolves the vendor at ingestion from the full IEEE registry (all 24-, 28- and 36-bit blocks, about 53,000 prefixes) instead of a 500-row table compiled into the sensor, which left any manufacturer outside it with no vendor at all. A vendor the device itself reported, through an agent, an interrogation, a connector or an import, is never overwritten, and the registry's answer replaces one an older sensor looked up in its own table. A backfill brings every existing asset up to date from its MAC identifiers: it starts about two minutes after inventory-service does, works through each organization in batches, records the registry snapshot it finished under, and is retried hourly for anything it could not complete. A release with a refreshed registry runs it again. Sensors need no upgrade for this.

  • A Smart device class for consumer and office connected devices: TVs and streaming players, smart speakers, doorbells, plugs, bulbs and locks, game consoles and appliances. Roku, Vizio, Ring, Sonos, Bose, Nintendo, PlayStation, Philips Hue, Nest, GE Lighting and Amazon devices are classified from their MAC, and Cast receivers and Matter nodes from what they advertise on the LAN. IoT device keeps its meaning of the enterprise and building estate: cameras, sensors, badge readers and building controls. The learned classifier was retrained with the new class; its answers still go to Approvals for review.

  • Classification from a host's DHCP vendor class. Windows clients, Android devices, Cisco access points and HP JetDirect printers are classified from the vendor class identifier (DHCP option 60) they send when they ask for a lease. Catalog ▸ Classification rules accepts a new dhcp_vendor_class rule kind, an anchored regular expression over that string, so a platform administrator can add rules beside the shipped ones.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The bundled NATS server is upgraded from 2.10 to 2.14. The NATS project no longer patches 2.10; datastores.nats.image.tag is now 2.14-alpine (2.14.7 when built). JetStream streams, durable consumers, their acknowledgement state and stored messages are read in place from the existing volume. A direct 2.10 to 2.14 start was tested on a platform-shaped workload with a durable consumer holding unacknowledged messages, and the stream, acknowledgement floor and backlog came through intact; the NATS project documents upgrading one minor version at a time, so back up before you upgrade. Rolling the chart back afterwards is not clean: NATS 2.10 rebuilds the stream index on its first start and logs corrupt state file, with messages and consumer state intact in testing. Snapshot the nats-data-nats-0 volume first if you need a clean rollback. A values file that pins datastores.nats.image.tag keeps the old server until the pin is removed, and an external NATS is unaffected. See Releases & Versioning (Upgrading → Bundled NATS server). The Docker Compose files, nightly integration job and local integration-test script already ran 2.14. (#2314)

  • The bundled NATS server is probed over HTTP, not by opening its TLS port. The probes were a TCP connection to port 4222, which speaks TLS by default (datastores.nats.tls.enabled); each probe closed the connection before the handshake, so NATS logged TLS handshake error: EOF every ten seconds. That line came from the probes, not from any client. The StatefulSet now probes /healthz on the monitoring port (8222, plain HTTP in both modes): a startup probe (js-enabled-only, every 5 seconds for up to about ten minutes, for a large JetStream store to recover), a readiness probe (js-enabled-only, every 5 seconds) and a liveness probe (js-server-only, every 10 seconds, so a broken stream or consumer can never restart-loop the pod). The nats Service had no readiness probe and could be routed to before the server was ready; it no longer is. The pod template changes, so the NATS pod restarts once on upgrade. (#2328)

  • The documented signature-verification commands now anchor the signing identity. The cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp values printed by helm install and published in the install guide and README were …@.*, which accepts a run of the release workflow from any ref. For Core it is now ^https://github\.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Core/\.github/workflows/release-core\.yml@refs/tags/v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-[A-Za-z0-9.]+)?$, a release tag only. The commercial line's regexp accepts a release tag or main, because the 4.4.0 commercial release was run from main and carries that identity. Verification of every published 4.x release is unchanged; checked against the 4.3 and 4.4 images and charts. Core images are now built from a Go builder pinned to the exact patch in go.work, including when the Docker Hardened Image base is used. See Releases & Versioning. (#2329)

  • The helm test pod image is updated to curlimages/curl 8.22.0 (from 8.10.1). No action needed. (#2314)

  • Two unused cross-tenant lookups are removed from compliance-engine. Nothing called them. (#2321)

  • Scheduled scans are set up in plain language, not cron. Pick every few hours, daily, weekly on chosen days, or monthly, at a time in your own time zone, and a sentence confirms when it will run; the schedule list reads the same way. A custom cron expression remains available and is validated before saving. Existing schedules keep running exactly as before.

  • Dashboard posture shows its evidence, not a bare percentage. A risk-band donut distinguishes high, medium, low, assessed-clean and unassessed assets; the overview also uses clearer inventory wording and bars for overlapping observed external-connection measures.

  • Discovery navigation groups what you deploy separately from what ran. Discovery Jobs now includes the run outcomes and failure messages that were on Job Logs. Old Job Logs links redirect there, and the rail makes the section hierarchy and activity clearer.

  • An asset still shown as an unknown host is reclassified as evidence accumulates, without a reviewer. A host first seen by ARP and later heard on mDNS, or whose vendor arrives in a later frame, is now classified over everything the inventory holds about it (its MAC identifiers, the services it advertised, its LLDP and CDP capabilities, and a vendor or model from the device itself) rather than the latest frame alone. A sweep runs about five minutes after inventory-service starts and every six hours afterwards, so assets already in the inventory are asked again; each move is recorded in the asset's class history and nothing the sweep decides is added to Approvals. A class a person declared, or a reviewer rejected, is never touched, only a rule's answer is applied (a learned-model answer still goes to Approvals), and an asset that already holds a real class is left as it is. Expect the unknown-host count to fall after the upgrade.

  • Classification rules are written against manufacturer names, not MAC prefixes. Catalog ▸ Classification rules now carries one oui_vendor rule per manufacturer whose products are all one kind of thing, resolved through the IEEE registry. The 496 per-prefix oui rules Vista shipped are retired on upgrade; an oui rule an administrator edited or added is kept, and, as the more specific statement about its MAC, still applies before a vendor rule. Prefix rules remain available for administrator overrides.

docs.title: Discovery pipeline and identity clean-up (rc.4)
docs.text:
Each entry below describes what a user or tenant administrator sees; the upgrade consequences are collected under "Upgrade notes in full".

  • One classifier and one external-connections writer for discoveries. The discovery processor no longer classifies network ownership, evaluates the tenant's auto-approval rules or writes 3rd Party Connections itself: it imports every discovery, third-party ones included, and inventory-service classifies each one once (honouring a cloud resource's cloud segment), evaluates the auto-approval rules against that answer, and either resolves it to an asset or records the connection. The import reports per finding what happened and which rule approved it, which is what the discovery row is stamped with; a third-party row is now observed (it was auto_approved when the processor wrote the connection itself). The internal network-segments/classify-asset route, whose only caller was the processor, is removed, and the import no longer reads a caller-supplied asset_status (#2374).

  • 3rd Party Connections keep the full certificate assessment, and never invent a source. The one writer now carries the certificate's validation status and quality flags — Certificate Transparency (an explicit "no SCT" stays a no), known-bad issuing CA, EV, OCSP status — read by the same shared reader the certificates table uses, plus the destination name with its provenance and the passive key-exchange label. A third-party discovery with no source address is no longer stored with source 0.0.0.0: it is dropped, reported as dropped / third_party_no_source_ip and counted on the batch's audit record (third_party_dropped_no_source_ip). Certificate validity times in the older sensors' format now parse on every path (#2374).

  • A direct scan of a known asset now shows its ports on that asset, and a host's agent report closes the ports it no longer lists through the same identity decision. When a completed TLS or SSH exchange (or a host's own report) is only supporting evidence for exactly one asset, its ports now appear on that asset's Services & Endpoints tab instead of waiting in Discovery → Observations for a Link; its names and addresses are still held for review, and evidence that points at two assets, or at an archived or denied one, attaches nothing. A host inventory's identity and sockets are decided in one place: a report that drops a listening socket marks it closed in the same step that recognises the host (never for a report the platform could not tie to the host), a report without a network-interfaces section is still matched by the address the platform reached it at or the agent reported, and addresses on a host's virtual interfaces (container bridges, tunnels) are kept as evidence rather than used to match other hosts (#2374 WP7, closes the open half of #2205).

  • Hosts on carrier-grade NAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10) are now internal candidates, not 3rd Party Connections. Overlay networks such as Tailscale and ZeroTier hand out these addresses; a host on one that matches no network segment now appears as an Unknown asset for review, as any unregistered private address does, instead of being written to 3rd Party Connections. It reports network type private, so an approval rule on network.type:private now also matches it. Probing is unchanged: automatic scans and sensor enrichment still leave 100.64.0.0/10 alone unless you register the range as a network segment, and a segment learned or imported over it is still public. Behind this, every component now reads one definition of private address space (shared/network/addrscope) instead of four that disagreed — the discovery processor's fallback also now counts loopback as private — and make audit fails on a new copy (#2374).

  • An import reads the tenant's network segments once, not several times per finding. Ownership classification, segment tags, segment enrichment and the identity intake's scoping each used to re-read every network segment of the tenant for every finding; an import of fifty findings now makes one read of the segment list and one of the identity snapshot, and a batch of posted sightings likewise. Fifty cloud resources in one VPC also find (or create) its segment once. The classify route answers from one read instead of two, and Reclassify all reads the segments once for the whole pass. A DHCP lease that changes a segment's posture mid-import makes the next finding read the segments again (#2374).

  • Discoveries reach the processor as soon as they are written (#2374 WP1). Every writer of the sensor_discoveries ingestion queue — sensor batches, TLS enrichment and self-observation in sensor-manager, scan-plan units from the Platform Sensor and tenant sensors, device-interrogation results, host-inventory connections, cloud discovery, and PCAP uploads — now publishes discovery.queue.ready (new DISCOVERY_QUEUE stream) after its transaction commits. discovery-processor wakes on it and drains every claimable batch, instead of claiming one batch per 15-second poll. A writer with no NATS client logs a WARNING once rather than silently relying on the poll.

  • DISCOVERY_POLL_INTERVAL now defaults to 60 seconds and is only the fallback (a lost message, NATS unavailable, a failed row's retry). The poll is no longer tripled when NATS is connected.
  • discovery-processor no longer wakes on discovery.jobs.submit, which is cluster-sensor-service's scan-job subject: a stuck-job republish no longer fires processor polls, and a PCAP upload no longer asks cluster-sensor to run a job that does not exist. Its old discovery-processor-poll-trigger consumer is deleted at start-up.
  • A failed row no longer rejects its whole batch. A failed import chunk or external-connection upsert now costs only its own rows: they keep processed_at NULL with the attempt and the error recorded in the new sensor_discoveries.process_attempts / process_error columns, and are retried after a backoff; only they are settled rejected (with the error) once the failure is permanent or DISCOVERY_MAX_RETRIES attempts are spent (default 7, backing off 30 s doubling to 10 min, so a rolling restart of inventory-service is ridden out; DISCOVERY_RETRY_BACKOFF_BASE is honoured exactly). A row that fails to scan, or that landed but could not be stamped processed, is counted the same way, and a TLS-enrichment row folded into a failed survivor shares its failure. Rows that landed are marked processed as before, and the chunks after a failed one are still sent. The processor no longer sleeps between retries while holding the batch and its NATS message.
  • Compliance evaluates an asset once per discovery import, not once per event about it. An import announces a changed asset on compliance.asset.changed and once more for every crypto configuration it created (inventory.lifecycle.crypto.configuration_added), and compliance-engine re-evaluated the asset for each of them with identical results. Requests for the same asset that arrive within two seconds of each other now share one evaluation. A request is only folded into an evaluation that had not started when it arrived, so a late or missing event still gets its own evaluation and a failed evaluation is retried for every request that joined it (#2374).

  • A discovered cloud KMS key (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS) now takes one path into inventory. Each key used to be written three times: to the key inventory (Inventory → Keys), to a separate kms_keys table that no page reads, and into the discovery queue, which classified and identified it as a Key Store Infrastructure Asset with no endpoint. The key inventory now creates or refreshes the Key Store asset itself, with the same identity, class, cloud segment and approval rules as before, so it appears without passing through the discovery queue and existing Key Store assets keep matching. kms_keys is no longer written; the table is kept for now and will be dropped in a later release, together with the experimental endpoints that still read it. Because the key inventory is now the only record, a run whose keys could not be recorded there reports the KMS type as failed instead of logging a warning (#2374).

  • Crypto evidence for an unapproved asset is held in one place and replayed by one path (#2374 WP5). Certificates and crypto configurations found on an asset that is not yet monitoring used to wait in three stores — an array in the asset's metadata (replayed only by Discovery → Approvals or an agent install), discovery payloads retained under identity admission enforce (replayed by the identity sweep), and the observations the enrichment pass re-resolved into them. They now wait in the new deferred_crypto_findings table and are replayed by one path on every route to monitoring: at once on Accept in Approvals and on an agent-driven approval, and within a minute when an auto-approval rule, an Active Scan or an operator's Link on an observation approves the asset — which previously left the crypto parked for good. A replay publishes the same events a live ingest does. At most 50 findings are held per asset; the oldest observed are dropped first. identity_observation_payloads now holds passive host observations only.

  • IPv6 unique-local and link-local addresses are private. A host seen at an IPv6 unique-local address (fc00::/7) used to be classified as a public network with a third-party owner, so an approval rule on network.type:private never matched and the asset stayed pending. RFC 1918 IPv4, IPv6 unique-local, link-local and loopback addresses are now private; everything else is public. (#2371, #2374)

  • Every interface MAC an interrogation reports becomes an identifier. A multi-homed device interrogated through its management interface used to keep only its primary MAC as an identifier, so a sensor later hearing it from another interface's MAC opened a merge proposal. Each usable interface MAC (not empty, malformed, zero, broadcast, locally administered or virtual-router) is now attached to the device. (#2370)

  • Two devices that share a name but not hardware become two assets. When a controller reports two clients (for example two plugs of one model that share a DHCP hostname) with different MACs and addresses, the second used to open a merge proposal, or silently take the first one's MAC. It is now created as its own pending asset, with the shared name staying on the original. Relayed adverts and a changed address on the same MAC are unchanged. (#2372)

  • A class proposal closes when Promote applies that class, and a proposal is never an ancestor of the current class. Approvals no longer asks a reviewer to approve a class the asset already holds, and a measured workstation is no longer offered computer by a vendor rule. Stale proposals leave the queue and the Approvals count. (#2373)

  • A held host inventory no longer closes live ports. When the platform keeps a host report as supporting evidence only, it writes no ports from it and no longer closes the ports the report did not match. (#2366)

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A newly discovered asset's History shows one "created" entry, not two. The identification engine's creation record and the context the asset was created with (tags, metadata, ownership, attributes) are now one row; before, the asset appeared to have been created twice. Existing duplicate rows are left as they are.
  • Ingest reads each identifier's owner once per finding. Discovery ingest built every finding's identity observation twice and looked each identifier up twice — once to decide whether the finding belonged to a denied, elevated or suppressed asset, and again to resolve it. Both decisions now rest on one read, taken under the identifier locks on the same transaction, which also removes the window in which the two reads could disagree. Denied, third-party, suppressed and archived findings behave as before.

  • A provisional asset (a device first heard about across VLANs, #1898) now triggers the 60-second automatic scan sweep as soon as it appears, like any other new asset; it previously waited for the 15-minute full sweep (#2374).

  • Purging a tenant now also removes its rows in class_floor_sweep_state and oui_vendor_backfill_state, the two classification state tables that had a tenant_id but no cascading foreign key to tenants.

  • The asset timeline no longer gets an "updated" entry every time an observation describes itself differently. A host that announces two services, or that two collectors hear in turn, sends a different description of the sighting each time (the capture interface, which mDNS service answered and on which port, whether a reflector relayed it, which collectors heard it). Those were stored as the asset's metadata, replaced as a whole on every observation, and counted as a change, so one quiet host wrote about a hundred entries an hour. They describe the sighting, not the asset, and now never earn an entry on their own, as the batch and sensor ids never did. They are still stored and still show the latest sighting. Entries already written are not removed. (#2289)

  • Passive QUIC is reported once per flow, not once per packet. A QUIC connection opens with a burst of Initial packets, and the sensor sent every decoded one on, so each flow produced about sixteen identical discoveries. QUIC now goes through the sensor's connection cache like passive TLS and VPN detection: one report per flow per dedup window (capture.dedupTTLMinutes, default 60 minutes), keyed on the destination, the client address, the QUIC version, the server name and the ALPN, and not on the client's ephemeral port. external_connections.observation_count for QUIC now counts sensor reports, as it does for TLS, not packets. Upgrade the sensor to benefit. (#2338)

  • "Scan anyway" scans the rest of the selection. When an Active Scan includes assets outside your registered networks, the platform asks before anything runs; 4.4.0's fix resent only the held assets, so the others in the selection were never scanned while the page said one asset had started. The refusal now carries pending_asset_ids, the assets a confirmed resend must carry: the whole request normally, because nothing ran, and only the held assets when the platform judged an asset after other batches had already gone out, so a dispatched asset is never sent twice. The dialog resends exactly that set and says which assets are scanned with it. Discover Assets' own "Scan anyway" is unaffected. (#2340)

  • A device interrogation that spends its whole time limit no longer fails at the last step. The job ran under one five-minute context and every write after the device answered (findings, discoveries, the completion mark) used it, so a slow device, or a worker shutting down, left the final update to fail with failed to interrogate device: failed to mark job completed: context deadline exceeded and the results unsaved. Those writes, the failure stamp and the discovery-job record now run on their own bounded context (two minutes; thirty seconds for the failure stamp). Stored job errors are redacted and capped at 2,000 characters by eliding the middle, so the failing step stays at the head and the cause at the tail, and an error with an empty message is named by its type. (#2340)

  • Probes of a device the platform has already confirmed at a DHCP address attach to that device. An SSH, TLS or QUIC probe of an address whose owner a sensor confirmed by MAC within the last day now matches that owner instead of waiting in Discovery → Observations as "Matches an asset" for a person to link. The address is still a lease: it follows the MAC when another device takes it, and a probe that carries a different NIC, or arrives past the window, is held for review as before. Nothing is back-filled, so an address becomes eligible after its device's MAC is next seen there (minutes on a sensored network), and rows already waiting in Observations stay until you link or dismiss them.

  • A sensor installed with the install command now actually enrolls. The Linux and Windows installers registered the sensor themselves, with a made-up version of 1.0.0, which used up the single-use registration code before the sensor could. The sensor then never sent a heartbeat or submitted a discovery, and the console showed it at v1.0.0 marked as needing an upgrade. The installers now let the sensor enroll itself (its private key never leaves the host), wait until it has, and print its ID and real version. A rejected code stops the install with instructions instead of leaving a service that retries forever. The Windows installer checks for Npcap before it changes anything. A sensor installed with an earlier installer never enrolled and its code is spent: generate a new registration key, run the new installer with it, and delete the old row. Re-running the installer with the key that enrolled a host keeps its identity and upgrades the binary in place.

  • The sensor now runs as a Windows service. The Windows installer registered crypto-sensor.exe as a service, but the sensor never told the Service Control Manager it had started, so starting the service failed with error 1053 and Windows killed the process. The sensor now reports to the Service Control Manager: it shows as Running once it is capturing, and Stop-Service or a system shutdown sends its last discoveries before it exits. As a service it logs to data\logs\sensor.log under the install directory, rotated at 10 MB, and writes start and stop events to the Application event log. A restart requested from the console now brings the service back up. The installer shows the sensor's log when registration fails, and stops and disables the service if the registration code was rejected.

  • The Linux device-agent installer preserves a registration key unless the host can safely store enrollment. It installs the agent as a hardened service with an owned data directory, and waits until the agent has enrolled. A failed enrollment save is fatal, and a manual start checks that its data path is writable before it contacts the platform, so the key is not spent on an agent that could not keep its certificate. An agent from an earlier release that logged Failed to save certificates to disk cannot be recovered: delete it in the console, generate a new key and install again.

  • Merge proposals now offer "Merge as is", "Review merge" and "Keep separate". The recommended selection is previewed before a one-click merge; conflicts that need a field choice always open review, and merge notes are optional because the audit records the decision details independently.

  • A sensor's own host report can reconcile its physical NICs without treating container bridges as host identity. A verified installation identity keeps its asset match, while a MAC held by another asset opens a reviewable merge proposal; virtual interfaces are excluded unless they carry the control-plane route.

  • Uploaded captures now report truncation and preserve more observations. The packet-capture job identifies packets cut short by its snapshot length (the upload page warns when a capture was truncated, for example by a gateway's built-in capture tool), TLS reassembly handles retransmitted and reordered TCP segments, every observed host is retained, and QUIC conversations are reported once in the same form as live sensor observations. Results are returned to the platform over service-mesh mTLS. Captures processed before the upgrade read as not truncated.

  • Scan jobs no longer stop being picked up after an upgrade or restart. The platform-owned durable consumer remains when a pod drains, where it used to be deleted by the pod that created it, leaving the new pod subscribed to a subject nothing delivered to while queued scans waited. The stuck-job sweep also recreates a consumer that is missing before it republishes queued work. During the upgrade from 4.4.0, whose pods still delete the consumer as they drain, a queued scan can wait until that sweep next runs.

  • A queued scan no longer counts as its own concurrent job. The rate-limit check excludes the job being picked up, so an organization at exactly its concurrent-job limit no longer has its oldest queued scan failed with "too many concurrent jobs" while nothing is running, and Start scan now identifies the exhausted limit in its 429 response.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• Go toolchain 1.26.8 to 1.26.9, which fixes nine standard-library advisories in crypto/tls, net/http and mime/multipart (GO-2026-6603, 6605, 6607, 6608, 6610, 6611, 6612, 6613 and 6617). Every builder image and CI job moves with it. This supersedes the next entry's statement that no Go advisories were open: they were fixed in 1.26.9, which arrived after it was written.

  • Go toolchain 1.26.6 to 1.26.8, and the public runtime image alpine 3.24.1 to 3.24.2. These are bug-fix patch releases (1.26.7 carries net/http fixes; 1.26.8 carries cgo, compiler, runtime and debug fixes). They fix no Go security advisories: every advisory against Go 1.26 was already fixed in 1.26.6. The bump is taken for the bug fixes and to stay current. (#2312)

  • The web server in the web-ui and admin-ui images is rebuilt. Caddy 2.11.4 becomes 2.11.7, built on Go 1.26.8 with newer versions of its dependencies (cel-go, now cel.dev/cel-go, 0.32.0; OpenTelemetry 1.47.0 and otlploggrpc 0.23.0; klauspost/compress 1.20.1; chi 5.3.2). This clears every finding the image scanner reported against the 4.4.0 user-interface images: three of Medium severity (GHSA-gcjh-h69q-9w9g, CVE-2026-81871 and CVE-2026-81872) and four of Low severity (CVE-2026-81870). govulncheck on the new binary finds no vulnerability the code calls; the only residual is GO-2026-5932 in golang.org/x/crypto, which has no upstream fix and is not called. gRPC stays at 1.83.2, because 1.84 is affected by GO-2026-6443. The runtime image is re-pinned to the 2026-10-05 build of caddy:2-alpine. The Node builder for these images is now dhi.io/node:24-alpine3.24-dev; if you build them yourself with NODE_BUILDER, use that or an equivalent Node 24 image. (#2326)

  • Go modules are refreshed across every module, including the AWS and Azure SDKs, go-redis 9.23, quic-go 0.63 and gopacket 1.7.4, with every dependency at one version everywhere. govulncheck reports no vulnerability that the code calls. It lists one in a module the code requires but does not call, GO-2026-5932 in golang.org/x/crypto, which has no upstream fix. Major versions of the Azure SDK compute, network and storage packages and of stripe-go are available and not taken. (#2318)

  • npm packages are updated to the latest minor and patch releases across the workspaces and the user interfaces, with no major-version changes. The source-map-js and postcss-selector-parser advisories are cleared. One advisory remains, in braces (GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm): no fixed release exists, and it is reached only through Tailwind CSS 3's build-time dependencies, which read static paths in this repository and are not in any image or run at runtime. It is accepted until Tailwind CSS 4 migrates the user interfaces. (#2315)

  • Redis, PostgreSQL and InfluxDB images are unchanged. The chart's redis:7 and postgres:17 lines are current in their supported series. InfluxDB stays on 2.8: 2.9 migrates API tokens to a hashed form on first start, which cannot be undone. (#2314) InfluxDB was later removed altogether in rc.6 (see "Removed" under "Chart, signing and scale (rc.6)").

docs.title: New in rc.6
docs.text:
• Pin the datastore storage class before you upgrade a chart install. datastores.storageClassName now defaults to "", which leaves the class to the cluster's default StorageClass, instead of longhorn. A StatefulSet's volume claim templates cannot be changed, so if your release relied on the old default an unpinned upgrade fails with Forbidden on the Postgres, Redis and NATS StatefulSets. Read the class your volumes use and pass it:
kubectl -n <namespace> get pvc
helm upgrade ... --set datastores.storageClassName=<class>

A release that already sets datastores.storageClassName (or a per-datastore class) needs nothing. New installs get the cluster default. - InfluxDB is removed. Nothing in the platform used it. Delete any datastores.influxdb block from your values file before upgrading: the chart's values schema now refuses it and the render fails. The upgrade deletes the influxdb StatefulSet; its data volume carries a keep annotation and stays. Once you are sure you do not need it, delete it with kubectl -n <namespace> delete pvc <influxdb data claim> (find it with kubectl get pvc). The influx-* keys drop out of the generated Secret on the next render. In Docker Compose the influxdb service is gone; remove its leftover volume with docker volume rm if you want the space back, and the INFLUXDB_* lines in .env are no longer read. - Regenerate signed CBOM artifacts (Enterprise). Artifacts signed by earlier releases used a shared-secret HMAC; they now verify as signature_valid: false with the reason legacy-hmac; regenerate, and there is no fallback. Generate a new artifact for the same scope to get an Ed25519 signature, and give recipients the public key from GET /cbom/signing-keys (pin the kid you send them). The chart generates the signing key in Secret <release>-cbom-signing and keeps it across upgrades; set cbomSigning.keyPEM to pin your own, or cbomSigning.existingSecretName with platform.generateSecrets=false. Enterprise Docker Compose installs generate a key on first start. - mcp-service now requires Redis. It checks every cached sign-in against the same revocation list as the other services, which lives in Redis. The chart and the Compose files already wire REDIS_URL into it; a custom deployment that runs mcp-service on its own must give it one, or revoked tokens keep working until the cache expires. In production, mcp-service no longer derives its OAuth discovery address from the request's Host header: the chart sets OAUTH_CALLBACK_BASE_URL from your hostname, and a Compose production install must set it (or MCP_ALLOW_HOST_FALLBACK=true), or the discovery endpoint answers 503. - Plan assignment needs platform.billing. Assigning a plan to a tenant, and the tier impact-analysis preview, now require platform.billing instead of platform.settings. The stock Super Administrator and Platform Admin roles hold both and are unaffected. Give platform.billing to any custom platform role whose holders assign plans; they also still need platform.settings to reach Plans & Pricing. - Sensors and device agents migrate to a per-collector secret on their own. A collector enrolled earlier keeps its registration key until its next certificate rotation, which issues the secret and removes the key from its config file. No re-enrolment and no action; a re-run of the same install command still recognises the enrolment. - GitOps installs are opt-in. platform.generateSecrets defaults to true, so an existing install renders as before. To move a release under Argo CD or Flux, pre-create the Secrets the chart would otherwise generate and name them (platform.existingSecretName, platform.existingDatastoreSecretName, install.existingSecretName, jwtSigning.existingSecretName, cbomSigning.existingSecretName), copying the current values out of the generated Secrets so the database passwords and the encryption key do not change; the render fails, listing what is missing, until they are all named. The schema-migration and rls-roles Jobs no longer delete themselves ten minutes after they finish; the next upgrade that changes the schema replaces them. - The persisted crypto-risk judgement fills itself after the upgrade. Every existing configuration starts out marked for re-judging; a background sweep works through them every five minutes, and a Crypto Risks read judges any it has not reached yet, so the first reads after the upgrade can be slower. No action needed.

docs.title: New in rc.4
docs.text:
• First upgrade to this release moves deferred crypto evidence into deferred_crypto_findings: the schema migration moves every pending asset's held findings out of its metadata, and every unmaterialized discovery payload out of identity_observation_payloads, once. Findings an older pod holds during the rolling upgrade are moved by inventory-service within a minute. Nothing is lost and nothing is replayed twice; an asset already approved whose held findings never replayed has them replayed on the first sweep.
  • Rolling upgrade: producer pods still on the previous version do not publish discovery.queue.ready; their rows are picked up by the processor's 60-second fallback poll until they are replaced. No action needed.
  • The schema adds two columns to sensor_discoveries (process_attempts integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, process_error text); the add is metadata-only, with no table rewrite.
  • A TLS endpoint the sensor saw passively and then probed is now one discovery, not two. The sensor's TLS enricher reports its probe of an endpoint as a second row next to the passive sighting that triggered it, and both used to be classified, run through the approval rules and imported (or written to 3rd Party Connections) separately. The discovery processor now merges each unambiguous pair (same destination address, port and protocol) into one finding before classification: the probe's measured version, cipher suite, certificate chain and quality flags win, the passive sighting supplies the client address, the requested name and everything the probe did not measure, and an explicit "no" (such as no Certificate Transparency) is kept as a "no". Both rows are marked processed with the same outcome. Pairs that cannot be matched with certainty are left as two discoveries, as before.
  • Crypto configurations are now unique in the database, and existing duplicates are collapsed on upgrade (#2374). Ingest has avoided writing a second row for a configuration it already holds since 0.11, but the table never enforced it, so the copies written before then stayed and inflated configuration counts, lists and the PQC-readiness percentage. A configuration is now unique per asset, endpoint, protocol, measured components and discovery method. On upgrade, each set of duplicates is folded into its oldest copy: certificate, algorithm, key and library links and tickets move to it, it keeps the earliest first-seen and latest last-seen times and the most recent evidence, and the other copies are retired (soft-deleted), so their findings resolve on the next evaluation. Merging two assets that share a configuration now folds it the same way instead of keeping two copies.

Upgrade note: the first helm upgrade to this release collapses the duplicates and builds the new index in the schema-migration Job, which may take noticeably longer on a large inventory. Discovery writes to crypto configurations wait while it runs; allow for it in helm upgrade --wait's timeout. Later upgrades skip the step. As always, pg_dump first.

  • Go 1.26.9 (see Dependencies) needs no action; the rebuilt images carry it.

docs.title: As published with rc.3
docs.text:
The summary in CHANGELOG.md now carries a shorter form of these notes. The complete text, unchanged:

Back up your database (pg_dump) first, as always. Upgrade from 4.4.0. The schema upgrade is additive except for one deletion, described below: it turns on row-level security for the compliance score history table and every audit-log partition, adds two bookkeeping tables (oui_vendor_backfill_state, class_floor_sweep_state), one nullable column on asset_identifiers (device_confirmed_at) and two on pcap_upload_jobs, and widens the rule kinds classification_rules accepts. As in earlier releases, pass a helm upgrade --timeout that covers the migration plus the rollout.

  • In production a service refuses to start on a missing or weak platform secret. With ENV=production (the chart default), INTERNAL_AUTH_SECRET and ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY must be present and at least 32 bytes, and JWT_SECRET, if set, at least 32 bytes (a token-verifying service may omit it once ES256 verification keys are configured). Secrets the chart generates, and openssl rand -hex 32, pass. If your platform Secret holds a short custom value, replace it before upgrading: the new pods exit naming the variable, and a rolling upgrade stalls with the old pods still serving. Changing ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY has no in-place re-key, so stored credentials (integrations, devices, connectors) must be entered again afterwards. The Compose production files set ENV=production and follow the same rule. See secrets-management.md.
  • jwtSigning.acceptLegacyHmac now defaults to auto. A fresh install never accepts legacy HS256 tokens; an upgrade stops injecting JWT_SECRET into every service except auth-service and admin-service once the signing Secret is older than jwtSigning.legacyHmacWindowHours (192). Set true to keep the old behaviour. With --reuse-values the old default (true) is carried forward; use --reset-then-reuse-values to take auto. helm template and Argo CD cannot read the cluster and keep the secret until you pin acceptLegacyHmac: false. The notes helm upgrade prints say which mode was chosen.
  • Docker Compose installs now connect as crypto_app, with crypto_bypass for the cross-tenant paths, through a one-shot db-roles service. Run docker compose up -d (with --build as usual); no new secret is needed. If db-roles exits non-zero because the volume's schema predates the roles, re-apply the schema as its log describes (the command is in the full list of changes).
  • Rolling back to 4.4.0 after this upgrade needs your backup, not helm rollback. The 4.4.0 schema re-adds the narrower rule-kind constraint on classification_rules, which the new oui_vendor and dhcp_vendor_class rules violate, so its schema job would stop. Together with the NATS note below, plan a rollback as a restore.
  • The shipped per-prefix MAC classification rules are retired. The upgrade deletes the 496 oui rules Vista shipped and nobody edited, and the seed supplies one oui_vendor rule per manufacturer in their place. An oui rule an administrator edited or added is kept, and, being the more specific statement about its MAC, still applies before a vendor rule. Catalog ▸ Classification rules shows what remains.
  • Vendors and classes fill in after the upgrade, in the background. A backfill resolves every existing asset's vendor from its MAC identifiers, and a sweep (after start-up, then every six hours) reclassifies assets still shown as unknown hosts; each move is recorded in the asset's class history. A vendor a device agent, interrogation, connector or import reported is kept. Sensors need no upgrade for this.
  • The lease-fresh DHCP rule starts empty. Nothing is backfilled: an address becomes eligible after the platform next sees its device's MAC there (minutes on a sensored network), and a probe is matched this way only within 24 hours of that sighting. Until then probes behave as in 4.4.0, and a row already waiting in Observations stays until you link or dismiss it.
  • A sensor or device agent installed by an earlier installer must be installed again, with a new registration key. Earlier installers spent the single-use code themselves, so such a sensor shows at v1.0.0 with no heartbeat. Generate a new key (Discovery → Sensors & Agents → Register), run the new installer and delete the old row; re-running it with the key that enrolled a host upgrades in place. A device agent that logged Failed to save certificates to disk must be deleted and installed again with a new key. Windows sensors need Npcap installed first.
  • During the rolling upgrade a queued scan can wait briefly. The 4.4.0 pods delete the scan-job consumer as they drain; the new pods own it, and the stuck-job sweep re-creates it before republishing queued work. Nothing is lost, and the next upgrade does not repeat this.

  • Single-sign-on sign-ins in progress during the upgrade must be started again once, for staff sign-in to the admin console and, on Enterprise, tenant and platform sign-in. An external Redis must be 6.2 or later.

  • The bundled NATS server upgrades from 2.10 to 2.14, and rolling back is not clean. JetStream data is read in place. A later rollback to a release on NATS 2.10 rebuilds the stream index on first start and logs corrupt state file; messages and consumer state were intact in testing. Snapshot the NATS volume (nats-data-nats-0) before upgrading if you need a clean rollback. A values file that pins datastores.nats.image.tag keeps the old server until you remove the pin; use --reset-then-reuse-values. An external NATS is unaffected. The NATS pod also restarts once for its new health probes. See the "Bundled NATS server" note in releases.md.

  • Set networkPolicy.clusterInternalCIDRs to your cluster's real pod and Service ranges. The Platform Sensor now refuses scan targets inside them, whatever networks a tenant has registered. The default is RKE2's (10.42.0.0/16, 10.43.0.0/16); on another network plugin the default protects the wrong ranges and may block scans of addresses that are the customer's own. Scans run by a tenant's own sensor are unchanged.
  • The edge's auth rate limit drops from 200 to 50 requests a second (burst 100) per source address. If a load balancer or proxy sits in front of Traefik, set edgeRateLimit.ipStrategy.depth to the number of trusted proxies (1 behind a single ALB); otherwise every client shares one bucket and a busy office can throttle everyone. A wrong non-zero depth, longer than the X-Forwarded-For list, makes Traefik answer 500 on rate-limited routes, so check that two clients do not share a bucket. edgeRateLimit.api and edgeRateLimit.auth set the ceilings.
  • Platform-admin sign-in is rate limited: five attempts a minute per account, twice that per address (ADMIN_LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT). A throttled attempt answers 429 with Retry-After.
  • Sign-in answers differently. A wrong password gets the same invalid-credentials answer for an unknown, deactivated or single-sign-on-only account, and POST /auth/methods no longer returns the organization's id except where single sign-on needs it. Integrations that read those distinctions from a failed sign-in stop seeing them.
  • PUT /auth/me with a different email answers 403 email_change_not_supported. No screen used it.
  • Pending sensor registration keys need sensors.create. GET /sensor-manager/sensors/pending refuses viewers and any role without it.
  • Tenant administrators can no longer edit or delete platform-wide alert rules, the admin console API (/admin-service/admin/**) refuses tenant tokens, and a tenant role can no longer be named platform_admin.
  • Tenant single sign-on endpoints must be https:// when saved (Enterprise). A provider saved with an http:// URL keeps working until its URL is edited; embedded credentials in a URL are refused.
  • ai.allowPrivateEndpoints: true no longer allows a model on the pod's own loopback (Enterprise), and CONNECTOR_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS=false now also disables private AI endpoints. Private-network and in-cluster addresses are unchanged.
  • GET and PUT /sensor-manager/admin/settings are removed and answer 404. They let a tenant member read, and a holder of settings.update overwrite, registration limits shared by every tenant, and no screen or client used them. The limits are fixed at their previous defaults (50 pending sensors, a 60-minute key lifetime, address validation off).
  • PUT /tenant/ui-config needs a platform identity and platform.settings. A tenant token gets 403 whatever its role is called; it used to trust the token's role string. The admin console's per-tenant ui-config route is unchanged.
  • The user list's and external connections' search treat % and _ literally.
  • Request bodies are capped: 1 MiB on anonymous sign-in routes and evaluate/multiple (at most 100 frameworks), 32 MiB on agent submissions with at most 10,000 discoveries per batch. A request over a limit is refused.
  • The edge Content-Security-Policy is connect-src 'self' in production. A deployment whose user interface calls another origin is blocked from doing so.
  • Platform-admin sessions: resetting a password, deactivating or deleting a platform user ends their refresh sessions; an access token already issued keeps working until it expires (up to one hour). The OAuth consent decision and the MSP dashboard WebSocket now reject cross-site requests, and the WebSocket requires an Origin.

docs.title: Highlights as published with rc.3
docs.text:
• Account takeover through the profile closed. PUT /auth/me let any valid access token change the account's sign-in email, and the forgot-password flow then delivered to the new address. It now answers 403.

  • Sign-in tells an attacker nothing. Before the password was checked, the sign-in routes disclosed whether an address was unknown, deactivated, single-sign-on only or a platform administrator, and answered unknown addresses faster. They no longer do. Platform-admin sign-in is rate limited per address and per account, and the edge's auth-tier limit is lower and configurable.

  • Platform-administrator sessions end when they should. Resetting a password, deactivating or deleting a platform user ends that user's sessions, and signing out revokes the access token it was given.

  • Authorization tightened where it was loose. Pending sensor registration keys need sensors.create; tenant administrators cannot change platform-wide alert rules; the admin console API refuses tenant tokens; the sensor registration settings no tenant member should have been able to change are gone; usage metering ignores a caller-chosen tenant. Row-level security is now tested against the application's database role.

  • Outbound requests and scans stay out of the cluster. Scans run by the Platform Sensor refuse the cluster's own pod and Service ranges; webhooks and staff sign-in refuse loopback, metadata and private addresses; and tenant single sign-on and the AI assistant's private-endpoint setting (Enterprise) refuse loopback, metadata and cluster addresses.

  • Bounded requests and a stricter edge. Anonymous sign-in routes, agent intakes and bulk evaluation cap their request bodies; the edge Content-Security-Policy is same-origin for connections; OAuth consent and the MSP dashboard socket reject cross-site requests; sensor registration keys and OAuth codes are no longer logged; packet-capture jobs open only the tenant's own upload directory.

  • Weak platform secrets stop a production install, and legacy tokens stop on their own. In production every service refuses to start when INTERNAL_AUTH_SECRET or ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY is missing or under 32 bytes, and credential encryption can no longer be silently off. jwtSigning.acceptLegacyHmac defaults to auto, so the chart removes the legacy HS256 shared secret from token-verifying services by itself.

  • Row-level security reaches Docker Compose, score history and audit partitions. Compose services connect as the application role instead of the table owner, and the compliance score history and the audit-log partitions are tenant-isolated.

  • The agent port and the edge expose less. The sensor and device-agent mTLS port serves only agent routes, and seven service-to-service routes are no longer published at the edge.

  • Single sign-on is bound to the browser and uses PKCE. Staff sign-in to the admin console, and tenant and platform sign-in (Enterprise), close a login-CSRF path.

  • Verification commands are anchored. The documented cosign verify identity regexps accept only the release workflow run from a release tag (the commercial line also from main).

  • Far more of the inventory is classified. MACs resolve against the full IEEE registry (about 53,000 prefixes) on the platform; a new Smart device class covers consumer devices; a host's DHCP vendor class (option 60) classifies Windows, Android, access points and printers; and unknown hosts are reclassified as evidence accumulates. A class a person declared or a reviewer rejected is never touched.

  • Installers that actually enroll. The sensor installers used to spend the single-use registration code themselves, so a sensor installed with the install command never sent a heartbeat. The Linux and Windows installers now let the sensor enroll itself, wait until it has and print its ID and version; the Linux device-agent installer does the same and never spends a key it cannot save; and the sensor now runs as a Windows service.

  • Scheduled scans in plain language. Pick every few hours, daily, weekly on chosen days or monthly, at a time in your own time zone, and a sentence confirms when it will run. Existing schedules keep running as before; a custom cron expression remains available.

  • DHCP addresses a device was just seen at decide a match. An SSH, TLS or QUIC probe of an address whose owner a sensor confirmed by MAC within the last day attaches to that owner instead of waiting in Discovery → Observations as "Matches an asset".

  • Clearer screens. A posture donut on the dashboard, run outcomes on Discovery Jobs (Job Logs links redirect there), and Merge as is / Review merge / Keep separate on merge proposals.

  • Operational fixes. Passive QUIC is reported once per flow instead of about sixteen times; Scan anyway scans the whole selection; a device interrogation that uses its full time limit completes with its results; the bundled NATS server's probes no longer log a TLS error every ten seconds; scan jobs are still picked up after an upgrade or restart, and a queued scan no longer counts as its own concurrent job; uploaded packet captures report truncation and keep more of what they observed; and a sensor's own host report can reconcile its physical NICs without treating container bridges as host identity.

  • The bundled NATS server is 2.14, replacing 2.10, which the NATS project no longer patches.

  • Dependencies are current. The user-interface images' web server (Caddy 2.11.7) is rebuilt and clears every finding the image scanner reported against 4.4.0. Go 1.26.8 and alpine 3.24.2 are bug-fix patch releases and fix no security advisories; Go modules and npm packages are refreshed, with no called Go vulnerability and one accepted, build-time-only npm advisory.

  • The asset timeline no longer grows with each sighting's own description, the remainder of what 4.4.0 began.

docs.title: Vista Platform 4.6.0 — full list of changes
docs.text:
Covers 4.6.0 through its release candidates. The date on the final release is stamped when it ships. The release summary — highlights, what to do before upgrading, what each edition includes, and how to verify the signatures — is in the CHANGELOG published with that release. This page is the complete, per-change record behind it.

4.6.0 is a platform-maintenance and clean-up release. The admin console gains a Maintenance section: backups of the platform database (optionally with the encryption keys and install secrets, encrypted under a passphrase), a banner and page that say when a newer release exists, and a one-click update that backs up first, verifies the chart signature, runs the upgrade as a Job and offers a rollback. A new Core maintenance-service does the work and is the only backend with a Kubernetes credential.

The release also finishes retiring resource-tracker-service, in four steps that each shipped behind the previous one: the AWS Cost Explorer sync nothing read was removed; resource-metrics ingest moved to auth-service; every reader moved to the metering table, dropping the generated figures the old readers filled gaps with; and the service itself was deleted. The algorithm reference table was reviewed row by row against current NIST guidance, and two fixes make the Observations review page stop growing with every repeat run of a controller.

Entries are grouped by kind, as they were recorded while the release was built.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Back up the platform from the admin console. The new Maintenance → Backups page (platform group, needs platform.maintenance) takes a pg_dump of the platform database as a downloadable file, keeps the newest few (maintenance.backups.retention, default 5) and lists who ran what in a run history. Ticking Include encryption keys and install secrets also packs the master key, JWT signing key, install identity, generated datastore passwords and CBOM signing key, encrypted with a passphrase you choose (AES-256-GCM, key from Argon2id); the passphrase is stored nowhere. Restoring is a documented procedure, with a bundle-decrypt tool to open an encrypted file. See docsv4/core/operate/maintenance.md.
  • The admin console tells you when a newer release exists. A banner on every admin page ("Vista Platform X is available") and Maintenance → About & Updates compare the running version with the tags of the chart's OCI repository, so an install that pulls from a mirror checks its mirror. maintenance.updateCheck.{enabled,interval,includePrereleases} control it; enabled=false makes no outbound call, for air-gapped sites. About & Updates also ports the per-service version table and skew badge the tenant About page has.
  • Update the platform from the admin console. Maintenance → About & Updates → Update to X runs pre-flight checks, takes a database backup, verifies the chart's cosign signature, then runs helm upgrade --reset-then-reuse-values as a Job, with a progress page that survives the services restarting and a Roll back button when the upgrade or smoke step fails. maintenance.updates.{skipSignatureVerify,timeout,plainHttp} tune it for air-gapped mirrors. A release that changes the updater's own Role must be applied once with helm upgrade from the command line.
  • New Core maintenance-service (port 8102) behind all of these. It is the only backend holding a Kubernetes credential: a namespace-scoped ServiceAccount and Role, no ClusterRole, rendered only when maintenance.enabled (default on; false removes the service, its RBAC, the backups volume and the console section). It detects installs not managed by Helm (GitOps, not Kubernetes) and says so instead of offering an update. The new permission platform.maintenance is granted to Platform Administrator.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Algorithm catalogue aligned with current NIST guidance. The algorithm reference table was reviewed row by row against SP 800-131A Rev. 2, FIPS 186-5, SP 800-56A Rev. 3, SP 800-52 Rev. 2 and SP 800-227, and against the draft transition documents (SP 800-131A Rev. 3, IR 8547). Key sizes NIST disallowed in 2013 (RSA-1024, DH-1024, DH-768, P-192, the RFC 5114 1024-bit group), DSA (withdrawn by FIPS 186-5) and RC4 in Kerberos (RFC 8429) now grade obsolete / Critical, matching their already-obsolete siblings; five shipped obsolete rows that scored below the Critical band the Catalog dialog promises are raised to it, and a guard test now pins that floor. Triple DES stays deprecated but its mapping and date now say encryption was disallowed after 2023. Mappings that overstated NIST approval are corrected: X25519 / X448 are not SP 800-56A key-agreement schemes and ChaCha20-Poly1305 is not an approved cipher (strength ratings unchanged). HMAC-SHA-1 is rated one way everywhere (deprecated, approved until 2030): the Kerberos AES-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96 types move from strong to acceptable, and the RFC 8009 Kerberos AES-SHA2 encryption types are added so they have an alternative to recommend. Every quantum-vulnerable public-key row now carries the IR 8547 (draft) 2030 deprecation date and names the 2035 disallowance in its guidance; the TLS and SSH PQ/T hybrid key exchanges share one convention; SHA-512/256, SHA-512/224, SHA3-224 and the SP 800-208 stateful hash signatures (LMS/HSS, XMSS, rated at their weakest approved parameter set) are catalogued; one SSH row that claimed a positive quantum category for classical X25519 and two inconsistent classical strengths are fixed. Existing installs pick the changes up on upgrade; rows a platform admin has edited are left alone.

  • Nothing reads from resource-tracker-service any more. Its four readers now take their figures from the metering table directly (third step of the service's retirement, issue #1263):

  • the MSP dashboard's API-call and data-ingestion series are real hourly buckets of tenant_resource_usage; its response-time, error-rate and throughput KPIs carry a measured flag and an empty series instead of the generated "realistic-looking" trend and placeholder constants they shipped with (the old fallback listed four services with made-up error rates);
  • inventory-service's tenant activity summary reads the tenant's 30-day API calls by SQL;
  • monitoring-service's tenant performance summary reads 24-hour API calls by SQL for throughput (it used to ask through a gateway URL that does not exist on Kubernetes and silently reported 0);

  • tenant-health's cost optimization factor is no longer scored: its inputs were an estimated price and an invented efficiency score. The breakdown keeps the key as null, unavailable_sources always lists cost-metering (as it does resource-metering), and the index is the three remaining factors at 25/20/15 over 60. Health indices move for every tenant on upgrade; the admin console shows the factor as "Not measured".

  • Resource-metrics ingest moves to auth-service. Every service's API-call metering middleware and monitoring-service's host collector now POST their samples to auth-service's HMAC-only /internal/resource-metrics, which writes tenant_resource_usage (the billing usage source) under the tenant bound into the request signature. The NATS METRICS stream and metrics.system subject are gone; the one publisher already spoke the HTTP shape. RESOURCE_TRACKER_URL is no longer read; RESOURCE_METRICS_INGEST_URL overrides the ingest URL in full. resource-tracker-service still accepts the old route for this release (second step of its retirement, issue #1263).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Observations: a repeat interrogation of the same controller no longer re-creates every client it could not admit. Each run's sightings carried a new interrogation:<job> source ref, so every run of a UniFi controller added a fresh unresolved row per unadmitted client (one lab tenant reached 95 unresolved observations from four runs of one router). A run's observations now group by the interrogated device, so a repeat run is another receipt on the row the first made: the occurrence count rises, the row names the run its evidence came from, and the unresolved list stops growing per run. Rows created before the upgrade keep their old grouping and age out or can be dismissed; new runs do not add to them.
  • Observations review: a row that already belongs to one asset is offered as Link ahead of "needs a network" / "needs a sensor", and a hardware-address-only row is no longer told to add a network. The suggestion ladder consulted the network and collector state before ownership, so on a tenant whose sensors were all offline every blocked row read "needs a sensor" even when its identifiers already matched exactly one asset, and the one-click bulk Link was never offered. Ownership now decides first (one linkable owner → Link; several, or one that cannot be linked → review), "needs a network" is only suggested when the evidence carries an address a segment could cover, and a MAC-only unplaced row is marked likely noise with the new explanation code no_address_to_place. The SQL twin that filters and counts the page moved in lockstep; the Go-vs-SQL matrix now covers both polarities.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• resource-tracker-service removed entirely (issue #1263, last of four steps). Everything it did that mattered now lives elsewhere: usage metering is written by auth-service's /internal/resource-metrics ingest and read from tenant_resource_usage by billing, the MSP dashboard, inventory-service and monitoring-service. Gone with it: its nine read endpoints (none had a UI caller), the resource_alerts table and active_resource_alerts view, its OpenAPI spec and typed client, its chart backend, routes and middlewares, its compose services, its place in the release matrices and the ECR/Harbor image lists, and RESOURCE_TRACKER_HOST_PORT. The commercial image set is 19 images (17 backends + 2 UIs) and Core is 18. The schema migration drops the two objects on upgrade. After upgrading, delete the orphaned METRICS JetStream stream (nats stream rm METRICS) and the service's Harbor repository by hand.

  • AWS Cost Explorer sync removed from resource-tracker-service. The sync job, its platform_integrations-backed credential loader, the aws_cost_data and aws_cost_sync_jobs tables with their three summary views and the cleanup_old_aws_cost_data() function are gone, and the service no longer pulls the AWS SDK into Core. Nothing read the data: no console page showed it, no peer called the cost endpoints, and the aws_costs block of GET /stats was an "estimated" stub on every deployment without an AWS integration record. The schema migration drops the objects on upgrade. ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY is no longer required by resource-tracker-service. First step of retiring the service (issue #1263; plan in docsv4/internal/developer/design/platform/resource-tracker-retirement-plan.md).

docs.title: Vista Platform 5.0.0 — full list of changes
docs.text:
Covers 5.0.0 through its release candidates. The release summary — highlights, what to do before installing, what each edition includes, and how to verify the signatures — is in the CHANGELOG published with that release. This page is the complete, per-change record behind it.

5.0.0 is the DCIM release and a fresh install: there is no upgrade path from 4.x. It adds the DCIM object model (sites, racks, device types, interfaces, IPAM, cables, circuits, virtualisation, VPN and wireless) on a re-baselined database schema. Removed routes and renamed concepts are listed under Removed and Changed below.

Entries are grouped by kind, as they were recorded while the release was built.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Tenant navigation now treats DCIM as the Infrastructure workspace. The former Inventory section is grouped by Assets, Facilities, Network & Connectivity, Compute, Organization, Catalog & Data, Cryptography, and Lifecycle. Operational records and catalogs move out of Settings; Scopes and Audit Log move to Risk & Compliance, and notification delivery history moves to Remediation. Existing /settings/* bookmarks redirect to the new routes.

  • Settings → Locations is replaced by Settings → Sites (row 2.1). A location is now a place inside one site; the 4.x location types (region, country, data centre, cloud region, office, site, colo, building, floor, rack) are gone. An asset's free-text site is replaced by its Site; an import's site name is matched to the site of that name or creates it. The /api/v2/inventory-service/locations routes are removed (use /dcim/locations and /dcim/sites), and the operational summaries are per site: /operational/sites-summary, /operational/sites/{id}/environments[/{env}/assets] replace the /operational/locations… routes.

  • The database schema is re-baselined for 5.0.0 (asset-inventory ADR-0010 D11). scripts/database/schema.sql carries every object's final shape in its one definition: each later ADD COLUMN folded into its CREATE TABLE, each enum ADD VALUE into its CREATE TYPE, every RLS policy defined once, and the 4.x data backfills, retired-object drops and the whole POST-MIGRATIONS tail removed (25,789 lines to 22,519). A fresh install builds a database identical to 4.6's, proved by a normalised pg_dump diff (scripts/database/tools/schema-normalised-dump.sh). Applying the 5.0 schema over a 4.x database is not supported. The unused POST /api/v2/inventory-service/network-segments/migrate-from-spaces route is removed.

  • Cloud networks are prefixes, not assets (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.5f; asset-inventory ADR-0009 amendment). A cloud discovery no longer creates Virtual network or Subnet assets: an AWS VPC, Azure VNet or GCP network and its subnets appear in Inventory → Networks as prefixes, each naming the network it belongs to, and an instance's network is the prefix its address falls in. The two classes are removed from the class taxonomy, the contains edges from a VPC to its subnets and instances are no longer written, and the cloud.vpc_id / cloud.subnet_id facts are retired (rows already stored are unchanged). A cloud resource imported as a finding is no longer placed in a per-VPC network segment; it is placed in its region's location.

  • SNMP devices no longer get a net.interfaces fact either (row 1.5d): the SNMP collector's interface list is stored as interfaces and addresses (see Added). Facts it wrote before are unchanged.

  • Hosts no longer get a net.interfaces fact. The device agent's interface list is stored as the host's interfaces and IP addresses instead (see Added); the fact key is marked retired in the fact registry, which gains a status: retired state with a required reason. Facts other collectors already wrote are unchanged, and a query on fact.net.interfaces still parses. Since row 1.5b the same holds for everything a UniFi controller reports: its devices' and clients' interface lists and the site's networks are stored as interfaces, IP addresses, prefixes and VLANs, and no UniFi net.interfaces or net.vlans fact is stored. UniFi ports are now named by number (Port 3), not by the label set in UniFi. A UniFi controller reached at an IP address that is none of the site's UniFi gateway's is no longer made the gateway of the site's networks.

  • Palo Alto, Cisco, FortiGate and F5 BIG-IP no longer get net.interfaces / net.vlans facts, and no longer teach network segments. Their interfaces, addresses, connected prefixes and VLANs are stored as objects instead (see Added). Interrogations of these devices no longer create network segments or claim the device as a segment's gateway; the prefixes they record take that role as segments retire (row 1.6). Until then, a finding at a public address no registered segment covers lands on the interrogated device rather than as a separate asset.

  • A network segment's auto-approve covers sensor discoveries only. The segment editor's "Cloud discoveries" source never took effect (the cloud intake did not evaluate rules) and is removed; a rule that scopes on a segment and names the cloud source is refused. Cloud resources are auto-approved per account (see Added).

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Inventory → Cabling, the asset faceplate, Connect, the bulk cable editor, cable tracing and the port crypto overlay (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 3.4). Every cable in one lens with both ends as asset:port, type, status (proposed cables from LLDP show as "Proposed"), length, colour, site and rack; a row opens the cable drawer. The asset page's Ports tab draws the device's ports as a faceplate in the device type's template order; a port opens Connect (site › rack › asset › port, or a circuit end, with incompatible pairs explained inline), Disconnect and Trace, a hop-by-hop diagram through patch panels and circuits with the far end highlighted and "Copy as text". "Edit cables as table" takes rows pasted from a spreadsheet and applies them one by one with a result per row. The crypto overlay tints each port by the weakest cipher or protocol version measured behind it (GET /dcim/assets/{id}/interface-posture).

  • Cables, terminations and cable paths (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 3.2; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D6). A cable joins two component ends (interface, console, front/rear port, power, circuit termination); the compatibility matrix refuses impossible pairs; paths are materialised through patch panels so /{kind}/{id}/trace answers from either end. A far end that is not yet in the inventory is an unresolved termination, never an invented object. The Interfaces and Ports tabs gain a Cable column with Connect and Disconnect.

  • Console ports, console server ports, front and rear ports, device bays, power ports and outlets (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 3.1). Instantiated from the device type's templates; front ports map to rear ports by position; the asset page gains a Ports tab.

  • Modules, module bays, inventory items and virtual chassis (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 2.4). Applying a device type creates its module bays; installing a module type creates the module's interfaces and ports with {module} resolved to the bay position, adopting any port a collector already measured; removing a module deletes only what it created and carries no measured data. SNMP (entPhysicalTable) and Cisco (show inventory, show switch) report inventory items, modules and stack membership; a person's values are never overwritten. The asset page gains a Hardware tab; Settings → Module Types.

  • Inventory → Racks and rack elevations (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 2.5). Racks of every site with their utilisation; the rack page draws the front and rear elevation, places devices by drag (the overlap rule is enforced server-side), and tints each device by its crypto posture using the shared rating bands.

  • Circuits (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 4.1; NetBox circuits/*). Providers, provider accounts and networks, circuit types, circuits and their A/Z terminations on a site or an interface; Inventory → Circuits lens; Settings → Circuit Providers.

  • Virtualisation (row 4.2). Cluster types and groups, clusters with their hosts, virtual machines as assets, virtual disks; Inventory → Clusters lens; Settings → Cluster Types & Groups; the asset page's Virtualization card.

  • VPN tunnels and IKE/IPsec policy (row 4.3). Tunnel groups, tunnels and terminations, IKE and IPsec proposals, policies and profiles, L2VPNs; every algorithm in a proposal is scored through the algorithm catalogue, so a weak IKE group or hash is a crypto finding like any other. Inventory → Tunnels lens; Settings → VPN Policies.

  • Wireless LANs and links (row 4.4). WLAN groups, WLANs with their authentication type and cipher scored through the catalogue, point-to-point wireless links. Settings → Wireless.

  • Cloud as DCIM (row 4.6; asset-inventory ADR-0009). One enumeration per account with a per-region outcome; a resource that disappears is a lifecycle event, not a deletion; Tier-1 classes and collectors across AWS, Azure and GCP with security groups as assets; Inventory → Cloud lens faceted by class, provider, account and region; cloud accounts, regions and VPCs in the Placement and topology hierarchy.

  • Custom fields (row 5.1). Tenant-defined fields on assets, interfaces, prefixes, VLANs, circuits and the other DCIM objects, validated on every write, queryable as cf.<name>; Settings → Custom Fields; a Custom Fields panel on each object.

  • Inventory → Changes (row 5.2). The substrate's change record as a lens: per-object diffs, related-object changes, retention; a Changes tab on every DCIM object.

  • Config contexts (row 5.3). Weighted JSON contexts assigned by site, role, platform, business unit or tag, merged and rendered per asset; Settings → Config Contexts.

  • Saved filters per object kind (row 5.4) and export templates (row 5.5) — text formats (a hosts file, a config snippet, an XML feed) rendered from any object list; Settings → Export Templates.

  • NetBox sync for circuits, virtualisation, VPN and wireless (Enterprise; row 4.5). Twenty-two further NetBox object kinds sync both ways on the same engine as Business Units, IPAM and interfaces, each class behind its own switch (off by default on existing connections). Pre-shared keys are reduced to a "key is set" flag on read and never pushed. Virtual machines, VM interfaces and virtual disks are not yet synced.

  • Device42 import (Enterprise; row 5.6). Settings → Integrations → Device42 (import): customers, buildings, rooms, racks, hardware models, devices with their rack position, ports, cables, subnets, IPs, VLANs and circuits, planned in a dry run per class and applied in dependency order; a cable whose far end is not imported parks as an unresolved termination.

  • Sites, regions, site groups and locations (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 2.1; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D4). Settings → Sites builds the Region › Site group › Site › Location tree (create, edit with each object's Changes and Journal, delete; a site holding assets is deleted only by choosing where its assets go). An asset has a Site and a Location inside it, chosen on the asset form (the location list is the site's) and shown under the asset's name as Site › Location. Inventory → Sites lists the sites; each opens a site page with its address, time zone, counts, locations, findings by environment and change log. A connected cloud account gets a site of its own, its regions become locations of it, and its networks are scoped to their region. New query fields site, site.id, site.group, site.region and location; the Site facet shows site names. API: /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/{regions,site-groups,sites,locations} (dcim.read / dcim.manage). Bulk CSV import and export gain a Sites kind, and the Locations kind now names each location's site and its path inside it (and needs dcim.manage).

  • Contacts, contact roles and image attachments (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 2.8). Contacts (a person or a team, optionally grouped under another contact), contact roles (owner, technical, billing, on-call and NOC built in) and assignments of a contact in a role to any object, under /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/{contacts,contact-roles,contact-assignments} and /dcim/objects/{kind}/{id}/contacts. Image attachments on any object: multipart upload (PNG, JPEG, WebP or SVG, at most 5 MB, type decided from the bytes, scripted SVG refused), kept in object storage (dcim_images, or the service's local disk until enabled) and served through the API; a device type's front and rear image are set by uploading with slot=front|rear. Settings -> Infrastructure -> Contacts manages contacts and roles; the asset Overview has Contacts and Images sections. See docsv4/core/inventory/contacts.md.

  • Bulk CSV import and export (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 2.7). Settings -> Infrastructure -> Import takes a CSV for one object kind (business units, sites, locations, manufacturers, device roles, platforms, device types, assets, interfaces, RIRs, aggregates, VRFs, VLAN groups, VLANs, prefixes, IP ranges, IP addresses), shows every row as create / update / unchanged / error with the reason, and applies it on your confirmation. The template download gives the header and an example row. Export buttons on the Networks and VLANs lenses and Business Units download the rows you are looking at; an export re-imports to no change. Needs the permission to edit the kind. See docsv4/core/inventory/import-export.md.

  • Device catalogue: manufacturers, device types, module types, device roles, platforms (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 2.2; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D4).
