NetBox-shaped catalogue tables with their nine component-template kinds (interface, console, console server, front and rear port, module bay, device bay, power port, power outlet), under /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/{manufacturers,device-types,module-types,device-roles,platforms} and /dcim/device-types/{id}/<kind>-templates. Platform rows are readable by every tenant and refused on write (403 read_only); a tenant adds its own. One device role is seeded per hardware and virtual asset class. An asset gains a device type, device role, platform (OS), serial and asset tag (/dcim/assets/{id}/hardware); POST /dcim/assets/{id}/device-type assigns a type and creates its interfaces, merging by name with the interfaces collectors already measured (never duplicating them, never overwriting a measured MAC, speed or status). The query language gains device_type, device_type.manufacturer, device_role, platform, serial and asset_tag. The hardware classes' asset_tag attribute is now the asset_tag column.

  • Racks, rack reservations and rack placement (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 2.3; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D4). Settings → Racks lists each site's racks with their location, role, status, utilisation and device count; a rack is created or edited there (an optional rack type supplies its height, numbering and width), its Reservations tab reserves units for someone, and deleting a rack takes its devices out of it. The asset page's Placement card shows Site › Location › Rack › U · Face and places an asset in a rack (site, location and rack selects, a half-unit position, front or rear). A device spans its device type's height (1U without one), a full-depth device takes both faces, and a placement or reservation over units a device or reservation already holds is refused, naming what is in the way — two people placing into the same units at once cannot both succeed. Five rack roles are seeded (compute, network, storage, patching, power). The site page counts racks, the asset CSV export gains Site, Location, Rack, U and Face columns, and the query language gains rack, rack.id, rack.site, rack.role, position and face. API: /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/{rack-roles,rack-types,racks,rack-reservations}, /dcim/racks/{id}/elevation and /dcim/assets/{id}/placement (dcim.read / dcim.manage).
  • A seeded device-type catalogue and a library import (row 2.2). Every install now carries 154 device types from the NetBox community device-type library (CC0-1.0) — Cisco Catalyst 9200/9300/9500 and Nexus 9300, Arista 7050/7280, Juniper EX4300/EX4400/QFX5120/SRX, FortiGate 60F–600F, Palo Alto PA-220–PA-3400, F5 BIG-IP i-series, Ubiquiti UniFi, Dell PowerEdge, HPE ProLiant, Supermicro and APC PDUs — with their interface, console, power and port templates, and the OUI registry's vendors as manufacturers. POST /dcim/device-types/import takes library YAML (one or many documents) and creates the tenant's own types for anything the catalogue lacks. tools/devicetype-import regenerates the subset from a library checkout.

  • Settings → Device Types, Manufacturers, Device Roles and Platforms (OS), and an asset's Hardware (row 2.2). Browse the device catalogue by manufacturer and search, open a type to see its interfaces and ports, import types from the device-type library by pasting or uploading their YAML, and create your own. The asset form gains Device type, Device role, Platform (OS), Serial and Asset tag; the asset page's Hardware card shows them and Apply templates creates the type's interfaces, merged with the ones discovery measured. See docsv4/core/inventory/device-types.md.

  • Network devices report their interfaces, addresses, prefixes and VLANs (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.5c; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D3). Interrogating a Palo Alto, Cisco (IOS / IOS-XE / IOS-XR / NX-OS / ASA), FortiGate or F5 BIG-IP now fills the device's Interfaces tab: ports with their type from the media they report, state, MTU and speed; switch ports in access or trunk mode with their VLANs; port-channels, aggregates and trunks with their member ports; sub-interfaces and VLAN interfaces under their parent; each address with its length, in the VRF of a non-default virtual router, VDOM or route domain. The device's connected prefixes and VLANs appear in Inventory → Networks, and the device's record address is its primary IP. Cisco collection adds show interfaces status and show interfaces trunk; FortiGate adds monitor/network/arp; F5 adds net/trunk, net/route-domain and net/arp and reads VLAN members. Their ARP tables follow the SNMP rule: an address already in the inventory gains the MAC it answered with, an unknown one is kept aside for 30 days, and nothing is created. A device's own serial and interface-MAC updates no longer move one of its addresses to another of its interfaces.

  • Cloud instances, NetBox devices, spreadsheet rows and hand-added devices carry their interfaces (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.5f; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D3). A cloud discovery records each EC2 instance's ENIs (and each Azure VM's and GCE instance's network interfaces) as interfaces on its Interfaces tab with their private addresses at their subnet's prefix length, and an ENI's public address as the instance's NAT outside addresses. A NetBox import declares each device's interfaces and their active addresses, linked to their NetBox records for the sync. The spreadsheet import takes optional Interface, Prefix length and VLAN columns beside the IP and MAC columns, shows each row's interface in the preview and offers a template CSV; and Discovery → Devices → Add device takes the MAC and interface the address is on when a device is added by hand. An interface with no name is named by the platform.

  • Sensors report interfaces and addresses (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.5e; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D3). A sensor's own host now shows its real interfaces by name on its Interfaces tab, each with its MAC and addresses with their prefix length, and the interface the sensor captures on is named in the asset's discovery details. A device the sensor (or an uploaded PCAP) only watched keeps its MAC and address on one observed-1 interface, and each address now records how it was last seen — DHCP for a lease, ARP, or Passive. A DHCP acknowledgement's subnet mask becomes a DHCP-managed network in Inventory → Networks, pending approval.

  • NetBox bidirectional sync for Business Units, IPAM and Interfaces (Enterprise; 5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.9; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D7). A NetBox connection can now sync Business Units, RIRs, prefix roles, VRFs, route targets, aggregates, ASNs, VLAN groups, VLANs, prefixes, IP ranges, FHRP groups, IP addresses and interfaces in both directions, field by field: Settings → Integrations → NetBox → Sync shows the last plan per object kind, runs a dry run or applies, edits who wins each field (observed here, declared here, NetBox, merge, newest change) and the schedule. Two sides that disagree inside their authority become a conflict in Discovery → Approvals (keep ours, take NetBox's, ignore until changed); a delete on either side is only ever a proposal. Objects keep a stable round trip through a hidden vista_id custom field the sync creates in NetBox. Diode push is a setting that is not built yet. The import and Drift stay read-only.

  • The device agent reports each host's interfaces (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.5a; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D3). A host with the device agent now shows its real network interfaces on its Interfaces tab — name, MAC, addresses with their prefix length, MTU, link speed (Windows) and up/down state — with a VLAN sub-interface (bond0.100) under its parent carrying its VLAN, and a bond's member NICs under the bond. Container, loopback and tunnel interfaces are left out. The address the agent reports for itself is the host's primary IP. Linux collection now runs ip -d -j addr (adds each link's kind and VLAN id). This is the first of the intake changes that make every discovery source write interfaces and IP addresses; network devices, SNMP, the sensor and cloud follow.

  • UniFi interrogation records interfaces, VLANs, prefixes and client addresses (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.5b). Interrogating a UniFi controller now fills in, on each managed device's own asset, its Interfaces: a switch's ports (Port N, typed from the medium, with speed, state and access/trunk VLANs) and link aggregations (LAG N), an access point's radios (one wireless interface per SSID, typed by band, with its BSSID) and the gateway's bridge interfaces with its address on each network and its WAN address. The site's networks become prefixes (with VLAN, DHCP and purpose) and VLANs in Inventory → Networks, and each client's MAC and address land on the client's own asset. Each device's management address is its primary IP. SSID passphrases, port authentication keys and WAN credentials are never kept.
  • Generic SNMP devices report their interfaces, addresses and VLANs (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.5d; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D3). A switch, router or appliance interrogated over SNMP now shows every port and virtual interface on its Interfaces tab: name in the vendor's long form, type (from IF-MIB ifType and speed; a LAG is lag, a VLAN or loopback interface virtual), MAC, MTU, speed, administrative and operational state, the addresses on it with prefix length and static/leased origin, the LAG a port belongs to, a sub-interface's parent, and — where the device answers the Q-BRIDGE tables — each port's native and trunked VLANs and the VLANs themselves. The device's management address becomes its primary IP. The ARP cache is supporting evidence only: an address another asset holds gains its MAC, an unknown one is parked until a device with that MAC appears, and ARP never creates an asset. The community string is removed from anything the device echoes back (sysDescr, contact, location) and a port's free-text description is not collected.
  • Discovered addresses live on interfaces (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.4; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D3). Identification now reads an asset's addresses from its interfaces and IPAM: every address discovery reports is an IP address on one of the asset's interfaces (shown on the asset's Interfaces tab and in Inventory → Networks), and a MAC on any of an asset's interfaces — including a further MAC added by hand — identifies it. A value whose source named no interface lands on an observed-1-style interface that is renamed when the device reports the real name. Each asset gets a primary IPv4/IPv6 address by rule, and a service's endpoint links its IP address. Address scoping and the DHCP rule follow IPAM prefixes (DHCP managed on a prefix) before network segments; auto-approval rules and probe consent can scope on a prefix (network.prefix_id, read before segment rules), and a prefix marked sensitive or active-probes-disabled is never probed automatically. Merge proposals in Discovery → Approvals name the interface a matching MAC or address is on. Searching by IP (ip.address:, id.ip_address:, free text) finds interface addresses.

  • MCP read tools for interfaces, IPAM and Business Units (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.10). An AI assistant connected through the MCP server (now 32 tools) can list interfaces across your assets or for one asset (find which asset owns a MAC address), browse prefixes with their utilisation and free space, list IP addresses and VLANs, ask "what holds 10.1.2.3?", list Business Units, and read the recorded change history of any one object. All read-only; the platform applies your own DCIM and IPAM permissions to every call. The interface operations in the inventory-service OpenAPI document now declare 401, and the assigned_kind and scope_kind filters declare their values.

  • Interfaces (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.2; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D3). An asset now has Interfaces — one list for physical and virtual interfaces alike: name, type (the NetBox interface-type list), enabled, management-only, MAC addresses, speed, duplex, MTU, 802.1Q mode with untagged and tagged VLANs, LAG membership, parent and bridge. Open an asset → Interfaces tab to add, edit and delete them; LAG, parent and VLAN-mode rules are enforced (a LAG member must point at a LAG on the same asset; tagged needs tagged VLANs; tagged-all takes none). Names from different sources (Gi1/0/24, GigabitEthernet1/0/24) fold to one interface. API: /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/interfaces (dcim.read / dcim.manage), filterable by asset, name, type, MAC, LAG and VLAN. Search the inventory by interface with interface:( … ), e.g. interface:(mac_address:"00:11:22:33:44:55"). Discovery populates them through the intake rows (the device agent first, see above).

  • Inventory → Networks and VLANs, and Settings → IPAM (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.3, part 3). Networks shows one VRF's prefixes as a tree with utilisation, status, role, VLAN and counts; a prefix's panel lists its child prefixes, free prefixes and addresses, IP ranges, IP addresses and the asset holding each, with its change log and journal, and pending discovered prefixes and addresses can be approved there. Find says which prefix, address and asset hold an address in every VRF. VLANs lists VLAN groups and VLANs with the prefixes each carries. Settings → Infrastructure → IPAM maintains VRFs, aggregates, RIRs, prefix roles and ASNs. The inventory query language gains ip., prefix., vlan. and vrf. fields (ip.address:10.10.0.0/24, vlan.vid=10). See docsv4/core/inventory/networks.md.
  • IPAM API (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.3, part 2). /api/v2/inventory-service/ipam/ serves list, create, edit and delete for RIRs, aggregates, VRFs, route targets, prefix roles, prefixes, IP ranges, IP addresses, VLAN groups, VLANs, FHRP groups and their assignments, and ASNs (reads need ipam.read, writes ipam.manage; every write is in the change log). A prefix's page carries its parent, depth, direct children, utilisation and the free prefixes and addresses inside it; /ipam/prefixes/tree returns a VRF's prefix tree and /ipam/find?address= says which prefix, address and asset hold an address in each VRF. Addresses are unique within a VRF that enforces it, except anycast and virtual-IP roles. The Networks and VLANs pages that use it follow.
  • IPAM tables and address arithmetic (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.3, part 1). The schema gains RIRs, aggregates, VRFs and route targets, prefix roles, prefixes, IP ranges, IP addresses, VLAN groups and VLANs, FHRP groups and ASNs (NetBox 4.x-shaped, tenant-isolated by row-level security), a per-prefix utilisation cache, and primary_ip4_id, primary_ip6_id, oob_ip_id on assets and ip_address_id on endpoints. RIRs and prefix roles are seeded. shared/dcim/ipam computes containment, the prefix tree, available prefixes and addresses, utilisation and longest match within a VRF, following NetBox's rules. Nothing writes the tables yet; the API and the Networks and VLANs lenses follow.
  • Business Units (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.1; asset-inventory ADR-0010 D2). Assets now point at a Business Unit (a NetBox tenant) instead of carrying free text. Settings -> Organization -> Business Units manages a tree of units (four levels deep), with delete-and-reassign; the asset form, bulk edit and imports assign them; the Inventory facet shows unit names. business_unit in the query language is now object-valued (business_unit.id, and business_unit.parent to include every descendant). A NetBox import maps each device's tenant onto a unit. API: /api/v2/inventory-service/dcim/business-units; assets.business_unit and network_segments.business_unit became business_unit_id, and the asset's business_unit is now {id, name, slug}.

  • Internal: DCIM scale fixture (shared/testdb/dcimfixture, BUILD_PLAN row 0.7): a deterministic, phase-aware generator for DATA_MODEL §12's tenant, a budget helper, and make test-dcim-scale; test infrastructure only.

  • The cloud account is an asset, and cloud resources are auto-approved per account (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 0.5; asset-inventory ADR-0009 D1, D5). Adding a cloud integration declares its AWS account, Azure subscription or GCP project as an approved Cloud Account asset; every resource any cloud collector records hangs off it with a hosted_on relationship, so the account's Relationships tab lists what it hosts and the map draws the stored edge instead of a synthetic account box. Each integration's Auto-approve resources switch (Discovery → Cloud, on by default) approves the resources discovered in its account through the same auto-approval rules as everything else (source:cloud and cloud.account_id="…", a new observation field). The integration card shows the account, the switch and the last run's per-type outcomes. Contested identities still go to Approvals as merge proposals, and removing an integration keeps the account asset.

  • Interface, port and cable type registries (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 0.4). standards/interface-types.yaml and standards/cable-types.yaml hold the interface, console, front/rear port, power port/outlet, cable and wireless-channel choice lists (taken from NetBox v4.3.5) and the cable termination compatibility matrix. make generate emits them as Go constants (shared/dcim), TypeScript unions (@vistasecurity/primitives/dcim) and the InterfaceType, CableType, PortType and ConsolePortType OpenAPI enums; make audit fails on drift. Nothing reads them yet; the interface and cable pages that offer these choices ship later in the 5.0.0 build.

  • A product vocabulary registry and guard (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 0.1). standards/vocabulary.yaml is now enforced: make generate emits the ObjectKind enum for Go (shared/dcim), TypeScript (@vistasecurity/primitives/dcim) and the inventory-service OpenAPI contract, plus a customer glossary at docsv4/core/concepts/vocabulary.md; make audit fails on generated-file drift, on a retired synonym in UI strings, OpenAPI names, schema identifiers or customer docs, and on a table that carries the object substrate with no registry row. Retired words are enforced phase by phase (after_phase), so the guard is green on today's wording.
  • Permissions for the 5.0.0 infrastructure-mapping programme. The tenant permission catalogue gains dcim, ipam, circuits, virtualization, vpn and wireless (each read · manage) plus business_units.manage and custom_fields.manage. Tenant Administrators and Security Administrators hold the six families in full, Viewers hold read, and the last two are Tenant Administrator only. No route uses them yet; they ship ahead of the pages that will, and the inventory-service gateway prefix already covers the new route groups.
  • A change log, journal and tags for every infrastructure object (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 0.3). The asset page gains a Changes tab — the change log (who changed what, from where, which fields) and a journal of dated notes — and a tag editor under the asset's name backed by one organisation-wide tag list. Underneath, every DCIM object shares the same substrate: object_changes (monthly partitions kept ahead and expired by audit-service's partition job, following the audit retention policy), journal_entries, tags / object_tags, image_attachments and unresolved_terminations, all tenant-isolated. Changes are recorded by the service that makes them, with the person and the request id, and secret-named fields are redacted from the before/after images. Reading needs dcim.read; writing needs dcim.manage.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • Network segments are retired; the tenant's networks are prefixes (5.0.0 DCIM build, row 1.6). The network_segments and network_spaces tables, the /network-segments routes (list, create, bulk, edit, delete, claim) and Settings → Network Segments are gone. A network is an IPAM prefix in Inventory → Networks, which now carries what a segment did: network type, environment, DHCP posture (three-valued: yes, no, unknown), auto-approval of sensor discoveries, active-scan exclusion, the sensitive flag, its gateway, the sensor that reaches it, the FHRP groups (VRRP, HSRP, …) whose virtual address is in it, and Claim as ours on a prefix learned from a device. Auto-approval rules, scan consent, Discover Assets targets, automatic scans, DHCP-lease rules, gateway links, asset placement (prefix_id replaces network_segment_id), the map, the topology tree, the inventory facet (prefix) and the spreadsheet import all read prefixes. A bookmark to /settings/segments lands on Inventory → Networks. Domain and IP-range segments have no successor: a name scopes to the tenant. Two cloud networks with the same CIDR are two prefixes, told apart by the network they belong to. A device's own sighting records the prefixes it reports before its addresses are scoped, so under enforced identity admission a switch, firewall or controller admits itself and its neighbours on the networks it teaches. The internal source-import route is /internal/sources/prefixes, and NetBox run summaries count prefixes_created / prefixes_matched / prefixes_skipped_duplicate.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• FortiGate discovery accepts the credential FortiOS actually supports. Add Device now asks for a read-only FortiGate REST API token and sends it as a bearer token, whether the platform connects directly or a device agent does. Identity is read from the current monitor/system/status endpoint, with the older CMDB endpoint retained for compatible appliances.

  • HBOM no longer labels an unclassified address as hardware without hardware evidence. An unknown_host appears in the HBOM only when a collector measured a hw.* fact for it; it remains visible in the full inventory. When several sources report the same fact value, the export emits that property once and keeps source-qualified duplicates only for genuine disagreement.

  • Deleting a DCIM object no longer strands its polymorphic references. Tags, journal entries, contacts, images, L2VPN/tunnel terminations and parked terminations are swept when their object is gone; dangling scopes and assignments on prefixes, VLAN groups, clusters, addresses, inventory items and circuit terminations are cleared. The sweep is tenant-scoped, idempotent and runs daily. power_feed and power_panel, which had no backing tables, are no longer advertised as object kinds until power infrastructure ships.

  • The admin console's update check and one-click update work against a chart mirror signed by a private CA. maintenance-service's registry client, its cosign verify and the update Job's helm upgrade all used the image's public trust store, so an internal registry (Harbor behind an organisation CA, an air-gapped mirror) failed every one of them with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. The service now honours EXTRA_TRUSTED_CA_PATH — the variable monitoring-service already reads for its synthetic checks — by adding the CA to the public store (never replacing it), passing a combined bundle to cosign as SSL_CERT_FILE, and the chart renders backends.maintenance-service's extraEnv / extraVolumes / extraVolumeMounts into the update Job as well, whose script exports the same bundle before helm runs. Documented under "Signature verification, mirrors and credentials" in the maintenance guide.

  • Backups and the one-click update work in the commercial (obfuscated) maintenance-service image. The build obfuscated the Kubernetes client libraries too, which register their API types by reflected name, so every backup or update Job the service tried to create failed with no kind "…" is registered for version "batch/v1" (the Core image, which is not obfuscated, was unaffected). Obfuscation is now scoped to Vista Platform's own code for that service, and the Dockerfile guard refuses a Kubernetes-client consumer's release build without that scope.
  • The one-click update no longer fails at render time on every install. The chart's render-time validations told "no cluster" from "genuinely missing" by looking up the kube-system Namespace, a cluster-scoped read the console updater's namespace-scoped Role can never be granted, so helm upgrade from the console stopped with namespaces "kube-system" is forbidden before touching anything. The probe now reads the release namespace's own default ServiceAccount first and falls back to kube-system only when the namespace does not exist yet (a cluster administrator's first install), and the cert-manager prerequisite check runs at install only. A chart test refuses any other cluster-scoped lookup.

docs.title: Vista Platform 5.1.0 — full list of changes
docs.text:
Covers 5.1.0 through its release candidates. The release summary — what 5.1.0 adds, what to do before upgrading, and how to verify the signatures — is in the CHANGELOG published with that release. This page is the complete, per-change record behind it.

5.1.0 completes the DCIM model introduced in 5.0.0 — virtual device contexts, power, floor plans, spares and RMA, the commercial asset lifecycle, change notifications and DCIM hygiene controls — and upgrades a 5.0.0 installation in place.

Entries are grouped by kind, as they were recorded while the release was built.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Virtual circuits, ASN ranges and VLAN translation (DCIM gap 10, NetBox 4.2 parity): virtual circuits over a provider network with interface terminations (Circuits lens → Virtual circuits, the interface page, virtual_circuit.* query fields); ASN ranges with their free numbers (IPAM workspace); VLAN translation policies and rules (VLANs lens → Translation policies) picked per interface; NetBox sync class Virtual circuits, ASN ranges and VLAN translation (NetBox 4.2+), off by default. Adds six tables and interfaces.vlan_translation_policy_id (on upgrade).
  • NetBox sync — virtual machines: NetBox virtual machines, VM interfaces and virtual disks sync both ways (class Virtual machines, off by default) as virtual_machine assets, interfaces on them and their disks; a new VM comes in through the identity engine and your approval policy, a pending one is never pushed, and NetBox's device and VM id spaces never meet. An address NetBox assigns to a VM interface is no longer read as the device interface with the same id. Widens sync_conflicts.object_kind (on upgrade).
  • Spares, stock and RMA (DCIM gap 8): an inventory item can be a spare at a stock location with a quantity and a stock state (in stock, reserved, out for RMA, retired); install a spare into an asset (a row splits; optionally into a module bay), remove a part from an asset to stock, and follow a return case from open through shipped and received (the replacement lands in stock) to closed — Infrastructure → Catalog & Data → Spares & RMA, a Spares card on the site page, and To stock / RMA on the Hardware tab; query field inventory_item.stock_state; a spare is never pushed to NetBox. Makes inventory_items.asset_id nullable, adds location_id, quantity, stock_state and the rma_cases table.
  • Floor plans (DCIM gap 9): a location carries a grid floor plan (width × depth in m or ft) and its racks a place on it (x, y, rotation); the site page's Floor plan tab draws it with racks coloured by unit or power utilisation (80 / 95 %), drag-to-place, an Unplaced racks tray and arrow-key nudging, bounds-checked by the server (GET /dcim/locations/{id}/floor-plan, the rack PATCH). Adds floor_plan_* to locations and floor_* to racks (on upgrade).
  • Inventory change notifications reach discovery changes from every path: a rule that includes discovery now also receives changes from discovery data that arrived over the message bus (the discovery pipeline import), cloud discovery runs and background passes (LLDP cable proposals, evidence re-resolution, same-device merges); delivery falls back from NATS to an HMAC-only compliance-engine route (POST /api/v1/compliance-engine/internal/alerts/raise) and logs a notification as lost only when both fail; notification-service logs a routing-rule row it cannot read instead of skipping it silently.
  • Columns menu on Inventory → All assets: show or hide any column the list knows — the optional ones, the lifecycle dates (warranty end, end of support, purchased, seller) and all of a class's attributes — with search and Reset to default, remembered per user in the browser; the selection export adds every shown column it did not already carry. interfaces.vdcs is dropped on upgrade, after any names a 5.0 database still holds there become virtual device contexts.
  • Palo Alto vsys display names: a discovered virtual system's context takes the display name its administrator set as its description (a rename on the firewall follows; a declared context's description is never overwritten).
  • Automatic end-of-life catalogue links: a device type or platform with no catalogue entry is linked to the single entry that fits (vendor and model or part number; platform name), when created or imported and daily; ambiguous matches are left alone and a person's link is never replaced; the edit form says whether a link was made automatically or by you.
  • Discovered virtual device contexts (DCIM gap 1, part 2): interrogating a FortiGate (VDOMs, root included), Palo Alto (vsys), F5 BIG-IP (route domains) or Cisco Nexus (VDCs, show vdc membership) records its contexts and the interfaces each owns, pending until the asset is approved; a declared or NetBox-synced context of the same name is matched and never overwritten, and a context the device stops reporting goes stale after the asset stale window, never deleted.
  • Virtual device contexts (DCIM gap 1): an asset's VDOMs, vsys, VDCs and route domains (NetBox VirtualDeviceContext) with identifier, status, business unit and primary IPs, on the Hardware tab; interfaces join them from the Interfaces tab (Context column, virtual_device_context_ids); query field interface:(virtual_device_context:…); NetBox sync class Virtual device contexts (off by default) with the interface vdcs membership. Adds virtual_device_contexts and interface_virtual_device_contexts; names a 5.0 database holds in interfaces.vdcs become contexts on upgrade.
  • DCIM hygiene controls (DCIM gaps 4 + 6). Inventory Hygiene gains IH-007 to IH-015: rack-mountable assets racked and positioned, no planned cable older than 90 days, declared cables confirmed by LLDP/CDP (asked only of assets that report neighbours), typed interfaces, no duplicate address within a VRF, no expired warranty, nothing past or within 12 months of end of support — each a hygiene finding that names the page to fix it on, and not assessed where the record holds nothing to judge.
  • Asset commercial lifecycle (DCIM gap 4). Assets record purchase date, cost and currency, purchase order, seller, warranty, support contract, install and decommission dates (Hardware tab → Lifecycle card, the asset import, the API and the query language); device types and platforms carry end-of-sale / support / life dates with an end-of-life catalogue fallback, and every asset read reports its warranty and end-of-support state — unknown when nothing is recorded.
  • Dashboard → Facilities: a fifth dashboard rolling up free rack space per site, fullest racks, switches and prefixes nearing full and the ageing cabling backlog from one GET /dcim/capacity read.
  • IP Addresses tab on the asset page — every address an asset holds in one table, with Primary and OOB badges and Set as primary / Set as OOB actions; the ip-addresses list gains an asset_id filter and PATCH /dcim/assets/{id}/primary-ips writes the asset's primary IPv4, IPv6 and OOB address.
  • Inventory change notifications and webhooks (DCIM gap 5): a routing rule with the new Inventory changes source delivers object creates, updates and deletes — filtered by object kind and action, discovery and sync changes opt-in — to any channel; webhooks carry the change fields at the top level. Adds tenant_notification_rules.change_filter (added on upgrade).
  • Power panels, feeds and power cabling (DCIM gap 3, row 6.1): power panels and feeds (NetBox-shaped, with available power) on the site and rack pages; power ports and outlets with their draws on the asset's Ports tab; Connect, trace and bulk cabling for power ends, traced from a server through its PDU to the feed; power_feed.* search fields; NetBox sync of panels and feeds. Adds power_panels and power_feeds, and widens the cable termination and path kinds (on upgrade).
  • Rack power budget and PDU collection (DCIM gap 3, row 6.2): a rack's power budget per feed and leg (NetBox Rack.get_power_utilization) on the rack page's Power card, a power overlay on the elevation, a Power column on the Racks list and Racks over power budget on the Facilities dashboard (GET /dcim/racks/{id}/power); SNMP PDU collectors (APC PowerNet-MIB, Raritan PDU2-MIB, Eaton EATON-EPDU-MIB, ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB power supplies) record measured outlet state, current and power beside the declared draws. Adds measured_* columns to power_ports and power_outlets (on upgrade).
  • Prefixes, VLANs, circuits, cables and interfaces each have a page of their own (/inventory/prefixes/:id, /vlans/:id, /circuits/:id, /cables/:id, /interfaces/:id) with Back to the lens, and every one shows custom fields, tags, contacts, images, changes and journal.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The in-cluster cache is now Valkey 8 instead of Redis. The chart ships valkey/valkey:8.1.10-alpine (BSD-3-Clause) in place of redis:7-alpine (Redis 7.4, RSALv2/SSPL), and every compose file moves from redis:8-alpine to the same image. Valkey speaks the Redis protocol; the datastores.redis key, the redis Service, REDIS_URL and REDIS_PASSWORD keep their names. Upgrading a 5.0.0 install starts the cache empty: Valkey cannot load Redis 7.4's RDB files, so it keeps its own files beside them on the same volume (a helm rollback finds the Redis data again). Pending password-reset and email-verification links and in-progress SSO sign-ins are lost, and access tokens revoked in the hour before the upgrade (JWT_EXPIRY) are accepted until they expire; refresh tokens stay revoked. Upgrade with --reset-then-reuse-values — --reuse-values keeps Redis. See "The cache server changed from Redis to Valkey" in the production checklist.

  • Chart: minimum Traefik is now v3.4 when serviceMtls is on. The backends-mtls ServersTransport uses rootCAs (- secret: platform-ca-secret) instead of the deprecated rootCAsSecrets, which Traefik v3.7 warns about on every load. rootCAs first appeared in Traefik v3.4.0; on an older Traefik the field is ignored and backend verification fails, so upgrade Traefik before upgrading the chart. The chart's own api-gateway image is Traefik v3.6.

  • The tenant, admin and QA web applications now build with Tailwind CSS 4. Their existing appearance and browser defaults are preserved while removing Tailwind 3's vulnerable build-time dependency chain. The production builds and application tests are unchanged at runtime. (#2674, #2677, #2678)

  • Go builder images now use the exact patch declared by go.work. Public and hardened builder fallbacks, Compose generation, seed utilities and the public-tree export all pin the exact patch (Go 1.26.10 at release) instead of a floating 1.26 tag. A repository guard rejects future floating or stale builder tags. (#2671)

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Stored framework scores honour each control's population: stored framework scores no longer count assets outside a control's population as passing — the Posture scorecards and framework preview scores now agree with the control results, so a control with nothing in its population (no racked asset, no warranty date recorded) reads Not assessed and scores may move down to their honest values.
  • IH-011 no longer flags the platform's own placeholder interfaces. An address no collector named an interface for is filed on an observed-N placeholder interface; Inventory Hygiene's Every interface has a type control counted those, so every sensor-discovered host without a named interface failed it and the finding could never be cleared. Placeholders are now skipped; an interface a collector reported without a type is still flagged.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Go 1.26.10 (GO-2026-6809, crypto/x509): every Go module, builder image and the toolchain pin move to the patched release.

  • Bundled maintenance tools and external dependencies were refreshed. The maintenance image now carries cosign 3.1.3 and Helm 3.22.1, removing the critical finding present in the prior cosign binary. Azure Identity, the AWS SDK for Go v2 family, Go cryptography and networking modules, and pinned runtime/CI images move to current patch releases. The called-code vulnerability gate remains clear. (#2667, #2668, #2669, #2670)

docs.title: Vista Platform 5.2.0 — full list of changes
docs.text:
Covers 5.2.0 through its release candidates. The release summary — what 5.2.0 adds and fixes, what to do before upgrading, and how to verify the signatures — is in the CHANGELOG published with that release. This page is the complete, per-change record behind it.

5.2.0 makes the published Enterprise chart installable again, which 5.1.0's was not, by moving the database SQL out of the chart and into a release image. It also separates assets with nothing cryptographic to assess from assets still waiting to be scored, scores at-rest encryption, and assesses cloud KMS keys and Secrets Manager secrets. Sensors and discovery agents share one panel layout, and discovered wireless networks follow their access point's approval. You can declare a certificate no sensor can reach and get expiry alerts for it, verify it where it is served, have it re-checked nightly and merge it into the certificate actually found there; the Overview gains a world map of sites and cloud regions; and a TLS or SSH listener alone no longer classifies a host as a server. The database schema adds nullable columns and indexes for declared certificates; nothing existing changes.

Entries are grouped by kind, as they were recorded while the release was built.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• The Overview now shows where your estate is, and what is missing from it. The top panel gains a world map of your sites and cloud regions, each pin coloured by the worst risk band among its assets; click a pin to see its riskiest assets, risk bands, classes and locations beside the map. Assets Monitored adds nine linked counts (sites, AWS regions, racks, prefixes, VLANs, cloud accounts, clusters, certificates and assets to approve), and the Data quality card lists the assets with no owner, no class, no site or gone stale, each opening exactly those assets. A count that cannot be loaded shows a dash, never a zero. The map needs no internet access.
  • Declare a certificate you cannot scan. Infrastructure → Cryptography → Certificates → Add certificate now has a Declare tab: enter a certificate's common name and expiry date (and optionally its issuer, names, serial number, owner, a note and where it is served) and the platform raises the usual expiry alerts for it, even when no sensor can reach it. A declared certificate is listed with the source declared, can be edited or removed from its drawer while nothing has measured it, and never shows a made-up fingerprint. The button that read Upload cert is now Add certificate; its Upload PEM tab is the old upload, unchanged. The Certificates lens gains a Source filter. See Certificate monitoring.

The database schema adds nullable columns to certificates and one partial unique index; nothing existing changes. GET /certificates/expiring now returns asset_id: null (it was "") for a certificate with no asset, and adds declared_host. - Check a declared certificate where it is served. When you say where a declared certificate is served, Add and verify (or Verify now in its drawer) makes one TLS connection to that host and port from the sensor that sees it, or else the platform sensor, and records what it found as the certificate's Observation: Observed (a certificate declared by name and date is then filled in from the one served and checked like any discovered certificate), Not observable with the reason in plain words, or Different certificate served, which adds the served certificate as its own entry, links it, and fails the new Certificate Hygiene control CH-005 "Declared certificates match what is served". Nothing else on the host is contacted and the host is not added as an asset; a host outside your registered networks is asked about first. The lens gains an Observation filter.

Sensors report a new capability, verify_certificate_v1; an older sensor is passed over for the platform sensor. The schema adds the nullable column certificates.declared_addresses and one index on discovery_jobs. - Declared certificates are checked again every night, and can be merged into the certificate served. A declared certificate whose location is Unverified, Not observable or serving a Different certificate is verified once more each night (one check per certificate per day, a bounded number per organisation, from the sensor that last tried), and a host outside your registered networks is only checked again if someone already confirmed it. When a verification links your declaration to a certificate the platform already holds, or the host serves a renewal you accept, Merge into the certificate served in the drawer's Observation section moves your note, ownership and location onto it and removes the declaration, never overwriting anything already recorded there (POST /certificates/{id}/merge-into-observed). After a certificate has been observed, Edit location still changes where it is served and the note; moving the host, port or SNI resets the observation to Unverified. Certificate monitoring is now listed as available on the release-status page. No schema change. - At-rest encryption is scored. A nightly pass reads every at-rest record (S3 buckets, managed databases, Secrets Manager secrets) and raises crypto/unencrypted_at_rest for each resource measured as unencrypted. The score comes from the new AT-REST-PLAINTEXT row in the algorithms catalogue, so editing that row changes it. An asset whose cryptography is entirely at rest and fully measured counts as assessed. One whose encryption could not be read (for example, AccessDenied on GetBucketEncryption) stays Not assessed; it is never treated as clean. Whether the provider or the customer holds the key is a Data Protection lens distinction, not a risk. - AWS Secrets Manager secrets get at-rest records. Cloud discovery now records each secret's encryption (AWS-managed or customer-managed KMS key), which shows in the Data Protection lens and feeds the pass above. Previously a secret reached the inventory with no crypto record. - Discovery agents can send their recent log lines to the console, as sensors already could. The request rides the agent's heartbeat answer; the agent masks credentials before the lines leave its host and the platform masks them again. Lines are held in Redis for a day and are never written to the database. New routes: GET /api/v1/device-interrogation-service/agents/{id}/logs (sensors.read) and POST …/agents/{id}/logs/request (sensors.update). Agents from earlier releases cannot send logs; their Logs tab says so. - Approve button on pending wireless LANs and wireless links (Settings → Wireless), for users with wireless.manage.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• "Not assessed" now means there is something left to score. Dashboard → Cryptographic Posture splits the assets that have no risk score into Not assessed (cryptography was seen but not yet scored) and No crypto observed. An asset is in No crypto observed when it has no TLS, SSH, IPsec or other crypto endpoint, no crypto configuration and no at-rest record, and is not a key store, secret store, VPN gateway, CDN distribution or API gateway. risk:not_assessed now matches only the first group; the new risk:no_crypto_observed matches the second. The facet rail, the asset page and the risk summary carry the split: the summary gains not_assessed and no_crypto_observed, while unknown_risk still counts every unscored asset. Asset reads add crypto_surface.
  • Sensors and discovery agents are managed from one panel layout on Discovery → Sensors & Agents: the same tabs in the same order (Overview · Discoveries · Health · Jobs · Logs · Settings), each device showing the ones it supports. Both Health tabs open with the same connection and settings-sync block. A new Jobs tab on both lists the last 10 jobs as one line each with a status, and a click expands a job to show its payload and reply; the sensor's command history no longer prints every command's JSON in a list that grew without bound. Log export has its own Logs tab on both and reads as text. The sensor's Control tab is now Settings, where both devices also have Restart.
  • GET /api/v1/device-interrogation-service/jobs accepts agent_id to list one discovery agent's jobs.
  • Discovered wireless LANs, and the VLANs they put clients on, take their status from the access point that reports them, as its interfaces do: active from an approved device, pending from one awaiting approval, and promoted at the next interrogation after the device is approved. Previously every discovered one stayed pending and the Wireless page offered no way to approve it. A WLAN or VLAN a person added, archived or rejected is not moved.
  • Wi-Fi clients are recorded as wireless stations. When a UniFi controller reports which SSID a client joined, the client's interface becomes an 802.11 station on that wireless LAN, so the asset's Interfaces tab shows the network and wireless_lan.ssid: queries find the client. Clients with a randomised MAC address are not joined, and a client never creates a wireless LAN. The weak-wireless-authentication finding still names only access points.
  • New release image: schema. ghcr.io/vistasecurity/schema (Core) and docker.io/vistasecurity/schema (Enterprise, MSP), tagged and signed like every other image. A mirrored or air-gapped registry needs it alongside the others; schemaMigration.sqlImage.{registry,repoPrefix,repository,tag,digest} override where it is pulled from, each falling back to the product images' setting.
  • Chart maintenance. The chart no longer carries a copy of schema.sql; scripts/stage-chart-sql.sh stamps files/schema/schema.sha256 from scripts/database/schema.sql and make audit fails when the stamp is stale. scripts/chart-release-record-size.mjs simulates Helm's release record for the packaged chart and fails above 900 KB, in make standards-check and in both release workflows, after first proving that the 5.1.0 shape measures over the limit.
  • After upgrading from 5.1.0, the <release>-seed-NN ConfigMaps that 5.1.0 created as pre-upgrade hooks are no longer managed by the chart and can be deleted: kubectl -n <ns> delete cm -l app.kubernetes.io/component=seed-data (the <release>-seed ConfigMap is re-created by the next upgrade).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A TLS or SSH listener no longer makes a host a server. Every crypto finding from a sensor, an active scan or a device interrogation claimed the class server for the host it was about, and a host is classified by whatever creates it. Access points, switches, laptops and load-balancer addresses first found that way showed as servers, including UniFi access points whose controller reports them as access points. Such hosts are now unclassified until something says what they are. Assets already classified server keep that class; correct them with Edit on the asset page, or accept the class proposal for them in Discovery → Approvals where one is waiting.
  • The published chart installs again. Helm stores every chart file and the rendered manifest in one release Secret, which Kubernetes caps at 1 MiB. schema.sql and seed.sql (about 1 MB each) were in that record twice, so helm install of the 5.1.0 Enterprise chart failed with Secret "sh.helm.release.v1.vista.v1" is invalid: data: Too long before creating a single object, and the Core chart was one seed addition away from the same failure. The SQL now ships in a new release image, schema, built from source for both lines; the schema-migration and seed-data Jobs copy it out of that image in a fetch-sql init container, and the chart carries only the sha256 of schema.sql. The release record is about a quarter of the limit.
  • A chart can no longer apply the wrong schema. The schema-migration Job's init container compares the hash of the schema inside the image with the hash the chart was stamped with and refuses a mismatch, naming both, instead of recording a completion marker for a schema it did not apply. The schema image must therefore be the one of the same release (schemaMigration.sqlImage; the published Enterprise chart pins its digest like every backend's).
  • The Enterprise content bundle is still verified before it is applied. The bundle and its signature ship inside the Enterprise schema image (the image build verifies the signature too); the chart carries the public key, so the chart decides which key the bundle must be signed with. A chart with enterprise.contentBundle.enabled=true pointed at a Core schema image fails in the seed-data Job's init container rather than seeding an empty framework catalogue.
  • Cloud KMS keys are assessed. The crypto pass could not reach the key-store asset that a discovered KMS key belongs to, so every KMS key read Not assessed. Keys now reach their asset through the key's external reference and are scored like any other key.
  • POST /api/v2/inventory-service/infrastructure-assets/enrich-all answered 500 on every commercial (garble-obfuscated) install: the backfill's scan struct left three fields without db tags, garble renamed them, and sqlx found no destination for the ip column before reading a row. The fields are tagged, the handler now logs the underlying error, and a static test keeps every sqlx scan destination in the package tagged.
  • A UniFi controller interrogation recorded a TLS listener on port 8443 for every device the controller manages, whatever the device's state, without connecting to any of them. Each became a measured endpoint (and, for some, a crypto configuration with no protocol version), so access points and switches read as having cryptography nobody had observed. The collector now claims TLS only for the controller's own management interface, which it probes; the managed devices still reach inventory with their interfaces, neighbours and hardware facts. Endpoints recorded before this fix are not refreshed again and turn stale after 30 days; they are not closed automatically.
  • Active scans failed on our side when a device offered only legacy TLS. The scan engine's handshake had the Go client defaults: a TLS 1.2 floor and, since Go 1.22, no RSA key-exchange suites. An embedded broker that speaks only TLS 1.0/1.1, or only RSA-kex and DHE suites, was left as an open port with no endpoint or crypto configuration, so its weak TLS was never scored. The identifying handshake and the version enumeration now offer TLS 1.0+ and every suite Go implements. They measure; they do not trust. A TLS attempt that still fails records a bounded tls_handshake_error class (protocol_version, cipher_suite, timeout, reset, eof, alert, not_tls, other) next to its note.

docs.title: Vista Platform 5.2.1 — full list of changes
docs.text:
Covers 5.2.1 through its release candidates. The release summary — what 5.2.1 fixes, what to do before upgrading, and how to verify the signatures — is in the CHANGELOG published with that release. This page is the complete, per-change record behind it.

5.2.1 is a one-fix patch release for 5.2.0's declared certificates. In 5.2.0, asking the platform to verify a declared certificate where it is served never reached the executor as a verification: the job ran as a plain port probe, no observation was recorded, and the certificate stayed unverified. 5.2.1 forwards the verification plan, so Verify now, the nightly re-check and Merge into observed work as documented in Certificate monitoring.

docs.title: Upgrading from 5.2.0
docs.text: The schema and seed are unchanged from 5.2.0. The upgrade is a helm upgrade to the 5.2.1 chart; the schema-migration Job re-applies the same SQL and the wait-for-schema gates pass on the existing marker. Sensors and agents from 5.2.0 keep working; a sensor that verifies certificates must still be 5.2.0 or later.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Certificate verification never reached the sensor. "Verify now" on a declared certificate created a plain port-probe job: inventory-service's discovery-job proxy built the request to the scan engine by hand and dropped the verification plan, so the executor measured the port, no observation was recorded, and the certificate stayed unverified in both editions of 5.2.0. The plan is now forwarded, and a test drives the real proxy against a stand-in scan engine and reads the request it receives, so the wire itself is pinned rather than the helper behind it. Found by the release's own end-to-end check after 5.2.0 was installed: the declared certificate of a lab registry went to observed within a minute once the fix was in place.

docs.title: Vista Platform 5.3.0 — full list of changes
docs.text:
Covers 5.3.0 through its release candidates. The release summary — what 5.3.0 changes, what to do before upgrading, and how to verify the signatures — is in the CHANGELOG published with that release. This page is the complete, per-change record behind it.

5.3.0 is the first release under the Vista Platform License 1.0. The sensor and device agent are now published from a public agents repository under Apache-2.0, and Core's public home is the Distribution repository, which carries each Core release's install files and collateral. Core is no longer exported as source: its images are built from the source with the Enterprise half removed, promoted by digest to ghcr.io/vistasecurity and signed with a new identity. Every image states its own terms. Discovery → Sensors & Agents offers exactly the agents this platform version was qualified with; sensors and device agents must speak managed protocol 1, and agent and sensor mTLS is mandatory. The operator tools bundle-decrypt and catalog-bundle ship with every release.

docs.title: Upgrading from 5.2.1
docs.text:
Back up PostgreSQL before upgrading, as always. Every sensor and device agent built before managed protocol 1 is answered 426 after the upgrade and shown as incompatible under Discovery → Sensors & Agents: replace each with the agent that page offers, from the public agents repository, and re-enroll it.

Agent and sensor mTLS is mandatory. The chart refuses agentMtls.enabled: false and serviceMtls.enabled: false, so an install needs the two agentMtls passthrough hostnames; the datastore TLS toggles can still be turned off. The compose quickstart sets AGENT_MTLS_REQUIRED=true and publishes both agent listeners on the host.

The schema adds two nullable columns (protocol_error, protocol_error_at) to sensors and device_agents, applied by the chart's schema-migration Job with no data changes. The release set grows to 21 images (20 for Core) with the tools image. Core images from 5.3.0 on are signed by the platform's release-core.yml workflow on a core-vX.Y.Z tag (the exact identity is under Changed); releases up to 5.2.1 keep their old signing identity and the terms they were published with.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • The operator tools ship with every release. bundle-decrypt (opens a passphrase-encrypted backup for a restore) and catalog-bundle (exports the end-of-life and vulnerability catalogues for an air-gapped install) are no longer built from a source checkout: each Core release on the Distribution repository attaches them as static binaries for Linux (amd64, arm64), macOS (amd64, arm64) and Windows (amd64), named bundle-decrypt-<os>-<arch> and catalog-bundle-<os>-<arch> and listed in the release's signed SHA256SUMS, and both lines carry the same binaries in a new tools release image (ghcr.io/vistasecurity/tools, docker.io/vistasecurity/tools) with both tools on its PATH, so docker run --rm <image> bundle-decrypt … works wherever Docker is at hand. The release set is 21 images (20 for Core). The Windows and macOS binaries carry no native code signature; the signed SHA256SUMS verifies them.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• 5.3.0 is the first release under the Vista Platform License 1.0. The sensor and device agent are now published from the public VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Agents repository under Apache-2.0, and Core release collateral is published in VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Distribution.
  • Core is now released privately, as images and a chart. Core's source is no longer exported to a public repository: the Core images are built from a copy of the source with the Enterprise half removed (scripts/prepare-core-tree.sh), garbled like the commercial images, qualified in the internal staging registry and promoted by digest to ghcr.io/vistasecurity by release-core.yml on a core-vX.Y.Z tag. They are signed by that workflow: verify with the identity ^https://github\.com/VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform/\.github/workflows/release-core\.yml@refs/tags/core-v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$. Releases up to 5.2.1 keep their old signing identity and the terms they were published with. Sensor and device-agent binaries are no longer attached to Core releases; they move to the public agents repository.
  • Core's public home is the Distribution repository, VistaSecurity/VistaPlatform-Distribution: each Core release there carries the install files (compose.yaml, env.example, values-core.example.yaml, IMAGES.txt), VERIFY.md, AGENTS.md, the release-status feed and a signed SHA256SUMS; the repository holds the licence and terms, the dated notice of the change after 5.2.1, the issue tracker and the security-advisory intake, and its INSTALL.md covers back up and restore for compose and Helm. The Core docs site publishes to its GitHub Pages at docs.vistasecurity.io, and the console's update notes link the Distribution release page and that site.
  • Every image states its own terms. Each release image carries the Vista Platform License (version 1.0) at /usr/share/doc/vista/LICENSE.md, with TERMS.md and a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md generated from what that image contains, and sets its own OCI title, description, vendor, licence (LicenseRef-Vista-Platform-License-1.0), source, url and documentation labels instead of inheriting its base image's (#2831).
  • Agent downloads come from the tested Agents release. Discovery → Sensors & Agents offers, per operating system and architecture, exactly the sensor and device-agent files of the public Agents release this platform version was qualified with (GET /api/v1/sensor-manager/agent-artifacts), with the pinned SHA-256, the cosign verify line and the install steps; a platform build with no qualified agents offers none, and never a "latest".
  • Sensors and device agents speak managed protocol 1, and only it. Every agent call names the protocol in the Vista-Agent-Protocol header; a sensor or device agent that does not (any agent built before protocol 1) is answered 426 and shown as incompatible under Discovery → Sensors & Agents. Replace it with an agent from the public agents repository and re-enroll it. Enrollment requires a certificate signing request (the platform no longer generates an agent's key) and always issues the agent secret; job credentials are sealed with that secret only; every sensor job is a scan plan.
  • Agent and sensor mTLS is mandatory everywhere. There is no path-id-only mode. The compose quickstart sets AGENT_MTLS_REQUIRED=true and publishes both agent listeners on the host (SENSOR_MANAGER_AGENT_HOST_PORT, DEVICE_INTERROGATION_AGENT_HOST_PORT). The chart refuses agentMtls.enabled: false, and with it serviceMtls.enabled: false (the agent listener reuses the mesh certificates): an install needs the two agentMtls passthrough hostnames. The datastore TLS toggles can still be turned off.
